# TO THE BENEVOLENT READER
### AND THE LOVER OF LEARNED ANTIQUITY

->Sends Greetings <note>original: "S. D.", an abbreviation for the Latin "Salutem Dicit," a formal greeting meaning "wishes health" or "sends greetings."</note><-

# JOHANN ALBERT FABRICIUS.

<note>A decorative woodcut initial 'E' features a swan with its wings partially spread, set against a hatched background within a square frame.</note>

Behold, here for you is a distinguished midnight labor <note>original: "lucubrationem"; this term refers to scholarly work produced by intense study late into the night by lamplight.</note> by that *most illustrious man*, **ELIAS SCHEDIUS** <note>Elias Schedius (1615–1641) was a German historian and poet; this work is his famous "De Diis Germanis" (On the German Gods).</note>. This work, which has been sought after in bookshops for a long time now, has long since deserved to be restored by the benefit of the printing press, and thus [brought] as if into the light...

## FABRICIUS’S PREFACE.

...having been recalled, it might be handed over and commended once more to the hands of students by right of restoration <note>original: "postliminio," a legal term referring to the recovery of rights or property upon returning from abroad or captivity; here used metaphorically for a book returning to print.</note>. This work, now polished and expanded with various learned observations for your use, is offered by a distinguished man, who is not unknown to you through the published specimen of the *History of the Learned Academies of Italy*, which he released at Leipzig in the year 1725: Master **JOHANNES JARKIUS** of Stade. He shares this in common with Schedius: just as Schedius consecrated himself to more elegant literature in the first flower of his age and composed the present book, so too has Jarkius—enkindled by the same love of studies from his early years—made his own notes on that work public while still quite a young man. Nor should this [youth] be held to the discredit of either man, for to them it was given, through a wise heart, erudition, and industry, not only to equal but to surpass the maturity <note>original: "senium," literally "old age," referring here to the wisdom and gravity usually reserved for elders.</note> of many; indeed, it may serve as a just defense against the harsher critics and detractors.

I do not doubt that the example especially of *John Selden* <note>John Selden (1584–1654) was an English jurist and polymath whose work on ancient law and "De Diis Syris" (On the Syrian Gods) heavily influenced Schedius.</note>, a most eminent man—just as *Thucydides* was once moved by *Herodotus*—allu- <meta>catchword: allu- (allured)</meta>

<summary>Johann Albert Fabricius introduces Johannes Jarkius as the editor of this edition, noting that despite his youth, his scholarship matches the high standards of the original author, Elias Schedius. He also begins to credit the influence of the English scholar John Selden on Schedius's work.</summary>
<keywords>Johann Albert Fabricius, Johannes Jarkius, Elias Schedius, John Selden, scholarship, Leipzig, History of the Learned Academies of Italy, historiography</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the comparison between the English polymath John Selden and the author Elias Schedius. # FABRICIUS’S PREFACE.

->a 5<-

...to entice and challenge him. For just as Selden intended his book *On the Syrian Gods* <note>original: "De Diis Syris"</note> to be the first monument of his learning—a work published in London in the year 1617, through which he successfully established his name in the annals of fame—so too Schedius, as a display of a mind cultivated by learning, claimed for himself the subject of *The German Gods* <note>original: "De Diis Germanis"</note>. Just as Selden divided his work into *syntagmata* <note>term: "syntagmata" | A Greek-derived word meaning systematic arrangements or treatises.</note>, Schedius divided his elaborated book on this subject into *syngrammata* <note>term: "syngrammata" | A Greek-derived word for written compositions or books.</note>.

In this regard, however, fortune did not favor him as much as it did Selden. It was Selden’s lot to put the finishing touches on his book and personally submit it, completed, to the printing presses. Living and breathing, he was able to witness his own fame and the praises of the learned—who received his work with universal applause—for nearly forty years thereafter, during which time he won over the minds of many with far more numerous and significant works. 

But Schedius departed from this life before he had even passed his twenty-sixth year. Although he had several other works in progress in his desk, and some even ready for the press—such as the *Genealogy of the Princes of Mecklenburg* <note>original: "Genealogiam Megapolitanorum Principum"</note> and the *Franceid*, an epic poem <note>original: "heroo carmine"</note> modeled after the *Aeneid* and organized into twelve books—yet by no other monument...

<summary>Fabricius compares Schedius’s scholarly ambitions to those of the famed John Selden, noting that while both wrote definitive works on ancient gods in their youth, Schedius died at age twenty-five before he could finish his epic and genealogical projects.</summary>

# FABRICIUS’S PREFACE.

...having brought [this sample] of his talent into the light of day, he passed away. He left his book *On the German Gods* <note>original: "de Diis Germanis"</note> to be published by his father—the most grieving father of an only son—Georg Schedius, who at that time was serving with distinction as the Rector of the School of Güstrow <note>original: "Scholae Gustroviensis"</note>.

There is no need to recount how favorable a reception these treatises <note>term: "syngrammata" | A Greek-derived term used here to describe Schedius’s formal written compositions or books.</note> found among readers when they were first brought into the open air of light by his father. This was due to their fairness and refinement, the skillful talent of the writer, and the variety and abundance of matters pleasant to know, which were treated diligently and richly illustrated from ancient monuments of every kind. [John] Selden himself, who used this work on more than one occasion, by no means begrudged its author the praise of being a "most learned writer" in Book 1 of his work *On the Sanhedrins* <note>original: "de Synedriis" | Selden’s massive study on the high councils of ancient Israel.</note>, page 417 of the first edition.

Since, however, the history of the ancient Germans before the saving light of Christ was brought to our lands is shrouded in no less—and perhaps even greater—obscurity than the ancient history of the Syrians and other Eastern peoples, it is no wonder that Schedius, just like Selden, quite often had to rely on conjectures; or even that, as noted in the *Thomasian Library*... <note>original: "Bibliotheca Thomasiana" | Likely a reference to the scholarly catalogs or works of Christian Thomasius.</note>

<meta>catchword: Thomasiana</meta>

# FABRICIUS’S PREFACE.

...[Tho]masian [Library] <note>original: "Thomasiana"; this concludes the reference to the *Thomasische Bibliotheque* from the previous page.</note> (*) it is held against him as a fault that he occasionally indulged in rather long and somewhat tangential digressions. Yet, the sometimes unbelievable conjectures brought forward do not diminish the value of the *Ancient Germany* <note>original: "Germania antiqua"</note> by Philipp Clüver <note>term: "Philippus Cluverius" | A 17th-century scholar regarded as the founder of historical geography.</note>, nor that of so many other works by learned men which are highly esteemed and read with profit by everyone. Nor are the writings of [John] Selden <note>term: "Seldenus" | A renowned English jurist and polymath whose vast works on ancient law and history were essential to 17th-century scholarship.</note> any less eagerly pored over by scholars, even though one may notice frequent wanderings in them as well; yet any boredom these might cause the more curious reader is easily brushed away by the excellence and abundance of his observations.

I am therefore quite convinced that these *Gods of the Ancient Germans* <note>original: "Deos veterum Germanorum"</note>, described by the posthumous pen of Schedius and unearthed from Antiquity, will provide a lasting testament to the Author’s genius and learning, just as I remember these verses inscribed upon a portrait of Selden:

->*What he was in talent, or what he was in art, both*<-
->*the gods themselves and the stones will speak, if men should keep silent.*<-
<note>original: "Qualis et ingenio, vel qualis ab arte, loquentur / Diique ipsi et lapides, si taceant homines." These verses emphasize that Schedius’s work is so fundamental that the very subjects he writes about—ancient gods and monuments—attest to his skill.</note>

For this reason, I am also confident that this new edition of Schedius’s work—enriched with significant notes and additions by the esteemed Jark <note>term: "Jarkius" | Referring to Johann Jark, the editor who updated Schedius's work for this 1727 edition.</note>—will be welcomed and appreciated by scholars. Jark himself will strive to honor these students of literature with ever greater and more impressive examples of his diligence, seeking to leave a blessed mark of his reputation for the memory of future generations. And so, farewell, my reader—lover of the humanities and of antiquity—and look kindly upon the efforts and scholarly pursuits of this most excellent editor, just as you have also done for mine.

# THE EDITOR’S PREFACE.

The more the excellence of this book has become known, the fewer words will be needed to explain the reasoning behind the whole plan that specifically drove us to this new edition. For the shortage and rarity of copies demanded this; the more this scarcity increased day by day, the more strongly it testified to how much the labor of our author pleased those who love to explore the knowledge of antiquity. So that their needs might also be assisted in this way, the bookseller <note>term: "librarius" | In the 18th century, the *librarius* acted as both a book dealer and a publisher who financed the printing.</note> decided to submit the book to the presses once more. For this reason, he began to urge me that if I had anything to contribute toward preparing this renewed work, I should grant it to him.

After I took this task upon myself, I initially began to collect and arrange what I knew had been observed by others since this author’s time, or what had been wrongly understood. By this addition, I thought I would earn sufficient favor, since while the industry of his original work remained intact, the illumination of the subject matter itself would gain a significant increase. Nevertheless, while I was comparing the collected opinions in this way and found myself overwhelmed by such a diverse crowd of conflicting views, I looked for a more convenient way to extricate myself from these tangles. I could not bring myself to indulge in common laziness or to satisfy the requirement with a sterile hodgepodge <note>original: "farragine" | A "farrago" refers to a confused mixture or a medley of miscellaneous things, often used disparagingly in scholarly contexts.</note> of excerpts. Rather, I decided to test the powers of my intellect here and to try to what extent I could elucidate the understanding of the subject matter which this book encompasses. And so

<meta>catchword: que</meta>

<summary>Johann Jark introduces his new edition of Elias Schedius’s work, explaining that the rarity of the original text and the need for updated scholarly commentary prompted this 1727 publication.</summary>
<keywords>Johann Jark, Elias Schedius, publishing history, scholarship, German antiquities, 18th-century editing, book trade</keywords>

--- Page 20 ---
<meta>This page continues the "Editor's Preface" by Johann Jark. Jark is explaining his editorial method, specifically how he balanced respect for the original author, Schedius, and later commentators with his own corrections and additions.</meta>

# THE EDITOR’S PREFACE.

...and after the frequently rehashed opinions of learned men and a mature examination, I selected separately those which appeared most probable, supported not by mere conjectures but resting upon a solid foundation sought from the testimonies of the ancients. Hence, I could not be so bound by a futile devotion to the words of others that I did not occasionally depart from them and note what was erroneously written. Let those be content with that Cato <note>The editor refers here to a "Cato," a symbol for a harsh, humorless, or overly rigid critic, suggesting that some scholars are too traditional to enjoy the "pleasant freedom" of intellectual exploration.</note>, whose palate is without taste, and who for that reason wickedly suppress the pleasant freedom of studies. Meanwhile, I did not break out into such impudence as to snatch a bit of glory from the infamous detriment of others, or to sell this book to you by a deceitful concealment of what was read here differently than it ought to have been explained, and thus fraudulently impose upon you. 

But looking upon the learning of the author and others with veneration, and not departing from it rashly, I added sparingly from my own, lest I "bring owls to Athens" <note>term: "owls to Athens" (original: *noctuas Athenas*) | An ancient Greek proverb for performing a redundant or useless action, similar to the English phrase "carrying coals to Newcastle." Athens was already full of owls (the symbol of Athena).</note>, as they say. Therefore, I especially took care not to violate the bounds of modesty, since the truth of the matter itself ought to recommend itself to fair judges. If I seem to have observed this duty of moderation as is fitting, without the loss of truer learning, it will be all the more pleasing to me, because this kind of examination created a sharper annoyance for me, as it restricts one’s style within the certain barriers of other people's thoughts. 

I will say nothing of the errors of the printers <note>term: "typothetarum vitia" | Literally "the faults of the typesetters." In early modern printing, editors frequently complained about the mistakes introduced by the workers who physically set the lead type.</note>, and also the indices <note>term: "indices" | The alphabetical back-of-the-book guides which Jark has reorganized and expanded based on his new annotations.</note> restored to their proper order and expanded from the notes. With this work finished, if I understand that this labor has not displeased you, I will have reason to congratulate this writer, and I will silently applaud that I have now attained a sufficiently great reward for my effort. 

Farewell.

<summary>Johann Jark concludes his preface by describing his editorial rigor, noting that he corrected previous errors and improved the book's indices while trying to remain humble. He emphasizes that his goal was to provide a corrected, reliable text without overstepping his role as an editor.</summary>

<keywords>Johann Jark, editorial method, ancient testimony, scholarly criticism, printing errors, indices, owls to Athens, Cato, intellectual freedom</keywords>

### Most Noble, Magnificent, Most Distinguished, Most Expert, and Most Prudent Men, Leaders of the Muses and most honorable Patrons.

The plurality of gods—if we set aside the influence of the Devil—was introduced by the opinion of the common people and the ignorant. For these people, giving too much rein to their own reasoning, could not be persuaded that such a massive machine <note>The author uses "machinam" (machine) as a metaphor for the universe or the created world.</note> and so many various things of different natures within it could subsist unless they assigned a specific Deity to each one. From this, their gods began to be distributed into as many crowds as possible. And although some among the Romans invented thirty thousand gods—which might have been enough for their madness and impiety—a story is found of a Philosopher left in Rome by the Gauls after the city was captured and the Capitol besieged. This man, just as he was about to pay his debt to nature <note>A common Latin idiom for dying.</note>, spoke to the Senate who had come to visit him. He said he rejoiced because, at the time he had first come to Rome, he had seen a huge and unbearable disgrace: namely, that the city was quite poor in gods; but now, their number had increased to match the number of citizens. For just as there were two hundred and eighty thousand citizens, so too he was leaving behind just as many gods for the city—one for every person—adding that in the future, each person, content with his own household deity <note>term: "Lare" | The Lares were ancient Roman guardian spirits of the home and family.</note>, would not weary the public divinities of the city. 

And lest the vanity of these people remain entirely hidden from the unlearned, besides Janus, Saturn, Jupiter, the Genius <note>A personal guardian spirit or guiding impulse.</note>, Mercury, Apollo, Mars, Vulcan, Neptune, the Sun, Orcus <note>A god of the underworld or death.</note>, Father Liber <note>An ancient Italian god of wine and fertility, later identified with Bacchus.</note>, Earth, Ceres, Juno, Minerva, the Moon, Diana, Venus, and Vesta: they also adopted infinite others into the number of the gods from among men, based on the specific duties over which they were placed. Such were Cautius <note>A minor deity associated with caution or wariness.</note>, Lucina <note>The goddess of childbirth, who "brings light" to the newborn.</note>, Opis <note>A goddess of fertility and the earth.</note>, Vagitanus <note>The god who was said to open the mouths of infants to their first cry.</note>, Curia <note>A goddess of the curia or assembly.</note>, Rumina <note>The goddess who presided over breastfeeding.</note>, Stellinus <note>A god believed to give children the power of speech.</note>, Adeona <note>A goddess who protected children as they returned home.</note>, Mens <note>The personification of Mind or Intellect.</note>, Volumnus <note>The god who presided over the will.</note> and Volu- <note>meta: catchword "Volu-" likely refers to Volupia, the goddess of pleasure.</note>

...by authority <note>original: "authoritate"; completing the catchword "autho-" from the previous page</note> at least to **Apollo**, but also shrines were built for the so-called gods of the "lesser nations" <note>original: "minorum gentium"; a Roman term for gods of secondary importance in the pantheon</note>. First, **Mercury** presents himself to us in the marketplace of **Pharae**, a town in **Achaia** <note>a region in the northern Peloponnese of Greece</note>, in a manner that is more ridiculous than it is worthy of wonder. I shall be brief, so that our own happiness might be seen in contrast to the madness of those poor wretches.

A marble statue of **Vesta** <note>the Roman goddess of the hearth and domesticity</note> stood in the marketplace in front of the statue of **Mercury**. Attached to this were small bronze lamps soldered with lead. Those wishing to consult the god would first appease **Vesta** by burning incense, then they would light the lamps after pouring in oil. Next, they would dedicate a bronze coin, stamped with a local mark, on the right side of the altar. Once the petitioner had asked what he needed, he would press his ear to the image; then, leaving for the marketplace, he would cover his ears with his hands. As soon as he stepped out of the marketplace, he would remove his hands and take the first voice he heard as the response of the oracle, considering it to be the voice of the god.

**Bacchus** was famous for three oracles: two in **Thrace** and one in **Phocis**. At the oracle of **Hercules** in **Bura**, a town of **Achaia**, lots were drawn from a tablet using knuckle-bones <note>original: "talos"; ancient dice made from the ankle bones of sheep or goats, used in divination</note>.

Indeed, the frenzied worshippers of each of these would receive responses at their appointed times in various ways.

I have set forth, with as much brevity as possible, how the **Sons of Noah** <note>original: "Filii Noæ"</note> gradually fell away from the true, pure, and primeval religion. ...a native deity, and an interpreter and messenger of **God** (for that is what "Tuysco" means in the language of the Germans); thus they consecrated him and began to hold him as a **God**. *Concerning Germany. Its boundaries. Long unknown to the Romans, and for what reason. The origins of the Germans. A nation of many names <note>original Greek: "πολυώνυμος" (polyōnymos)</note>. ### A 2 ###
<meta>catchword: ...rus</meta>

...[the treatise] passed into neighboring nations. This region is separated from other nations by the Rhône, the German Ocean <note>The North Sea</note>, the Adriatic Sea, the Tanais <note>The Don River, which ancient geographers often considered the boundary between Europe and Asia</note>, and the Euxine Sea <note>The Black Sea</note>, according to Aventinus <note>Johannes Aventinus (1477–1534), a Bavarian Renaissance historian</note> in Book 1 of the *Annals of the Bavarians*. The Germans are truly most ancient and have been very little mixed by the arrivals and hospitality of other peoples. This is because, in former times, those seeking new homes were transported not by land, but by fleets; and the immense Ocean beyond—and, if I may put it so, the "opposite" <note>original: "adversus." Tacitus suggests the sea was hostile, lying "opposite" the known world, or difficult to navigate</note> Ocean—is visited by few ships from our world. (Tacitus, in his book *On the Customs of the Germans*).

However, they became known to the Roman people quite late, even though the dreaded name of the race had previously reached the most distant lands. The cause certainly seems to be the same as that which Josephus uses in Book 1 of *Against Apion* to excuse the ignorance regarding his own Jewish people: *"Regarding the antiquity of the Jews, nothing was written—even though they are the oldest of all—for the reason that the Jews inhabited neither a coastal region nor practiced commerce; their interaction with the Greeks was more remote. Nothing was offered in ancient times that would cause a mixing with the Greeks, such as the trade goods that the Egyptians both export and import."*

And this likewise happened regarding Europe; when concerning the Roman state—which had acquired power over such a long time and produced so many causes for war—neither Herodotus, nor Thucydides, nor anyone who lived alongside them, made any mention. It was only late in time, and with difficulty, that knowledge of them reached the Greeks. In the same way, they were ignorant of the Galatians <note>The Gauls</note> and Iberians. For these authors, of whom Ephorus <note>A Greek historian of the 4th century BCE known for writing the first universal history</note> is one, are considered the most meticulous writers...

...[so obscure] that he <note>Referring to the geographer Eratosthenes, mentioned on the previous page</note> considered the Iberians <note>The ancient people of the Iberian Peninsula (modern Spain and Portugal)</note>, who are known to inhabit the entire part of the land of Hesperia <note>original: "Hesperiae"; a Greek term for "the Western land," referring here to the Iberian Peninsula</note>, as if they were a single city-state. How then is it proper to wonder if our own people <note>the Germans</note> were not known with certainty by many, nor gave any occasion for writing about themselves? Thus far he [Josephus] speaks.

Furthermore, the name "Germany"—according to the testimony of Tacitus in his book *On the Customs of the Germans*—is a recent and only lately heard term. For those who first crossed the Rhine and drove out the Gauls were then called Tungri <note>A Germanic tribe located in modern-day Belgium</note>, and are now called Germans. In this way, the name of a specific tribe <note>original: "natio"</note>, rather than the whole race <note>original: "gens"</note>, gradually prevailed, so that at first all were called "Germans" by the victor to inspire fear, and now they are called so by themselves, using the name they invented.

In other respects, as recorded by Aventinus <note>Johannes Aventinus (1477–1534), a Bavarian Renaissance historian</note> in Book 1 of the *Annals of the Bavarians*, Germany is the largest of the European lands and is distinguished by many names. For it was also called Scythia <note>A vast region in central Eurasia often conflated with Germany in early modern geography</note>, and the region of the Getae <note>A Thracian tribe</note> where it touches the Euxine Sea <note>The Black Sea</note>; beyond the Vistula River toward the East it was called Sarmatia (though this is false); on this side [of the Vistula], however, it was called Galatia, Gaul, and Celtic lands; even now it is called Alamannia, Francia, and Teutonia.

I think I must speak first of Scythia. This is the same as Germany. The name is derived from King Scythes, about whose birth Herodotus indeed recorded wonders in Book 4: his mother Hylea * lived in a cave and was of a dual nature, both human and serpentine—a woman from the top down to the thighs, but a viper below. Hercules lay with her so that he might recover his stolen horses, and upon his departure gave the weeping woman a bow and a belt, which belt at its end...

# CONCERNING THE GERMAN GODS
### 11

[Aristo]tle <note>The text continues from the previous page's mention of the "Stagirite," referring to Aristotle's "Meteorologica."</note> in Book II of his *Meteorology* <gloss>original Greek: ῶν, a suffix for "Meteorologica"</gloss> contends that the Ister <note>The ancient name for the Danube River</note> rises there: which is, however, a river of Germany. Strabo also agrees with this in Book IV: *The Apennine mountain <note>Strabo likely refers here to the Carnic Alps; the "Apennines" usually refer to the Italian range, but ancient geography was often imprecise with these names</note> hangs over the Carni: having a lake flowing into the river Isara <note>The Isar river in Bavaria</note>. Which, having snatched another river along with it, is carried out into the Adriatic gulf. From the same lake, however, another river glides into the Ister, which they call the Atesinus <note>The Adige river</note>. For the Ister, divided into many heads from these mountains, takes its origin.* Suidas and Appian of Alexandria, in his *Celtic History*, also openly write that the Germans are called Celts; although that name is retained in only one part of Germany, Gelderland <note>original: "Geldria," a province in the Netherlands</note>. Polybius and Strabo, in their fourth books, record that the Celts migrated from Germany into Italy. Among these were the Boii, inhabitants of the Hercynian Forest <note>A vast, ancient forest that stretched across Central Europe</note> according to Appian, who sought new homes in the third year after Pyrrhus’s arrival in Italy; having been defeated again and again, they eventually struck a treaty with the Romans. Strabo asserts in Book IV that the Boii previously inhabited the Hercynian Forest.

The Hercynian Forest, moreover, belongs to Germany, as witnessed by the Divine Caesar in Book VI of his *Commentaries on the Gallic War*. It is also clear from Tacitus in his book *On the Customs of the Germans* <note>Commonly known as the "Germania"</note> that even the Senones—who devastated Rome under the leadership of Brennus—were Germans, and specifically of the Suebi nation; he writes that the Semnones record themselves as the oldest and most noble of the Suebi. After subduing the Gauls, these people moved their standards into Etruria. Then, when the Roman envoys came down into the battle line against the Law of Nations, they descended in a hostile column into Roman territory; once battle was joined at the Anio river, the victorious Senones occupied the City <note>The Sack of Rome in 390 BCE</note>. Titus Livius <note>The historian Livy</note> recorded in Book V from the founding of the City that these were the Senones: the Senones...

The people of Cologne, named after Agrippina the Younger, mother of Nero.</note> after the name of their founder, do not blush at their origin; having crossed over [the Rhine] long ago and having been stationed right on the bank of the Rhine as a test of their loyalty, they were placed there to block others, not to be guarded themselves. 

Of all these nations, the Batavians are preeminent in valor. They inhabit not so much the bank, but an island in the Rhine river. They were once a branch of the Chatti who, due to internal strife, crossed over into those lands where they became part of the Roman Empire. The honor and the mark of their ancient alliance remains. For they are neither held in contempt by tributes, nor does the tax-collector wear them down. Exempt from burdens and contributions, and set aside only for use in battles, they are reserved for wars like missiles and weapons. 

The same author [Tacitus] says in Book IV of his *Histories*: "As long as the Batavians lived across the Rhine, they were part of the Chatti; driven out by domestic discord, they occupied the furthest shores of Gaul which were empty of inhabitants, and at the same time an island situated between the shallows, which the Ocean sea washes in front, while the Rhine river flows around its back and sides. Not worn down by Roman wealth or alliance with stronger powers, they supply only men and arms to the Empire." Hence [they are called] brothers and friends...

...by the Gauls against the Germans. For when the Gauls, weary of the rule of the Germans, called upon the Romans according to their natural fickleness so that they might shake off the dominion of the Germans, Ariovistus <note>Ariovistus was a leader of the Suebi and other allied Germanic tribes in the 1st century BCE.</note> crossed over [the Rhine] not of his own accord, but having been requested and summoned by the Gauls. He claimed that this part of Gaul was his province, just as that other part belonged to the Romans. Just as it would not be right for him to be granted permission if he were to make an attack on Roman borders, so too he argued the Romans were unjust to interrupt him in the exercise of his own right. 

The same author <note>Julius Caesar, in his *Commentaries on the Gallic War* (*Bellum Gallicum*).</note> writes in Book II that among the Belgae there was a King Divitiacus <note>Not to be confused with Diviciacus the Druid; this Divitiacus was a king of the Suessiones.</note>, the most powerful in all Gaul, who held sovereignty over a great part of these regions as well as Britain. J. Campanus writes that Vespasian, having been sent by Claudius, clashed with the Germans thirty-two times. In fact, he fought with the Britons, not the Germans. 

Suetonius says of Claudius that he undertook only one expedition in total, and that a modest one, namely into Britain. In his life of Vespasian, he also states: *Under the emperor Claudius, through the influence of Narcissus <note>Narcissus was a powerful freedman and advisor to Emperor Claudius.</note>, he was sent as a legionary legate to Germany; having been transferred from there to Britain, he clashed with the enemy thirty times.* 

Hegesippus <note>A 4th-century writer whose work is largely an adaptation of Josephus’s *The Jewish War*.</note> also says in Book III that Vespasian acquired Britain for the Roman Empire by force of arms. Eutropius <note>A 4th-century Roman historian and author of the *Breviarium Historiae Romanae*.</note> writes in Book III that Vespasian clashed with the enemy in Britain thirty-two times. Therefore, these people whom Vespasian defeated in Britain were either Germans, or Britons descended from Germans. This is because Britain was subject to the Belgae, who are Germans. 

The glory of the Batavians was soon increased throughout Britain, as Tacitus relates in Book IV of his *Histories*, when cohorts were sent across to that place; according to ancient custom, these were commanded by the most noble of their own countrymen. Truly, this refers to the maritime part [of Britain], as witnessed by Caesar in Book V of his *Commentaries on the Gallic War*.

From this, the religious rites and teachings were transferred from the Germanic Belgae into Britain and remained characteristic of that people. 

Whence Caesar, in Book VI of his *Commentaries on the Gallic War*, considers that the <term>discipline</term> <note>Refers to the specialized religious and legal training of the Druids.</note> was discovered in Britain and from there transferred into Gaul. And even now, those who wish to understand that matter more thoroughly generally travel there for the sake of learning. 

Furthermore, the Gauls or Galatians were called "Germans" because of the whiteness of their bodies, as Saint Jerome <note>A 4th-century church father and scholar.</note> reports in his *Commentary on the Epistle of Paul to the Galatians*, citing Marcus Varro, the Sibyl, and Lactantius as authorities for his opinion. They called them "Milky ones" (Lacteos), as it were, because of their appearance; for the Greeks call milk *Gala*. These people, after devastating Greece, were summoned by the Kings of Bithynia <note>An ancient kingdom in modern-day Turkey.</note> and gave the name Galatia to the region after their own name...

### ON THE GERMANIC GODS.

...history <note>original: "λογίας" (logias), the conclusion of "Archaiologias" from the previous page, referring to Josephus's *Jewish Antiquities*.</note> as witnesses, the Germans were the guardians. Aurelius Antoninus and Maximinus, as Herodian testifies, placed their greatest trust in the loyalty of the Germans; they were the only ones whom the assassins—the punishers of the emperor—feared as potential avengers. Even when everyone else abandoned Vitellius, the Germans alone remained faithful until the very end. Galba also would not have been deserted by them, had they not lost their way. For they alone of all the soldiers, as Suetonius records, flew to his aid; but arriving too late, having been delayed on a roundabout route due to their ignorance of the terrain, they were the last to withdraw from Nero, as Tacitus relates. Caracalla was also avenged by the Germans after his assassin, Martial, was killed. Others also made use of them, including Herod, according to Josephus in Book 17 <note>Herod the Great utilized Germanic mercenaries in his personal guard, a fact noted by Josephus to highlight their presence even in Judea.</note>. For this reason, even now the Kings of France use Germanic Swiss as bodyguards, as do the Roman Pontiffs <note>A reference to the Swiss Guard of the Vatican, which was well-established by the time Schedius was writing in the 17th century.</note>. Indeed, an inscription on a stone at Interamna <note>Modern-day Terni in Italy.</note> reads as follows:

->HILARIUS, BODYGUARD OF NERO CAESAR, A FRISIAN BY NATION.<-

Nor is their nature capable of fraud; hatreds do not lurk under the titles of friendship, and the modest simplicity of the people is entirely ignorant of great crimes. Of candid soul, they do not diminish the virtues of others—their deeds or inventions, especially of those who are absent—with spiteful and swollen envy, but uplift them with sincere and almost immoderate praise. Hence, those pretentious men deserve to be mocked with the best of right and driven out of Germany; those who—without the agreement of authors and contradicting history itself—rely on their own brains and vomit up whatever comes into their mouths, claiming that several famous cities in Saxony were built by Julius Caesar, which he supposedly named after the number of the seven planets. They do not blush to lie openly about such things, when Caesar himself says that after eighteen days he returned from Germany into Gaul, having broken down the bridge. For the Roman Empire was always bounded by the Rhine and the Danube <note>original: "Istro". Domitius Ulpianus <note>A celebrated Roman jurist whose writings make up a large portion of the *Digest*.</note> writes in the *Digest* concerning captives and restoration of status <note>term: *postliminium* — a Roman legal doctrine where a person captured by an enemy regained all their former rights and status upon returning to Roman territory.</note>: *Enemies are those against whom the Roman People have publicly declared war, or who have declared it against the Roman People; others are called petty thieves or robbers.* Therefore, a slave captured by robbers is not the slave of the robbers, nor is the law of return necessary for him; but one captured by enemies—for example, by the Germans or the Parthians—is indeed a slave of the enemies, and he recovers his former status through the law of return. Saint Ambrose, writing on the time of Valentinian: *The Danube, cutting through the barbarian and Roman peoples from the Western parts until it is buried in the sea itself. The Rhine, directing its course from the ridge of the Alps even to the depths of the Ocean, is a wall of the Empire that must be remembered by the Romans against the fierce nations.* Josephus, in Book II of *The Jewish War* <note>original: "τῆς Ἁλώσεως" (The Capture).</note>: *What wonder is it if the Euphrates from the East and the Ocean from the West, likewise the most fertile region of Libya from the Southern tract, and the Rhine and the Danube from the North, are the limits of the Empire?* Claudianus, in his poem on the fourth consulship of Honorius:

> The Germanic treaties ennoble the ancient Drusi,
> but were bought with an uncertain war and many disasters.
> Who remembers the Rhine conquered by fear alone?

<note>Drusus was a famous Roman general who led early campaigns into Germany, though with heavy losses.</note>

Servius, in his commentary on Book VIII of the *Aeneid*: *The Rhine is a "two-horned" river because it flows through two channels. Through one, where the Roman Empire is; through the other, it flows between the Barba-* <note>The text cuts off here at the catchword "ba-", likely leading into "barbarians."</note>

<summary>This page discusses the historical and legal status of the Rhine and Danube as the definitive borders of the Roman Empire, distinguishing the Germanic tribes as "official enemies" of Rome rather than mere bandits.</summary>

And when these rivers were swollen with water, honor was paid to the gods and thanks were offered by all those who inhabited the shores of Gaul, the Raetias, the Vindelici, the Norici, Pannonia, and the Moesias <note>These represent the Roman provinces along the Rhine and Danube frontiers, stretching from modern France through Switzerland, Austria, Hungary, and the Balkans.</note>. But if the waters failed, or decreased due to drought, or if at last the ice joined the banks together, then every age and sex—men, women, the elderly, boys, and girls—proclaimed a public mourning <note>original: "justicium"; a period where public business was suspended, often during times of national crisis or mourning.</note> both publicly and privately. Holidays were established by the augurs, priests, and sacrificial officers; solemn supplications were decreed, and prayers were offered at all the couches <note>original: "pulvinaria"; platforms where statues of the gods were placed to "feast" during festivals.</note> of the Gods. Greater and lesser victims were sacrificed, and with special ceremonies, solemn rites, vows, and prayers, the minor Pontiffs and the High Priests <note>original: "Flamines maximi"</note> performed rites to **Jupiter Elicius** <note>A title of Jupiter meaning "The One Who is Called Down," specifically invoked to bring rain or lightning during droughts.</note>* in order to obtain rain and the flooding of these rivers, so that the way would not lie open to the Germans.

For this reason, no one will find in the ancient authors that Germany was ever fully reduced to the status of a Roman province. Even Strabo, in Book V, who witnessed the Empire at its most flourishing, records that the Romans never crossed the Elbe: "That region, indeed, which faces beyond the Elbe, is entirely unknown to us. For we have no record of any of our predecessors having completed a voyage to the East as far as the mouth of the Caspian Sea; nor did the Romans themselves cross the Elbe." One should not be swayed by the fact that many Emperors called themselves "Germanicus" after defeating the Germans. They boasted of this title falsely; for whether they defeated a few marauding soldiers of Germany in Gaul or other provinces with some small slaughter, or received them into friendship, or subdued a modest region of Germany, they soon claimed the whole...

These lines mock Caligula's "triumph," where he allegedly staged a fake victory, even hiring people to wear blonde wigs (lutea gausapa) to look like Germanic prisoners.</note>

## ON THE GERMAN GODS

->NERO CLAUDIUS CAESAR<-
->AUGUSTUS GERMANICUS, PONTIFEX MAXIMUS <note>The high priest of the Roman state religion.</note>, TRIBUNICIAN POWER, IMPERATOR.<-

Nero undertook no expedition against the Germans, but only expeditions to Alexandria and Achaia <note>A province of Greece.</note>, as Suetonius testifies in his *Life of Nero*. Nor did Nerva obtain any praise from Germany. Neither did Trajan, although he reduced Decebalus <note>The last king of Dacia (modern-day Romania), famously defeated by Trajan.</note> to submission and turned Dacia into a province. Nor did the later Emperors, who after Trajan and Constantine arrogated the name "Germanicus" to themselves; for even when Roman affairs were flourishing, they fought against the Germans with equal loss to both sides. 

Likewise, Tacitus testifies in his *Life of Agricola* that Domitian celebrated a false triumph over Germany: *He was inwardly conscious that his recent false triumph over Germany had been an object of ridicule, featuring people purchased through trade whose clothing and hair were styled to look like captives.* <note>original: "Inerat conscientia derisui nuper fuisse falsum e Germania triumphum, emptis per commercia, quorum habitus & crines in captivorum speciem formarentur."</note> 

From this, it is discovered that what is said regarding the Dacians—here called "peoples of Germany"—being conquered by Domitian is a false claim based on the preceding facts. Indeed, he triumphed more for the killing of Oppius Sabinus and Cornelius Fuscus, leaders of the legions, than for any actual subjugation of Dacia. Aurelian eventually abandoned this province after it had been seized. This is noted by Flavius Vopiscus and Jordanes in his work *On the Succession of Kingdoms*. 

Nor should we believe the official triumphs of the Romans; for as Strabo shows in Book III: Polybius recorded that three hundred cities of the Celtiberians were overthrown by Tiberius Gracchus, which was said in a "comic fashion" <note>Meaning it was an exaggeration or a joke.</note> of Tiberius Gracchus by someone who calls simple towers "cities," as is the custom in triumphal processions. And the Panegyric to Maximian <note>A formal public speech of praise delivered to the Emperor Maximian (reigned 286–305 AD).</note> states: here, regarding what was already falsely believed about the ancient Emperors, that the Roman standards across the Rhine...

*Our city was in its six hundred and fortieth year <note>Approximately 113 BCE.</note> when the arms of the Cimbri <note>A Germanic-Celtic tribe that threatened the Roman Republic.</note> were first heard, during the consulship of Caecilius Metellus and Papirius Carbo. Not the Samnites, nor the Carthaginians, nor the Spanish or Gallic provinces, nor even the Parthians have more frequently taught us a lesson. Truly, the liberty of the Germans is more fierce than the kingdom of Arsaces <note>The founder of the Parthian Empire; Tacitus argues German freedom is harder to suppress than Eastern monarchy.</note>. For what else could the East throw in our face but the slaughter of Crassus, especially since they themselves were thrown down by Ventidius after losing Prince Pacorus? But the Germans—by routing or capturing Carbo, Cassius, Aurelius Scaurus, Servilius Caepio, and Marcus Manilius—took five consular armies from the Roman People all at once. They even took Varus and three legions from Caesar <note>Referring to the Battle of the Teutoburg Forest in 9 CE, a catastrophic Roman defeat.</note>, and not without cost did Gaius Marius strike them in Italy, or the Divine Julius Caesar in Gaul, or Drusus, Nero, and Germanicus in their own homelands. Soon, the great threats of Gaius Caesar <note>The Emperor Caligula, whose German campaign was considered a farce.</note> were turned into a joke. Then there was peace, until taking the opportunity of our own discord and civil wars, they captured the winter quarters of the legions and even aimed for the Gallic provinces; and being pushed back from there, in recent times they have been more "triumphed over" than actually defeated.* <note>original: "Sexcentesimum & quadragesimum annum urbs nostra agebat... proximis temporibus triumphati magis, quam victi sunt."</note>

As even Baptista Mantuanus <note>A famous Italian Carmelite poet of the 15th century, known as the "Christian Virgil."</note> wrote to Roberto Sanseverino:

> *But neither the peaceful Indians, nor the soft Sabaeans,*
> *Nor the short Pygmies seize power; but the inhabitant of the Rhine,*

For it is well established that the Romans, although they were a terror to all others, feared the Germans. Thus, for example, the Tencteri and Usipetes <note>Two Germanic tribes who crossed the Rhine in 55 BCE and encountered Julius Caesar.</note> speak in Caesar’s *Gallic War*, Book IV: *The Germans never refuse to contend with arms if they are provoked, because this is their custom handed down from their ancestors: to resist whoever brings war.* Nor does Hirtius <note>Aulus Hirtius, a general under Caesar who wrote the eighth book of the Gallic Wars.</note> deny this in his addition to the *Gallic War*, stating that before Caesar's most excellent achievements in Gaul, the Germans denied aid to no one who fought against the Romans. For how could it be that they feared the Romans, when they were sending reinforcements to everyone who opposed Rome? They sent aid to Mithridates <note>Mithridates VI of Pontus, a persistent and powerful enemy of the Roman Republic.</note>, and even to the gladiators themselves in the very heart of Italy <note>A reference to the Third Servile War led by Spartacus, whose ranks included many Germanic and Gallic captives.</note>. See Orosius <note>Paulus Orosius, a 5th-century historian and theologian.</note>, Book V. Nor were the Germans quiet themselves; in frequent marching columns they devastated now Italy, now Gaul, and now the other Roman provinces. Claudian <note>Claudius Claudianus, the last great poet of classical Rome, writing around 400 CE.</note> puts it best in his work to Stilicho <note>The high-ranking general of Germanic (Vandal) origin who became the de facto ruler of the Western Roman Empire.</note>, Book I:

> *- - Once great*
> *Names, kings gleaming with blond hair on their long-haired heads,*
> *Who, though summoned by princes, gifts, and prayers, would never*
> *Have obeyed, now hurry at your command, and fear*
> *To have offended you by a sluggish delay. - -*

# 44

The same author <note>Referring to the poet Claudian.</note> writes in *On the Gothic War*:
> *Will posterity believe it? That Germany,*
> *Once so fierce in its people, who formerly could scarcely be held*
> *With all the weight of our emperors pressing upon them,*
> *Now offers itself peacefully to the reins of Stilicho.*

Yet, Stilicho <note>Flavius Stilicho (c. 359–408), a high-ranking general of the Western Roman Empire who was of Vandal origin.</note> drew them to his side not by force, but with a massive sum of gold, because he himself was a Vandal and a German. Indeed, the Poet is quite excessive in heaping praise upon Stilicho, though it is not established that he possessed such great virtue. These facts demonstrate more than enough that the Germans did not fight merely for liberty, but for empire and dignity. For although Drusus <note>Nero Claudius Drusus, a Roman general who led major campaigns across the Rhine.</note> alone for some time applied himself to reducing a very small portion of Germany into a province, he eventually yielded after being defeated at Bingen <note>original: "Bingium"; a town at the confluence of the Nahe and Rhine rivers.</note>. Far be it, then, from the truth that the Germans feared the Romans as masters of the world, when, on the contrary, the Romans very often purchased friendship and peace from the Germans with a great weight of gold. <margin>Claudian, *On Stilicho*, Book I</margin>
> *Those terrible men, whose custom it was*
> *To always sell their leisure, and to bargain for peace with a shameful price.*

So also Salvianus <note>A 5th-century Christian writer known for his critiques of Roman society.</note> complains in Book VI of *On the Government of God*: *The ancient Romans used to terrify; we are afraid. The barbarian peoples used to pay them taxes; we are the ones paying tribute to the barbarians. Our enemies sell us the very use of the light of day: our entire safety is a matter of commerce.* And the Divine Caesar took the Germans on the near side of the Rhine into his friendship, as Lucan <note>A Roman poet, author of the epic *Pharsalia*.</note> testifies in Book I of the *Pharsalia*:
> *And the Belgian, the docile driver of the beaked chariot.*

And:
> *—and the excessively rebellious*
> *Nervian, defiled with the blood of the slaughtered Cotta,* <note>Referring to the defeat of the Roman legate Lucius Aurunculeius Cotta by the Nervii and Eburones.</note>

<summary>Schedius argues that Rome's perceived dominance over the Germans was often a facade maintained by bribery and the influence of German-born Roman generals like Stilicho. He cites both poets and historians to show that Rome frequently bought peace from the tribes they could not defeat in battle.</summary>

Indeed, within the memory of our fathers, it was from Germany that architects were primarily sought, and thereafter painters, statue-makers, sculptors, mathematicians, and craftsmen of most skillful hand, as well as hydraulic engineers <note>original: "aquileges"</note> and surveyors <note>original: "septem pedariique mensores"</note>. ### ON THE GERMAN DEITIES.

Having already clarified the nature of the region and added its governance, one must investigate what further should be sought within it. And indeed, the highest good for a human in life must be most diligently investigated, and one must aspire most greatly to participate in it. Now, the highest good, according to Aristotle <note>The influential Greek philosopher (384–322 BCE). This definition comes from his *Nicomachean Ethics*.</note> in Book 1 of the *Ethics*, is the operation of the soul according to the best and most perfect virtue in a complete life. It is also called the highest good <note>original: "τὸ ἀγαθὸν" (*to agathon*)</note>, blessedness <note>original: "μακαρισμὸς" (*makarismos*)</note>, happiness <note>original: "εὐδαιμονία" (*eudaimonia*)</note>, prosperous fortune <note>original: "εὐτυχία" (*eutychia*)</note>, good action <note>original: "εὐπραξία" (*eupraxia*)</note>, or the blessed life <note>original: "εὖ ζῆν" (*eu zēn*)</note>. It is defined through action; for the perfection of a thing is judged by its operation. 

However, the highest blessedness is by no means found in pleasure. For it is common to beasts and irrational animals. For if pleasure makes one blessed, then beasts are certainly happier than we are, as they enjoy it more freely and pleasantly. Nor is it lasting. As Plautus <note>Titus Maccius Plautus (c. 254–184 BCE), a Roman playwright known for his comedies.</note> says in his play *Curculio*:

->— no good is perpetual for any man.—<-

Furthermore, hatred is joined to this pleasure. Boethius <note>An early 6th-century philosopher and statesman; this quote is from his *Consolation of Philosophy*, a staple of medieval and Renaissance learning.</note> writes in Book III, Meter 7:

> *Every pleasure has this trait:*
> *It drives those who enjoy it with stings,*
> *And like a flight of bees,*
> *Once it has poured out its sweet honey,*
> *It flies away, and strikes*
> *The wounded heart with a bite that lingers.*

> *Spurn pleasures; pleasure bought with pain is harmful.*

Virtue should not follow the matter <note>original: "rem"; referring here to material wealth, circumstances, or rewards.</note>, but the matter should follow virtue. **Therefore**, regarding the honors which many seek, Cato <note>Cato the Younger (95–46 BCE) was a Roman statesman famed for his stubborn integrity and refusal to take bribes or seek office through populism.</note> should not have sought them; rather, the state should have given them to him unasked because of his virtue, <term>Augustine, *The City of God*, Book 4</term> <note>St. Augustine (354–430 CE) was a foundational Christian philosopher; here he argues that true honor is a byproduct of character, not a goal in itself.</note>. The reward of virtue is glory, which is likewise bestowed upon good men, <term>Aristotle, *Ethics*, Book 4, chapter 3</term>. This is because honor is an external good—light, doubtful, fleeting, inconstant, and deceptive—partly due to the fickleness of the common people, and partly due to our own weakness. Honor also exists more in the one who bestows the honor than in the one who is honored, <term>Aristotle, *Ethics*, Book 1</term>. It is in the power of those who revere, not those who are revered, <term>Aristotle, *Ethics*, Book 1, chapter 5</term>. Moreover, honor is often acquired by the unworthy. The "Highest Good," however, is obtained only by the worthy.

The good man and the coward desire glory, honor, and power equally. But if the good man strives by the true path, the coward—because he lacks honorable skills—competes with tricks and deceits, <term>Sallust, *The War with Catiline*</term> <note>Sallust (86–35 BCE) was a Roman historian; this quote highlights the difference between earned merit and political machination.</note>. Hence Alphonso <note>Alfonso V of Aragon (1396–1458), known as "the Magnanimous," was a prominent Renaissance prince and patron of learning.</note>, as Panormitanus <note>Antonio Beccadelli (1394–1471), called "Il Panormita," was a famous Italian humanist and the court chronicler for King Alphonso.</note> records in Book 2 of his *Deeds of Alphonso*, was asked what he thought of honor that had no utility. He replied that it seemed to him like a man who could see very sharply and keenly, yet, struck by a thick mist, wanders lost in the darkness. He was noting those who aspire to great honors, but once they have obtained them, they do not have the character to live up to the title of that honor.

Such are the "gilded knights" <note>original: "equites aurati"; a class of knighthood often associated with the Holy Roman Empire, sometimes bestowed for merit, but here criticized as a vanity.</note> of today who, after a pilgrimage to St. James <note>The shrine of Santiago de Compostela in Spain.</note> or the Holy Sepulchre, call themselves gilded knights and show off painted coats of arms, even though they barely have enough travel money for a mile or two and are accustomed to traveling on foot. Therefore, once the obstacles of insane opinion are removed, crimes are weighed bare, and inspected bare; let the deceptive coverings, vain praises, and false glories be taken away, and their miseries will appear...

"Let there be heaped upon you," says **Seneca** in *Letter 16 to Lucilius* <note>Lucius Annaeus Seneca (c. 4 BCE–65 CE) was a Roman Stoic philosopher. His letters to Lucilius are famous for their practical moral advice.</note>, "whatever many wealthy men have possessed. Let fortune carry you beyond the private measure of money, cover you with gold, clothe you in purple, and lead you to such a degree of luxury and wealth that you hide the earth with marble—allowing you not only to possess riches, but to trample upon them. Let statues, paintings, and whatever any art has labored over for the sake of luxury be added; from these things, you will only learn to desire greater things. What does it matter how much lies in a man’s chest, or how much in his granaries, if he gapes after another's property, if he calculates not what he has acquired, but what is yet to be sought? For he is not poor who has less, but he who desires more. Nor is he rich who has more, but he who desires less. If you live according to nature, you will never be poor. If you live according to opinion <note>original: "opinionem"; here meaning social expectations, fashion, or the perceived need to keep up appearances.</note>, you will never be rich. Nature desires little; opinion desires the infinite."

Truly falling and fragile (as **Valerius Maximus** says in Book 6 <note>Valerius Maximus was a 1st-century Roman writer known for his collection of historical anecdotes used by orators to illustrate moral points.</note>), and consistent with children's rattles, are those things which are called human strength and wealth. They flow in suddenly and slip away quickly; they stand in no place, nor are they fixed in any person with stable roots. Instead, driven here and there by the most uncertain breath of Fortune, they abandon those whom they once raised on high, and after an unforeseen downfall, they plunge them miserably into a depth of disasters. Therefore, those things ought neither to be esteemed nor called "goods" which, by the bitterness of the evils they inflict, double the desire for them.

**Boëthius** rightly says of these things in Book 3, prose 8 of *The Consolation of Philosophy* <note>Boëthius (c. 477–524 CE) wrote this influential work while imprisoned; he argues that true happiness comes from the soul, not external circumstances.</note>: "I will demonstrate very briefly with how many evils riches are entwined. For what? Will you try to gather money? But you will snatch it from him who has it. Do you wish to shine with dignities? You will have to beg from the one who bestows them; and you, who desire to surpass others in honor, become cheapened by the humility of petitioning..."

# ELIAS SCHEDIUS

...of pleasure; these are the words of Bernard <note>St. Bernard of Clairvaux (1090–1153) was a primary builder of the Cistercian order and a highly influential mystic whose writings often focused on the soul's relationship with the divine.</note> in his 35th Sermon on the Song of Songs. ...divinity <note>original: *numinis*. The text begins mid-word, completing the thought from the previous page regarding the nature of the divine.</note>, and discussing the purification of the soul. This purification is so necessary for every human that it is impossible that God would not have provided some universal method for the purification of the human race. By what reasoning, then, is it possible that the fall of man occurred through the *phantasia* <note>Latin: *phantasia*. In this philosophical context, it refers to the "imagination" or the sensory faculty that acts as a bridge between the spiritual soul and the physical body.</note>, through which the body is joined to the soul? For higher things are not dragged down by lower things, but rather the opposite occurs. Indeed, these higher substances descend within themselves, from the intellect into the imagination, from spiritual things to material ones, from the highest to the lowest, and from the perfect to the imperfect. And those souls which could have remained firm and stable, had they been intent upon the one God—not so much by their own power as by God's, under whose form, as it were, they would have lived and acted—once they incline and lean toward matter, they fall away from themselves and sink below themselves. 

For this reason, the ancients teach that sin arrived and faithlessness or treachery was condemned in those substances that are capable of wavering toward material things, insofar as they loved the creatures and turned away from the Creator. Proclus <note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was a Greek Neoplatonist philosopher who sought to synthesize Greek philosophy into a single system.</note> says in his book *On the Soul*: *If the soul had remained whole with God, as Plotinus <note>Plotinus (c. 204–270 AD), the founder of Neoplatonism, who taught that the soul’s goal is to return to "The One."</note> desired, it would have preserved reason itself—which is like a ray to the soul—unblemished; and consequently, it would have directed all its actions in such a way that we would not have been made liable to sin.* 

Simplicius <note>Simplicius of Cilicia (c. 490–560 AD), a philosopher who wrote influential commentaries on Aristotle and sought to harmonize him with Plato.</note> indeed writes with great precision: *As long as the soul of man firmly adheres to its author, it remains whole and retains the perfection implanted by the Creator. But if it is torn away from him, as if cut off from its root, it immediately withers and fades away, and it cannot be restored to its original vigor unless it is joined once more to the First Cause.*

Muhammad, the author of the Quran, in Surah 81 <note>The text cites Surah 81, though the specific names of the idols listed—Wadd, Suwa, etc.—actually appear in Surah 71, titled "Noah."</note> lists the names of the idols: Proceeding further in his discourse, Noah said: "O God, they have followed those who, by no means imitating me but perpetrating as many deceits as possible—which gave them wealth and offspring only to their own ruin—persuaded others in turn not to abandon their images, which were a great occasion of error for many: namely, Wadda, Suwaha, Yajowth, Yahowk, and Nasera. Since they wandered further because of their blindness <note>original Latin: **caligamina**, referring to spiritual darkness or cataracts of the eye.</note> and became very guilty, they were submerged by our hand." Moreover, immediately, barely as the flood had left the lands, wicked idolatry took up its beginning once again. The most severe punishment <note>i.e., the Great Flood.</note> had escaped their eyes, and therefore it [idolatry] was renewed, as occurs throughout the writings of Eusebius in the *Preparation for the Gospel*, Theodoret, Epiphanius, and Clement of Alexandria, especially in the age of Serug and Terah <note>In biblical tradition, Terah was the father of Abraham and is often depicted as a maker of idols.</note>. To these, Said ibn Batriq <note>A 10th-century Melkite Patriarch of Alexandria, also known as Eutychius, who wrote a universal history in Arabic.</note> also agrees:

> And they sacrificed their sons and their daughters to demons; so God sent upon them a violent wind, and it was a flood of winds, and it broke [their idols]... <note>original Arabic: **وذبحوا بنيهم وبناتهم للشياطين بعث الله عليهم ريحا عاصفا وكان طوفان رياح وكسرت**</note>

the upper and lower world, and you will find this in their books; and they tell of Abraham’s condition, and they said these same words: that Abraham was born and raised in the land of those who serve fire. When he contradicted the opinion of that people, saying that there was another creator <note>original: *operator*</note> besides the Sun, they brought their arguments against him, among which they mentioned the operations of the Sun, which are manifest and appear to the sight throughout the entire universe, etc. And from this descended the most ancient custom of worshipping the stars and holding the celestial bodies as Gods. For the things that were worshipped by the ancients are either corporeal or incorporeal. Corporeal things include celestial bodies—the Sun, Moon, and Stars—or terrestrial ones, such as men, Heroes, and other animals <note>original: *bruta*</note>, along with herbs and plants. Incorporeal things are Demons <note>In the ancient sense of *daimones*, or intermediary spirits/intellectual beings, rather than the modern concept of evil spirits.</note>. # ELIAS SCHEDIUS #

...in Plato's *Cratylus* <note>The *Cratylus* is a dialogue by Plato regarding the origins of names and language.</note>, Anaximander, Alcmæon, Xenocrates, Theophrastus, Zeno, Cleanthes, and Socrates all attributed divine worship to the stars. From this point, all things that existed on the earth were also counted among the number of the Gods: the Earth, \* the Sea, the Air, the Winds, Fire, \*\* and the Crops; indeed, whatever provided a convenience or benefit to man was deified. Lucretius, in Book II of *On the Nature of Things*, sings elegantly of this:

> *If anyone here decides to call the Sea 'Neptune' and the grain 'Ceres,'*
> *And prefers to misuse the name of Bacchus rather than*
> *To utter the proper name of the liquid [wine];*
> *Let us grant that he may declare the globe of the Earth*
> *To be the mother of the Gods, provided that in truth it is not so.*
<note>original: *Heic si quis Mare, Neptunum Cereremque vocare / Constituet...* Lucretius, a Roman Epicurean poet, argued that while we use the names of gods as metaphors for nature (metonymy), we should not believe the physical elements are literally divine.</note>

Orpheus writes in the *Lesser Crater*:

> *Hermes is the messenger and interpreter of all things,*
> *The Nymphs are water, fire is Hephaestus, grain is Demeter,*
> *And the great Sea is Poseidon, the Earth-shaker.*
<note>original Greek: Ἑρμῆς δ’ ἑρμηνεὺς τῶν πάντων ἄγγελός ἐστι... These verses, attributed to the mythical poet Orpheus, illustrate the "interpretatio graeca," where natural elements are personified as specific deities.</note>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the Stoic "utility theory" of divinity, where ancient peoples assigned the names of gods to physical things that were beneficial to human survival. Having previously discussed the elements and stars, Schedius now turns to the extreme examples found in ancient Egypt, where animals and even vegetables were elevated to divine status based on their perceived usefulness or symbolic value.</meta>

-># ON THE GERMAN GODS #<-

<margin>81</margin>
<margin>F</margin>

*...that useful and healthful things should be called by the names of the Gods, so that they might not even say that those things were invented by the Gods, but were themselves divine.* <note>original Latin: "res utiles & salutares Deorum vocabulis esse nuncupandas..." This reflects the Stoic belief that the divine essence is permeated through all things that sustain life.</note> Afterward he adds: *Those very Egyptians who are mocked, consecrated no beast except for some utility which they received from it.* 

Herodotus <note>The "Father of History" (c. 484–425 BCE), whose second book, titled *Euterpe*, focuses on the customs and history of Egypt.</note> writes in his *Euterpe*: 

<note>original Greek: νομίζουσι δὲ καὶ τῶν ἰχθύων τὸν καλεόμενον λεπιδωτὸν ἱερὸν εἶναι, καὶ τὴν ἔγχελυν, καὶ τῶν ὀρνίθων τοὺς χηναλώπεκας. ἔστι δὲ καὶ ἄλλος ὄρνις ἱερὸς τὸ ὄνομα Φοῖνιξ.</note>

This is to say: *they considered among the fish that the one called the lepidotus <note>A scaly fish of the Nile, often identified as a species of barbel or carp.</note> was sacred, as was the eel; and among the birds, the sheldrake <note>original Greek: χηναλώπεκας; literally "fox-goose," referring to the Egyptian goose.</note>. There is also another sacred bird whose name is the phoenix.* 

But they even brought herbs into the number of the Gods; the Roman satirist Juvenal <note>Decimus Iunius Iuvenalis (late 1st/early 2nd century CE), famous for his biting "Satires" which mocked the perceived decadence and foreign superstitions of Rome.</note> mocks their madness in these verses from his fifteenth Satire:

> — Who does not know what kind of monsters mad 
> Egypt worships? One part adores the crocodile.

Furthermore:

> It is a sin to violate or break with a bite the
> Leek and the onion. O holy nations, for whom
> These divinities are born in the gardens!

Anaxandrides of Rhodes <note>A poet of the Middle Comedy (4th century BCE). This fragment is often cited to show the deep cultural divide between Greek and Egyptian religious practices.</note> beautifully agrees with this sentiment:

<note>original Greek: Οὐκ ἂν δυναίμην συμμαχεῖν ὑμῖν ἐγώ. / Οὔθ' οἱ τρόποι γὰρ ὁμονοοῦσ', ἔθ' οἱ νόμοι / Ἡμῶν ἀπ' ἀλλήλων δὲ διέχουσιν πολύ. / Βοῦν προσκυνεῖς, ἐγὼ δὲ θύω τοῖς θεοῖς. / Τὴν ἔγχελυν μέγιστον ἡγῇ δαίμονα, / Ἡμεῖς δὲ τῶν ὄψων μέγιστον παρὰ πολύ. / Οὐκ ἐσθίεις ὕεια, ἐγὼ δέ γ' ἥδομαι / Μάλιστα τούτοις, κύνα σέβεις, τύπτω δ' ἐγὼ</note>

I could not bring myself to be your ally,
For neither do our manners nor our laws agree,
But they stand far apart from one another.
You worship the ox; I sacrifice it to the gods.
You consider the eel a most great divinity;
We consider it the greatest of delicacies by far.
You do not eat pork; but I delight 
In it most of all. You revere the dog; I beat it <note>The fragment usually continues "I beat it when I catch it stealing my food."</note>

Divine Lactantius <note>Lactantius (c. 240–320 CE) was an early Christian author and advisor to Constantine I who wrote *The Divine Institutes* criticizing pagan beliefs.</note>, Book 1, chapter 20. Guevara <note>Antonio de Guevara (c. 1481–1545), a Spanish writer and court chronicler.</note> in *The Dial of Princes*, Book 1, chapter 12. Briefly, there were as many Gods for the Romans as there were citizens in the City. The philosopher Bruxellus—of whom Cicero <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero (106–43 BCE), the Roman statesman and orator.</note> makes mention in Book 1 of *On the Nature of the Gods*, based on the account of Parasmanis in Book 20 of *On the Liberty of the Gods* as cited in Guevara Book 1, chapter 6—says: just as there are two hundred and eighty thousand citizens, the Romans were most firmly convinced that two hundred and eighty thousand Gods were left to them by Bruxellus. Therefore, Prudentius <note>Aurelius Prudentius Clemens (c. 348–413 CE), a Roman Christian poet.</note> wrote rightly in Book 1 *Against Symmachus* <note>A polemic against the pagan senator Symmachus, who petitioned to restore the Altar of Victory to the Senate House.</note>:

> *Once vain superstition besieged the pagan hearts of the fathers,*
> *It ran uninterrupted through a thousand steps of generations;*
> *The young heir trembled in awe, and worshipped whatever*
> *The gray-haired ancestors had shown him to be venerable.*
> <note>original Latin: "Ut semel obsedit gentilia pectora patrum / Vana superstitio..."</note>

For as he continues further:

> *Whatever the earth, the sea, or the wondrous sky brings forth,*
> *They deemed to be Gods—the hills, the straits, the rivers, the flames;*
> *These elements, formed into various figures for themselves,*
> *The fathers established, and they inscribed the names of men*
> *Upon silent statues, either calling the Ocean "Neptune,"*
> *Or the hollow rivers the "dark-blue Nymphs,"*
> *Or the woods "Dryads," or the remote countrysides "Napaeae."* <note>Nymphs of the glens and wooded valleys.</note>
> *Fire itself, which was made to serve our use,*
> *Is held to be "Vulcan," and he is fashioned in supreme power;*
> *As a god, he has shrines assimilated both in name and appearance;*
> *Furthermore, he is said to reign in the furnaces*
> *And be the greatest craftsman of Aeolia or Etna.* <note>Volcanic regions associated with the forge of the gods.</note>
> *There are those who sought the Gods above in the conspicuous stars.*
> <note>original Latin: "Quicquid humus, pelagus, cælum mirabile gignunt..."</note>

# ELIAS SCHEDIUS

<page-num>86</page-num>

Therefore, since the whole world was corrupted, and even the very nation chosen by God the Best and Greatest, the Germans themselves also corrupted the religion of their homeland which they had received from their ancestors. They exhibited the honor due to God to the vain names of the stars, as some of the Romans believe. Julius Caesar, in Book 6 of the *Gallic War*, says: **"The Germans count among the number of the gods only those whom they perceive, and by whose power they are openly helped: the Sun, Vulcan <note>original: Vulcanum; here referring to the personification of Fire.</note>, and the Moon. They have not even heard of the others even by rumor."** Tacitus, in the book *On the Customs of the Germans*, writes: **"Of the gods, the Germans chiefly worship Mercury <note>The Roman name "Mercury" was commonly used by Latin authors to describe the Germanic god Wotan or Odin.</note>, to whom on certain days they consider it lawful to offer human sacrifices. They appease Hercules and Mars with permitted animals. A part of the Suebi also sacrifices to Isis. Collectively they worship Erthus <note>original: Erthum, id est, terram matrem</note>, that is, Mother Earth, and they believe that she intervenes in human affairs and is carried among the peoples."** The same author also states: **"They venerate the Mother of the Gods."** Herodotus, in the *Melpomene* <note>The fourth book of Herodotus's *Histories*.</note> concerning the Scythians—whom he considers to be none other than the Germans—recounts these things: **"The gods alone they appease are these: Vesta <note>original Greek: ἑςίην (Hestia)</note> most especially; then Zeus <note>original Greek: Δία (Dia)</note> and the Earth, believing Earth to be the wife of Zeus. After these, Apollo, the Heavenly Venus, and Hercules and Mars. For all the Scythians considered these to be gods."** <note>original: "Deos autem solos hos placant, Vestam quidem præcipue; postea Iovem ac Tellurem, Tellurem Iovis uxorem existimantes. Post hos Apollinem, cœlestem Venerem, & Herculem ac Martem. Hos enim omnes Scythæ Deos putarunt."</note> Therefore, before these authors are compared with one another by us, it is necessary that the rites which first...

...they used in invoking the Gods. Therefore, polyonymy <note>original: πολυωνυμία (polyonymia); the practice of using many names for a single deity.</note> was especially in use among the Gentiles, by which infinite names were heaped together, so that all the names of the Gods might finally be reduced to a single God. Indeed, many names were considered highly desirable, and that god was more illustrious who had more titles <note>original: indigitationes; specific ritual names used to invoke a deity for a particular purpose.</note>. For they believed that by a multiple heap of names, multiple power also accrued to their Gods. Hence Diana, in Callimachus, prays:

> "Grant me to keep eternal virginity, O Father, 
> and to be called by many names."
> <note>original Greek: Δός μοι παρθενίην αἰώνιον, Ἄππα, φυλάσσειν, καὶ πολυωνυμίην. From Callimachus's *Hymn to Artemis*.</note>
> *Grant me to keep eternal virginity, Father,*
> *And to be called by many names.*

Orpheus in his *Hymn to Mars*:

> "O King Mars, showerer of weapons, always spattered with slaughter, 
> rejoicing in the blood of men, shaker of war, terrible one, 
> who desires the unspeakable strife of swords and spears."
> <note>original Greek: Ἄρες ἄναξ δολόδεικτε, φόνοις πεπαλαγμένος αἰεὶ, Αἵματι ἀνδροφόνῳ χαίρων, πολεμόκλονε, φρικτὲ, Ὃς ποθέεις ξίφεσίν τε καὶ ἔγχεσι δῆριν ἄϋστον.</note>
> *Mars, King most terrible, always rejoicing in slaughter,*
> *Rejoicing in human blood, desiring war, harsh one,*
> *Who wishes to contend always with swords and spears.*

Bacchus, in Nonnus's *Dionysiaca*, book 40, prays to the Sun with a mystical voice:

In the 18th chapter of 1 Kings, verse 26: *And they took the bullock which was given them, and they prepared it, and called on the name of Baal from morning even until noon, saying, O Baal, hear us!* <note>original Latin: *Et acceperunt juvencum, quem concesserat eis, & paraverunt eum, & invocarunt in nomen Bahalis a mane usque ad meridiem dicendo, o Baal exaudi nos!*</note> For I am not persuaded to believe that they summoned Baal to their sacred rites by shouting only these two words, **O Baal, answer us** <note>original Hebrew: *ha-Ba'al 'anenu* (הבעל עננו)</note>, for six whole hours. This ritual of invocation was undoubtedly rebuked by our Savior Jesus Christ in Matthew, chapter 6, verse 7: *And when you pray, do not heap up empty phrases as the pagans do, for they think that they will be heard for their many words.* <note>The author quotes the Greek: *proseuchomenoi mē battologēsēte, hōsper hoi ethnikoi, dokousi gar, hoti en tē polylogia autōn eisakousthēsontai.* The word *battologēsēte* implies repetitive, stuttering, or babbling speech.</note> Writers even now report this same behavior among the Turks. Bartholomæus Georgieviz <note>A 16th-century Croatian scholar and former captive of the Ottoman Empire who wrote extensively on Turkish customs.</note> notes these things about the Turkish women: *They pray from the ninth hour of the night until the twelfth, which is midnight; and during the prayer, the body is continually agitated, and they afflict themselves strangely with outcries, so that they often fall prostrate on the ground, failing in strength and spirit.* Salomon Schweigger also writes about the Turks themselves in his *Travels to Jerusalem*. Next is **Mars**, to whom the name of **Vulcan** also belongs. **Apollo** is the same as the **Sun**. **Jupiter** is identified as the Heavens (**Caelum**); **Venus** as **Urania**, **Erthus** <note>Schedius likely refers to Nerthus, the Germanic earth goddess described by Tacitus.</note>, **Vesta**, and **Isis** is the **Moon** herself. For Vulcan is the inventor of fire and the various crafts that are prepared by fire, as **Tzetzes** <note>Johannes Tzetzes, a 12th-century Byzantine poet and grammarian known for his vast mythological commentaries.</note> records in *History 335, Book 10*:

This figure was even believed to be Fire itself, as **Orpheus** <note>Referring to the *Orphic Hymns*, a collection of ancient Greek poems dedicated to various deities.</note> has it in his *Hymn*:

> O Vulcan, strong-hearted, of great power, unwearied fire,
> Shining with flaming blasts, a light-bringing deity to mortals.
> <note>original Greek: Ἥφαιστ’ ὀβριμόθυμε, μεγασθενὲς, ἀκάματον πῦρ, Λαμπόμενε φλογίαις αὔραις φαεσίμβροτε δαῖμον. original Latin: Vulcane praestans, magnanime, perennis flamma, Splendens in flammeis auris peramabile numen.</note>

Therefore, he forged arms for Mars, since he was the blacksmith of the Gods, as the divine **Maro** <note>Publius Vergilius Maro, better known as Virgil.</note> sings in the eighth book of the *Aeneid*:

> *In another part, they were busily working for Mars on a chariot and flying wheels, with which he stirs up men, and with which he stirs up cities.*
> <note>original Latin: Parte alia Marti, currumque rotasque volucres Instabant, quibus ille viros, quibus excitat urbes.</note>

<margin>Diodorus Siculus</margin>...is said to have discovered the art of iron, bronze, silver, gold, and all things forged with fire. **Sol** <note>The Sun</note> must now be discussed by us, whom Tacitus indeed passes over in silence, though Caesar mentions him; Herodotus calls him Apollo.
