Truly, the Erycinian Venus was worshipped in Sicily with the greatest honor. Eryx first established a temple for her. **Servius** <note>A 4th-century commentator on Virgil</note>, in his commentary on Book 1 of the *Aeneid*: *Eryx was the son of Venus and Butas—though according to some, he was the son of Neptune—who, being of surpassing strength, challenged strangers to boxing matches with cestus <note>leather straps often weighted with metal</note> and slew those he defeated.* He was killed by Hercules and gave his name to the mountain where he was buried, upon which he had built a temple for his mother. Moreover, doves are always seen around the temple of the Erycinian Venus. Doves are dedicated to Venus, and she is even imagined to use them to pull her chariot. **Ovid**, in Book XV of the *Metamorphoses*:
> *And carried through the light breezes by her yoked doves,*
> *she approaches the Laurentian shore.*

Hence also the festivals of Venus are called the *Anagogia* <note>original Greek: ἀναγώγια; meaning "the departure," referring to a festival where the goddess was said to depart for Libya</note> among the Sicilians. **Aelian** <note>A Roman author and teacher of rhetoric</note>, in Book 1 of his *Various History*: *In Eryx in Sicily, where there is a temple of Aphrodite, majestic and holy, there at a certain time the Erycinians sacrifice...* <note>original Greek: ἐν ἔρυκι δὲ τῆς Σικελίας, ἔνθα ἐστὶν ὁ τῆς Ἀφροδίτης νεὼς, σεμνός τε, καὶ ἅγιος, ἔνθα κατά τινα καιρὸν θύουσιν οἱ ἐρυ-</note>

...the Departure festivals <note>original Greek: ἀναγώγια (Anagogia), festivals marking the "setting sail" or departure of a deity</note> are common, and they say that Aphrodite departs for Libya from Sicily; the doves vanish from the region, as if they are traveling abroad along with the goddess. During the rest of the year, however, it is agreed that a vast multitude of these birds frequents the temple of the goddess. 

That is to say: In Eryx <note>A mountain and city in western Sicily famous for its temple of Venus</note> in Sicily, where there is a venerable and holy temple of Venus, when at a certain time the inhabitants of Eryx offer the **Anagogia** <note>The "Departure" sacrifices</note> sacrifices, and they affirm that Venus sets sail from Sicily into Libya, the doves vanish from that place, as if they depart together with the Goddess. It is well established that for the remainder of the time, a huge abundance of these same birds is found around the temple of the Goddess. **Athenaeus** <note>A Greek rhetorician and grammarian, author of the *Deipnosophistae* or "Banquet of the Learned"</note>, in Book IX, Chapter XVI of the *Deipnosophistae*, relates that Venus herself returns in the form of a purple dove, accompanied by a great multitude of doves. 

For this reason, Venus is called **Rose-colored Aphrodite** <note>original Greek: ῥοδόχρως Ἀφροδίτα (rhodochrōs Aphrodita)</note> by **Anacreon** <note>A Greek lyric poet known for his poems on wine and love</note> in his *Ode to the Rose*. Moreover, among plants, the rose is dedicated to Venus. As Anacreon says in the same place:

> For this is the breath of the gods,
> This is also the joy of mortals,
> An ornament for the **Graces** <note>original Greek: Χάρισίν (Charisin), the goddesses of charm, beauty, and nature</note> in the seasons
> Of many-flowered loves,
> And the plaything of Aphrodite.
> This is also a subject of concern in myths,
> And a graceful plant of the Muses.

*For the Rose is the delight of the Goddesses;*
*This is the scent of men*—

As Pausanias in his *Description of Greece* (Book 6, *Elis II*) and Virgil in his *Seventh Eclogue* record:

> The poplar is most pleasing to Hercules <note>original Latin: Alcides, a name for Hercules derived from his grandfather Alcaeus</note>, the vine to Bacchus <note>original Latin: Iacchus, a ritual name for Bacchus/Dionysus</note>,
> The myrtle to beautiful Venus, and his own laurel to Apollo <note>original Latin: Phoebus</note>.

As for why the dove was pleasing to Venus, Publius Nigidius <note>Publius Nigidius Figulus (c. 98–45 BC), a Roman scholar and Pythagorean philosopher</note> writes in his commentary on the *Phaenomena* of Aratus: it is because a dove brooded over an egg of marvelous size that had been rolled out of the Euphrates river by fish, and from this egg the Goddess <note>Venus</note> was produced. Tibullus also writes in his first book of *Elegies*:

> The white dove is sacred to its Palestinian master. <note>The "Palestinian" here refers to the Syrian or Phoenician origins of the goddess Astarte, whom the Romans identified with Venus.</note>

Elsewhere, Aristophanes writes in his play *The Birds* that Cupid was born from an egg:

> There was Chaos, and Night, and black Erebus at first, and wide Tartarus.
> There was neither earth, nor air, nor heaven; but in the boundless laps of Erebus,
> Black-winged Night first brought forth a wind-egg <note>An egg produced without fertilization; in this context, a primordial "world-egg."</note>.
> From this, as the seasons rolled around, there sprouted forth the long-desired Love <note>original Greek: Eros</note>,
> His back gleaming with golden wings.

<note>original Greek: Χάος ἦν, καὶ νὺξ ἔρεβός τε μέλαν πρῶτον, καὶ τάρταρος εὐρύς. Γῆ δ’ οὐδ’ οὐρανὸς ἦν ἐρέβους δ’ ἐπ’ ἀπείροσι κόλποις Τίκτει πρώτιστον ὑπηνέμιον νὺξ ἡ μελανόπτερος ᾠόν. Ἐξ οὗ περιτελλομέναις ὥραις, ἐβλάστανεν Ἔρως ὁ ποθεινὸς Στίλβων νῶτον πτερύγοιν χρυσαῖν.</note>

> At first there was Chaos, and Night, and black Erebus, and then deep Tartarus.

> Black-winged Night first brought forth an egg conceived of the wind.
> From this, as the hours glided by, there then sprouted forth Cupid,
> With his back shining with golden wings.

This completes the sentence from the previous page regarding the Syrian veneration of the dove.</note> Furthermore, according to Hesychius, *Semiramis* denotes a "mountain dove." <note>original Greek: Σεμίραμις περιστερὰ ὄρειος ἑλληνιστί, translated by the author as "Semiramis is a mountain dove in Greek."</note> Regarding Semiramis, see more in Hyginus (*Poetical Astronomy*, fable 117), Ovid (*Metamorphoses*, Book 4), Athenagoras (in his *Apology*), Tzetzes (*Chiliades* 9, chapter 235), and Phurnutus <note>Lucius Annaeus Cornutus, a Stoic philosopher known for his work on the nature of the gods.</note> (*On the Nature of the Gods*). ->*The Cytherean goddess, carried through the middle of the air in a light chariot,*<-

Because Venus was placed in charge of loves and marriages by the ancients, she was called *Babia* and worshipped by the Syrians, because she protected boys and infants against dangers. Thus Damascius writes in his *Life of Isidore*, as preserved by Photius in the *Myriobiblon* (Codex 242): <note>original Greek: βαβια δὲ οἱ Σύροι, καὶ μάλιστα οἱ ἐν Δαμασκῷ τὰ νεογνὰ καλοῦσι παιδία· ἤδη δὲ καὶ τὰ μειράκια ἀπὸ τῆς παρ’ αὐτοῖς νομιζομένης Βαβίας θεοῦ.</note> *that is, the Syrians, and especially those in Damascus, call newborn children "babia"; and indeed they even call adolescents by this name after Babia, who is considered a goddess among them.* That this is an office of Venus is not without reason. One should read Macrobius (*Saturnalia*, Book 1, chapter 19), whose words are these:

> The Egyptians also apply the symbolism of the caduceus <note>The staff of Mercury, often shown with intertwined serpents.</note> to the birth of human beings—which is called Genesis—noting that four guardian deities attend a person at birth: the Spirit <note>original Greek: daimon</note>, Fortune <note>original Greek: tyche</note>, Love <note>original Greek: eros</note>, and Necessity <note>original Greek: ananke</note>. And they wish for the first two to be understood as the Sun and the Moon...

...they hold that *the Sun is the author of the Spirit, the parent and guardian of heat and light for human life.* And for that reason, he is believed to be the *daemon* <note>A guiding spirit or lesser deity, from the Greek *daimon*.</note>—that is, the God—of one who is being born. The Moon is *Fortune* <note>original Greek: τύχη</note>, because she is the overseer of bodies, which are tossed about by the variety of chance events. Love is signified by a kiss, Necessity by a knot. And *Vettius Valens of Antioch*, in the 4th book of his *Anthology*, in the chapter which is called *the division of the four lots* <note>original Greek: τῶν τετάρτων κλήρων μερισμός</note>, as cited by the distinguished Selden in the 1st *Syntagma* <note>A systematic treatise or collection.</note> of *On the Syrian Gods*: *from the lot of fortune, of the daemon, of Love, and of Necessity, the temporal passions, benefits, and dangers are received* <note>original Greek: ἐκ κλήρου τῆς τύχης, τοῦ δαίμονος, ἔρωτος, καὶ Ἀνάγκης τὰ καιρικὰ πάθη καὶ αἱ εὐεργεσίαι καὶ οἱ κίνδυνοι παραλαμβάνονται</note>; that is, *temporal affections, virtues, and dangers are perceived from the chance of fortune, of the daemon, of Love, and of Necessity.* *Servius*, in his commentary on the 9th book of the *Aeneid*: We owe all things to the gods above as long as we live, for this reason: as the <term>Physici|Classical natural philosophers who studied the physical laws of the universe</term> say, when we begin to be born, we obtain our Spirit from the Sun, our body from the Moon, our blood from Mars, our intellect from Mercury, our desire from Jupiter, our longings from Venus, and our honor from Saturn—all of which we seem to return to each individual deity when we are deceased.

See Luke 1, verse 14; John chapter 16, verse 21; Titus 3, verse 5; from the root *he begat* or *she brought forth* <note>original Hebrew: ילד (*yalad*)</note>. *Then the remote thickets resound with melodious birds,*
*And the herds return to Venus <note>Meaning they return to the impulse of mating and procreation.</note> on appointed days;*
*Every field brings forth, and with the warm breezes of the West Wind*
*The fields loosen their bosoms; a tender moisture abounds in all.*

These verses signify Spring and Mother Earth. Macrobius <note>Ambrosius Theodosius Macrobius, a Roman provincial who wrote the *Saturnalia* in the early 5th century, a work focusing on ancient Roman religious lore and linguistics.</note> speaks clearly on this in Book 1 of the *Saturnalia*, chapter 21: *The statue of the Goddess Venus on Mount Lebanon is fashioned with her head veiled, with a sorrowful appearance, supporting her face with her left hand within her garment; it is believed by those looking on that a vision of tears flows from her. This image, besides being that of a mourning Goddess, represents the earth in winter, at which time, veiled by clouds and widowed of the sun, she lies dormant; the springs, acting as the eyes of the earth, flow more abundantly, and the fields, deprived of their usual cultivation, show a mournful face. But when the Sun has emerged from the lower parts of the earth and crosses the boundaries of the vernal equinox by increasing the length of the day, then Venus is joyful: the fields turn beautiful and green with grain, the meadows with grass, and the trees with leaves.* For this reason, our ancestors dedicated the month of April to Venus. Plutarch <note>A Greek-Roman philosopher and biographer.</note>, in his *Life of Crassus*, writes the following regarding the Syrian Goddess <note>Atargatis, the chief goddess of northern Syria, often identified by the Greeks and Romans as Venus/Aphrodite or Juno/Hera.</note> worshipped at Hierapolis: <note>original Greek: οἱ μὲν Ἀφροδίτην, οἱ δὲ Ἥραν, οἱ δὲ τὴν ἀρχὰς καὶ σπέρματα πᾶσιν ἐξ ὑγρῶν παρασχοῦσαν αἰτίαν καὶ Φύσιν νομίζουσι.</note> *Some consider her to be Venus, some Juno, and others the cause and nature that provides the principles and seeds for all things from moisture.* The sacred rites of both Goddesses were also the same; see Lucian <note>A Syrian-Greek satirist who wrote "On the Syrian Goddess."</note> and Apuleius <note>Author of "The Golden Ass," which contains descriptions of wandering priests.</note> in Book 8 concerning the priests of the Syrian Goddess, who used to travel through the streets and towns sounding cymbals and rattles,

This goddess was worshipped by the Germans among the Aviones, Angles, Varini, Eudoses, Suardones, and Nuithones <note>A group of Germanic tribes located in what is now northern Germany and Denmark.</note>. They collectively worship her as *Herthum* <note>original: *Herthum*</note>, that is, *Mother Earth*, and they believe she intervenes in human affairs and travels among the people.

> There is on an island in the Ocean a sacred grove, and within it a consecrated chariot covered with a cloth; only a single priest is permitted to touch it. He perceives the presence of the Goddess in her inner sanctum and follows her with great reverence as she is drawn by female oxen. Then follow days of joy and festive places, wherever she deigns to visit and be hosted. They do not enter into wars, they do not take up arms; all iron is locked away; peace and quiet are then alone known and loved! Until the same priest restores the Goddess to her temple, satisfied with her conversation with mortals. Presently the chariot, the cloths, and—if you are willing to believe it—the divinity herself are washed in a secret lake. Slaves perform the service, whom the same lake immediately swallows. From this arises a mysterious terror and a holy ignorance as to what that thing might be which only those about to die ever see. 
<note>This famous passage comes from Chapter 40 of Tacitus’s *Germania* (written c. 98 AD), describing the cult of the goddess Nerthus.</note>

But Tacitus is mistaken in the name; for "Earth" is not pronounced with a harsh breathing <note>The "h" sound at the start of the word.</note> among us, but with a smooth one. Indeed, in our language, Earth is called *Aerde*, not *Harthe*: for with that word we designate the hearth <note>original: *focum*</note>, which is very far removed from the earth. Therefore, the deity should have been called *Herthus*, *Erdus*, or rather *Erda*. But he [Tacitus] adapted it according to the Roman idiom, which he frequently does in other German-

# ELIAS SCHEDIUS

As for why the servants of Ops (who is the Earth) and Saturn perform sacred rites, Macrobius <note>Ambrosius Theodosius Macrobius (fl. 400 AD), a Roman provincial and author of the *Saturnalia*, a work discussing Roman history and mythology.</note> records in Book 1, Chapter 10 of his *Saturnalia*: *The Earth is called Ops, for by her aid* <note>original: "ope"</note> *the nourishment for human life is prepared; or perhaps the name comes from labor* <note>original: "opere"</note>*, through which fruits and crops are brought forth. To this Goddess, people offer their vows while sitting, and they purposefully touch the earth, demonstrating that Mother Earth herself is to be sought by mortals.* Philochorus <note>An Athenian historian (c. 340–262 BC) known for his history of Athens.</note> says that Cecrops <note>The mythical first king and founder of Athens.</note> established the first altar to Saturn and Ops in Attica, and that he worshipped these deities as Jupiter and the Earth. He also instituted the custom where the heads of families, once the fruits and crops had been gathered, would eat everywhere alongside the servants with whom they had endured the labor of cultivating the fields. *For the God is delighted by the honor shown to servants in contemplation of their toil.* It is for this reason that, following a foreign custom, we perform the sacred rite to this God with an uncovered head <note>The Roman "Greek rite" (*rito Graeco*) involved sacrificing with the head bare, unlike the "Roman rite" where the head was veiled.</note>. As for why female oxen are used, the reason is that they are instrumental for the fertilization of the countryside, for giving birth, and for plowing. Nor is it unfitting that the Bull <note>The constellation/sign Taurus.</note> is dedicated to Venus. For indeed, according to Macrobius in Book 1, Chapter 12 of the *Saturnalia*, the first month <note>March, the month of Mars.</note> was dedicated to Mars, the god who is most often the killer of men (as Homer says, knowing his nature: *Ares, Ares, bane of mortals, blood-stained, stormer of walls* <note>original Greek: "ἆρες ἆρες βροτολοιγὲ μιαιφόνε, τείχεσιπλῆτα" from the *Iliad* 5.31.</note>), while the following month <note>April.</note> was dedicated to the fertile Venus, who might soften his violence with her beneficial influence. Furthermore, among the twelve signs of the Zodiac—which are believed to be the fixed dwellings of certain deities—while the first sign, Aries, is assigned to Mars, the following one was received by Venus, namely, the Bull (Taurus). For this reason, oxen were not eaten by the Ancients; however, a later and "iron" age slaughtered them, as Aratus <note>A Greek poet (c. 315–240 BC) who wrote the *Phaenomena*, a poem on astronomy and meteorology.</note> describes in his *Phaenomena*:

*And Theon adds the reason for this passage:* and in this he sufficiently complains about those who first began to eat plowing oxen, since the previous generation had not yet done this. For the ancients took care to guard working oxen from being sacrificed. For this reason, Homer also says: *a heifer unbroken, which a plowman has not yet led under the yoke.* <note>Homer, *Odyssey* 3.382. In ancient ritual, an animal that had worked for humans was often considered "tainted" or too "humanized" to be a pure sacrifice to the gods.</note> For it seemed impious to slaughter a "plowman" <note>Here, Schedius refers to the ox itself as a fellow laborer or "plowman" (*aratorem*).</note>. The Athenians were the first to taste such oxen. They say that the companions of Ulysses also ate such cattle. Indeed, the Sun was enraged; because plowing oxen, who are the reason we behold the Sun <note>By providing the food that sustains our life and sight.</note>, exist as the providers of nutrition, and through this they produce the vital power that remains for all.

<note>The preceding section is Schedius providing both the Greek text and a Latin translation of the commentary by Theon of Alexandria, a 4th-century scholar, regarding the myth of the "Cattle of the Sun" from the *Odyssey*.</note>

Perhaps we have also observed another origin for this ritual, and why the bull is said to be sacred to Venus. For the Goddess is said to have placed a bull’s head upon her own head as a royal insignia, and after wandering the world, to have found a star fallen from the air, <term>a star fallen from the sky<note>original Greek: ἀεροπετῆ ἀστέρα (*aeropetē astera*). This refers to a legend recorded by the Phoenician writer Sanchuniathon regarding the goddess Astarte (often identified with Venus), who found a meteorite and consecrated it in the holy city of Tyre.</note></term>

### ELIAS SCHEDIVS

Hence Ceres was even called "the green one," because when the crops sprout, they abound with a pleasing greenery. As Euripides left us in these lines:

> But I am going straight to the city: for I must sacrifice
> A ram to Demeter of the Greenery.
> <note>original Greek: "Ἀλλ' εὐθὺ πόλεώς εἰμι θυ̃σαι γάρ με δει̃ / Κριὸν χλόῃ Δήμητρι." original Latin: "Sed recte ad urbem eo: sacrificare enim me decet / Arietem virenti Cereri." This fragment is from Euripides' lost play *Erechtheus*. "Ceres" is the Roman name for the Greek "Demeter."</note>

Since Isis and Ceres are one and the same deity, the mythologists say she is the Earth. Servius, in his commentary on Book VIII of the *Aeneid*: *Isis, in the language of the Egyptians, is the earth, which they wish to be Isis.* <note>Servius was a 4th-century grammarian known for his extensive commentary on Virgil’s works.</note> Macrobius, in Book I, chapter 20 of the *Saturnalia*: *Isis is celebrated in all religion as either the earth or the nature of things lying beneath the Sun. This is why the entire body of the Goddess is thickened with continuous breasts, because the whole universe is nourished either by the earth or by the nature of things.* <note>Macrobius was a late Roman provincial official and author; his *Saturnalia* is a collection of ancient lore. The "continuous breasts" refers to the "Polymastos" or "Multimammia" iconography, often seen in statues of Artemis of Ephesus, whom Schedius here conflates with Isis/Ceres as a symbol of nature’s fertility.</note> Diodorus Siculus, in Book I of his *Library*, interprets Isis as "ancient," <note>original: "antiquam." Diodorus likely connects the name Isis to the Greek word "is" (strength) or "eisi" (to go/be), though Schedius focuses on her eternal nature.</note> saying that this name was given to her because of her ancient and eternal generation; and they add horns\* to her because that is the appearance of the Moon when it grows and shrinks in the shape of a sickle, and because she has the bull Apis consecrated to her among the Egyptians. And rightly so. For thus Maro <note>Publius Vergilius Maro, better known simply as Virgil, the Roman national poet.</note> in Book I of the *Georgics* understands the Moon:

> —O you brightest stars of the world,
> Who lead the gliding year through the sky,
> Liber and bountiful Ceres.
> <note>original: "Vos ô clarissima mundi / Sidera, labentem cælo quæ ducitis annum. / Liber & alma Ceres." While Virgil likely refers to the Sun and Moon, Schedius uses this to identify Liber (Bacchus) and Ceres (Isis) as celestial bodies.</note>

Servius: *The Stoics say there is only one God, and that there is one and the same power which, according to the reason of the duty—* <note>The Stoics believed in a single divine principle—the Logos or Fire—that manifested in different forms as various gods depending on its function in nature.</note>

---

\* Vossius <note>Gerardus Vossius (1577–1649), a Dutch classical scholar and theologian.</note> proves in *On Idolatry*, Book II, ch. 76 and Book VII, ch. 10, that the "Moon" appears under the name of Atergatis. <note>Atergatis was a Syrian mother goddess, often depicted as a mermaid.</note> The illustrious Millius executes this learnedly in his elegant *Dissertation on Gad and Meni*, section VII. <note>original: "Cl. Millius in eleganti Diss. de Gad & Meni." David Millius was a Dutch orientalist. "Gad" and "Meni" are deities of fortune and fate mentioned in the Hebrew Bible (Isaiah 65:11), which Millius and Schedius link to the Moon and planetary worship.</note>

<meta>This page continues Elias Schedius’s exploration of religious syncretism, where he argues that the numerous deities of antiquity are merely different names for the same celestial powers. Having previously linked Isis and Ceres to the Earth, he now expands on their identification with the Moon and the Sun, illustrating how cultural attributes—like "horns"—are shared across Phoenician, Greek, and Roman mythologies.</meta>

# ON THE GERMAN GODS.

[The deity] is called by various names according to their different duties. Hence, they call the same [power] the Sun, Liber, and Apollo. Likewise, they say the Moon is the same as Diana, Ceres, Juno, and Proserpina: according to those who invoked Liber <note>An ancient Italian god of fertility and wine, often identified with Bacchus or Dionysus.</note> and Ceres on behalf of the Sun and Moon. And for this reason, Astarte <note>A Phoenician goddess of fertility and war, often associated with the planet Venus or the Moon.</note> is depicted with a bull’s head, because Astarte is the same as the Moon. \* For so says *Lucian* in his book *On the Syrian Goddess*: *I believe Astarte to be the Moon.* <note>original Greek: "Ἀσάρτην δ’ ἐγὼ δοκέω σεληναίαν ἔμμεναι"</note> Consult also, if you wish, what *Achilles Tatius* <note>A 2nd-century Greek writer known for his romance novel *Leucippe and Clitophon*.</note> writes in his first book. And what could be said to be more "horned" than the Moon? Thus *Orpheus* <note>Refers to the *Orphic Hymns*, a collection of ancient Greek poems attributed to the mythical singer Orpheus.</note> calls her "horned":

> Hear, O Queen Goddess, Bringer of Light, Divine Moon,
> Bull-horned Moon, walking by night, wandering through the air.
> <note>original Greek: "κλῦθι θεὰ βασιλεία, Φαεσφόρε, δῖα σελήνη, Ταυρόκερως Μήνη, νυχτίδρομε, ἠεροφοῖτι." The Latin translation provided in the original text reads: "Audi Dea Regina, luminis author, divina Luna. Cornuta Luna, noctu incedens, alte currens."</note>

Therefore, the altar of the God is fashioned with horns—horns which the sister Diana gave to her brother Phoebus <note>A common epithet for Apollo, meaning "bright" or "pure."</note> for the construction of an altar, as *Ovid* writes in the *Letter of Cydippe*:

> *I marvel at the altar constructed from countless horns.*

Indeed, the island of *Cyprus* was once called *Cerastia*, as *Xenagoras* <note>An ancient Greek historian and geographer.</note> records in his second book *On Islands*, because it was inhabited by people who seemed to have many swellings, like horns, on their heads—since horns are called *kerata* <term>original Greek: κέρατα</term> by the Greeks, and the horned are called *kerastai* <term>original Greek: κεράσται</term>,

Servius <note>Maurus Servius Honoratus, a late 4th-century grammarian famous for his commentary on Virgil’s poetry.</note>: "Some report that Hecate was so named because she is the same as Diana and Proserpina. > *“Have you never heard in the country that on the eighth day of the lunar month—the moon being called Jana—both while waxing and, conversely, while waning, that those things which ought to be done while the Moon is waxing, some are nevertheless better done after the eighth day of Jana than before?”*

The same author, in Book V of *On the Latin Language*, calls Jana by the name Juno:
> *“Whether the Nones <note>The Nones were a day in the Roman calendar, usually the 5th or 7th day of the month.</note> are to be on the fifth or seventh day, the pontiffs in the Calabra court <note>A place on the Capitoline Hill where the start of the month was proclaimed.</note> on the Capitoline would proclaim it thus five times: ‘I call you, New Juno,’ or seven times: ‘I call you, New Juno.’”* <note>original: *Calo Iuno Novella*. The word 'Calo' (I call) is the root of 'Calends'.</note>

Some people substitute "Jana" for this, though quite foolishly. Indeed, Macrobius <note>Ambrosius Theodosius Macrobius (fl. 400 CE), a Roman provincial and author of the *Saturnalia*.</note> in Book I of the *Saturnalia*, chapter 15, openly objects, writing thus:
> *“Since our ancestors observed the beginnings of the months from the rising of the Moon, they rightly dedicated the Calends to Juno. They believed the Moon and Juno to be the same, either because the Moon travels through the air—whence the Greeks also called the Moon Artemis <note>original Greek: ἄρτεμιν</note>, as if she were an ‘air-cutter’ <note>original Greek: ἀεροτόμην</note>, because she cuts the air—or because Juno is the mistress of the air; therefore, they deservedly consecrated the beginnings of the months, that is, the Calends, to this Goddess.”*

This goddess was also placed in charge of weddings, which is why she was called the *pronuba* <note>A title for Juno as the matron of honor or patroness of marriage.</note>. The Carthaginians <note>referred to here as the *Poeni*.</note> worshiped her most religiously. Maro <note>The poet Virgil.</note> in Book I of the *Aeneid*:
> *This one land, they say, Juno cherished more than all others,*
> *setting even Samos aside.*

And Horace in the Book of Odes, Book II, Ode I:
> *Juno, and whichever of the gods were more friendly*
> *to the Africans.*

St. Augustine, in *Questions on Judges*, Book II, question 16, writes that this goddess was actually Astarte:
> *“Without a doubt, Juno is called Astarte by them (namely, the Carthaginians). And since those languages (Punic and Phoenician) do not differ much from one another, it is rightly believed that the Scripture says this concerning the children of Israel...”*

<meta>This page continues the philological discussion of the Moon’s various names and identities, moving from the previous page's focus on the Roman names Jana and Juno to their equivalents in other cultures, specifically linking them to the Phoenician and Punic deities Baal and Astarte.</meta>

## ELIAS SCHEDIUS ##

...because they served the *Baals* and the *Astartes*, just as they served *Jupiters* and *Junos*. <note>The author is likely quoting a Church Father, such as Augustine, discussing why these names appear in the plural in the Bible.</note> It should not be troubling that he did not say *Astarte* (that is, *Juno*) in the singular, but rather used the plural name as if there were many *Junos*. For he intended the meaning to refer to the multitude of idols, since each individual image of *Juno* was called *Juno*. And through this, he wanted as many *Junos* to be understood as there were statues.

The same author says: It is often said that among the people of those regions, the name *Baal* belongs to *Jupiter*, and *Astarte* to *Juno*, which the Punic <note>The language of ancient Carthage, related to Phoenician.</note> language is thought to demonstrate. For it seems the Punic people say *Baal* for "Lord." Whence they are understood to say *Baalsamen* as "Lord of the Heavens"; for among them *samen* is the name for "heavens." *Juno*, however, is without doubt called *Astarte* by them. 

Furthermore, *Herodian* <note>A Roman civil servant and historian of Greek origin (c. 170–240 CE).</note> in Book V, writing on the *Pseudo-Antoninus* <note>Refers to the Emperor Elagabalus, whom contemporary historians often viewed as a false claimant to the Antonine name.</note>, calls this *Astarte* or *Astroarche* <note>Astroarche literally translates to "Queen of the Stars" or "Ruler of the Stars."</note> the Moon:
> The Africans indeed call her *Urania*; but the *Phoenicians* name her *Astroarche*, intending her to be the Moon. <note>original Greek: Λίβυες μὲν οὖν αὐτὴν Οὐρανίην καλῶσι· Φοίνικες δὲ Ἀστροάρχην ὀνομάζωσι, Σελήνην εἶναι θέλοντες</note>

Indeed, *Dio* <note>Cassius Dio (c. 155–235 CE), a Roman consul and historian.</note> records the same; see *Xiphilinus* <note>Joannes Xiphilinus, an 11th-century monk who epitomized the lost books of Cassius Dio's Roman History.</note> on the *Pseudo-Antoninus*. 

But also, in that passage of *Varro*, some read *Covella* instead of *Novella*. <note>Referring to the proclamation "I call you, New Juno" (Juno Novella) mentioned on the previous page.</note> and this is indeed excellent. For the ancients called the sky *Covum*, as *Sextus Pompeius* <note>Sextus Pompeius Festus, a 2nd-century Roman grammarian.</note> holds. ### ON THE GERMANIC GODS ###

->Q 3<-

<meta>catchword: Cæsar.</meta>

...until it was divinely permitted <note>original: *fas*; refers to what is allowed by divine law as opposed to human law</note> to contend in battle before the New Moon, * while the light of the heavenly body was decreasing. See Caesar, Book 1 of his *Commentaries on the Gallic War*. Among the Germans, it was the custom that the mothers of their families would declare through lots and prophecies whether it would be advantageous to engage in battle or not. These women declared that it was not divinely permitted for the Germans to be victorious if they joined in battle before the New Moon. Therefore, Caesar, learning this from deserters, provoked them to battle and, attacking them while they were hindered by such a religious scruple, he put them to flight. For thus Polyænus writes in Book VIII of his *Stratagems*: Caesar, not daring to commit to a fight as the Germans approached because he had learned their prophets had forbidden them from fighting before the new moon, led his army away as if he were afraid; the Germans were then destined to fight with less enthusiasm because of the prophecy. Thus, at a favorable time, the Romans utterly defeated the Germans. See also Frontinus, Book II, chapter 1, and Plutarch in his *Life of Caesar*.

For the Lower Germans, it is *Maen*; for the Upper Germans, *Mond*, from which, following the Roman custom for the second day of the week, they said *Montag*; the Lower Germans say *Maendach*, the Swedes *Mandagh*, the Danes *Maendag*, and the English *Mundag* <note>Monday</note>.

### ELIAS SCHEDIUS ###

<margin>Caesar.</margin> The Greeks also, and especially the Spartans among them, used to observe the Moon with great superstition before embarking upon any undertaking. Euripides notes this poorly <note>The author, Schedius, suggests Euripides may be slightly inaccurate in his historical or religious detail here.</note> when, in *Iphigenia in Aulis*, Agamemnon replies that his daughter will then be married when the "right circle of the Moon" <note>original: *dexter circulus*; this refers to the moon's waxing phase as it completes its disk</note> has arrived. Clearly, he was referring to the full moon. Lucian, in his short treatise *On Astrology*, openly reports that Lycurgus established a law for the Spartans that they should not enter into battle before the full moon. Aristophanes jokes about this superstition with the phrase *at the full moon* <note>original: *tē panselēnō* (τῇ πανσελήνῳ)</note>, signifying something that would happen very late or perhaps never at all; see Theodor Zwinger, Book IV, Volume XXI.

The cause for this was as Pausanias writes in his *Description of Greece*: *The Athenians sent Philippides as a messenger to the Spartans regarding the Persian invasion of Attica; he, upon his return, reported that the Spartans were slow to lead out their troops because they were hindered by religious scruple from marching with the army before the Moon had filled its orb.* Consult also Herodotus, Book VI.

How great the fear of the ancients was, and how great their trembling when the Moon failed <note>original: *deficeret*; referring to a lunar eclipse</note>, Tacitus reports in Book I of his *Annals*: *For the Moon was suddenly seen to fade in a clear sky. The soldier, ignorant of the rational cause, took this as an omen of his present situation; likening the failure of the heavenly body to his own hardships, he believed that the things they were undertaking would turn out successfully if the brightness and clarity of the Goddess were restored to her. Therefore, they made a clamor with the clashing of bronze and a concert of trumpets and horns; according as she grew brighter or darker, they would either rejoice or mourn. And after rising clouds obstructed their sight, and it was believed she was buried in darkness—as minds once struck with terror are prone to superstition—they believed that eternal labor was portended for them, and that their own deeds...*

\* In rites of atonement, no metal was used as frequently as bronze, because the common people affirmed for certain that it was sufficient either to ward off the anger of the Gods or to cure any manner of evils. An ancient commentator on Theocritus, citing Apollodorus in his book *On the Gods*, observed that the excellence of bronze in early ages was so great that it was used for every holy consecration and purification <note>original Greek: πρὸς πᾶσαν ἀφοσίωσιν, καὶ ἀποκάθαρσιν; Latin: *ad omnem sanctiorem lustrationem*</note>. For the same reason, Pignorius thinks, in his exposition of the *Isiac Table*, that many vessels cast from bronze were believed sufficient either for the proper celebration of sacred rites or for engaging in battles under a more favorable omen.

### ON THE GERMANIC GODS.

<meta>Chapter</meta>

Thus far, we have discussed Isis, Erthus, and the Moon, who have been believed by certain writers of Germanic history to be distinct; yet our dissertation proves that they are one and the same divinity. For indeed, Venus, Urania, Vesta, Minerva, the Great Mother of the Gods, Astarte, Erthus, Isis, the Moon, Diana, Juno, Lucina, and Hecate are a single deity, identified by her various powers.

And this is so certain that, for this reason, that Isis was called *myrionymos* <note>original Greek: μυριώνυμος, meaning "of the myriad names"</note>. This is especially true since all the pagan divinities of the male gods are traced back to the one Sun, as Macrobius <note>A 5th-century Roman provincial official and author whose *Saturnalia* is a major source for ancient religious lore</note> maintains in the first book of his *Saturnalia*. Therefore, it is most fitting and justified that the divinities of the female sex be reduced to the one Moon. For so says Aristotle in his book *On the Universe* <note>original Greek: περὶ κόσμου (*peri kosmou*). Schedius provides the quote in both Greek and Latin: "Though he is one, he has many names, being named for all the effects that he himself brings about."</note>. Furthermore, more regarding the Moon, or the Celestial Goddess, may be seen in the works of Apuleius in *Florida* IV; Ammianus Marcellinus in book XXII; Capitolinus in his lives of *Pertinax and Macrinus*; Trebellius Pollio in *Celsus*; Salvian in chapter VIII of *On the Providence of God*; Saint Augustine in book II of *The City of God*, chapter IX; and Turnebus in *Adversaria*, book XXII, chapter XXIV.

---

* In the works of Gruter <note>Jan Gruter, a Flemish-Dutch classicist known for his massive collection of Roman inscriptions</note>, this inscription is read: **TO THEE, WHO ART THE ONE AND ALL, THE GODDESS ISIS**, etc. See also Gisbert Cuperus in *Harpocrates*, p. 11; Joannes Oliva, *Exercises on the Isiac Marble*, p. 28 and following; and Petrus Zornius, *Library of Antiquities and Exegesis*, Vol. I, p. 655.

<summary>Schedius argues for a syncretic view of ancient religion, asserting that various goddesses from Germanic, Roman, and Egyptian traditions are all manifestations of a single Moon goddess. He supports this by citing classical authorities like Macrobius and Aristotle who applied similar logic to male gods and the Sun.</summary>

### CHAPTER X.

*A true opinion on what has been written thus far. An analogy is derived from the Hebrew language. There was originally one single language. Hebrew was the first of all. Theodoret <note>A 5th-century influential theologian and bishop of Cyrrhus</note> is refuted. How widely the language once extended. By what means it migrated into various dialects. It remained uncorrupted only among the people of Abraham. The Punic language <note>The language of Carthage</note> was derived from Hebrew. The Punic column of the Phoenicians fleeing from Joshua <note>A reference to a legend mentioned by ancient historians like Procopius, claiming an inscription existed in Africa marking the flight of Canaanites from the biblical Joshua</note>. Different dialects in Canaan during the captivity. The Syrian language is a mixed one. The characters of the Chaldeans and Hebrews were once different. The error of Benjamin of Tudela <note>A 12th-century Jewish traveler</note> regarding the Samaritans is exposed. The Jews are enemies of the Samaritans. Ashima <note>A deity worshipped by the people of Hamath, mentioned in 2 Kings 17:30</note>. Daniel is instructed in the letters and language of the Chaldeans. Which script the Angel of the Lord used at the feast of Belshazzar. The sacred language was rejected by the pagans. The names of the vowel points are Chaldaic. Testimonies of the Rabbis. The change of letters detracts nothing from the authority of Scripture. Causes. From this language, as if from the first language, the analogy of the most ancient deities in Germany is to be derived. This analogy was not always accurately maintained in investigating the names of the Gods.*

Having now understood the origin and names of the Celtic <note>Schedius uses "Celtic" as a broad term encompassing the Germanic and northern European peoples</note> Gods, it is necessary that we also reveal the true opinion concerning them. For the first step of wisdom is to recognize what is false, as Lactantius <note>A 4th-century Christian author often called the "Christian Cicero"</note> reports. Therefore, before we affirm anything true about these matters and derive their origin from the Hebrew language, it seemed best to inquire into the very first language of all. For order demands and necessity commands that it be seen which language the ancients used, so that we may more conveniently reach our intended goal. For indeed, from this most ancient language are to be derived those deities which were proposed for worship to posterity by the ancient heroes. Then also, the division of languages and the genealogy of Tuysco <note>A legendary ancestor of the Germanic people mentioned in Tacitus's *Germania*</note> must be considered; for he was the first father of the Germans or Celts,

And first, there was a single language in the whole world. Therefore, Philastrius <note>A 4th-century bishop and writer on heresies</note> is rightly to be rejected in his **Catalogue of Heresies**, **chapter 106**, where he twists the words of Moses as follows: *Moses says the earth was of one lip because, although there were various kinds of languages, everyone nevertheless understood each other; and there was one language and the same speech for everyone, not indeed through the use of the same vocabulary, but through the same understanding shared by all speakers and listeners.* He was deceived by the figure of speech which the Greeks call *hysteron proteron* <note>A rhetorical device where what should come last is put first; literally "latter-former"</note>, which occurs very frequently in the Sacred Scriptures. However, since Moses defined nothing certain regarding this interpretation, we must stand on the side of the elders. 

And first, indeed, the etymology of names given to persons and things clearly teaches us that this language was the first. For it was from this language that names were imposed by Adam upon the animals according to the nature of each—a feature that occurs in no other language. The first father also called his spouse **Chava** <note>Eve</note>: <note>original Hebrew: "כי הוא היתה אם כל-חי"</note> *because she was the mother of all living,* namely, from the root *chayah*, meaning "she lived." The Eastern languages, however—dialects of Hebrew—were subsequently furnished with new words through commerce and the abundance of wars; these do not "taste of" Hebrew in the least, and they were corrupted by other harsh sounds of pronunciation. Time also not infrequently depraves a language. The Holy Scripture is witness in Genesis chapter 31, verse 47, that the Aramaic language had departed from the Hebrew. <note>In this Bible verse, Laban (an Aramean) and Jacob (a Hebrew) give different names to a stone heap, signifying the divergence of their languages.</note> Only about two hundred years, more or less, had passed from the departure of Abraham until the time of Jacob.

And Franciscus Junius <note>A significant Huguenot theologian and linguist (1545–1602) known for his work on Old Germanic languages and biblical philology.</note> writes in the preface to his *Grammar* that the Indic, Persian, Babylonian, Armenian, Syrian, and Arabic languages are most closely joined to Hebrew. This, however, is false. These things are said concerning the ancient Eastern Dialects, all of which are established to have flowed from the first Hebrew language. This language alone remained in the house of Abraham, even preserved untainted during the Egyptian captivity; just as Elias <note>Elias Levita (1469–1549), a prominent Renaissance Hebrew scholar and teacher to many Christian Hebraists.</note> reports in the preface to *The Translator* <note>original: *Methurgeman*, Levita’s influential dictionary of the Aramaic Targums.</note>: that the Israelites in Egypt changed these three things: their names, their clothes, and their language. Nevertheless, from its first origin, the language degenerated into various and different idioms. For this reason, Daniel did not understand Chaldean <note>A term often used historically for Aramaic.</note>, nor did the Jews understand the Aramaic language. And St. Jerome demonstrates this most excellently in his preface to the Book of Daniel:

> *When I was a young man, after the reading of Quintilian and Cicero and the flowers of Rhetoric, I had shut myself up in the treadmill* <note>term: *pistrinum*. Jerome uses this to describe the grueling, repetitive labor of learning a new language, comparing it to the mill where slaves were forced to grind grain.</note> *of the Hebrew language. With much sweat and over a long time, I had scarcely begun to sound out the gasping and strident words; it was as if I were walking through a dark crypt and saw only a rare light from above. Finally, I stumbled into the book of Daniel: and I was affected by such weariness that, in a sudden fit of despair, I wanted to despise all my old labor. But a certain Hebrew man encouraged me, frequently repeating to me in his own language that "relentless labor overcomes all things."* <note>original: *labor improbus omnia vincit*, a famous quote from Virgil’s *Georgics*.</note> *Thus, I who seemed to myself a bit of a scholar among the Hebrews, began once more to be a student of Chaldean. And to tell the truth, even to the present day I am better able to read and understand the Chaldean language than to speak it.*

lest anyone torment themselves too much, and demonstrate that it happened against the grain <note>original: *genio invito*, a Latin idiom meaning against one's natural inclination or will</note>, that Chaldean descends from Hebrew: and should adduce the words of Saint Jerome in Volume 5 of his *Commentary on Daniel*, Chapter 1: *“Philo thinks that the language of the Hebrews is itself Chaldean, because Abraham was from the Chaldeans. If we accept this, we must ask how it is that Hebrew boys are now ordered to be taught a language they already knew: unless perhaps, according to the opinion of some, we say that Abraham knew two languages, both that of the Hebrews and that of the Chaldeans.”* <note>St. Jerome (c. 347–420 AD) was the primary translator of the Vulgate Bible; here he grapples with why the youths in the Book of Daniel had to "learn" Chaldean if it was supposedly the same as their ancestral tongue.</note> Let one look at the idiom of the French <note>original: *Gallorum*, the Gauls</note>, which in that first century was Roman, imposed by the Romans upon the conquered, and see how far it differs from the Roman tongue; so much so that even one most skilled in the Roman language would not understand a Frenchman delivering a speech, not even by a single word. I pass over Spanish: which the resident Roman speech established, but once established, error, time, and native barbarism destroyed it. Truly, the more recent Syriac language is not that ancient one, but is a composite of Jewish, Chaldean, and Palestinian. And the Jerusalem Talmud, written around the year of Christ 230 by Rabbi Yochanan <note>Rabbi Yochanan bar Nappaḥa, a central figure in the compilation of the Palestinian or Jerusalem Talmud</note>, consists of a most impure style, which reeks of Jewish speech and various dialects of the Aramaic language; it also contains many Greek, Latin, Arabic, and barbarian words. I do not deny that they were different. For thus Saint Jerome says in his *Helmeted Prologue* <note>original: *prologo galeato*, the famous preface to the Books of Kings where Jerome defends his translation; he called it "helmeted" because it was meant to defend the work against critics</note>, which is placed before the books of Kings: *“That there are twenty-two letters among the Hebrews is also testified by the language of the Syrians and Chaldeans, which is for the most part closely related to Hebrew. For they also have twenty-two elements with the same sound, but with different characters.”* The Samaritans also habitually write the Pentateuch of Moses with the same number of letters, differing only in their shapes and flourishes <note>original: *apicibus*, referring to the small strokes or points that distinguish one script from another</note>. And it is certain that Ezra the scribe and teacher of the law—after the capture of Jerusalem and the Restoration of the temple under Zerubbabel—found other letters, which we use now <note>This refers to the "Square script" or *Ashuri*, which replaced the older Paleo-Hebrew script</note>, whereas until that time the letters of the Samaritans and Hebrews had been the same. Joseph Scaliger <note>A leading 16th-century scholar of history and chronology</note> writes the following in Book VII of *On the Emendation of Time*: *“The Samaritans read the Pentateuch in characters that are not corrupted, as those of the Jews are, but in the pure Mosaic characters, as was clearly reported by Postel, and as the matter itself speaks.”* Therefore, let the opinion of Benjamin of Tudela be dismissed, along with all those who agree with him, who writes: *The Samaritans lack three letters—Ayin, Het, and Yod <term>ע ח י</term>—as if they were struck from the names of the Patriarchs Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.* Therefore, they argue, the Pentateuch and other books of Scripture could not have been written in that character before Ezra. However, Saint Jerome testifies that this is false,

...who flourished long before him, as did Postel <note>Guillaume Postel (1510–1581) was a French polyglot and one of the first European scholars to study the Samaritan language.</note>, who published a complete Samaritan alphabet. For how sharply the Jews pursued the Samaritans after they returned from Babylonia is evident from the fact that a Jew was not permitted to eat bread with a Cuthite <note>Cuthite (Cuthæus) is a derogatory Jewish term for Samaritans, implying they were merely foreign settlers from the city of Cuthah.</note> or Samaritan, according to the proverb: *“He who eats Samaritan bread is just as if he eats the flesh of a pig.”*

...not only [the Earth] (as the common people of the Hebrews explain) but also all the knowledge in which these young men were trained by the Chaldeans. Symmachus <note>A 2nd-century translator of the Old Testament into Greek known for a more literal style than the Septuagint.</note> renders it thus in chapter 1, verse 17: **God gave them understanding and wisdom in all literature and wisdom** <note>original Greek: σύνεσιν καὶ φρόνησιν ἐν πάסῃ γραμματικῇ καὶ σοφίᾳ</note>. See also Rabbi Saadia <note>Saadia Gaon (882–942), a prominent Jewish philosopher and exegete.</note> and Abenezra <note>Abraham ibn Ezra (1089–1167), a celebrated Spanish Jewish scholar and biblical commentator.</note> on this passage, who translate "book" <note>original Hebrew: *sepher* (ספר)</note> as "writing" <note>original Hebrew: *ketav* (כתav)</note>.

And the letters indeed were in the Holy Language, but the words were in the Aramaic language* <note>original Hebrew: ויבא המלאך ויכתב לו על הקיר בששר נוכח מנורת המלך ואלה אשר כתב חשב שכר והפריש אבל האותיות היו לשון קדש והמכתב לשן ארמית</note>. 

Now, the Chaldean or Aramaic tongue was the native language of the King as well as the Magi; it would be absurd to suggest they did not know its letters if they had matched the Hebrew letters as they do in our own century. But those characters were the ancient Hebrew or Samaritan ones, which the Chaldeans had not learned. Indeed, Holy Scripture affirms that they could neither read the writing nor show the interpretation to the King. In this matter, Pererius <note>Benito Pereira (c. 1535–1610), a Jesuit scholar whose commentaries on Daniel were influential in the late Renaissance.</note> in Book VI of his *Commentary on Daniel* is clearly hallucinating <note>A scholarly idiom meaning he is profoundly mistaken.</note> against the text, for he claims that the Chaldeans could easily read that writing but were unable to extract a certain meaning from it. But this is done "against the grain" <note>original Latin: *invita Minerva*, a classical idiom meaning to act against one's natural ability or against common wisdom.</note>. For this writing was Hebrew, as Rabbi Saadia testifies in his commentary on chapter 5, verse 24 of Daniel: *[It was] in the Holy Scripture, and our wise men were not able to read it* <note>original Hebrew: בכתב הקדש ולא יכלו חכמנו לקרותו</note>.

Indeed, I do not deny that those points existed, but rather that the names of the points are Chaldean. For the Hebrew language can by no means subsist without points. [In chapter 10], he writes that the <term>shekel</term><note>The shekel was the standard unit of currency and weight in ancient Israel.</note> is equal to four Attic <term>drachmas</term><note>A silver coin of ancient Greece.</note>, which is to say one <term>stater</term><note>A "stater" simply means a "standard" coin; in the New Testament period, it was often used to refer to a four-drachma coin.</note>, or half an ounce. For this reason, **Symmachus** <note>An author of one of the Greek versions of the Old Testament (late 2nd century AD).</note> in this place uses the word "staters" <note>original Greek: στατῆρας (*stateras*)</note> instead of "shekels," as he is mostly accustomed to doing, as does **Aquila** <note>Another 2nd-century translator of the Hebrew Bible into Greek, known for his extreme literalism.</note> as well. And that this is the true weight of the silver shekel is demonstrated by the most ancient shekels, weighed on a most precise balance.

One of these was formerly given to me as a gift of friendship by a man most worthy of eternal memory—not only for his Hebrew printing and his excellent knowledge of that language, but especially for his singular integrity of mind and sincerity—**Daniel Bomberg** <note>Daniel Bomberg (died 1549) was a pioneering printer in Venice who produced the first "Rabbinic Bible" (*Mikraot Gedolot*), revolutionizing Hebrew scholarship.</note>. On the other face, where one sees that small vessel in which the **manna** was kept in the Ark, the inscription is: *Shekel of Israel* <note>original Hebrew: שקל ישראל (*Shekel Yisrael*)</note>. 

Furthermore, above that cup of manna, two letters are visible, **Shin** (ש) and **Mem** (מ), which I believe are an abbreviation for *King Solomon* <note>original Hebrew: שלמה מלך (*Shlomo Melekh*). Modern numismatists usually interpret these letters as dates, such as "Year 2."</note>. Such a coin, struck with the **Samaritan character** by the Jews themselves as well as by Masius <note>Andreas Masius (1514–1573), a Flemish priest and noted Hebraist and Syriac scholar.</note>, is cited by **Theodore Beza** <note>A major French Protestant theologian and successor to John Calvin.</note> in his *Major Annotations on the New Testament*, Part I, at Matthew chapter 17, verse 23, in these words:

"Of this coin—that is, the half silver stater, which when whole was four drachmas, such as the Jews themselves once stamped—we have [caused] a true image here..."

I have taken care to have an engraving made, *reproduced from a true coin of pure, bright silver, given to me by that faithful servant of Christ and man of blessed memory, Master Ambrosius Blaurer.* <note>Ambrose Blaurer (1492–1564) was an influential German reformer and contemporary of Schedius. The "pure silver" emphasizes the coin's authenticity.</note> This coin, marked with Samaritan letters, features on one side that sacred urn in which the Manna was stored <note>The "golden jar of manna" (Exodus 16:33) was kept in the Ark of the Covenant as a memorial of God's provision in the desert.</note>, with the letter *Aleph* placed above it. This indicates that it was a simple *Shekel* <note>original: *Siclus*</note>—specifically, one of two <term>drachmas</term>—whereas a double shekel would be four drachmas. It bears the inscription "Shekel of Israel" <note>original Hebrew: שקל ישראל (*Shekel Yisrael*)</note>. On the other side is that budding rod of Aaron <note>In the Book of Numbers, Aaron’s staff miraculously sprouted blossoms and almonds to prove his divine selection for the priesthood.</note>, with the inscription "Holy Jerusalem" <note>original Hebrew: ירושלים קדשה (*Yerushalayim Kedoshah*)</note>. So says the author. However, it is not believable that the Samaritans minted these coins, but rather the Judeans. The Samaritans detested Jerusalem; they would never have decorated a coin with such a venerable title for a city that was their greatest enemy. It is now clearer than sunlight that the character of the ancient Hebrews was different from the modern one. However, one should not conclude from this that the Holy Scripture was corrupted or depraved by Ezra and those scribes who transcribed the Old Testament <note>original: *V. Instrumentum*, referring to the *Vetus Instrumentum* or Old Testament.</note> into Chaldean characters <note>The "Chaldean characters" are the square Hebrew letters used today, which tradition says Ezra adopted during the Babylonian exile to replace the older "Samaritan-style" Paleo-Hebrew script.</note>. For they were **holy men of God** <note>original Greek: ἅγιοι Θεοῦ ἄνθρωποι (*hagioi Theou anthropoi*)</note>, gifted with divine **infallibility** <note>original Greek: ἀναμαρτησίᾳ (*anamartēsia*), meaning "freedom from error."</note> and privilege. Thus, they were entirely immune from any error in doctrine. Indeed, as stated in Ezra chapter 7, verse 6, he was **a scribe skilled in the Law of Moses** <note>original Hebrew: סופר מהיר בתורת משה (*sopher mahir be-torat Mosheh*)</note>. But it is not our intention to treat this question at greater length. Since it is more than sufficiently established that the **Hebrew** language was the first, and that our first parents spoke in this tongue and announced the true word of God, we shall derive **the names of the German Gods and their entire religion** from this source. We shall demonstrate that many **names of the Gods** which they—

...they used, were Hebrew, and that many sacred rites were sought from that source. For even the Greeks sought the naming of their Gods from grammar. Thus **Aphrodite** descends from *foam* <note>original: *aphros*. In Greek myth, Aphrodite was said to be born from the sea foam.</note>, **Hermes** from *interpreting* <note>original: *hermeneuein*. Hermes was the messenger god and the patron of communication.</note>, **Hades** from *voicelessness* <note>original: *audes*. This is a classical etymological play suggesting the silence of the dead.</note>, **Cronus** from *time* <note>original: *chronos*</note>, and **Zeus** from *living* <note>original: *zen*</note>, or from *boiling* <note>original: *zein*</note>. * The **Latins** derive **Sol** <note>The Sun</note> from *alone* <note>original: *solo*, as in "the only one of its kind"</note>, **Pomona** <note>Goddess of fruit trees</note> from *fruit* <note>original: *pomis*</note>, **Cluacina** <note>An epithet of Venus as "The Purifier"</note> from *cleansing* <note>original: *cluere*</note>, **Venus** from *coming* <note>original: *veniendo*</note>, **Trivia** <note>An epithet of Hecate or Diana</note> from *crossroads* <note>original: *triviis*</note>, and **Cinxia** <note>A goddess of marriage who presided over the ungirdling of the bride</note> from the *girdle* <note>original: *cingulo*</note>. But not all names proceed according to such rules of analogy. \*And each language has this unique trait\* (may the famous Taubmann grant me this from his own work, *The Pot of Gold*, act 1, scene 1) <note>Friedrich Taubmann (1565–1613) was a German philologist; *Aulularia* or *The Pot of Gold* is a play by Plautus on which Taubmann wrote a famous commentary.</note> \*that it breaks the rules of those masters—namely, the Grammarians—and runs out into a freer field: those who have taken offense at this as if it were a foreign thing deserve little credit from good writers.\* But to escape any criticism regarding this origin derived from Hebrew, we shall first speak of **Tuysco** <note>Schedius identifies "Tuysco" (the Germanic deity Tuisto) as a historical figure and descendant of Noah.</note>: we shall now demonstrate that he held the true worship of God, was instructed in the true religion by his grandfather **Noah**, and first used the Hebrew language; and that later, even in the confusion of tongues <note>A reference to the Tower of Babel</note>, he retained those names of the true God and transmitted that worship even to his descendants.

See **Ménage** <note>Gilles Ménage (1613–1692), a French scholar.</note> on Diogenes Laertius VII. 147, **Gataker** <note>Thomas Gataker (1574–1654), an English theologian and critic.</note> on Antoninus [Marcus Aurelius] IV. § 23 and V. § 27, and **Elsner** <note>Jakob Elsner (1692–1750), a Prussian theologian.</note> in *Sacred Observations* page 451.

## CHAPTER XI.

*The first age was free from heresies. Adam knew the mystery of the Holy Trinity. He displayed the character of Christianity. Seducing angels. From these, Giants were born. The father of the Germans. When the corruption of languages emerged. Not all men gathered for the building of the tower. Noah was still alive at that time. Neither Peleg nor Eber were participants. Nimrod was the instigator. Though language changed, among the Celts the proper names of God remained intact. The name Jehovah, the name of God, was known to Noah. The words Hesus, Belenus, and Tharamis <note>These are ancient Celtic/Gaulish deities: Hesus (associated with Mars or Mercury), Belenus (with Apollo), and Tharamis (with Jupiter/Thor).</note> are names of Gods. Samothes is the same as Tuyscon <note>Samothes was a legendary figure believed by some Renaissance historians to be the first king of Gaul and Britain.</note>. Ashkenaz is the sacred name for Tuyscon. Under Serug, idolatry began. Terah the statue-maker. Haran was the first to die before his father. Tuyscon retained the sacred rites of the fathers. The cause of longevity. His memory is celebrated by the Germans.*

### ON THE GERMAN GODS.

**Franciscus Junius** <note>Franciscus Junius the Younger (1591–1677) was a pioneer of Germanic philology who studied ancient Gothic and Anglo-Saxon texts.</note>, in the preface to his *Grammar*, writes that not only are the Indian, Persian, Babylonian, Armenian, Syrian, and Arabic languages most closely joined to **Hebrew**, but the **Gothic language** is as well. He notes that many proofs of this matter exist in the works of **Procopius**, **Agathias**, and **Jornandes** <note>Procopius, Agathias, and Jordanes (Jornandes) were late antique historians who wrote extensively about the Goths and other Germanic tribes.</note>. Furthermore, this dispersion of languages—which was the punishment for the pride and recklessness in building the Babylonian tower—was finally lifted by the miraculous outpouring of the **Holy Spirit** on the feast of **Pentecost**. Thus, those nations once scattered through a diversity of tongues were gathered back into the unity of faith by the gift of the Holy Spirit.

Indeed, I believe this **Tuysco** <note>Tuisco or Tuisto, the legendary ancestor of the Germanic peoples mentioned by the Roman historian Tacitus.</note> was also called **Samothes**, or by <term>apheresis<note>The linguistic process of dropping the first syllable of a word.</note></term> among the Romans, **Dis** <note>original: "Ditem"; referring to Dis Pater, the Roman god of the underworld from whom Julius Caesar claimed the Gauls believed they descended.</note>. If, however, anyone should think that he was called **Ashkenaz** <note>original: "אשכנז"</note> in the Sacred Scriptures—derived from *esh* <note>original: "אש"</note> meaning "fire," and *nezar* <note>original: "נזר"</note> meaning "he sprinkles," as if to say "sprinkled fire," as **Benedictus Arias Montanus** <note>A 16th-century Spanish orientalist and editor of the Antwerp Polyglot Bible.</note> maintains in his *Genealogy of Noah*—I do not object. For it accords with the timeline: if **Gomer** was born in the second year after the deluge and fathered **Ascanius** <note>Ashkenaz</note> in the year 1760 <note>This follows the Anno Mundi or "Year of the World" chronology common in the 17th century.</note>, everything coincides.

Yet, if someone else wishes to call him a son of **Noah**, given such great discord among sources and the rarity of Germanic writers, I leave the matter to their own judgment. Certainly, religion remained pure regarding the true God until the division of languages under **Serug** and **Peleg** <note>Biblical patriarchs during whose lifetimes the dispersion of humanity was said to have occurred.</note>; the division of tongues took place in the twenty-third year of this Serug. Thereafter, following Serug, **idolatry** first began to exist among men, as **Epiphanius** <note>A 4th-century Church Father known for his "Panarion," a treatise against heresies.</note> writes.*

Finally, understanding and considering that Tuysco <note>Tuysco, or Tuisco, was regarded by early modern scholars—following the Roman historian Tacitus—as the earth-born founder of the Germanic people.</note> himself, the father of the Germans and Sarmatians <note>The Sarmatians were a confederation of Iranian peoples whom Schedius here groups with the Germanic tribes.</note>, realized that without justice and the fear of religion, the state could not flourish nor could the license of men be restrained, he gave rights and laws. For He shares other titles with the Angels and men; but He claims one most excellent name for Himself, consisting of four elements or letters <note>The Tetragrammaton, יהוה (YHVH).</note>, the pronunciation of which has remained unknown from the reading of books until now*, because it does not exist written with its own vowels or points by which it should be uttered. That name is the sublime and most holy יהוה <note>The Tetragrammaton, often rendered as YHVH or Yahweh.</note>, which must be observed by men with great reverence; in its place we often say אדני <note>Adonai, meaning "My Lord."</note>, and sometimes אלהים <note>Elohim, meaning "God."</note>. ...out of a certain zeal, they abstained from its pronunciation, * lest daily use should lead to it being taken in vain. Moreover, it was called the *name of four letters* <note>original Hebrew: שם בן ארבע אותיות (Shem ben Arba Otiyot)</note>. For it consists of the four letters יהוה <note>YHVH</note>, from which it is also called the *Tetragrammaton* <note>original Greek: τετραγράμματον; meaning "four-lettered"</note> by the Greeks. It is also called *The Name* <note>original Hebrew: השם (HaShem)</note>. They prove this from that passage in *Leviticus* [24:11]: *and the son of that Israelite woman blasphemed the Name* <note>original Hebrew: ויקב בן־האשה הישראלית את־השם (va-yikov ben-ha-ishah ha-yisre'elit et-ha-Shem)</note>. Which *Jonathan* <note>Referring to the Targum Pseudo-Jonathan, an Aramaic translation/paraphrase of the Torah</note> renders as *the great and glorious name* <note>original Aramaic: שמא רבא ויקירא (Shema Raba ve-Yakira)</note>. The *Jerusalem Targum* <note>An ancient Aramaic translation of the Hebrew Bible</note> calls it *the explicit name* <note>original Aramaic: שמא מפרשא (Shem HaMephorash)</note>. They therefore abstained from the pronunciation of this name and read in its place *Adonai* <note>original Hebrew: אדני; "My Lord"</note>, whose vowel points were added to the letters יהוה <note>YHVH</note>, with a simple *sheva* <note>a Hebrew vowel sign indicating a very short "e" sound or a break</note> placed instead of a *chateph-patach* <note>a composite vowel sign used for certain phonetic reasons in Hebrew</note>. 

However, when *Adonai* precedes it, *Elohim* <note>original Hebrew: אלהים; "God"</note> is substituted; for otherwise, one would have to read "Adonai, Adonai" twice. And that this is true is clear from the Elders <note>The seventy translators of the Septuagint</note>, who, before the birth of Christ, explained this word יהוה <note>YHVH</note> as *Lord* <note>original Greek: κύριος (Kyrios)</note>, just as the Hebrews did with *Adonai*. Likewise, the Latin translators rendered it as *Lord* <note>original Latin: Dominus</note>. 

The primary reverence for this name among the Jews soon turned—as almost everything does—into superstition. Pronunciation of it was forbidden to the common people under penalty of death; the high priests pronounced it in the temple at Jerusalem, nowhere else and only once a year, during that solemn blessing of the people (Numbers 6, verses 24–25) on the feast of expiation <note>Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement</note>. But as superstition easily spreads, so here too it soon grew even further.

> "To the Jews it is 'ineffable' because, as Rabbi Moses of Egypt <note>The medieval philosopher Maimonides</note> indicates, the rank of this name is sublime, for it denotes the very essence of God. And I believe it is called 'ineffable' not because it cannot or should not be spoken, but because it is sacrosanct. For this reason, it should not be taken up by the mouths of men or in writing for profane matters; just as among us Christians, it is considered a sin to bestow the name of Jesus Christ upon any man, so they abstained out of reverence for God, lest that name become common through frequent use." Thus he wrote.

From this it also appears that the word *Tav* <note>The final letter of the Hebrew alphabet, תו</note> was substituted for the <term>Tetragrammaton</term> <note>The four-letter Name of God, YHWH</note>. Indeed, this small word is used for "Jehovah" in the sacred scriptures, such as in Job 31:35: *Behold my sign, the Almighty* <note>original Hebrew: הן תוי שדי (Hen Tavi Shaddai). However, a single God was worshiped by the Celts, who was called "Theutates" by their descendants, though he was first called "Thau." For they did not establish more than one God. 

And if we look more closely, we will find that other nations also established one God. Indeed, **Orpheus**—whom **Justin Martyr** in his *Oration against the Nations* identifies as the first author of a plurality of divinities—writes quite excellently about God in his <term>Palinodia</term> <note>A poem in which the author retracts a previous sentiment; here, Orpheus supposedly retracts polytheism in favor of one God</note>:

> *He is one, self-begotten, and from this one all things have been made.*
> *He is present within them, and no mortal*
> *sees Him, yet He sees all.*
> <note>original Greek: Εἷς δ’ ἔϛ’ αὐτογενὴς, ἑνὸς ἔκγονα πάντα τέτυκται, Ἐν δ’ αὐτοῖς αὐτὸς περιγίγνεται, οὐδέτις αὐτὸν Εἰσοράει θνητῶν, αὐτὸς δὲ γε πάντας ὁρᾶται.</note>

And elsewhere:

> *Zeus was first, Zeus is last, the wielder of the thunderbolt,*
> *Zeus is the head, Zeus the middle, from Zeus all things are made.*
> *Zeus is the foundation of the earth and the starry heaven.*

**Iamblichus** <note>A Syrian Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) who emphasized the use of ritual and the soul's ascent to the Divine.</note> in *The Mysteries*, chapter 1: 

> “The essential knowledge of divine things, which is perpetual to the soul, is not truly 'knowledge' in the usual sense, because we enjoy God. > “...incomprehensible, incomparable, uniform, who far surpasses all causes, and who created that substance of the Gods in which some appearance of good is seen. **Alexander of Aphrodisias**, in his work *On Providence* addressed to Antoninus, left this for memory: *that one God provides for all; that He is capable of whatever He wills.* <note>Alexander of Aphrodisias was a celebrated commentator on Aristotle (c. 200 AD) who sought to reconcile Aristotelian thought with the concept of divine care.</note> **Theophrastus** treats this same subject in an entire book in his work *On Flavors*. This fragment completes the description of the Divine essence from the previous page.</note> Likewise, in Book II: *A city or a house cannot endure for even a tiny amount of time without someone to manage and care for it. Could such a great and beautiful construction as the world be managed so disorderly, by chance and as it happens, without a governor?* <note>original Greek: "πόλιν μὲν ἢ οἶκον μὴ δύνασθαι διαμένειν, μηδ’ ὀλιγοστὸν χρόνον, δίχα τοῦ διοικοῦντος καὶ ἐπιμελεμένου. τὸ δ’ οὕτω μέγα καὶ καλὸν κατασκεύασμα, εἰκῆ καὶ ὡς ἔτυχεν οὕτως ἀτάκτως οἰκονομεῖσθαι, ἐστὶν ἄνευ τοῦ διοικοῦντος." This is a common argument from design: complexity implies a designer.</note> That is to say: a city or a house cannot stand for even a moment or a point in time without management and a governor; and could this world, endowed with such great breadth and magnitude, be administered by chance and accident, with no order? There is, therefore, some governor of it.

**Pythagoras**, moreover, speaks thus according to **Cyril**: *God is one, not—as most people think—removed from the administration of the world, but entirely within the whole. The "torch of heaven" refers to God as the source of all celestial light and order.</note>

**Philolaus**, the disciple of Pythagoras, says: *God is one, the prince of the universe, who always is: singular, unmoving, and like unto Himself.*

**Archytas**: *God is the beginning, the end, and the middle of all things that are accomplished according to justice and right reason.* <note>original Greek: "ὁ Θεὸς ἀρχή τε καὶ τέλος καὶ μέσον ἐστὶν τῶν μετὰ δίκαν τέ καὶ τὸν ὀρθὸν λόγον περαινομένων." Archytas was a Greek philosopher and mathematician who believed that divine harmony governed both the stars and human law.</note>

**Hierocles** writes that He was called *Zena* and *Dia*, because through Him all things exist and live. <note>Hierocles of Alexandria was a Neoplatonist. He uses Greek etymology here: the name "Zena" (Zeus) sounds like the verb *zen* (to live), and "Dia" (the accusative form of Zeus) is identical to the word for "through." Thus, God is He "through" whom we "live."</note>

**Alcyphron**: *God does not grant a long time for living; do not let it slip away by wasting it on riddles and nonsense.* <note>original Greek: "οὐ μακρὸν δίδωσιν ὁ δαίμων χρόνον τοῦ ζῆν, μὴ λάθης τοῦτον εἰς αἰνίγματα καὶ λήρους ἀναλώσας."</note>

**Synesius**, in his book *On Dreams*: *Faith in God is the best guardian when something is entrusted according to God's will.* <note>Synesius was a philosopher-bishop who combined Neoplatonism with Christianity.</note>

Every span of life is as nothing, as is the present moment. But that which occurred thirty years ago is like the evening, and not the morning. <note>original Greek: πᾶν βίου διάστημα τὸ μηδέν ἐστι, καὶ τὸ νῦν. ἀλλὰ μὴ πρὸ ἐτῶν τριάκοντα, τοιοῦτόν ἐστι, οἷον τὸ δείλης, ἀλλὰ μὴ πρωὶ</note> *That is, in the eyes of God, the entire span of human life, and even the present moment, is nothing; for thirty years in His sight are like the twilight, if not merely a morning hour.* <note>original Latin: id est, apud Deum enim universæ humanæ spacium vitæ, atque adeo præsens momentum nihil est: cum anni triginta, in illius conspectu veluti crepusculum, ne dicam hora sint matutina.</note>

**Also:** God is certainly not ignorant of the disposition and nature of each person, being by nature more capable of perceiving the soul than the body. <note>original Greek: ὁ Θεὸς οὐκ ἀγνοεῖ δήπου, τὴν ἑκάστου διάθεσιν καὶ φύσιν, ὅ, τε δὴ ψυχῆς μᾶλλον ἢ σώματος αἰσθάνεσθαι πεφυκώς</note> *That is, God does not ignore the feelings and nature of anyone, since He exists as the examiner of the soul more than the body.* <note>original Latin: id est, Deus uniuscujusque affectum ac naturam haud ignorat, utpote qui magis animæ, quam corporis, scrutator existit.</note> In the book *To an Uneducated Ruler*. <note>Plutarch’s essay *Ad principem indoctum* argues that a ruler must first be a subject of reason and divine law.</note>

Justice is the goal of the law, the law is the work of the ruler, and the ruler is the image of God who orders all things. <note>original Greek: δίκη μὲν νόμου τέλος ἐστὶν, νόμος δὲ ἄρχοντος ἔργον, ἄρχων καὶ εἰκὼν Θεοῦ τοῦ πάντα κοσμῶντος</note> *That is, Justice is indeed the end of the law, while the law is the ruler's work, and the ruler is the likeness of God who administers the whole universe.* <note>original Latin: id est, Iustitia quidem legis est finis, lex autem principis opus, princeps vero Dei simulacrum, administrantis universa.</note>

In the book *On Exile*: <note>referring to Plutarch’s *De fuga*</note>
God is the one King and Ruler, holding the beginning, the middle, and the end of the universe. <note>original Greek: εἷς καὶ βασιλεὺς καὶ ἄρχων Θεὸς, ἀρχήν τε καὶ μέσα καὶ τελευτὴν ἔχων τοῦ παντὸς</note> *That is, there is one King and Prince, which is God, who holds the beginning, the middle, and the end of all things.* <note>original Latin: id est, unus autem Rex, & princeps Deus est, principium, medium ac finem universi tenens.</note>

Book 1 of *The Opinions of the Philosophers*: <note>A work traditionally attributed to Plutarch, though now often assigned to Aetius, summarizing various schools of thought.</note>
God is Mind, a separate form—that is, unmixed with any matter and not entangled with any passive thing. <note>original Greek: νοῦς ὁ Θεὸς, χωριστὸν εἶδος, τουτέστι τὸ ἀμιγὲς πάσης ὕλης, μηδενὶ παθητῷ συμπεπλεγμένον</note> *That is, God is Mind, a certain detached form, meaning He is mixed with no matter whatsoever and joined to no subject capable of suffering.* <note>original Latin: id est, Deus mens est, abjuncta quædam forma, id est, nulli omnino materiæ mixta, nulli patibili rei coalita. The term "passive" or "subject capable of suffering" refers to the philosophical concept of *impassibility*—that God cannot be changed or harmed by external forces.</note>

**Philostratus** in his life of *Scopelianus*: <note>Philostratus was a 3rd-century author known for his biographies of sophists and orators.</note>
Men are the playthings not only of God, but also of one another. <note>original Greek: οἱ ἄνθρωποι μὴ Θεοῦ μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἀλλήλων παίγνια</note> *That is, humans are a source of sport not just for God, but one for another.* <note>original Latin: id est, homines non Dei solum, sed etiam sibi invicem alter alteri sunt in ludibrium.</note>

**Lucian** in *The Philopatris*: <note>Lucian of Samosata was a 2nd-century satirist. *The Philopatris* is a dialogue that discusses religious and political themes.</note>
God brought man from non-existence into being, and He is in heaven watching both the just and the unjust, recording their deeds in books... <note>original Greek: ἄνθρωπον ἐκ μὴ ὄντων Θεὸς ἐς τὸ εἶναι παρήγαγε, καὶ ἔστιν ἐν οὐρανῷ βλέπων δικαίους τε κ' ἀδίκους, καὶ ἐν βίβλοις τὰς πράξεις ἀπογραφόμενος ἀν-</note> *That is, God brought man from non-existence into existence, and He is in heaven looking upon the righteous and the unrighteous, recording their actions in books...* <note>original Latin: id est, hominem ex non entibus Deus ad esse produxit, & est in coelo intuens iustos & iniustos, atque in libris facta annotans...</note>

*...and He contemplates the seas; He protects the interests and lives of men. What can be so open and so clear, once we have looked up at the sky and contemplated the celestial bodies, than that there is some divine power <note>original Latin: *numen*</note> of a most excellent mind, by whom these things are ruled?* <note>Schedius is quoting Marcus Tullius Cicero, the Roman statesman and philosopher, from his work *On the Nature of the Gods* (*De Natura Deorum*).</note> *The same author says: we see that the advantages we use, the light we enjoy, and the breath we draw, are given and imparted to us by God. Rightly, therefore, did* Varro say, as quoted by Augustine in *The City of God*, Book IV, Chapter IX...
