<header>### ON THE GERMAN GODS.</header>

The teachers of the Gentiles <note>non-Christians or heathens</note>, although they named many Gods and Goddesses, intended them all to be understood as being contained within one Jove <note>original: *Jove*, the name for Jupiter, the supreme Roman deity</note>. They held that those various gods and goddesses were merely His powers and duties; however, they specifically worshipped Jove as the one who was venerated as the one God without statues and idols—which must be regarded as the true worship of the true God. See also Irenaeus <note>Saint Irenaeus (c. 130–202 AD), a Greek bishop and theologian.</note>, Book III, Chapter 41, and Lactantius <note>Lactantius (c. 250–325 AD), an early Christian author who often used pagan sources to argue for Christian truths.</note>, Book VII, Chapter 22. Although the Poets have partially corrupted the hidden secrets of the truth, the matter itself is found to be more true because they agree with the Prophets; this is sufficient proof of the matter for us. The greatest of the Sibyls <note>The Sibyls were prophetesses in the ancient world; early Christian writers often cited the "Sibylline Oracles" as pagan prophecies of the one God.</note> produced these verses:

> He alone is God the creator, existing as the uncontainable,
> ->He Himself fixed the forms and shapes of men,<-
> He Himself mixed the nature of all life's generation.
> <note>Original Greek: *Ὁ μόνος ἐστὶ Θεὸς κτιστὴς...* / Original Latin translation: *Vnus est Deus creator...*</note>

And also these verses:

> But God is the only one, far the most excellent, who
> ->made<-
> Heaven, and the Sun, and the stars, and the moon,
> The fruit-bearing earth, and the surges of the flowing
> ->sea.<-
> <note>Original Greek: *Ἀλλὰ Θεὸς μόνος εἷς...* / Original Latin translation: *Sed Deus unus est...*</note>

What does he mean when he says, *I swear by the first Voice of the Father, which he brought forth from his mouth*? <note>original Latin: "Vocem juro Patris, primam, quam prodidit ore."</note> Here he uses the term "Audēn" <note>original Greek: Αὐδὴν</note>, that is, "Voice," to name the "Logos" <note>original Greek: λόγον</note>—the Word of God. It is through this Word that heaven, earth, and every living creature were established, just as the divine prophecies of holy men teach us. These were things that the poet himself understood, in part, while applying himself to his studies in Egypt: that every creature was made by the Word of God. Accordingly, where he says:

> *I swear by the first Voice of the Father which he brought forth from his mouth.*

He joins those words to these:

> *When he himself established the whole world by his counsel.* <note>original Latin: "Consilio ipse mundum cum conderet omnem."</note>

In this context, he uses the term "Voice" instead of "Word" to accommodate the poetic meter of the song. <note>The "meter" refers to the rhythmic structure of the verse; the author argues the choice of words was based on the "beat" of the poetry rather than a different theological meaning.</note> That this is the case is quite clear from what he said shortly before; for when the meter of the song permitted it, he did indeed use the name "Word." For he says:

> *Looking toward the divine Word, attend to this always,* <note>original Greek: Εἰς δὲ λόγον θεῖον βλέψας, τώτῳ προσέδρευε</note>
> *Directing the intellectual vessel of the heart, and rightly follow* <note>original Greek: Ἰθύνων κραδίης νοερὸν κύτος, εὖ δ᾽ ἐπίβαινε</note>
> *The path; look only upon the immortal Maker of the World,* <note>original Greek: Ἀτρεπὸ, μῦνον δ᾽ ἐσόρα κόσμοιο τυπώτην / Ἀθάνατον</note>
> *Whom the ancient word declares.* <note>original Greek: παλαιὸς δὲ λόγος περὶ ὧ δὲ φαείνει</note>
> *That he is perfect, etc.* <note>original Greek: Ὡς ἔς᾽ αὐτοτελὴς, &c.</note>

> *Looking toward the Word of God, be present with it always*
> *Fixing the intellectual vessel of the heart, and stand upright on the*
> *Path; look only upon the immortal Former of the World,*
> *Whom the ancient discourse declares.*
> *That he is perfect.* <note>This is the author's Latin translation of the preceding Greek verses, here rendered into English.</note>

...letters; they may be read indeed, but not understood. All things are centered around the King of the Universe <note>original: "Regem Vniversi"; a reference to Plato's *Second Letter* 312e</note>; all things exist because of Him and for His sake, and He is the cause of all things that are seen as beautiful. Furthermore, around the Second are the second things, and around the Third are the third things, etc.

*Numenius in his book On the Good:* <note>Numenius of Apamea was a 2nd-century philosopher who bridged the gap between Platonism and Pythagoreanism; he is famous for calling Plato "Moses speaking Attic Greek."</note>
Whoever desires to know the First and Second God must first distinguish them correctly, and above all, must quiet his mind; then, having called upon the name of God, he may bring forth the treasure of his thoughts. Let us begin in this manner: I say that the First God, who exists within Himself, is simple; He is consistent with Himself in every way, being one within Himself and never divided. The Second and Third God are also one. We must think of the Father as being the First of him who is called the Creator <term>Creator: original 'opifex', referring to the Platonic Demiurge or craftsman who shapes the material world</term> of all things.

*Plotinus, Ennead V, Book 1:* <note>Plotinus (3rd century) was the founder of Neoplatonism. Schedius here summarizes his core doctrine of the "Three Hypostases."</note>
There are three primary hypostases <term>hypostases: the underlying substances or distinct levels of divine reality</term>: the One or the Good, Mind or Intellect, and the World Soul. One should not speak of these things without first imploring God's help and with a settled mind. If you ask by what means one generates the other, we are dealing here with eternal matters. Therefore, no one should imagine a temporal birth here. For when we speak of "generation," we are considering only the cause and the logical order.

*Ennead V, Book 8, Chapter 5:*
What benefit shall he gain who has contemplated God? Truly, that he has seen God begetting the Son <note>Schedius uses the term "Filium" (Son) to translate Plotinus's concept of the Divine Mind (Nous), making the text sound more compatible with Christian theology.</note>, and in the Son, all things. And he has seen that Son, once conceived, holding all things without effort, even though this world, which pleases us so much, is but his image.

*Ennead VI, Book 13, Chapter 27:*
God is at once both the Beloved and Love itself. Moreover, this love is a love of self. For He is beautiful in Himself and by Himself. But as for the statement that He is said to coexist entirely with Himself, this cannot take place,

...unless that which exists and that which coexists are entirely one and the same. If, however, that which coexists and that to which it coexists are one, and likewise that which desires and that which is desired are one: then surely Desire and Essence will be one and the same. *Iamblichus in his book On the Mysteries, chapter 39,* <note>Iamblichus (c. 245–325 AD) was a Syrian Neoplatonist who emphasized theurgy, or ritual, as a way to reach the divine.</note> writes thus: **The First God exists before being, and is alone; He is the father of the first God, whom He begets while remaining in His own solitary unity, and this is "beyond the intelligible." He is His own exemplar, and is called the father of Himself, the son of Himself, the one father and the truly good God.** For He is greater and first, the source of all things and the root of those things which are first understood and which themselves understand—namely, the Ideas. From this One, the self-sufficient God unfolded Himself. Therefore, He is called self-sufficient of Himself, the father, and the self-ruling prince. *Porphyry, explaining Plato’s Letter to Dionysius as cited by Cyril in Book I of Against Julian, says:* <note>Porphyry was a student of Plotinus; Cyril of Alexandria, a prominent Christian bishop, cited Porphyry's commentary on Plato to argue that pagans had a partial understanding of the Trinity.</note> **The Essence of God extends to three Hypostases or substances. For there is the supreme God, who is properly called the Good; after Him is the second, who is the Maker of the Universe; and finally the Third, the Soul of the World; for divinity is extended even to the soul.** <term>Maker of the Universe: original 'Opifex Vniversi', the craftsman or Demiurge; Soul of the World: 'Anima mundi', the spirit that animates the physical cosmos</term> This is what Plato intended when he established three "Kings": for although all things depend on these three, they depend on them in such a way that the first depends on the First, then the second on Him who is from the First, and thirdly on the third who proceeds from the second, in that order. *Proclus in his book On the Patriarchs:* <note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was a late Neoplatonist who attempted to synthesize all previous Greek philosophy into a single system.</note> For he teaches that the Intellect is indeed eternal, but there is a certain "pre-eternal" <note>original: προαιώνιον (*proaiōnion*)</note> one to whom it adheres, because that Pre-eternal one is beyond all things. For in the eternal Essence, there is a Second and a Third, and between the Pre-eternal and the eternal, Eternity sits as the middle. *Amelius, a most fierce enemy of the Christian name:* <note>Amelius was a student of Plotinus who was known for acknowledging the similarity between the opening of the Gospel of John and Platonic philosophy.</note>

Chalcidius <note>A 4th-century philosopher known for his Latin translation and commentary on Plato’s "Timaeus," which was the primary source of Platonic thought in the West for centuries.</note> writes as follows in his commentary on Plato’s *Timaeus*: *The origin of things, from which substance is provided for all other things that exist, is the highest and ineffable God. <note>original Greek: "τοῦτο ταῖς Περσῶν ἱερατικαῖς ἐμφέρεται φήμαις, καὶ εἰσέτι Μάγοι τὰ Μνημόσυνα τοῦ Τριπλασίου Μίθρου τελοῦσιν."</note>

...oath, which is recounted in the *Golden Verses* of Pythagoras:

I do not know for certain what he means by the **Tetractys** <note>The *Tetractys* is a mystical symbol consisting of ten points arranged in a triangle, which the Pythagoreans believed explained the organization of the universe.</note>. *Pythagoras met with the Prophets of the Egyptians, for whose sake he was even circumcised, so that by entering their inner sanctuaries <note>Latin: adyta</note> he might learn the mystical philosophy of the Egyptians; he also associated with the most excellent of the Chaldeans and the Magi. And that which is now called the **Church** is signified by that which, in his own system, is the **gathering of listeners** <note>original Greek: ὁμακοεῖον (homakoeion), the communal school or assembly of Pythagoras’s followers</note>.*

And in Book V of the *Stromata* <note>A work by Clement of Alexandria, c. 150–215 AD, titled "Miscellanies"</note>: "Pythagoras, Socrates, and Plato, in saying that they heard the voice of God, all contemplated the condition of the universe as being accurately made by God, and held together by Him without end." For they heard Moses saying: *He spoke and they were made* <note>original Latin: "dixit & facta sunt." A reference to the creation narrative and Psalm 33:9</note>, describing the world as the work of God.

St. Ambrose, in Book I, Letter VI: "For since Pythagoras is thought by many to have drawn his lineage from the people of the Jews, he also derived the precepts of his mastery from their discipline." See Numenius <note>A 2nd-century philosopher who famously asked, "What is Plato but Moses speaking Attic Greek?"</note> as cited in Origen’s first book of *Against Celsus*.

Furthermore, the **mystical name of four letters** is that which surrounded those who alone entered the inner sanctuary. What makes the power of the **number four** <note>Latin: quaternarii numeri</note> so admirable is primarily that, by a silent consensus, almost all nations express the principal name of God with only four letters; this is a fact that does not seem possible without a more divine inspiration.

For what we now call **God** <note>Latin: Deum</note>, the Egyptians call **Theut** <note>Thoth</note>; the Persians say **Sire**; the discipline of the Magi says **Orsi**, from which **Oromasis** <note>The Greek form of Ahura Mazda, the supreme deity in Zoroastrianism</note> originated. Now, among the Hebrew people, the sacred name of God consisting of four letters is famous, which for that reason they call the **Tetragrammaton**; it is also expressed by another word, which is **Adonai**, though among them it is written **Adni** <note>Refers to the Hebrew consonants Aleph-Dalet-Nun-Yod (אדני)</note>, and it means **Our Lord**. Among the Greeks, however, He is called **Theos** <note>original Greek: Θεὸς</note>.

To the ancient Germans He was **Diet** <note>original: "Diet," an old Germanic term for "the people" or "the folk," here used to imply a national deity</note>, to the more recent ones **Gott**, to the Arabs **Allah**; however, we received the saving name of Jesus from the Angel. Nor was the knowledge of the Tetragrammaton hidden from the Sibyl <note>The Sibyls were legendary prophetesses in the ancient world whose oracles were often cited by early Christian writers to prove that pagans had foreknowledge of monotheism</note>. *To the Moors, by their own will, Juba is God.* <note>original: "Juba Mauris volentibus Deus est." Juba was a common name for Numidian and Mauretanian kings, here linked by the author to a divine origin.</note> Indeed, if you contract the elements <note>letters or sounds</note> slightly, the name **Juba** will result from **Jehovah** <note>Hebrew: יהוה</note>. For the idiom of the Phoenicians or Moors was forged from the Hebrew language. Traces of this appear most clearly in the *Poenulus* of **Plautus** <note>A Roman comedy containing rare passages of the Punic (Carthaginian) language, which is closely related to Hebrew.</note>. For that word *Avo* <note>a Punic greeting</note> used by Hanno descends from the Hebrew *Adon* <note>אדון, meaning "Lord"</note>; and his *Donni* <note>my lord</note> is from the Hebrew *Adon* <note>אדן</note> by means of **apheresis** <term>apheresis: the loss of a letter or sound from the beginning of a word</term>; and their *Souffetes* <note>the chief magistrates of Carthage</note> or Judges comes from the Hebrew *Shofetim* <note>שופטים</note>; and *Elsa* <note>the name Elissa, another name for Dido</note> from *El* <note>אל, "God"</note> and *Asher* <note>עשר, "blessed"</note>; and *Ditho* <note>Dido</note> from *Dod* <note>דוד, "beloved"</note>.

Furthermore, the **Iao** <note>Ἰαὼ</note> and **Ieuo** <note>Ἰευὼ</note> of the Greeks descend from this name, as is evident from **Diodorus Siculus** (Book I), **Clement of Alexandria** (*Stromata*, Book V), **Eusebius** (*Apodixis*, Book IV), and **Theodoret** (Question 15 on Exodus). See also **Philo of Byblos**, who reports that **Sanchoniathon** <note>An ancient Phoenician author whose works are lost but were summarized by Philo of Byblos; he was said to have written about Jewish history around the time of the Trojan War</note> wrote on Jewish affairs during the time of the Trojans: "having received memoirs from **Jerombalus**, the priest of the god **Ieuo**" <note>original Greek: εἱληφότα ὑπομνήματα παρὰ Ἱερομβάλου τοῦ ἱερέως θεοῦ τοῦ Ἰευὼ</note>. If you contract this name and apply a Latin termination, it will become **Jovis** <note>The genitive form of Jupiter, used here to suggest the Roman god's name is a derivative of the Hebrew Jehovah.</note> *.

Hence Saint Paul, in Acts chapter 17, verse 28, says: "as even some of your own poets have said, 'for we are also his offspring'" <note>original Greek: ὡς καί τινες τῶν καθ᾽ ὑμᾶς ποιητῶν εἰρήκασι, τοῦ γὰρ καὶ γένος ἐσμέν.</note>. This verse ** belongs to **Aratus**, in his *Phaenomena* <note>Aratus was a Greek poet whose work on astronomy was widely read; Paul quotes him during his sermon at the Areopagus in Athens to show that even pagan poets recognized a supreme creator.</note>...

But because in all sacrifices and prayers the divine fathers were called upon, the name of *Jove* <note>Iovis</note> took on the word for "father," having been derived from the word *Iewo* or *Iao* <note>Schedius is asserting that the Roman name for the god Jove (Iovis) is actually a linguistic corruption of the Hebrew name for God, Yahweh (Jehovah).</note>, and from this it became *Jovispater*; from there it passed into *Jupiter*. For *Jupiter* was not so named as if he were the "Helping Father" <note>original: "Iuvans pater"</note>, as Lactantius <note>An early Christian apologist (c. 250 – c. 325 AD).</note> (Book I, Chapter 11), Gellius <note>Aulus Gellius, a 2nd-century Roman grammarian.</note> (Book V, Chapter 12), Cicero, and Cato (in *On Agriculture*, Chapter 141) would have it, but rather from *Iewo*. From this also comes *Jupiter Sabazius* or *Liber Sebadius*, as Macrobius <note>A 5th-century Roman writer.</note> writes in *Saturnalia* (Book I, Chapter 18), derived from *Jehovah Sabaoth* <note>original: "Iehova Sabaoth"; "Sabaoth" is the Hebrew term for "Hosts" or "Armies," a title for God.</note>.

...to employ superstition. But this cannot be achieved without the invention of fables and illusions. For, as Synesius <note>Synesius of Cyrene (c. 373–414 AD), a philosopher-bishop who struggled with the tension between Neoplatonism and Christianity.</note> says in his *Praise of Baldness* <note>original: *Encomium Calvitii*</note>: "the common people will mock what is easiest [to understand]. Just as it happens with coals, which are easily ignited by torches moved near them—if I may use the words of Synesius of Cyrene <note>A Neo-Platonist philosopher and later Bishop of Ptolemais.</note> from Book I of *On Providence* <note>original: *De Providentia*</note>—because they are already predisposed to catch fire: so is the nature of the Demon. Since his nature teems with passions—or rather, is a kind of living passion possessing the power of movement—when he approaches the soul, he stirs up the passion already within it and brings that potential into action. For whatever he does, he does by making an impression. 

Whatever receives an action becomes similar to that which affects it. Thus, demons kindle lust, anger, and whatever evils are innate to these in our souls through their habitual presence, acting through those parts of us that are compatible with them. These parts naturally feel the demons' presence, and when they are agitated by them, they are strengthened to rise up against the mind, until they either subjugate the whole soul or despair of conquering it. This battle is the greatest of all; for they never cease to attack at any time, in any way, or in any place—and from where one would least expect it, from that side they assault... <note>The text cuts off here at the word "assault" (original: *adoriuntur*), as indicated by the catchword "riun-" on the bottom of the page.</note>

...writes these things in the *Parashah* <note>The weekly portion of the Torah read in Jewish liturgy.</note> *Shemini* <note>original: שמיני</note>: in "man" <note>original: איש (*Ish*)</note> and "woman" <note>original: אשה (*Ishah*)</note> is contained the name of God, *Yah* <note>original: יה, the first two letters of the Tetragrammaton</note>. Hence the Druids erected a statue in their innermost sanctuaries, dedicating it to Isis—or rather to the Virgin—from whom that son was to come forth. Philipp Nicolai <note>A German Lutheran theologian (1556–1608) who wrote extensively on the Apocalypse.</note> also agrees with this in his explanation of the Revelation of John.

### ON THE GERMAN GODS.

...everyone might marvel at them. And Cicero, in Book II of *On Divination*, writes: "Let us observe the Sibylline books; we must call upon some King, if only we wish to be safe." For in the Sibylline poems it was read that as soon as the Romans had restored the King of Egypt, the Lord of the World would appear. <note>The Sibylline Oracles were a collection of oracular utterances in Greek hexameters ascribed to the Sibyls, prophetesses who uttered divine revelations in a frenzied state. > *Now comes the final age of the Cumaean song,*

> *Bright offspring of the Gods, great seed of Jove.*

> ->seed.<-

Through the reading of these verses, many of the heathens were made Christians. And Cicero, in Book III of *The Republic*, writes thus concerning Christ, who would bring other laws: "There is indeed a true law, right reason, congruent with nature, diffused among all, constant, everlasting, which calls to duty by commanding and deters from fraud by forbidding; yet it neither commands nor forbids the virtuous in vain, nor moves the wicked by its forbidding or commanding. It is not permitted to repeal this law, nor is it allowed to detract anything from it, nor can it be entirely abolished. Nor indeed can we be released from this law by either the Senate or the people, nor should another explainer or interpreter of it be sought. There will not be one law at Rome, another at Athens, one now, and another hereafter; but one eternal and immutable law will hold sway among all nations and at all times, and there will be one common, as it were—"

### ON THE GERMAN GODS.

...we follow. The words of Tertullian <note>Tertullian (c. 155 – c. 220 AD) was a prolific early Christian author from Carthage and a key figure in the development of Western theology.</note> in his *Apology* <note>original: *Apologeticum*, one of Tertullian's most famous works, written to defend Christianity against pagan charges.</note> are to be noted, in which he drives out the demons and scorns their empty anger:

> *Let someone be produced here before your tribunals who is clearly known to be driven by a demon. When commanded to speak by any Christian at all, that spirit will as truly confess itself to be a demon as it elsewhere falsely claimed to be a god. In the same way, let someone be produced from those who are thought to be under the influence of a god: who conceive the malicious divinity of the air from the smell [of sacrifices], who are cured by blinking, or who prophesy by gasping. Unless that very celestial power itself—the promiser of rains—confesses itself to be a demon (not daring to lie to a Christian), then and there shed the blood of that most insolent Christian. No one lies to their own disgrace, but rather for their honor. They will not say that Christ was a Magician, nor of a common condition, nor stolen from the tomb; but rather the power of God, his wisdom, and the Word existing in heaven, from whence he shall come to judgment. Nor indeed will they deny that they are unclean spirits, already damned for their malice, awaiting his terrible judgment, truly fearing Christ in God and God in Christ, and being subjected to the servants of God and of Christ, etc.*

Let us say therefore, with Philippe de Mornay <note>Ph. Mornæus (1549–1623) was a French Protestant writer and diplomat known for his defenses of the Christian faith.</note> in chapter 32 of *On the Christian Religion*: Jesus is without doubt God and the Son of God, just as he spoke to us; and for that reason, we ought to hear him, listen to him, follow him, and worship him as God himself. God, I say, and man, the unique <term>Mediator</term> <note>A theological term for Christ's role as the "go-between" or bridge between God and humanity.</note> of the human race, who died for our sins and was raised from the dead for our justification. To whom be praise, honor, and glory for ever and ever. AMEN.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the Druid order, specifically completing a sentence from the previous page regarding their social and religious functions. ### ON THE GERMAN GODS.

...are concerned with divine **matters, they look after public and private sacrifices, and they interpret religious questions.** <note>original Latin: *bus divinis intersunt, sacrificia publica ac privata procurant, religiones interpretantur*</note> Strabo <note>a Greek geographer and historian</note> in Book IV of his *Geography* writes: *Among all three nations everywhere, the Bards, Vates, and Druids are held in exceptional honor. The Druids, in addition to the study of natural causes, practice moral philosophy.* Diodorus Siculus <note>a Greek historian of the 1st century BCE</note> in Book V of his *Library of History* says: *There are among them philosophers and theologians whom they call Druids, and they deem them worthy of great honor.* Lucan <note>a Roman poet</note> in Book I of his *Pharsalia* writes:

> *And you, Druids, after laying down your arms, have returned to your barbaric rites and the sinister custom of your sacrifices.*

Furthermore, we certainly maintain that these <note>the Druids</note> also existed among the Germans, despite the objection of Caesar, who writes in Book VI of his *Commentaries on the Gallic War* <note>original: *Com. bell. Gall.*</note> that *the Germans have neither Druids to preside over divine matters, nor do they devote themselves to sacrifices.* This report goes against the reliability of other authors. Indeed, Tacitus <note>the primary Roman historian for Germanic culture</note> openly contradicts this, and the facts themselves testify that there were priests among these people and that sacrifices were performed. For Tacitus says in his book *On the Customs of the Germans* <note>original: *l. de mor. Germ.*, commonly known as *Germania*</note>: *If the public interest is being consulted, the priest of the state prays to the Gods.* In the same work: *Silence is commanded by the Priests.* Also: *it is permitted for only the Priest to touch [the sacred objects].* A little later: *Until the same Priest returns them to the temple.* In Book I of his *Annals*: *In the nearby groves were barbaric altars at which they had slaughtered tribunes and centurions of the first rank.* And Diodorus Siculus in Book V of his *Library* reports: *All those peoples spread out as far as Scythia and situated near the Ocean and the Hercynian mountain <note>The Hercynian Forest was a vast, ancient mountain range and forest in central Europe</note> are called Gauls; but the Romans include all these nations under the single name of Gauls.* Now, if the inhabitants of the Hercynian region and those dwelling as far as Scythia are called Gauls, then surely the Druids themselves—

...of the Nations, they are just as much for the Germans as they are for the Gauls. But the Germans themselves inhabited these places, as has been shown in the preceding sections, and the evidence itself speaks loudly. Indeed, Tertullian <note>an influential early Christian author from Carthage, c. 155–220 CE</note> agrees with us most elegantly in the book he wrote *On the Soul*: *Or if it is the privilege of Philosophers,* he says, *and specifically the Greeks; as if the Scythians and Indians do not also philosophize.* <note>original Latin: "aut si privilegium Philosophorum est... quasi non & Scythae & Indi philosophentur."</note>

And some once called these Philosophers by another name, *Tarabosteseos*, and likewise *Pileati* <note>meaning "the capped ones," referring to the felt caps worn by the Dacian and Getae nobility to distinguish them from the long-haired commoners</note>; from among these they were accustomed to appoint priests and kings in the manner of the Egyptians, as noted by Johannes Magnus <note>a 16th-century Swedish archbishop and historian</note> in Book I, chapter 33; Cranz <note>Albert Krantz, a German historian of the 15th century</note> in Book II on the Swedes, chapter 55; Bonfinius <note>Antonio Bonfini, an Italian humanist who wrote on Hungarian history</note> in Book II of the first Decade; and Saxo Grammaticus <note>a medieval Danish historian and author of the Gesta Danorum</note> in Book I.

Three types of Mathematicians <note>in this context, the term refers to practitioners of the occult, astrology, or high magic rather than modern arithmetic</note> once performed miracles of an unheard-of kind through various illusions among the Northern peoples. The first of these were men of a monstrous race, whom antiquity called Giants, surpassing the standard of human size with the extraordinary greatness of their bodies. The second were the Magi <note>Wizards or Sages</note> following after these, who, obtaining the primary art of natural philosophy, possessed the Pythian art <note>the art of prophecy or divination, named after the Pythia, the priestess of Apollo at Delphi</note>; as much as these were inferior to the former in physical stature, they excelled them by just as much in the lively talent of their minds. Between these Magi and the Giants, there were continuous wars fought for supreme power, until the Magi, as victors, secured for themselves not only the right to rule, but also the reputation of divinity. Both of these groups, through the highest skill in deceiving the eyes, knew how to overshadow their own faces and those of others with various images of things, and to obscure true appearances with enticing forms. But the third kind were called "Gods"; springing from the alternating union of the groups mentioned above, they [shared] the nature of their authors, but neither in the size of their bodies nor in their arts...

...responded to the exercise of their [magical] arts. Through these illusions, however, a belief in their divinity was instilled in the deluded minds of the barbarians. And Olaus Magnus <note>a 16th-century Swedish historian and geographer</note> in Book I, chapter 1 and Book III, chapter 10, notes that the Northern Bothnians, Lapps, and Finns are most excellent magicians. Likewise the Biarmians <note>inhabitants of the legendary region of Bjarmaland, likely in Northern Russia</note>, who live beneath the North Pole, take on whatever shape they wish. They also investigate things happening in another world, whether concerning friends or enemies, by paying a price with a linen garment or a bow. Regarding the other gifts of Gaul, Marcus Cato <note>Cato the Elder, Roman statesman and author, 234–149 BCE</note> in the second book of his *Origins* says: *For the most part, Gaul pursues two things most industriously: military matters and speaking eloquently.* <note>original Latin: "Plerumque Gallia duas res industriosissime persequitur, rem militarem, & argute loqui."</note> Saint Jerome <note>the scholar and priest who translated the Bible into Latin, c. 347–420 CE</note> writes to Rusticus of the *Studies of the Gauls, which are most flourishing.* <note>original Latin: "Studia Galliarum, quae vel florentissima sunt."</note> In his work *Against Vigilantius*, he writes: *Gaul alone has not had monsters, but has always abounded in the bravest and most eloquent men.* <note>original Latin: "sola Gallia monstra non habuit, sed & viris semper fortissimis & eloquentissimis abundavit." Jerome likely refers to "monsters" in the sense of major heretical movements which were less common in Gaul at the time.</note> And this reputation for eloquence proceeded from the labor of the Druids, who were held in the highest esteem among the Gauls and Germans, as Aventinus <note>Johannes Aventinus, a 16th-century Bavarian historian and humanist</note> testifies in the first book of his *Bavarian Annals*. But Druids were also found among the Britons, as Caesar in the sixth book of his *Commentaries on the Gallic War* and Tacitus in the fourteenth book of his *Annals* have recorded for posterity.

...[Caesar] <note>Julius Caesar, in his *Gallic Wars*, Book VI</note> considers that the discipline of the Druids was discovered in Britain, and from there transferred into Gaul. And even now, those who wish to understand that matter more carefully usually travel there for the sake of learning. Hence Hector Boece <note>a Scottish philosopher and historian, 1465–1536</note> in Book II records that they were first established by Fynnanus, King of the Scots, and were called *Durcerglii* <note>meaning "guardians of the sacred"</note>, being the overseers and interpreters of sacred rites. Among the Spaniards, these are called *Turduli*, or even *Turditani*. Indeed, the Spaniards drew their origin from the Celts, and together with that origin they drank in their religion: hence they are called Celtiberians, from the mixing of the Celtic and Iberian races, as Diodorus Siculus <note>a Greek historian of the 1st century BCE</note> records in Book V of his *Historical Library*. For these Turduli possessed written laws of great antiquity; and therefore among the Spaniards, before veins of gold and silver were discovered and the Spanish wars were waged, many practiced philosophy, and the people lived securely and peacefully with the holiest of customs. Individual tribes were governed by an annual magistrate, men outstanding in learning and integrity; affairs were settled with equity and goodness. There were no lawsuits or controversies among the citizens, and yet if any did exist, they were concerning the emulation of virtue. Learned men would discourse publicly on appointed days regarding the nature of the Gods, the principles of nature, and upright morals. Juan Luis Vives <note>a Spanish humanist and scholar, 1492–1540</note> in his commentary on Book VIII of Augustine’s *City of God* notes this; Aventinus <note>Johannes Aventinus, a Bavarian Renaissance historian, 1477–1534</note> on the other hand, in Book I of the *Annals of the Bavarians*, records that they were established by an author named Druys, who was the fourth descendant from Samothes <note>a legendary king often cited in early modern histories as the first ruler of Britain and Gaul</note>, and is believed to have founded them. But I judge it more likely that they were established by Tuysco <note>Tuisto, the divine ancestor of the Germanic peoples mentioned by Tacitus</note>. For he, being equally knowledgeable in divine and human wisdom, foresaw that a republic could neither hold together nor could the license of men be restrained without justice and the fear of religion,

...along with religion, he also established Priests, and handed over both Philosophy and Theology to be cultivated by them. However, Johannes Metellus <note>Jean Matal (1520–1597), a Burgundian scholar and jurist</note> objects, who, when speaking of the Kabbalah <note>the ancient Jewish tradition of mystical interpretation of the Bible</note>, writes as follows:

> The Kabbalah <note>original: *Cabala*</note> is nothing other than the true discipline of philosophy. Indeed, it teaches very skillfully through certain symbols—once all earthly things are set aside and the physical matter of things is removed—how to draw forth form from form, until one reaches and descends to that first uniform matter, which they call formless. Therefore, whatever the Magi among the Persians, the Chaldeans <note>priests and astronomers of ancient Mesopotamia</note> among the Babylonians and Assyrians, or the Gymnosophists <note>literally "naked philosophers" of ancient India</note> among the Indians, and the Druids among the Gauls, and those called the *Semnothei* <note>a term used by ancient writers like Diogenes Laertius to describe Celtic philosophers</note> discovered; they received these things from the Jews. For the Jews were the first of all Philosophers, and Egypt had Jewish Prophets. Moreover, Pythagoras and Plato, having changed the name from "Kabbalah" to "Philosophy," explained to their own people in Greek those things received from the Jews, not from the Greeks or Romans.

So he claims. But from where did the Germans receive these things from the Jews? Certainly not through the founding of colonies, and much less through the practice of trade. In fact, the Jews were never known to the Germans in those times, as neither nation traveled back and forth for the sake of commerce. Even the early Romans did not know of the Jews until ambassadors were sent to Rome for the purpose of striking a treaty <note>referring to the embassy of the Maccabees in the 2nd century BCE</note>.

Perhaps, however, his argument rests on the foundation that the Germans (or Scythians <note>Schedius, like many early modern historians, identifies the Scythians as the ancestors of the Germanic peoples</note>) drew in this Philosophy when Madyes, King of the Scythians—as Herodotus testifies in the book titled *Clio* <note>the first book of Herodotus's *Histories*</note>—devastated all of Media and Persia along with Palestine all the way into Egypt, which Justin <note>a Roman historian of the 2nd century CE</note> also records in Book II. But never...

I am not led to believe that during those twenty years, the Scythians—while they were waging war in Asia—simultaneously devoted themselves to Philosophy.

> *Fair Clio <note>the Muse of history and learning</note> and the fierce madness of terrifying Mars <note>the Roman god of war</note> do not agree well,*
> *nor do they stay in one place.*

And it is well known what happened to Musonius Rufus <note>a famous Stoic philosopher of the 1st century AD</note>, a man of the equestrian order, when he attempted to promote the study of Philosophy and the tenets of the Stoics—explaining the blessings of peace and the nature of war among armed men—as Ludovicus Vives <note>Juan Luis Vives (1493–1540), a Spanish humanist and educator</note> records in Book II of *On Concord and Discord*, citing Tacitus. But rather, I believe that Tuysco <note>Tuisto, the legendary divine ancestor of the Germanic peoples mentioned by the Roman historian Tacitus</note> established these institutions; he is the one from whom all Germany drew the origin of its religion, its political order, and its lineage. From him, so many peoples, so many Kings, so many Princes, and so many Caesars <note>Emperors</note> have traced their descent.

And indeed, this fits the office of the Druids most closely, which was to examine the hidden things of nature and from there to draw out the truth. For these were the most ancient teachers among the Celts, and more excellent than even the wise men of Greece, who followed the sect of the Druids after a long course of time.

ELIAS SCHEDIVS

...begin. We shall start, however, with the head. And here, the first thing we encounter is reddish hair <note>original: "rutilus crinis"</note>, which is effectively the hallmark of the Germanic people. Diodorus Siculus, in Book V of his *Historical Library* writes: *They not only wear their hair red by nature, but they also strive to increase this natural quality of color through artifice. For they frequently wash their hair with a lye of lime <note>A strong alkaline solution used here as an early form of bleach or hair dye</note>, and they twist it back from the forehead to the crown, and from there to the neck, so that it may be more conspicuous. In this way, they resemble Satyrs and Pans in their appearance. By this treatment, the hair is thickened so much that it differs in no way from the bristles of horses. Some shave their beards, while others grow them moderately. The more noble among them smooth their cheeks by shaving, but let their mustaches grow long so that their mouths are covered. Therefore, when they eat, food becomes entangled in the hair; when they drink, the liquid flows through as if through a strainer.* Tacitus, in his book *On the Customs of the Germans*, notes: *reddish hair, large bodies, and powerful only for a sudden onset.* Hence the Batavians <note>A Germanic tribe living in the modern-day Netherlands</note> are called "golden-haired" by Silius Italicus in Book III:

->*But a boy already dreaded by the golden-haired Batavian.*<-

> Leaf of gold more golden from the hair itself? <note>The author uses the term *bractea*, referring to a thin foil or leaf of beaten gold, to emphasize the metallic brilliance of the hair.</note>

For there is such grace in a person's hair—these are the words of Francesco Barbaro in Book I, Chapter 5 of *On Wifely Duties* <note>original title: *De re uxoria*, a 15th-century treatise on marriage</note>—that it is enough for Homer very often to call his Helen beautiful based on this one elegance of her hair alone. Did not our Maro <note>The poet Virgil, whose full name was Publius Vergilius Maro.</note> also, when he described a wise man and wished to make him beautiful in a few words, add this part of beauty, saying:

> In face and shoulders like a god; for his mother 
> Herself had breathed upon her son a beautiful head of 
> Hair, the glowing light of youth, 
> And joyful honors upon his eyes.

Believe me, if Mars had seen Venus with her hair shorn, that passion by which the most warlike god was moved would have vanished instantly, so much so that he would never have been ensnared by the devices of Vulcan <note>This refers to the mythological tale where Vulcan, the god of fire and smithing, caught his wife Venus and the god Mars in a finely-wrought metal net to expose their affair.</note>. To this beauty of which I speak...

<meta>This page continues Schedius’s examination of Roman social and aesthetic standards, specifically focusing on hair. # ON THE GERMANIC GODS.

Matrons were never given blonde hair <note>original: "flava coma"</note>, but always black. Blonde hair was therefore given to Dido as if she were shameful. <note>Dido was the Queen of Carthage in Virgil's *Aeneid*; blonde hair was often used by Roman poets to signal foreignness or a lack of matronly virtue.</note> Hence Messalina in Juvenal’s *Satire VI*:

> *And with a yellow wig hiding her black hair,*
> *She entered the warm brothel with its old quilt.*
<note>Juvenal describes the Empress Messalina sneaking out of the imperial palace to work in a brothel under the pseudonym "Lycisca," wearing a blonde wig to disguise her identity and appeal to the tastes of the clientele.</note>

Therefore, unchaste women—so that they might be more pleasing to their lovers, as Cato records in his *Origins*—would smear their hair with ash so that the hair might become reddish-gold. *Tertullian*, in *On the Apparel of Women*, chapter 6: "I see some women even changing their hair with saffron. They are ashamed even of their own nation, that they were not born Germans or Gauls; thus they transport a foreign homeland into their hair. They portend poorly and most wickedly for themselves with a flaming head, and they think that beautiful which they actually defile. Yet the power of the medicinal treatment burns a loss into the hair; and the constant application of any pure moisture preserves destruction for the brain; then there is the desirable heat of the Sun for enlivening and drying the hair at once. What is beauty combined with injury? What is loveliness along with filth? The Christian woman heaps saffron upon her head as if upon an altar. Behold, they desire to make it blonde instead of white or black, for easier grace; though they also try to make it black from white, those who have regretted living until old age." <note>Tertullian, an early Christian author, argues that by dyeing their hair blonde, Roman women were effectively trying to "become" Germanic or Gallic, which he views as a rejection of their God-given identity.</note>

*Cyprian*, in *On the Discipline and Dress of Virgins*: "With bold endeavor and sacrilegious contempt you dye your hair; with an evil omen of things to come, you already portend flaming hair for yourself." <note>Cyprian suggests that the "flaming" blonde hair of the fashion-conscious woman is a prophetic sign of the fires of Gehenna (Hell).</note> *Jerome* to Laeta: "Neither burden your head with gems, nor redden your hair, lest you sprinkle upon it something of the fires of Hell." *Clement of Alexandria*, in Book III of *The Pedagogue*, chapter 2: "And indeed, that woman who made her own hair blonde, the comic poet Menander drives from the house:"

<meta>This page continues the discussion of hair as a symbol of identity and spiritual power. While the previous page established how the Athenians used the "crobylus" knot and golden cicadas to signal their status and connection to the land, this page explores the darker, supernatural beliefs regarding hair, moving from Athenian nobility to the "charms of silence" used by magicians and the biblical example of Samson.</meta>

### ELIAS SCHEDIUS ###

...a knot <note>original: "κρώβυλον" (krobylon). A hairstyle where the hair is gathered into a tuft or knot.</note>, which is a type of braiding, they bound up, decorating it with the insertion of golden cicadas. Being truly native to the soil, they were renowned—though perhaps with a certain lack of refinement—for their pride. That is to say: *The leaders of the Athenians, moreover, who seek civic governance, grow long beards down to their ankles as a sign of virtue; they wrap their beards and surround them with a knot—a kind of weaving—decorating them with the binding of golden cicadas, thus emphasizing their native or true origin through what some might call a foolish impurity.* <note>The cicada was a symbol of "autochthony," or being born from the earth itself, as the Greeks believed cicadas emerged from the ground.</note> 

But even among magicians, there was believed to be a "charm of silence" <note>original: "fors silentii." A magical spell or amulet supposed to prevent a prisoner from speaking or feeling pain during interrogation.</note> hidden in the hair, as Paolo Grillando <note>A 16th-century Italian jurist and writer on witchcraft and demonology.</note> in his treatise on inquiries, question 4, number 14, and Hippolytus Marsilius <note>A famous Italian lawyer (1451–1529) known for his works on criminal law and torture.</note> write. They claim that this charm of silence was often found in the hair of magicians, who otherwise seemed to sleep through their torments as if they were entirely devoid of pain. 

Consequently, Grillando, who had seen many such cases, was advised to say: *Lord, open my lips, and my mouth shall declare your praise,* <note>original: "Domine labia mea aperies, &c." This is a quote from Psalm 51:15, used here as a counter-spell to break the magician's silence.</note> and in this way, they would begin to feel pain and speak the truth. Jean Bodin <note>A 16th-century French jurist and political philosopher who wrote "On the Demon-Mania of Witches."</note> writes of this in Book 4, chapter 1. Furthermore, an Inquisitor of Como, in the territory of Valtellina <note>original: "Varniferano agro."</note> on the borders of Milan, condemned forty-one witches to the fire in the year 1485. All of them, after their hair had been shaved off and their clothes changed, confessed without even being questioned. 

It is read in the works of Philostratus of Lemnos <note>Author of the "Life of Apollonius of Tyana."</note> that the Emperor Domitian once did the same to the magician Apollonius of Tyana, ordering him to be stripped and shaved. For the Inquisitor Sprenger <note>Jakob Sprenger, co-author of the "Malleus Maleficarum," a famous manual for hunting witches.</note> says that if a magician possesses the charm of silence, he will experience no pain during torture and will never confess the truth. 

Nevertheless, the long hair of Samson nurtured an immense strength within him, as seen in the Book of Judges, chapter 17. <note>The author cites chapter 17, though the story of Samson's hair and the Philistines is primarily found in Judges 16.</note> For this Nazirite <note>A "Nazirite" was a Hebrew person consecrated to God, bound by a vow to never cut their hair or drink wine.</note> could never be captured by the Philistines, nor did the power of the Lord desert him,

## CHAPTER V.

*The fair face. A face whitened with chalk in Petronius. Roman women washed their faces with donkey's milk. They plastered their faces. They are rebuked by the Church Fathers. ...flesh already liquefied by poisons: they insult the Maker of all things, as if He had not granted them beauty for their husbands. From this, I believe, it came to be that on the first day of marriage, brides were wrapped in the <term>flammeum<gloss>a large, flame-colored or deep yellow veil worn by Roman brides.</gloss></term>. Although the Scholiast <note>An ancient or medieval commentator on a classical text.</note> on Juvenal’s *Satire VI* offers another reason: *“The flammeum is a type of garment with which women cover themselves on their wedding day. It is blood-red for the sake of preserving a modest blush.”* Festus Pompeius, in Book VI, writes: *“The bride is dressed in the flammeum for the sake of a good omen, because it was used constantly by the Flaminica—that is, the wife of the Flamen <note>The Flamen Dialis was the high priest of Jupiter; his wife, the Flaminica, was a symbol of marital stability as they were not permitted to divorce.</note>—who was not allowed to seek a divorce.”* Nonius Marcellus defines it as: *“The flammeum is a garment or covering with which matrons cover their heads.”* Pliny the Elder, in Book XXI, chapter IX of his *Natural History*, and the Glossaries state: *“The flammeum is a virginal <term>mavorte<gloss>A Latin term for a veil or mantle, often associated with the goddess Mars or later simply any head-covering.</gloss></term>.”* Indeed, in later ages, a 'mavorte' came to mean any kind of head covering.

---

\* *“The flammeum,”* says Octavius Ferrarius <note>A 17th-century Italian archaeologist and scholar of ancient clothing.</note> in his *Analects on Ancient Dress*, chapter XXIV, page 1099, Volume VI of Graevius’s collection, *“takes its name from its color, with which the head of the bride was veiled—whence the term 'nuptials' [from 'nubo', to veil or cover] is derived. However, that veil was not a long garment that hung down to the feet or was thrown back over the shoulder, but rather a covering for the head, chest, and shoulders only.”* You may see the *flammeum* itself, as it is depicted on ancient monuments, with your own eyes in the work of Jacob Spon, in his *Curious Researches into Antiquity*, dissertation V, page 88; in Lorenz Beger, Volume I of the *Brandenburg Treasury*, page 100; and in Bernard de Montfaucon’s *Antiquity Explained*, Volume III, Part 2, Book I, chapter 9, section 2, page 220. # ELIAS SCHEDIUS <note>Elias Schedius (1615–1641) was a German historian and polymath known for this work, *De Diis Germanis* (On the Germanic Gods), where he explores the culture and religion of the ancient Germanic tribes through a classical lens.</note>

## Chapter VI.

*Eyes. The soul resides in the eyes. Blue eyes among the Germans. Terrible in appearance. Roman women used to paint themselves with <term>stibium<gloss>A mineral-based black pigment, also known as antimony, used as eyeliner in antiquity.</gloss></term>. The power of stibium. Eyebrows were dyed with soot. A passage from Petronius.*

We must now speak of the eyes, the most precious part of the body, which distinguish life from death by the use of light, as Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder (23–79 AD), a Roman author and natural philosopher who wrote the encyclopedic *Natural History*.</note> says in Book 11, Chapter 37. Indeed, in no other part are there greater signs of the soul for all animals, but most especially for man—that is, signs of moderation, clemency, mercy, hatred, love, justice, and joy. Their gaze is likewise manifold: fierce, grim, burning, solemn, sidelong, slanting, downcast, or charming. Truly, the soul dwells in the eyes. Among the Germans, moreover, the eyes were blue. Tacitus <note>Publius Cornelius Tacitus (c. 56–120 AD), a Roman historian whose work *Germania* is the primary source for the early Germanic tribes.</note> says in his book *On the Customs of the Germans*: *Hence their physical appearance, although the same for everyone in such a great number of people, consists of fierce and blue eyes.* Juvenal <note>A Roman poet of the late 1st and early 2nd centuries AD, famous for his *Satires*.</note> asks in Satire 13:

> Who has ever been astonished by the blue eyes of a German? <note>original: "Cærula quis stupuit Germani lumina?"</note>

Moreover, the color <term>glaucus<gloss>A blue-grey or sea-green color, often associated with the shimmer of water.</gloss></term> was a sign of constancy to the ancients, just as they used to praise the Germans for their <term>caesius<gloss>A Latin term for bluish-grey or cat-like eyes.</gloss></term> eyes. But these eyes also struck terror into their enemies. Diodorus Siculus <note>A Greek historian of the 1st century BC.</note> says in Book 5 of his *Library*: *They are terrible to look upon.* Julius Caesar <note>The famous Roman general and statesman; these quotes come from his *Commentaries on the Gallic War*.</note> in Book 1 of his *Commentaries* relates that the Gauls declared the Germans were of immense physical size, possessed incredible courage and training in arms, and that often when they met them, they could not even bear their expression or the sharp flash of their eyes. Indeed, for this reason, many have also called it <term>Platyophthalmon<gloss>A Greek term meaning "wide-eyed."</gloss></term>, because in the <term>calliblepharis<gloss>From the Greek for "beautiful eyelids," referring to cosmetic preparations meant to enhance the eyes.</gloss></term> of women, it dilates the eyes. Hence, proud women used to paint their eyes with it, as Clement of Alexandria <note>Clement of Alexandria (c. 150–215 AD) was a Christian theologian who frequently wrote against the "pagan" vanities of his era.</note> clearly indicates in Book III of *The Instructor*, Chapter II: *For so it seems to me that women who wear gold, and busy themselves in curling their hair, and are occupied in anointing their cheeks and dyeing their eyes, and pursue other vanities with wicked art, decorating their carnal vanity and truly imitating the Egyptians, attract unfortunate lovers.* They dyed their eyebrows, however, with soot. > *Though you lie hidden, stored in a hundred boxes,*
> *your face does not sleep with you. You put on in the morning*

And so as not to display only these riches, he bared his right arm, adorned with a golden bracelet and an ivory circle joined by a shining plate.*

Pliny, in Book 33, chapter 1, writes that in the <term>Iliac times<gloss>The era of the Trojan War, as described in Homer’s Iliad.</gloss></term> there were no rings; a view shared by Porphyry in his 15th Question, Eustathius in his commentary on the *Odyssey* (Book 12, at the end), the Scholiast <note>An ancient commentator.</note> of Sophocles in *Oedipus Rex*, and Plutarch in his work on Homer. However, from the Sacred Histories <note>Referring to the Bible.</note> it is clear that the use of rings is far more ancient. It is certainly evident that for a long time, not even the Roman Senate possessed gold rings. Indeed, only those who were to go as ambassadors to foreign nations [wore gold] rings...

...to **Tiro** <note>Marcus Tullius Tiro, the freedman and secretary of the orator Cicero.</note> in Book 16 of the *Letters*: *Just as I remember our mother used to do; she would seal even empty wine-jars, so they would not be said to be empty if any had been secretly drained.* <note>original: "Sicut olim matrem nostram facere memini; quae lagenas etiam inanes obsignabat, ne dicerentur inanes, ubi qua fuissent, quae furtim essent exsiccatae."</note> From these gold rings, therefore, the **right of gold rings** <term>jus aureorum annulorum<gloss>A legal privilege in Rome that allowed a freed slave to wear the gold ring of a free-born citizen, effectively raising their social status.</gloss></term> descends. * And he who obtains this right is indeed considered **free-born** <term>ingenuus<gloss>A person born free, as opposed to a "libertus" or freedman who was born in slavery.</gloss></term>, but not in every respect, according to Law 1 of the Code *on the right of gold rings* <note>original: "l. 1. C. d. jur. aur. ann."</note>; for the **Patron** <note>The former master of a freed slave.</note> retains his legal right over him, and is not excluded from his inheritance, as seen in the Law *He who has the right* in the Digest *on the right of gold rings* and Law 3 of the Digest *on the services of freedmen*. He is also a participant in a legacy left to him. Likewise, he may not summon his patron to court without permission, according to the Law *But also if*, section *patron*, in the Digest *on summoning to court*. Furthermore, for the murder of a Patron, he can be tortured just like other freedmen, according to the Law *The same shall be*, in the Digest *on the Silanian Decree of the Senate*. It is, therefore, a lesser thing to have the right of gold rings than to have the **right of birth** <term>jus natalium<gloss>A higher legal grant that fully restored a freedman to the status of a free-born person, severing all ties to the former master.</gloss></term>, and both are granted solely by the favor of the **Prince** <note>The Emperor.</note>.

But today, under the most recent law of the **Authenticae** <term>Authenticum<gloss>A collection of the "Novels" or new laws issued by Emperor Justinian after his initial Code.</gloss></term>, because those who are **manumitted** <note>Formally released from slavery.</note> are declared Roman citizens, they immediately receive by that very manumission both the right of gold rings and of **regeneration** (that is, the right of birth), so that they thus become free and free-born without any other indulgence from the Prince. This remains permanent provided they offer to their manumitters and their sons the **deference** <note>original: "obsequium"</note>—that is, the reverence and veneration introduced by the laws. This is explained more broadly in the *Authenticum*, the section *That freedmen henceforth, etc.*, paragraph *therefore when*.

### CHAPTER VIII.

*Clothing. Striped cloaks. The color purple. Sacred to the celestial Gods. Dedicated to Emperors and Kings. Tyrian purple. Tight-fitting clothing. Pure garments in sacred rites. And these being white. The color white is the most simple. Germanic women clothed in linens. The more proud [clothed] in Babylonian textiles. Babylonian weaves. Feathers of birds. Feather-workers. Peacock garments. Priests among other nations used male attire, while among the Eastern peoples they used female attire.*

<margin>
* There were, says **John Doughty** <note>John Doughty (1598–1672), an English divine and author of *Analecta Sacra*.</note> in part 1 of the *Sacred Analects*, page 161, as it seems, multi-colored garments, either embroidered with a needle in the Phrygian style, or otherwise interwoven with various colored segments; these were in very frequent use especially among the more Eastern peoples. Furthermore, they were held in the highest luxury and honor, as they were worn not so much by private individuals and common people, but by princes and the leaders of the people, usually for the sake of luxury or some mark of distinction. Compare **Joseph Maria Suares** <note>A French bishop and antiquarian.</note> in his singular dissertation *on lettered garments* <note>original: "de vestibus literatis," referring to garments with woven patterns or inscriptions.</note>, published in Vaison, 1652, in quarto. **Philip Rubens**, Book 2 of *Selected Works*, chapter 3. **Albert Rubens**, Book 1 of *On the Matter of Clothing*, chapter 10. And **Stephen le Moyne** in *Exercises on Jeremiah 23:6*, page 101 and following.
</margin>

Clothing now comes to our attention, regarding which nothing certain is found among the authors. **Diodorus Siculus** in Book 5 of the *Library of History* says their clothing is remarkable: for they wear tunics dyed with various colors and sprinkled as if with flowers, and leggings (which are called **breeches** <term>bracae<gloss>A type of trouser or leggings worn by ancient Germanic and Celtic peoples, which the Greeks and Romans considered a mark of "barbarian" dress.</gloss></term>). They also wear **striped cloaks** <term>virgata saga<gloss>Heavy woolen cloaks or mantles, often striped or checkered, typical of northern tribes.</gloss></term>, thick for the winter and thinner for the summer, distinguished by frequent checkered patterns like flowers, held with brooches...

Otherwise they remain uncovered, spending whole days by the hearth and fire. The wealthiest are distinguished by a garment, not flowing like that of the Sarmatians and Parthians, but tight and showing each limb. They also wear the skins of wild beasts..."

Having cut off her hair, the husband expels the naked woman from the house in the presence of her kinsmen, and drives her with lashes through the entire village. For there is no pardon for public loss of chastity; neither beauty, nor age, nor wealth will find her another husband. For no one there laughs at vices, nor is corrupting and being corrupted called "the spirit of the age."* 

*Even better are those states in which only virgins marry, and where the hope and vow of a wife is settled once and for all. ## CHAPTER X.

*There was a High Priest among the Druids, as there was a Pontifex Maximus among the Romans. The Sacrificial King. Kings formerly performed priestly duties. The Roman Pontiff. His lust must be restrained. He is subject to Caesar. Who is able to abolish the Pontificate.*

**B**ut since without authority <note>original: *imperio*</note> neither any house, nor city, nor nation, nor the whole human race could stand, nor the whole nature of things, nor the world itself, as Cicero writes in Book III of *On the Laws*: it was certainly necessary to place a High Priest <note>original: *Pontificem*</note> over the Druids. For ruling and being ruled <note>original Greek: "τὸ γὰρ ἄρχειν καὶ ἄρχεσθαι" (to gàr árchein kaì árchesthai)</note> is not only among those things that are necessary, but also those that are beneficial. To rule and to be ruled [is found] not only among necessary things, but also useful ones. Aristotle, *Politics*, Book I, Chapter III. And that is the bond—as Seneca says in *On Clemency*—by which republics hold together: that vital spirit which these many thousands draw in: they would be nothing by themselves but a burden and a prey, if that mind of authority were withdrawn. It was certainly necessary that a certain High Priest be placed over them, who might judge those in dispute, or decide if any legal suit <note>original: *litis*</note> arose among them. Moreover, the whole nation of the Gauls is very much devoted to religious matters, as the Divine Caesar <note>Julius Caesar, in his accounts of the Gallic Wars.</note> writes in Book VI of his *Commentaries on the Gallic War*: Therefore, one man presides over all the Druids, who holds the highest authority among them. Among the Romans, Numa Pompilius <note>The legendary second king of Rome, credited with establishing many of its religious institutions.</note> first created the *Pontifex Maximus* <note>The supreme priest of the Roman state religion.</note>, according to the testimony of

<meta>This page continues the comparison between the religious structures of the ancient Celts and Romans, moving from the general necessity of leadership to the specific duties and historical development of the Roman Pontifex Maximus as a model for the Druidic High Priest.</meta>

<page-num>418</page-num>

<header>ELIAS SCHEDIUS</header>

Livy <note>original: *Liv. l. 1.*; referring to Titus Livius's *History of Rome*, Book 1, Chapter 20.</note> writes that, as one who was the master of the greatest matters in divine worship, he should judge the sacrifices; he should establish laws in things regarding the Gods, and indicate to others at which altars, to which Gods, with which victims, on which days, and at which temples sacred rites ought to be performed. There were, however, four [pontiffs] from the beginning, as L. Fenestella <note>A Roman historical writer (c. 52 BC – AD 19) known for his work on Roman customs.</note> reports in his book *On Roman Priesthoods*, chapter 8. But after the common people <note>original: *plebs*</note> obtained a share of the highest honors through the motions of the tribunes, they wanted access to the priesthoods and sacrosanct powers to be open to them as well. Therefore, it was decided that four other Pontiffs be created from the common people, during the consulship of M. Valerius and Q. Apuleius.

One man had been placed over them all by Numa Pompilius <note>The legendary second king of Rome, credited with establishing many of its religious institutions.</note>, and he was called the <term>Pontifex Maximus</term> <note>The High Priest; literally "the greatest bridge-builder" between the human and divine.</note>. He possesses within his own records all the sacred rites written down and sealed, [specifying] with which victims, on which days, and at which temples sacred rites ought to be performed. In such divine matters, the Pontiff is also concerned with where the funds for the expenses ought to be disbursed; and all other sacred rites, both public and private, are subject to the Pontiff's sacred authority. Indeed, when there is a dispute concerning religion or sacred matters, the people proceed to consult him.

Pompilius, the author of this priesthood, thought it would be very useful so that divine law <note>original: *jus divinum*</note> would not be disturbed by neglecting ancestral rites and adopting foreign ones. It belongs to the same Pontiff not only to lead celestial ceremonies, but also to oversee proper funeral rites and the appeasement of the <term>Manes</term> <note>The spirits of the departed ancestors, who required specific rituals to remain peaceful.</note>. In his keeping there is also said to be a tablet in which eclipses of the Sun and Moon are observed—whenever darkness falls upon the light—as well as the calculation of the year, months, and the <term>fasti</term> <note>The official Roman calendar that designated which days were permissible for legal and public business.</note>. Originally, however, they were chosen from the patrician fathers, as Pomponius Laetus <note>A 15th-century Italian humanist who wrote extensively on Roman antiquity.</note> records in his book *On Priesthoods*; see his work. But also among the Romans...

...among us <note>The text likely refers to "among the Romans" in continuity with the previous page.</note> was the <term>Rex Sacrificulus</term> <note>Literally the "Sacrificial King"; a priest who performed the religious duties formerly handled by the Roman kings.</note>, whom the same author writes was established by the Romans for this reason: First, they chose Gaius Manius Papyrius <note>A legendary figure often associated with the early collection of Roman laws.</note> from the Fathers <note>The Senators.</note>, and they subjected that priesthood to the Pontiff, so that the honor of the royal name, added to their new liberty, would not be an obstacle. This Papyrius was most devoted to peace. He is remembered as the same man who brought back into public view the laws of Numa <note>Numa Pompilius, the second king of Rome, credited with the city's religious foundations.</note> which had been inscribed on oaken tablets by Ancus Martius <note>The fourth king of Rome.</note>. The occasion for creating this office, as Fenestella <note>A Roman historian of the Augustan age.</note> writes in chapter 11, was that when the Kings had recently been driven out, many sacred rites which were usually performed by the Kings alone seemed to be neglected by their expulsion. Since the people took this very poorly—as it seemed that divine worship had been diminished by the expulsion of the Kings—it was decided that a Priest should be created. To ensure he did not lack authority, they decorated him with the royal name, calling him the "King of Sacred Rites." For it was customary, among both the Greeks and the Romans, for Kings to perform priestly duties. Whence Virgil, speaking of King Anius of Delos, thus sings:

> ->*King Anius, both king of men and priest of Apollo.*<-
> <note>original: *Rex Anius, Rex idem hominum, Phœbique sacerdos.* From Virgil's *Aeneid*, Book 3, line 80.</note>

See also Book 2, and see Dionysius of Halicarnassus <note>A Greek historian (c. 60 BC – 7 BC) who wrote extensively on Roman history.</note>. And even now, the Roman Pontiff <note>The Pope.</note>, following in those footsteps, enjoys that imaginary title and fictitious power. He cleverly represents the persona of the Sacrificial King, but with greater authority, having deluded the highest Princes with imaginary worship and feigned piety. See Covarruvias <note>Diego de Covarrubias (1512–1577), a Spanish jurist and canon lawyer.</note> in the chapter *Alma Mater*, part 1, section 1, number 4, on the sentence of excommunication in book 6. They talk such nonsense as saying that he [the Pope] stands as far above the Emperor <note>original: *Caesari*</note> as the Sun stands above the Moon, gold above lead, or the soul above the body. ...they never even contend for supreme power with arms. And it is read that this type of duel <note>original: "duellum." In this context, it refers to a judicial duel or trial by combat, a legal method used to settle disputes.</note> is most ancient. Thus David killed Goliath, Romulus killed Acron, and Manlius Torquatus and Valerius Corvinus killed the Gauls. And the **Lombards** \*, whenever proof was lacking, would prove their case to the judge by a duel, according to Alciatus in *On the Duel*, book 4. And Cujacius brings forward controversies decided by duel in his commentary on the *Books of Feuds*; as do Hotoman, Borcholt, and Tiraqueau in *On the Right of the Prince*. But a duel is also sometimes undertaken for the safety of the fatherland, as noted by Ferdinand Vasquius and Alciatus. A leader, however, ought not rashly present himself, lest by failing he creates misfortune for his soldiers, according to Castolus. Nor is it a wonder that the Germans fought among themselves with arms. For as Tacitus witnesses in his book *On the Customs of the Germans*, they do nothing, whether in public or private business, unless they are armed. And as it pleases the crowd, they sit down armed. If a proposal displeases them, they reject it with a roar; but if it pleases them, they clash their <term>frameas</term> <note>A framea was a versatile Germanic spear or javelin with a short, narrow iron head, used for both close and distant combat.</note> together. To praise with arms is the most honorable type of assent. Their arms, however, as Diodorus Siculus writes in Book V of his *Historical Library*, are shields, extended to the height of a man and decorated with their own unique markings. Some carry bronze images of beasts, as much for defense as for ornament—

\* *That the **Lombards** were named from the length of their beards <note>original: "a longitudine barbae."</note>, Paul the Deacon (Warnefrid), himself a Lombard, held for certain in his "History of the Lombards," book I, chapter 9. Or they may be named from the extensive stretch of soil inhabited by them—"from the long border" <note>original: "von der langen Börde."</note>—as is favored today by Meibom, Gryphiander, and others. Or even from the double-axe <note>original: "a bipenni."</note>, the <term>halberd</term> <note>original: "Hellebard."</note>, according to the opinion of Rudbeck in his "Atlantis."*

...they display [shields] that are skillfully made. Furthermore, they fortify themselves for an attack with bronze helmets featuring large attachments made for extensive display. For these helmets have either horns affixed to them, or the faces of birds and four-footed animals fashioned upon them. They also use barbaric trumpets according to their custom, which, when blown, produce a harsh bellowing sound suited to inspiring warlike terror. They put on iron breastplates made of hooks <note>original: "hamatos." This likely refers to chainmail, where iron rings are "hooked" or linked together.</note>. Others, content with what nature has provided, fight naked. Instead of short swords, they carry long <term>spathas</term> <note>A spatha was a straight, long sword, much longer than the standard Roman gladius, used for reaching over a shield or from horseback.</note> which hang obliquely from iron or bronze chains upon the right thigh. Some gird their tunics with gilded or silvered belts. Additionally, they carry spears before them which they call lances, the iron points of which equal a <term>cubit</term> <note>An ancient unit of length based on the forearm, roughly 18 inches or 45 centimeters.</note> in length, or even exceed it. The width of these points is not far from two <term>palms</term> <note>A palm was roughly the width of a human hand, about 3 to 4 inches.</note>. Indeed, their swords are no smaller than the <term>saunions</term> <note>A saunion was a heavy, all-iron javelin or spear used by various ancient peoples.</note> of others. However, the edge of these saunions is larger than that of the swords. A portion of these are forged straight, while others have curved bends throughout, so that upon impact they do not merely cut, but actually break the flesh; when the spear is pulled back, it mangles and tears the wound apart.

**Tacitus** in his book *On the Customs of the Germans*: *Indeed, they proceed to business, and no less often to banquets, while fully armed.* <note>original: "Quin & ad negotia, nec minus sæpe ad convivia procedunt armati."</note> From this arise frequent brawls, as is common among those full of wine; these are rarely settled by mere insults, but more often by slaughter and wounds. **Diodorus Siculus**, Book V: *Among the feasts themselves, having seized upon some cause for a quarrel however it arose, they are accustomed to rise up and, considering the loss of life as nothing, they fight it out with swords among themselves upon the slightest provocation.* <note>original: "Inter ipsas quoque epulas causa ex jurgio quomodocunque arrepta insurgere, & ex provocatione, nihili vitæ jacturam æstimantes, inter se digladiari solent."</note> And **Athenaeus** touches upon this custom in Book IV of *The Philosophers at Dinner*: *And some—namely the Germans—stand by bearing their shields behind them, while others...* <note>original Greek: "καὶ οἱ μὲν... τοὺς θυρεοὺς ὁπλοφοροῦντας ἐκ τῶν ὀπίσω παρεστᾶσιν, οἱ δὲ..."</note>

## CHAPTER XIII.

*Justice is necessary for humans. The Druids were most just. They differed from the Romans in religion. The most just Germans and Scythians live not by laws, but by good morals. They especially venerate their philosophers and theologians. They decide public controversies. Types of punishments.*

But since the force of Justice is so great—as Cicero says in Book II of *On Duties*—that not even those who feed on crime and wrongdoing can live without some small portion of Justice; it was necessarily provided that men famous for justice should be chosen to administer it. For if justice is removed, what are kingdoms but great robberies? <note>original: "Remota enim justitia quid sunt regna, nisi magna latrocinia?" The use of wool and clothing is unknown to them; and although they are nipped by constant cold, they nevertheless use the skins of wild beasts and sea creatures. This self-restraint has also instilled in them a justice of character, as they covet nothing belonging to others; for the desire for wealth exists only where there is also the use of it. And if only other mortals had a similar moderation and abstinence from what belongs to others! Certainly, so many wars would not persist through all ages in all lands; nor would iron and weapons snatch away more people than the natural condition of fate. It truly seems marvelous that nature gives to them what the Greeks—despite the long-standing doctrine of wise men and the precepts of philosophers—cannot achieve, and that refined morals [benefit] by comparison with unrefined barbarism...*

<meta>This page continues the discussion from the previous page regarding the natural virtue and justice of the ancient northern peoples. While the previous page focused on the moral character of the Scythians and Germans, this page shifts to the specific judicial roles of the Druids and priests, using classical authorities to show how spiritual and legal authority were intertwined in ancient Gaul and Germany.</meta>

<page-num>427</page-num>

<header>CONCERNING THE GERMAN GODS.</header>

...to be surpassed by instruction. Ignorance of vices is so much more profitable among them than the knowledge of virtue is among others. For this reason, according to Diodorus Siculus in Book V of his *Historical Library*, they honor their Philosophers and Theologians with exceptional distinction. For they are considered the most just of all, and according to the testimony of Strabo in Book VII of his *Geography*, both private and public legal judgments are entrusted to their good faith by common consensus. Hence, as the Divine Caesar says in Book VI of his *Commentaries on the Gallic War*, they decide on almost all public and private controversies. At a certain time of year, they assemble in a consecrated place within the territory of the Carnutes <note>A Celtic tribe located in central Gaul, near modern-day Chartres; their territory was considered the spiritual "navel" or center of the region.</note>, which is considered the central region of all Gaul. Everyone with a dispute gathers here from all directions and obeys their decrees and judgments. If any crime has been committed, if a murder has occurred, or if there is a dispute regarding an inheritance or property boundaries, they are the ones who decide the matter and establish rewards and punishments. Furthermore, according to Tacitus in his book *On the Customs of the Germans*, no one is permitted to bind, punish, or even flog a person except the priests—not as a form of criminal penalty, nor by order of a general, but as if commanded by God. Silence is also commanded in the assembly by the priest, who at that time possesses the right of enforcement. Natalis Comes <note>Natale Conti (1520–1582), an influential Italian mythologist whose work was standard for understanding classical references in the Renaissance.</note> writes quite skillfully about the Greeks in Book IX [of his work].

---

<margin>* To inflict capital punishment on the accused was once not considered a mark of infamy. In the most ancient times, the priests and Druids themselves carried out the law, binding and flogging [offenders], as Caesar testifies in Book V <note>Though the text cites Book V, Caesar’s primary description of the Druids is found in Book VI of the *Gallic Wars*.</note>. Compare the celebrated Keysler <note>Johann Georg Keysler (1693–1743), a German scholar of northern antiquities.</note> in *Select Northern and Celtic Antiquities*, page 166 and following. Concerning Duke Henry of Lüneburg executing a sentence of hanging, read Krantzius in *Saxonia*, Book X, chapter 30, page 278. Regarding Count Baldwin of Flanders, see Lipsius, *Political Monitor and Examples*, Book 2, chapter 9.</margin>
