<header>ELIAS SCHEDIUS</header>

IX. The author of the *Mythology* <note>original: "Mythol."; likely referring to the influential mythographer Natalis Comes (1520–1582), whose work "Mythologiae" was a standard reference for classical lore.</note> writes that it was brought about that great reverence, sacrifices, and religion were accorded to the Gods and to the priests themselves, because among the Greeks, priests were chosen only from the most noble families and participated in all public councils. For, just as if the Gods—to whom we must believe nothing is unknown—were present, so too in the presence of the priests, all public deliberations were proposed. This was seen with the *Manteis* <note>original: "Mantibus"; from the Greek *manteis*, meaning seers or diviners who interpreted the will of the gods through omens.</note> among the Athenians, and with the Augurs <note>Priests in the ancient world who interpreted the will of the gods by observing the flight of birds.</note> who sat beside the King among the Spartans. Nor would they undertake any public or private business of great weight after consultation until they had consulted the Delphic Oracle, or the Oracle of Ammon <note>original: "Ammonium"; the famous oracle of Zeus-Ammon in the Siwa Oasis of Egypt.</note>, or the Oracle of Dodona <note>original: "Dodonæum"; the oldest Hellenic oracle, where the god Zeus was said to speak through the rustling leaves of a sacred oak tree.</note>, or had sought the will of the Gods themselves by some other means. 

Thus, in subsequent times, it became established by custom, and was later confirmed by laws, that the senate could not be legitimately held except in the Temples of the Gods or in sacred places; it was as if they made the Gods themselves witnesses to everything that was done and said, and to their own conscience and equity. Afterward, indeed, the wisest bringers of civil laws each introduced various Gods as the authors of their laws, since every law was considered trivial and empty if it did not have the consensus of the immortal Gods. From this, the ancient Theology of the ancestors began to attract the studies and minds of men to itself. *Thus says that author.* 

Hence, at the council of the Druids, as is evident from the Divine Caesar in Book VI of his *Commentaries on the Gallic War* and Tacitus in his book *On the Customs of the Germans*, it is permitted to bring accusations and even to seek the death penalty. A distinction of punishments is made based on the crime: Traitors and deserters they hang from trees; the cowardly, the unwarlike, and those who have shamed their bod— <note>original: "corpore"; the text cuts off mid-word, likely continuing on the next page to describe "shameful acts against the body" which were punished by drowning in marshes.</note>

<meta>This page continues Schedius's exploration of ancient Germanic and Celtic judicial systems. While the previous page discussed how the Greeks integrated divine authority into public councils, this page examines the specific punishments used by the Germans and Druids to maintain social and religious order, moving from physical capital punishment to the spiritual "death" of excommunication.</meta>

<page-num>429</page-num>

<header>ON THE GERMAN GODS.</header>

...those infamous for their deeds are drowned in mud and swamp, with an iron grate thrown over them. <note>original: "infames cœno, ac palude, injecta insuper ferrea crate mergunt." Schedius is quoting Tacitus, *Germania* 12, describing how the ancient Germans distinguished between types of crimes through the method of execution.</note> The diversity of punishment looks to this principle: that crimes of violence <note>original: "scelera"</note> ought to be exposed to the light while they are being punished, but shameful acts of disgrace <note>original: "flagitia"; often referring to unnatural or hidden vices</note> should be buried and hidden away. But for lighter offenses, according to the measure of the penalty, those convicted are fined a certain number of horses and cattle. For even homicide is atoned for by a specific number of herds and livestock, and the entire household receives satisfaction. This is a practice useful for the public good, because feuds <note>original: "inimicitiæ"</note> are more dangerous in a state of high liberty. Moreover, a portion of the fine is paid to the King or the state, and a portion is paid to those who are being avenged, or to their relatives.

## CHAPTER XVI.

*Severity must be applied. Hence the Druids used to forbid the wicked from the sacred rites. The same custom existed among the Greeks. The excommunicated. The Ban. Its power. Those under the ban are not members of the Empire. They lose their privileges. The Bolt of Jupiter <note>original: "Diale fulmen"; a metaphor for excommunication, likening it to a divine strike from Jupiter that removes one from the community.</note>. Burial denied in ancient times to the impious. As also to usurers, Jews, the excommunicated, and those who took their own lives <note>original: Αὐτοχείροις (*Autocheirois*).</note>.*

Severity is necessary to stir up religious devotion: for without it, no government—let alone religion—can remain secure for long. Therefore, punishment was devised to restrain the minds of men, lest the state or religion should crumble. For, if any person, whether a private citizen or a public official—as Julius Caesar testifies in Book VI of his *Commentaries on the Gallic War*—did not abide by the decree of the Druids, they would forbid him from the sacrifices. This punishment was the most severe among them. Those who were thus interdicted were counted among the number of the impious...

## CHAPTER XV.

*They prevent wars. The authority of the Priests among the Romans. An attendant <term>Lictor; an officer attending a magistrate, carrying the fasces</term> preceded them. The curule chair <term>Sella curulis; a folding inlaid chair used as a seat of high authority</term>. The litter. The ceremonial cap. The carriage. The dignity of the Vestal Virgins.*

They possessed such great authority that those about to engage in battle <note>original: "Martem collaturi," literally "those about to bring Mars together," referring to joining in combat.</note>, as Strabo testifies in Book IV of his *Geography*, would desist at their command. Diodorus Siculus, in Book V of his *Library*, notes that both enemies and friends listen to these priests, as well as to the lyric poets, not only in matters of peace but even in wars. These men often step into the middle of opposing battle lines while the armies are fighting with drawn swords and leveled spears; as if they were taming wild beasts with incantations, they break up the battles. Thus, even among the most ferocious Barbarians, anger yields to wisdom, and Mars <note>The god of war.</note> respects the Muses <note>original: "Mars reveretur Musas." The Muses represent the arts, music, and the civilizing influence of knowledge.</note>.

But also among the Romans, the office of the high priesthood reached such a pinnacle of honor and excellence that when the Praetor Gnaeus Cornelius insulted Marcus Aemilius Lepidus, the Chief Priest <term>Pontifex Maximus; the supreme head of the Roman state religion</term>, a fine was imposed; they believed the priest was closest in rank to royal dignity. For an attendant <term>lictor</term> would appear before him, and he was distinguished by a royal curule chair and a litter <note>A portable couch or sedan chair.</note>, which he was accustomed to keep visible before his entrance; at his doors, as a sign of his splendid dignity, a green laurel was seen fixed. And while others who had held high offices were compelled to give an account of their administration, the Chief Priest, because of the majesty of the office he held, could most especially be compelled to give an account; <note>The Latin "maxime cogi poterat" suggests a high degree of accountability, though historically the Pontifex Maximus was often exempt from secular judgment; the author may be emphasizing his supreme responsibility to the gods or the state.</note> and for them...

so that there might be even more dignity in their command and power, it was permitted for them to wear the ceremonial cap <term>galerus; a skullcap made of the skin of a sacrificed animal, typically worn by the Flamines and Pontiffs</term> and to enter the city in a carriage <term>carpentum; a two-wheeled covered wagon, usually reserved for women of high rank or religious officials</term>, just as was allowed for the rest of the priests. <margin>* Regarding the Vestal Virgins, besides the specific work of Justus Lipsius, see also Saubertus *On Sacrifices*, Chapter VIII; Casalius *On the City of Rome*, page 372; Johannes Braunius *On the Clothing of Priests*, pages 537, 542; Licetus *On Lamps*, pages 38, 190, 415; Ezechiel Spanheim in his *Discourse on the Coin of the Smyrnaeans, or on Vesta and the Greek Prytanes*, Volume V of Graevius’s *Treasury*; and Thomas Hyde *On the Religion of the Persians*, page 142 and following.</margin>
The dignity of the Vestal Virgins * among the Romans was also once of the highest order, and mention of no other divine cult occurs more frequently in Roman histories than that of Vesta. Numa <note>Numa Pompilius, the legendary second king of Rome, credited with establishing many of its religious institutions.</note> established a salary for them from the public treasury and made them venerable through their vow of perpetual virginity and other ceremonies. They used a carriage, and magistrates would rise in their presence; if they happened to encounter someone being led to execution, that person was exempt from the death penalty. However, an oath was required from the Virgin to testify that the encounter had been accidental and unplanned, rather than premeditated. *Plutarch in his Life of Numa; Aulus Gellius, Book I, Chapter XII, Attic Nights; Alexander ab Alexandro, Book V, Chapter XII, Genial Days.*

## CHAPTER XVI.

->*Concerning the disciples of the Druids. An oath was usually required from them. The duration of their training. Sons were not present with their parents. The disciples of the Romans. Stirred by such great honors and rewards, as the Divine Caesar reports in Book VI of his *Commentaries on the Gallic War*, many join this training of their own accord, and others are sent by their parents and relatives. To those who keep the oath, may it be well and may the AFOREMENTIONED GODS be favorable; but to those who break the oath, may the opposite occur.” This means: I adjure all who come across this, by the sacred circle of the Sun, the irregular courses of the Moon, and the powers of the remaining Stars, and the Zodiacal circle, that they keep these things in hidden places; nor should they communicate them to the unlearned or the profane—

<note>Hippocrates (c. 460 – c. 370 BCE) was a Greek physician often called the "Father of Medicine." Schedius includes this oath to demonstrate that ancient "secret" or specialized knowledge, whether in medicine, astrology, or Druidic religion, was protected by sacred bonds between teacher and student.</note>

*to hold my teacher in this art equal to my own parents; to share my life with him, and to supply him with the necessities of life if he be in need; to regard his offspring as equal to my brothers in the male line, and to teach them this art, if they desire to learn it, without fee or written contract; to impart precepts, oral instruction, and all other learning to my own sons, to those of my teacher, and to pupils who have signed the covenant and taken an oath according to the medical law, but to no one else,* <note>original: "ἡγήσασθαι δὲ τὸν διδάξαντά με τὴν τέχνην ταύτην, ἴσα καὶ γενέτῃσι ἐμοῖσι, καὶ βίου κοινώσασθαι, καὶ χρεῶν χρηΐζοντι μετάδοσιν ποιήσασθαι, καὶ γένος τὸ ἐξ ἑωυτέου ἀδελφοῖς ἴσον ἐπικρινέειν ἄῤῥεσι, καὶ διδάξειν τὴν τέχνην ταύτην, ἢν χρηΐζωσι ἄνευ μισθοῦ καὶ ξυγγραφῆς, παραγγελίης τε, καὶ ἀκροήσιος, καὶ τῆς λοιπῆς ἁπάσης μαθήσιος μετάδοσιν ποιήσασθαι υἱοῖσί τε ἐμοῖσι καὶ τοῦ ἐμὲ διδάξαντος, καὶ μαθηταῖς συγγεγραμμένοις τε καὶ ὡρκισμένοις νόμῳ ἰητρικῷ, ἄλλῳ δὲ οὐδενί"</note> *that is, that I will bestow upon my teacher, by whom I was taught this art, no less than upon a parent by whom I was begotten: sharing my life with him, and providing all things which I understand to be necessary for him according to my strength: holding his offspring in the place of brothers, teaching them this art without payment and without agreements: freely and faithfully handing down all precepts to my own children and the children of my teacher, and to other disciples who have bound themselves by the laws of medicine and have been sworn, and to no one else besides.*

Meanwhile, during the time they were devoting effort to their discipleship, they did not go out, nor was it permitted for them to be present with their parents: as the **Divine Caesar** records in Book VI of his *Commentaries on the Gallic War*; *In the other customs of life, they differ from others in this respect: that they do not permit their own children to approach them publicly unless they have grown up so that they can sustain the duty of military service; a son—*

<note>Julius Caesar’s "Gallic War" is the primary source for the customs of the Druids. Here, Schedius highlights the strict separation between the private world of education and the public life of the community, noting that Druidic sons were kept apart from their fathers until reaching adulthood.</note>

<summary>Schedius compares the secretive oaths of ancient astrologers and the medical students of Hippocrates to the educational rigors of the Druids, emphasizing the sacred bond between teacher and student. He cites Caesar to illustrate that Druid youths were kept in isolation from their families until they reached the age of military service.</summary>

## CHAPTER XVII.

*The disciples learned verses. In early life, Poets are to be read. Pedagogues. Scholastics. Rhetoricians. Sophists. Orators. They did not rush their students. The reason why.*

The disciples of the Druids <note>Ancient Celtic priests, teachers, and judges whose influence extended into Germanic territories; their training was famously rigorous and oral-based.</note> are said to learn a great number of verses by heart. Julius Caesar testifies to this in Book VI of his *Commentaries on the Gallic War*, and he believes they established this for two reasons: because they did not wish their secret teachings to be spread among the common people, nor did they want those who learn to rely on the written word and thus pay less attention to memory. It commonly happens to many that, with the help of writing, they relax their diligence in learning thoroughly and allow their memory to weaken. Petronius Arbiter <note>A Roman courtier and writer under Nero, author of the *Satyricon*.</note> also advises this in his *Satires*:

-> Let him give his first years to verses, <-
-> And drink from the Mæonian spring with a happy heart. <-
<note>Mæonia is an ancient name for Lydia, the legendary home of Homer; the "Mæonian spring" refers to Homer’s epic poetry.</note>

Lucian <note>A Syrian-Greek satirist of the 2nd century AD.</note> in *Lexiphanes*: <note>original Greek: ἀρξάμεν@ δὲ ἀπὸ ἀρίστων ποιητῶν καὶ ὑποδιδασκάλοις αὐτ@ ἀναγν@, μέτιθι ἐπὶ τοὺς ῥήτορας καὶ τῇ ἐκείνων φωνῇ συντραφείς, ἐπὶ τὰ Θουκυδίδου καὶ Пλάτων@ ἐν καιρῷ μέτιθι</note> That is: starting with the best poets and listening to the teachers of life, move on afterwards to the rhetoricians; once accustomed to their way of speaking, move in due time to the writings of Thucydides and Plato. Julius Severianus <note>A 5th-century Roman author on rhetoric.</note> says: "The frequent reading of Speeches, and Histories, and Poems is necessary." Servius <note>A 4th-century grammarian famous for his commentary on Virgil.</note>, on *Eccl. IV*, says that in a proper order, first the Poets, then the Historians, and finally the Philosophers must be read. Among the Romans, those who were pedagogues or instructors of youth were called "Scholastics" <note>original: "Scholastici"</note>.

<summary>This page discusses the oral education of the Druids as described by Julius Caesar, emphasizing why they preferred memory over writing, and outlines the classical curriculum order of poets, historians, and philosophers.</summary>

The Emperor Antoninus <note>Better known as Marcus Aurelius, the Stoic philosopher-emperor.</note> in his book *On His Own Life* <note>The *Meditations*.</note> says: <note>original Greek: καὶ τὸ μήτε ἀντι- να εἰπεῖν, μήτε ὅτι οἰκογενὴς βέρνακλος, μήτε ὅτι σχολαστικὸς, ἀλλὰ ὅτι ἀνὴρ πέπειρος</note> *and this, neither about to say to another, nor because he is a Sophist, nor because he was born in our house, a domestic servant, nor because he is a Scholastic, but because he is a mature man.* <note>The Emperor is describing the qualities of a man valued for his maturity and character rather than his professional status as a teacher or household-born slave (*vernaculus*).</note> And Rhetoricians were called by the same name. The author of the *Dialogue on Famous Orators* <note>Often attributed to Tacitus.</note> writes: *Young boys are led onto the stages of the Scholastics, whom they call Rhetoricians.* Lucian, in his *Precepts for Rhetoricians*: <note>original Greek: ἐρωτᾷς, ὅπως ἂν ῥήτωρ γένοιο, καὶ τὸ πάνδημον ὄνομα σοφιστὴς εἶναι δόξης</note> that is, *you ask how one may become a Rhetorician, and for the universal name of 'Sophist' to be considered an honor.*

Marius Victorinus <note>A 4th-century grammarian and rhetorician.</note> in his Commentary on Book 1 of Cicero’s *On Invention*, defines the Rhetorician and the Sophist in this way: *A Rhetorician is one who teaches literature and transmits the arts of eloquence. A Sophist is one with whom the craft of speaking is learned.* Advocates <note>In Rome, "advocates" were legal representatives or lawyers.</note> are also called Scholastics in Law 2 of the *Theodosian Code* <note>A collection of Roman laws compiled in the 5th century.</note> concerning the granting of advocates, and in the law *Praeter* of the Code concerning the profits of advocates. They are also called Scholars, as seen in Law 3 regarding the privileges of Scholars. Julius Severianus <note>A minor Latin author of a manual on rhetoric.</note> says: *Ancient Orators are to be read and current ones are to be heard. Beyond this, one must frequently write, act, and declaim. And no one can be instructed in the oratorical arts unless they have natural talent and frequent study. First, let there be a certain natural power of the mind, then voice, lung capacity, grace, moderation, and patience for labor.*

And it was most excellent that the Druids <note>Schedius compares the long, oral training of the Celtic Druids to the best practices of classical education.</note> did not rush their disciples, lest the finest talents be corrupted by premature haste. Petronius Arbiter <note>A Roman courtier and satirist under Nero.</note> treats this very well in his *Satires*: *For first, like all things, they surrender their hopes to ambition: then, when they hurry toward their desires, they thrust their still-raw studies into the forum,*

...[they want], and they clothe children, while still newborns, in eloquence—an art which they admit is the greatest of all. But if they permitted the progression of books to take place, so that studious youths might be tempered by rigorous reading, so that they might steady their minds with the precepts of wisdom, so that they might dig out words with a sharp pen <note>original: "atroci stylo"; implying a laborious or rigorous style of writing</note>, and listen for a long time to what they wished to imitate, then nothing that merely pleased children would seem magnificent to them: that grand oratory would then possess the weight of its own majesty. Now, boys play in schools, and youths appear in the forum <note>The public square where legal and political business was conducted.</note>, and what is more shameful than either: whatever one learns wrongly, he is unwilling to admit in old age. Thus, the Author of the *Dialogue on Famous Orators* <note>The *Dialogus de oratoribus*, a work on the decline of rhetoric traditionally attributed to Tacitus.</note> rightly writes that the mind must first be imbued with the honorable arts, recording it thus:
> "The ancients persuaded themselves of these things, and they understood that to accomplish these things, there was a need not to declaim in the schools of the Rhetoricians, nor to exercise the tongue and voice in fictitious controversies that in no way approached the truth; but rather to fill the heart with those arts in which one disputes concerning good and evil, the honorable and the shameful, the just and the unjust."

<margin>* Concerning the Germans who were formerly ignorant of the secrets of letters, see *Heumann's Poecile*, Vol. I, Part V, no. 9.</margin>

However, it must not be believed that the Celts or Germans were entirely devoid of letters; inasmuch as Caesar, in the fourth book of his *Commentaries on the Gallic War* <note>original: "Cæs. l. IV. comm. Bell. Gall."</note>, writes: *they use Greek letters in almost all other matters, both public and private records.* And in Book 1, he relates that *tablets written with Greek letters were found in the camp of the Helvetii <note>A Celtic tribe living in what is now Switzerland.</note> and brought to Caesar, on which tablets a detailed account had been made, by name, of the number who had left home who were able to bear arms, and likewise separately the boys, the old men, and the women: the sum total of all these people was 263,000 <note>original: "CCLXIII"</note> Helvetii, 36,000 <note>original: "XXXVI"</note> Tulingi, 13,000 <note>original: "XIII"</note> Latobrigi, 23,000 <note>original: "XXIII"</note> Rauraci, and 32,000 <note>original: "XXXII"</note> Boii. Of those who could bear arms, there were about 92,000 <note>original: "XCII"</note>. The total sum was about 368,000 <note>original: "CCCLXVIII."</note>*

And Tacitus, in his book *On the Customs of the Germans* <note>Commonly known as the *Germania*.</note>, reports that certain monuments and burial mounds inscribed with Greek letters still exist on the borders of Germany and Raetia <note>A Roman province encompassing parts of modern-day Switzerland, Germany, and Austria.</note>. Aventinus <note>Johannes Aventinus (1477–1534), a Bavarian Renaissance humanist and historian.</note>, in the first book of his *Annals of the Boii*, relates that Tuisto <note>original: "Tuyfconem"; a legendary ancestor-god of the Germanic peoples mentioned by Tacitus.</note> also invented letters. The Roxolani <note>A Sarmatian people living near the Black Sea.</note> still use their own letters, he says, which are not unlike the Greek. There is preserved at Regensburg <note>original: "Reginoburgi"</note> in the Church of Saint Emmeram <note>original: "B. Haimerani"</note> a very ancient charter <note>original: "diploma"</note> given by Charlemagne <note>original: "Carolo M."</note>, written indeed in the Latin language, but with different letterforms. Some think they are Lombardic, others Greek; they are very similar to Greek. Truly our own language, especially that of the Saxons, [is related to Greek] by the nature and power of its letters, the force and number of diphthongs, the pronunciation of syllables, the clarity, the articles, and the accent (which our [language]...

<meta>catchword: language</meta>

...the body. But the Mind is properly that which we call Man—namely, a divine living being which can in no way be compared to other animals, but most rightly to the Gods themselves, if it is not even said to excel them. For the dwellers in heaven cannot descend to earth without leaving heaven; yet man, although he stands upon the earth, measures the heavens with his thought. Thus, a terrestrial man is like a mortal God, while a heavenly God is like an immortal man.

Anacharsis: <note>Anacharsis (c. 6th century BCE) was a Scythian philosopher who traveled to Athens and became known as a "wise barbarian" for his pithy, observational wisdom.</note>
**The body is the instrument of the soul, but the soul is of God.**
<note>original Greek: ψυχῆς ὄργανον τὸ σῶμα, Θεοῦ δὲ ἡ ψυχή</note>
*that is, the body is the instrument of the soul, but the soul belongs to God.*
<note>original Latin: anima instrumentum corpus, Dei vero anima.</note>

Plato in the *Crito*: <note>The author attributes this quote to the *Crito*, though the sentiment and phrasing are famously central to Plato's *Phaedo*, which discusses the soul's journey after death.</note>
**But the soul, being invisible, departs to such another place, noble, pure, and invisible—to Hades** (meaning the house <note>original: οἶκον / domum</note> of the unseen) **truly to the good and wise God.**
<note>original Greek: ἡ δὲ ψυχὴ χἄρα τὸ ἀειδὲς, εἰς τοιοῦτον τόπον ἕτερον οἴχεται, γενναῖον καὶ καθαρὸν καὶ ἀειδῆ εἰς ᾅδε, ... ὡς ἀληθῶς παρὰ τὸν ἀγαθὸν καὶ φρόνιμον Θεὸν</note>
*that is, the soul, which is a certain invisible thing, migrates into a certain other place, excellent, pure, invisible, and hidden from us, truly to the good and wise God.*
<note>original Latin: anima vero, quæ invisibile quiddam est, in quendam alium locum migrat, excellentem, purum, invisibilem, nobis occultum, revera ad bonum sapientemque Deum.</note>

Plotinus, *Enneads* IV, Book III: <note>Plotinus (c. 204–270 CE) was the founder of Neoplatonism. His *Enneads* explored the mystical union between the individual soul and the "One" or the Divine.</note>
The soul has commerce with the Gods and is immortal; and Plato says that if it were granted to see the soul in its pure and clear state, we would undoubtedly speak of it thus. But because we sometimes see it disturbed, we judge it to be neither divine nor immortal; yet surely, he who desires to rightly weigh the nature of a thing ought to consider it naked, in its own substance, and stripped of everything foreign to it. For whatever is mixed with or joined to things hinders a perfect knowledge of them. 

Therefore, let each person look upon themselves stripped of every foreign thing, so that they are nothing but soul; they will surely feel themselves to be immortal when, I say, they have contemplated themselves in their pure and truly intellectual nature. <note>original Greek: ὃν γὰρ καλοῦσι πολλοὶ θάνατον, αὐτὸ τοῦτο ἦν ἀθανασίας ἀρχὴ, καὶ γένεσις μέλλοντος βίου: τῶν μὲν σωμάτων τῷ αὐτῷ νόμῳ καὶ χρόνῳ φθειρομένων, τῆς δὲ ψυχῆς ἐπὶ τὸν αὐτῆς τόπον καὶ βίον ἀνακαλουμένης</note>

*Aristotle in his book On the Soul:* **This intellect can be separated from the body, is not mixed with it, and is by its own substance incapable of suffering change.** <note>original: impassibilis</note> **It exists and subsists in actuality and through itself. Therefore, once it is separated, it remains immortal and eternal. Finally, it has nothing in common with the body, because it is none of those things that exist before it understands; and consequently, which of all the bodies could it possibly be?**

*Also, in Book II of On the Soul:* **What God is always, we are according to our own measure.** <note>The author suggests that humans participate in divinity in a limited, proportional way.</note> **But He is always separated from corporeal things; therefore, we also can eventually be separated.**

*Epictetus:* **Should we not be ashamed to lead a dishonorable life and yield to adversity? We are the kinsmen of God: we came from Him; let it be permitted for us to return to that place from whence we set out.**

*Heraclitus:* **We live the death of the blessed**—*that is, this life is a series of deaths*—**and we die into that same life**—*that is, our death is an entry into the blessed life.*

...to man, God gave reason and mind. *Philolaus* <note>Philolaus (c. 470–385 BCE) was a Greek Pythagorean philosopher who argued that the soul was harmoniously joined to the body.</note> *however, says:* the soul is bound to the body because of sins, and is buried in it as if in a tomb. <note>original: "animam corpori propter peccata alligatam esse, in eoque tanquam tumulo sepultam." But he anticipates the sentence of his Judge, because he condemns himself by death. *Alexander of Aphrodisias,* <note>A celebrated commentator on Aristotle (active c. 200 CE) known as "the second Aristotle."</note> *Book I of Problems:* This mind, which is within us, comes from the outside and is incorruptible. I say "incorruptible" because its nature is such, and this is that very thing which *Aristotle* proclaims glides in from the outside. *Book II of Problems:* If someone’s brain is damaged, the rational soul will not correctly perform the actions that proceed from the brain. Yet, within itself, it will nonetheless remain the same in regard to its essence, faculty, and power—immutable in its immortality—so that if it should obtain a good organ <note>The "organ" here refers to the physical body or brain, viewed as a tool used by the soul.</note> again, it could perform those actions no differently than before. *Claudius Galen in the book On the Doctrines of Hippocrates and Plato:* We must confess one of two things (which *Aristotle and the Stoics* are afraid to deny): that the soul is an ethereal and luminous body, or certainly an incorporeal substance, of which the [physical] body is like a vehicle, which communicates with other bodies through an intermediary. *And in his book On Conception:* Our soul is a certain flow from the universal soul, descending from the heavenly region; it is a substance capable of knowing, which always strives for the journey back to heaven and to a substance similar and kindred to itself. It willingly leaves behind these lower things to seek higher ones; it is a partaker of celestial divinity, and while it contemplates the things above the heavens, it often presents itself to Him who governs all things. *Phavor-* <note>The text cuts off mid-name; likely referring to Phavorinus of Arles, a Roman philosopher and rhetorician.</note>

...Favorinus <note>Favorinus of Arelate (c. 80–160 CE) was a Roman philosopher and orator who famously argued that "nothing is great on earth but man, and nothing in man but the mind."</note> says: **Nothing on earth is great except man; nothing in man is great except the mind; if you climb to that height, you transcend the heavens; if you look down upon the body, and then look up to the heavens, you see yourself as a fly, and even something less than a fly.**

*Strabo, in Book 15 of his Geography:* <note>Strabo (c. 64 BCE–24 CE) was a Greek geographer and historian. Here he discusses the beliefs of the Brahmans of India, comparing them to Greek philosophy.</note> **For one must think of this life here as being like the height of gestation; but death is a birth into the true and happy life for those who have devoted themselves to philosophy.** <note>original Greek: "νομίζειν μὲν γὰρ χρὴ τὸν μὲν ἐνθάδε βίον, ὡς ἂν ἀκμὴν κυομένων εἶναι. τὸν δὲ θάνατον, γένεσιν εἰς τὸν ὄντως βίον..."</note> *That is: this life must be thought of as a kind of vivid conception of men; but death is a birth to that true and happy life for those who have rightly philosophized.*

*Diodorus Siculus, in Book 1 of his Library:* <note>Diodorus Siculus (1st century BCE) was a Greek historian. He is known for his monumental universal history, "Bibliotheca historica."</note> **The Egyptians consider the time spent living to be of entirely little account; but they value most highly the memory of those who will be remembered after their end because of their virtue. They call the dwellings of the living "lodgings,"** <term>lodgings</term> <note>original Latin: "diversoria." The Greek "καταλύσεις" refers to temporary inns or places to unyoke animals, emphasizing that life is merely a brief stop on a longer journey.</note> **inasmuch as we inhabit them for only a short time.** *That is: the Egyptians surely think the time of the present life is to be made of small account, but the glory of the future, which is acquired through virtue, is to be esteemed most highly. They call our homes "inns," as if they were to be inhabited by us for only a brief duration.*

*Plutarch, in his book against Colotes the Epicurean:* <note>Plutarch (c. 46–119 CE) was a Greek Middle Platonist philosopher and biographer. Here he defends the immortality of the soul against the materialist views of the Epicureans.</note> **Death is a change of the soul, not its destruction.** <note>original Greek: "μεταβολὴ τῆς ψυχῆς, οὐ φθορά, ὁ θάνατος."</note> *Death is a change of place, not the extinction of the soul.*

*In his Platonic Questions:* **The soul, having partaken of mind, reason, and harmony, is not only a work of God, but also a part of Him. It was not made merely under Him, but from Him and out of Him.** <note>original Greek: "ἡ δὲ ψυχὴ νοῦ μετασχοῦσα... οὐκ ἔργον ἐστὶ τοῦ Θεοῦ μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ μέρος." This reflects the Platonic idea that the human soul shares a divine substance.</note> *That is: the soul, governed by reason and prudence, is not only a work of God, but also a certain part of God; and it is not just beneath Him, but from Him and out of Him.*

*Philo, in his book On the Creation of the World:* <note>Philo of Alexandria (c. 20 BCE–50 CE) was a Hellenistic Jewish philosopher who sought to harmonize the Hebrew Scriptures with Greek philosophy.</note> **The soul comes from nothing created...**

<note>original Latin: "Evolat. Hanc alta capitis fundavit in arce Mandatricem operum, prospecturamque labori." This poetic excerpt describes the soul or mind as a "commander" stationed in the head, the "citadel" of the body.</note>

And this is the most certain opinion concerning the state or immortality of souls. Now follows the second part of this doctrine: which concerns the <term>transmigration of souls</term> <note>Also known as "metempsychosis," the belief that after death, a soul moves into a new body.</note> into another body. Diodorus Siculus, in Book 5 of his *Library*, records that this belief also flourished among the Northern peoples. The opinion of Pythagoras <note>An ancient Greek philosopher (c. 570–495 BCE) famous for his teachings on reincarnation.</note> prevailed among the Celts: that the souls of men are immortal and, having entered into another body, they take up life again after a determined period of time. Julius Caesar, in Book 6 of his *Commentaries on the Gallic War*, writes: "Above all, they wish to persuade people of this: that souls do not perish, but after death pass from some into others." Lucan says in Book 1 of the *Pharsalia*:

->- - *If your songs speak known truths,*<-
->*Death is but the midpoint of a long life.* - - -<-
<note>original Latin: "Longae canitis si cognita vitae Mors media est." This famous line suggests that death is merely a transition in a continuous cycle of existence.</note>

And many of the ancient writers record that Pythagoras fostered this opinion. Hermias <note>A Christian apologist, likely Hermias the Philosopher (2nd or 3rd century CE), who wrote a satire on pagan Greek philosophies.</note>, the Christian Philosopher, criticizes this opinion with these words: *But when I look at myself, I am terrified of my body, and I do not know what to call it—a man, or a dog, or a wolf, or a bull, or a bird, or a serpent, or a dragon, or a chimera? For I am changed by the philosophers into all sorts of beasts: of the land, of the water, of the air; many-shaped, wild, tame, voiceless, vocal, irrational, and rational. I swim, I fly, I soar, I crawl, I run, I sit. There are even times when Empedocles* <note>A Greek philosopher who claimed he had previously been a boy, a girl, a bird, and a fish.</note> *makes me a shrub.* 

<note>original Greek: "ὅταν δὲ ἐμαυτὸν ἴδω, φοβέμαι τὸ σῶμα, καὶ οὐκ οἶδα ὅπως αὐτὸ καλέσω, ἄνθρωπον, ἢ κύνα, ἢ λύκον ἢ ταῦρον, ἢ ὄφιν, ἢ δράκοντα, ἢ χίμαιραν; εἰς πάντα γὰρ τὰ θηρία ὑπὸ τῶν φιλοσοφέντων μεταβάλλομαι, χερσαῖα, ἔνυδρα, πτηνὰ, πολύμορφα, ἄγρια, τίθασα, ἄφωνα, εὔφωνα, ἄλογα, λογικά. νήχομαι, ἵπταμαι, πέτομαι, ἕρπω, θέω, καθίζω. ἔστι δὲ ὅτε Ἐμπεδοκλῆς καὶ θάμνον μὲ ποιεῖ"</note>

That is to say: *But when I truly look at myself, I fear my body, and I do not know by what name to call it—whether man, or dog, or wolf, or bull, or bird, or serpent, or dragon, or chi-*

<margin>In the same place:</margin>
> *Souls are free from death; and always, having left*

> *All things change, nothing perishes; the spirit wanders, and from there*

> *it will; it passes from beasts into human bodies,*
> *and from ours into beasts, and never perishes through time.*
<note>original: "Morte carent animæ..." This is a classic definition of *metempsychosis*, or the transmigration of souls. The author uses Ovid's poetry to explain the philosophical belief that life is a continuous cycle where the spirit never truly dies, but merely changes its physical vessel.</note>

<margin>Horace, Book 2, Odes, Ode 20.</margin>
> *On no common or weak wing shall I be carried,*
> *a biformed poet, through the liquid air.*
<note>original: "Non inusitata, nec tenui ferar..." In this ode, the poet Horace describes himself transforming into a swan. By calling himself "biformed," he suggests that his identity exists in two states—the mortal man and the immortal bird/poet—echoing the themes of transformation discussed by the author.</note>

And the *divine* Maro <note>A common honorific for the Roman poet Virgil (Publius Vergilius Maro).</note> in *Book VI* of the Æneid:

> ->*All these, when they have rolled the wheel for a thousand years,*<-
> ->*God summons in a great column to the river Lethe:*<-
> ->*So that, indeed, forgetful of the past, they may revisit the vaulted sky above,*<-
> ->*And begin to wish to return again into bodies.*<-
<note>original: "Has omnes, ubi mille rotam volvere per annos..." from Virgil, *Aeneid* 6.748-751. The "wheel" refers to the cycle of time or purification; the River Lethe is the underworld stream of forgetfulness which souls drink from before being reborn so they do not remember their previous lives.</note>

Plato, moreover, the greatest <term>Philosopher</term><note>Latin: *summus Philosophus*.</note>, speaks thus in the *Meno*:
They say that the soul of man is immortal, and at one time it reaches an end—which they call dying—but at another time it is born again, and is never destroyed. For this reason, one must live out one's life in the holiest way possible. For those from whom Persephone shall receive the penalty for ancient grief, she gives back their souls to the sun above in the ninth year. From these arise noble kings, and men swift in strength and greatest in wisdom; and for the rest of time, they are called holy heroes by men. *That is: For they say that the soul of man is immortal, but then indeed it departs, which is called dying: and it returns again, but to perish and be extinguished never; wherefore life must be passed as holily as possible. For those who have already paid to Proserpina <note>Proserpina is the Latin name for the Greek goddess Persephone, queen of the underworld.</note> the penalties for ancient misery, she sends their souls back again to the sun above in the ninth year, and they become kings most excellent in glory, power, and wisdom, and are received into the number of the Gods or Heroes.*
<note>original: Plato, *Meno* 81b-c. In this passage, Socrates cites "priests and priestesses" or poets like Pindar to argue that learning is actually a process of "recollecting" knowledge the soul acquired in previous lives. The "ancient grief" or "ancient misery" refers to a primordial debt or sin that the soul must expiate before returning to a position of honor on Earth.</note>

...so that they were not only the first capable of producing human beings, but could even receive and protect newcomers, before coverings for the body were invented against the heat or cold, or before the defects of various places were softened by remedies sought out through art. They argued that **Egypt** had always been so temperate that neither the chills of winter nor the burning heats of the summer sun burdened its inhabitants: its soil was so fertile that no other land was more productive for the use of human nourishment. Therefore, it ought to be seen that men were first born there, where they could most easily be raised. 

In contrast, the **Scythians** <note>The Scythians were a nomadic people inhabiting the vast steppes of modern-day Ukraine and southern Russia; in antiquity, they were often contrasted with the "civilized" and settled Egyptians.</note> thought that the temperateness of the climate was no argument for antiquity. For they held that when Nature first distinguished the regions by the varying degrees of heat and cold, she immediately also generated animals capable of enduring those specific places: and indeed, the types of trees and crops were appropriately varied according to the condition of the regions. And just as the sky is harsher for the Scythians than for the Egyptians, so too are their bodies and minds more hardy. 

Furthermore, if the parts of the world which now exist were once a single unity, whether a <term>flood of waters</term> <note>original: *illuvies aquarum*</note> held the lands submerged at the beginning of things, or if **fire**, which also gave birth to the world, possessed all things: in either version of the origin, the Scythians take precedence. For if fire was the first possessor of all things, which, being gradually extinguished, gave a place for the lands, no part would have been separated from the fire by the rigor of winter sooner than the northern part, so much so that even now no region is more frozen with cold. **Egypt** and the whole **East**, however, were tempered most slowly, since even now they swelter under the scorching heat of the Sun. But if all lands were once submerged in the deep, surely the highest parts...

> ,,The same [Providence] at one moment adds strength to the earth, and at another diminishes it; and these opposites are arranged by divine providence for the harmony of the Universe. <note>original: *ad Universi concentum*</note> That same power introduced man into the World, gave him a body and limbs, heritages and co-heirs. Furthermore, it made sight and colors; yet sight and colors would be in vain without light. Therefore, it also created light itself. *Plutarch, On the Opinions of the Philosophers.* <note>Plutarch (c. 46–120 CE) was a Greek philosopher and biographer; this specific work, the *Placita Philosophorum*, is now often attributed to "Pseudo-Plutarch."</note> Certain others, otherwise students of Plato, twist his words in every way so that he might seem to deny the creation of the world and the soul, and to assert the eternity of time. But let them take care, lest by this reasoning they strip from him that excellent discourse of the Gods against the impious, than which nothing is more worthy of Plato, nor more Platonic. But what need is there to bring forward one or two passages? Since the *Timaeus* <note>Plato's dialogue *Timaeus* is the foundational Greek text describing the creation of the universe by a "Demiurge" or divine craftsman.</note> explains the creation of the world eloquently and by design. But one ought to believe that God is the Lord of all; therefore, He is also the creator of every individual thing. *Cicero, Book 1 of On Invention.* <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero (106–43 BCE), the Roman orator and statesman.</note> We were not born or created by chance or accident, but surely there was a certain power that took thought for the human race; nor would it produce or nourish that which, when it had exhausted all its labors, would then fall into the eternal evil of death. *Seneca, Book 1 On the Happy Life, Chapter 31.* <note>Seneca the Younger (c. 4 BCE – 65 CE), a Stoic philosopher and advisor to Nero.</note> And shall I not inquire what the beginnings of all things are, who the shaper of the world is, who separated all things when they were submerged in one mass and rolled up in inert matter? *Macrobius, Book 1 of the Saturnalia.* <note>Macrobius (c. 400 CE) was a Roman provincial and philosopher whose works preserved much ancient lore.</note> The world cannot but be quite new, since the knowledge of it does not exceed two thousand years. " 

And this is the truest opinion; from which even Lucretius <note>Titus Lucretius Carus (c. 99–55 BCE), a Roman poet and Epicurean philosopher who, despite being an atomist, argued the world had a beginning and would have an end.</note> in Book 5 of *On the Nature of Things* does not shrink:

Lucian used this term to mock Jesus, combining the idea of a philosopher/teacher with the "shameful" death of crucifixion.</note>—writes the following in his *Philopatris*: "God produced man from non-being into existence, and He is in heaven, watching both the just and the unjust; and He records their deeds and actions in books. He will repay all on that day which He Himself has appointed." <note>original Greek: "ἄνθρωπον ἐκ μὴ ὄντων Θεὸς ἐς τὸ εἶναι παρήγαγε..." This passage from the *Philopatris* (a dialogue traditionally attributed to Lucian but likely written later) reflects Christian doctrine regarding creation *ex nihilo* and the Last Judgment.</note> That is: *God brought forth man from nothing into essence; He is in heaven beholding the just and the unjust alike, and describing in books each one’s affairs and actions. He will repay all on that day which He Himself has predetermined.* In that place, you too shall endure your punishment, Lucian—you who, looking back upon the recognized light of truth, delivered your soul into the slavery of demons; you shall be their perpetual slave on account of your blasphemous mouth.

*The observation of time. They count nights. The night was prior. The Romans reckoned the day from midnight. Weddings celebrated at night. Boys carried torches before those being married. The color of Night.*

# ELIAS SCHEDIUS

<margin>See the celebrated Johann Georg Keysler in *Northern and Celtic Antiquities*, page 197 and following; and Cluverius, *Ancient Germany*, Book 1, Chapter 33.</margin>

In the observation of time, the Druids established a practice different from the Roman custom, as is clear from Tacitus's book *On the Manners of the Germans*: *they do not compute the number of days, as we do, but the number of nights. In this way they settle their affairs, and in this way they make their agreements: the night seems to lead the day.* <note>Tacitus (c. 56–120 AD) was a Roman historian; his work *Germania* is a primary source for the customs of the ancient Germanic tribes.</note> And the Divine Caesar in Book VI of his *Commentaries on the Gallic War* states: *they define the spans of all time not by the number of days, but of nights: and they observe birthdays, and the beginnings of months and years, in such a way that the day follows the night.* <note>Julius Caesar’s account of the Gallic Wars provides some of the earliest Roman descriptions of Druidic culture.</note> They correctly numbered the night first. For as the Poets relate, Night was first; as Aristophanes <note>An Athenian playwright known as the "Father of Comedy."</note> relates in *The Birds*:

->Chaos existed, and Night, and black Erebus first, and<-
->vast Tartarus;<-
->but there was neither earth, nor air, nor heaven.<-
<note>original Greek: "χάος ἦν, καὶ νὺξ, ἔρεβός τε μέλαν πρῶτον, καὶ τάρταρος εὐρὺς, γῆ δ' οὐδ' ἀὴρ οὐδ' οὐρανὸς ἦν." This passage describes the primordial void before the creation of the physical world.</note>
->*Chaos existed, and night, and black Erebus first, and dark Tartarus,*<-
->*but of the Earth there was neither air nor sky.*<-
<note>This is the Latin translation of the Greek verse above, which the author provides for his 17th-century readers.</note>

Hence Aratus <note>A Greek didactic poet (c. 315–240 BC) famous for his work on astronomy.</note> in his *Phaenomena* calls Night "ancient":

->But then ancient Night also placed the censer around that [constellation].<-
<note>original Greek: "Αλλ' ἄρα καὶ περὶ κεῖνο θυτήριον ἀρχαίη Νύξ." This refers to the constellation Ara (the Altar).</note>
->*But after ancient Night also placed the censer there.*<-
<note>The Latin translation of the Greek verse from Aratus.</note>

The same is called by Orpheus <note>The legendary poet and prophet of Greek myth; "Orphic" hymns were central to certain ancient mystery cults.</note> the parent of both men and Gods, while he sings thus:

->I shall sing of Night, the mother of the Gods and of men.<-
<note>original Greek: "Νύκτα Θεῶν γενέτειραν ἀείσομαι, ἠδὲ καὶ ἀνδρῶν."</note>

# ON THE GERMAN GODS

->I sing of Night, the mother of gods and men.<-

Moses also writes in Genesis, chapter 1, verse 5, that the first day consisted of "evening and morning." Indeed, as the notes of Tremellius and Junius observe, Moses places darkness, or evening, before the day and the light; this is partly because darkness existed first in time, as seen in verse 2. On this point, when Thales was asked whether the day or the night was created first, he replied: "One night was prior to the day," as recorded in the works of Laërtius. <note>Thales of Miletus (c. 624–546 BC) was one of the Seven Sages of Greece. Diogenes Laërtius was a biographer of Greek philosophers. The idea that darkness preceded light is a common theme in ancient cosmogonies.</note> Furthermore, it is because, following the logic of the Scriptures—which many nations have adopted—the civil day begins with the night.

Aulus Gellius, in Book III of his *Attic Nights*, writes that the Roman people also reckoned each day starting from midnight. Moreover, regarding the Tribunes of the plebs <note>The Tribunes were powerful Roman officials whose primary duty was to protect the common citizens (plebeians); by law, they could not be away from the city of Rome for a full day.</note>, who are not permitted to be absent from Rome for even a single day: when they depart after midnight and return after the lighting of the first lamps but before the following midnight, they are not said to have been absent for a "day." Since they returned before the sixth hour of the night <note>Midnight.</note>, they are considered to have spent some portion of that day within the city of Rome. Servius, commenting on that line in Virgil’s *Aeneid*, Book VI:

> *-- Under the first light of the Sun and its rising.*

*But, he says, Virgil spoke according to the Roman rite, by which the day is believed to begin at the middle of the night.* <note>Servius was a 4th-century commentator whose notes on Virgil are a primary source for Roman ritual and myth.</note> Even among the Romans, a new bride was led to her husband’s house at night, as Ambrose reports in *On Widows*: *When the night is conducted with lit torches. Does not the funeral procession seem to prepare more for a burial than the wedding chamber prepares...*

## CHAPTER XXII.

*They took care of sacrifices. Possessors of knowledge regarding the divine nature. Certain families among other nations. The Pinarii among the Romans. The Eumolpidae among the Athenians.*

As Caesar reports in Book 6 of his *Commentaries on the Gallic War*, the Germans or Celts utilized the <term>Druids</term> <note>The Druids were the high-ranking priestly class in ancient Celtic societies, responsible for religious rituals, legal judgments, and lore; Schedius here associates them with the Germanic tribes as well.</note> as administrators for their sacrifices. According to Diodorus Siculus in Book 5 of his *Library*, it was not lawful for anyone to perform a sacrifice without a "philosopher." They believed that through these men—as they were conscious of the divine nature and, so to speak, interlocutors of the gods—sacrificial offerings of thanks should be presented to the GODS; and that through these intermediaries, blessings should be sought from them. Moreover, as Strabo records in Book 4 of his *Geography*, they never sacrificed if the Druids were absent; this is also evident from Tacitus’s book *On the Manners of the Germans* <note>Commonly known as the *Germania*, written around 98 AD.</note>. There were also, among some nations, specific families who alone were initiated into the sacred rites of certain Gods. Thus, for Hercules, there were the Pinarii and the Potitii <note>These were two of the most ancient noble families in Rome, traditionally tasked with the cult of Hercules at the Ara Maxima.</note>, as is clear from Virgil's *Aeneid* Book 8, Livy Book 1, and Macrobius Book 3, chapter 6. Furthermore, in the rites of Ceres <note>The Roman goddess of agriculture, equivalent to the Greek Demeter.</note> among the Athenians, only the Eumolpidae <note>A priestly clan at Athens who oversaw the Eleusinian Mysteries.</note> were initiated, because Eumolpus was the first to celebrate those rites, as Acesorus testifies with these words: <note>original: "κατοικῆσαι δὲ τὴν Ἐλευσῖνα ἱστοροῦσι, πρῶτον μὲν τοὺς αὐτόχθονας, εἶτα Θρᾷκας τοὺς μετ’ Εὐμόλπου παραγενομένους πρὸς βοήθειαν, εἰς τὸν κατ’ Ἐρεχθέως πόλεμον. τινὲς δέ φασι καὶ τὸν Εὔμολπον εὑρεῖν τὴν μύησιν τὴν συντελουμένην κατ’ ἐνιαυτὸν ἐν Ἐλευσῖνι, Δήμητρι, καὶ Κόρῃ"</note> *They report that the indigenous people first inhabited Eleusis, and then the Thracians, who arrived with Eumolpus to provide aid in the war against Erechtheus. Some say that Eumolpus also discovered the initiation ceremony performed annually in Eleusis for Demeter and Kore.* <note>Kore, or "the Maiden," is another name for Persephone, Demeter's daughter.</note> That is, they tell that the indigenous people had lived previously in Eleusis, but then the Thra-

Those who had fully received the teachings were then able to instruct others and properly preside over the sacrifices. From this, it is clear from Suetonius's *Life of Caesar* that among the Romans, the "care of the forests" was numbered among the duties of a consul. <note>Suetonius, *Life of Julius Caesar* 19. The Roman Senate once tried to limit the power of incoming consuls by assigning them the "care of forests and paths" as their official province, rather than prestigious military commands.</note> This was decreed by the Senate to check the authority of a consulship gained by force. On this matter, Maro <note>The full name of the poet Virgil was Publius Vergilius Maro.</note> wrote in his fourth *Eclogue* to Pollio: *If we sing of the forests, let the forests be worthy of a consul.* <note>Virgil, *Eclogue* 4.3. The author argues that Virgil was intentionally elevating the status of nature poetry to match the political dignity of his patrons.</note> He did this so that, just as the Senate had lowered the Consul's dignity to the level of the humble forests, Virgil himself might raise the forests to the height of the consulship through his verses and the dignity of this new subject matter. Thus says Scaliger in Book I of his *Poetics*, chapter 4. <note>Julius Caesar Scaliger (1484–1558) was a prominent Renaissance scholar whose work on literary theory was highly influential.</note> Indeed, according to Servius's commentary on Book III of the *Aeneid*, a "sacred grove" <note>original: "lucus."</note> is never mentioned without a religious connotation. <note>Servius was a 4th-century grammarian; his commentaries are a primary source for understanding how the Romans interpreted their own literature and religion.</note> Furthermore, the ancient Romans in the time of Numa <note>Numa Pompilius, the legendary second king of Rome, who was believed to have established the city's religious laws.</note> did not yet worship idols, but performed their sacred rites in groves. This is clearly indicated by Tertullian in his *Apology*, chapter 25:

*And although a superstitious curiosity was established by Numa, religious matters among the Romans did not yet consist of either idols or temples; it was a frugal religion with modest rites, with no massive structures rivaling the Capitol, but rather simple altars made of turf, vessels still made of Samian earthenware, steam rising from pots, and God himself to be found nowhere.* <note>original: "Samia," referring to the simple pottery from the island of Samos. Tertullian, an early Christian author, is highlighting the simplicity of early Roman religion to contrast it with the decadence of his own era.</note>

For the first hundred and seventy years, though they built temples, they made no statue, whether molded or painted. For...

<header>### CONCERNING THE GERMAN GODS. ###</header>

...is taken for a grove or a thicket of oaks. Isaiah 1:29. <note>Isaiah 1:29 refers to the people being ashamed of the "oaks" or "sacred gardens" where they practiced idolatry.</note> And this opinion is confirmed by the cited verse of Genesis 18:1, because Abraham stood under those trees which were in a grove. Mention of a grove also occurs in Exodus 3:2, Judges 6:25, 1 Samuel 22:7, 1 Kings 14:23 <note>The Latin text cites 1 Kings 34:25, likely a printer's error for 14:23 or a different chapter numbering</note>, 2 Kings 21:12, and 23:4, 7, where the Hebrew word *Asherah* <note>original Hebrew: הָאֲשֵׁרָה</note> denotes a grove. It is so called either because men sought happiness <note>The Hebrew root "ashar" means to be happy or blessed.</note> in it, as a sacred and religious place, or by "antiphrasis" <note>A rhetorical device where a word is used in a sense opposite to its literal meaning.</note>—meaning it is not at all blessed—just as in Latin a grove is called *lucus* because it is "not at all shining" <note>original Latin: *lucus, quasi minime lucidus*. This is a famous ancient pun, *lucus a non lucendo*, suggesting that because a thick grove is dark, it is ironically named after light (*lux*).</note>.

But this term also sometimes denotes a statue or a wooden object. For so that passage in Judges 6:25 and 28 concerning Gideon <note>Gideon was a judge of Israel who destroyed his father's altar to Baal and the sacred pole (Asherah) beside it.</note> is to be understood: he destroyed the altar of Baal and cut down the grove <note>original Hebrew: הָאֲשֵׁרָה (*Asherah*)</note> which was upon it. For the Hebrew word *alaw* <note>original Hebrew: עָלָיו</note> must be translated as "upon it," not "next to it" as some do. Indeed, the Seventy-Two Elders <note>The translators of the Septuagint, the ancient Greek version of the Old Testament.</note> translated it as "upon it" <note>original Greek: ἐπ' αὐτῷ</note>, that is, upon the altar itself. And Rabbi David Kimchi <note>A famous medieval Jewish biblical commentator and grammarian (c. 1160–1235).</note> writes under the root *Asherah* that every piece of wood that is worshipped is called an *Asherah*.

But no images of the Gods were seen in those groves among the Celts and Germans, because they said the divine power of the Gods should not be enclosed in any place, as all things ought to be free and open to them, as Cicero writes in Book 2 of *On the Laws*. The Persians likewise used to mock those who made statues and worshipped them, as Herodotus <note>Known as the "Father of History," Herodotus (c. 484–425 BCE) wrote about the customs of the Persian Empire in his first book, titled *Clio*.</note> testifies in *Clio*: *As for the Persians, I know they observe these laws: they do not consider it lawful to set up statues, temples, or altars, according to their institutions; but they even charge those who do so with folly.* <note>original Greek: Πέρσας δὲ, οἶδα νόμοισι τέτοισι χρεωμένους, ἀγάλματα μὲν, καὶ νηούς, καὶ βωμούς, οὐκ ἐννόμῳ ποιευμένους ἱδρύεσθαι; ἀλλὰ καὶ τοῖς ποιεῦσι μωρίην ἐπιφέρουσι</note> That is to say, *The Persians, as I have learned, use these laws; they do not erect images, temples, and altars, according to their customs, but even those who...*

*...those who do these things, they accuse of madness.* <note>The author continues a quote from the previous page, likely referencing those who criticize the use of physical idols.</note> And the Romans **had no image of the Gods for many years: for Numa taught that God is pure mind, entirely uncreated, and not subject to the sight of mortals, and could be expressed by no human industry.** <note>Numa Pompilius was the legendary second king of Rome. Ancient historians like Plutarch claimed that for 170 years, Romans had no statues of gods, following Numa's Pythagorean-like belief that the divine cannot be represented in material form.</note> Demosthenes, in his *Orations against Aristogiton*, agrees with this, saying that the human breast is a temple pleasing to God, and the best and most venerable temple is one fortified by justice, modesty, and observance of the laws.

It was, however, the custom that certain nations, both Asian and European, performed their sacred rites in high places. Regarding the Persians, Herodotus says in his first book, *Clio*: <note>original Greek: οἱ δὲ νομίζουσι, Διῒ μὲν ἐπὶ τὰ ὑψηλότατα τῶν ὀρέων ἀναβαίνοντες θυσίας ἔρδειν, τὸν κύκλον πάντα τοῦ οὐρανοῦ Δία καλέοντες</note> *It is a sacred law for them to ascend to the highest peaks of the mountains to sacrifice to Jupiter, calling the entire circle of the heavens 'Jupiter.'* <note>original Latin: *id est, Istis vero sanctum est, ut in altissimos montium vertices ascendentes Jovi sacrificent, Jovem, universi cæli ambitum appellantes.* Schedius uses "Jupiter" to translate the Greek "Zeus," a common practice in early modern scholarship.</note>

Regarding the Jews, it is written in 2 Kings chapter 17, verses 32 and 33: *So they feared the Lord and appointed for themselves certain priests, who performed sacred rites for them in the shrines of the **High Places**. Thus they feared the Lord, yet they also worshipped their own gods, according to the custom of the nations from which they had been carried away.* <note>original Latin: *excelsorum* — literally "the high things." In the Bible, "High Places" were hilltop altars often associated with pagan or unauthorized worship.</note> Mention of these "high places" is also made in 1 Kings chapter 15, verse 2, and 2 Chronicles chapter 15, verse 16. Indeed, mentions of high places are found six hundred times throughout the sacred scriptures, so it would be superfluous to list them all here.

Regarding the Greeks, Apollonius of Rhodes writes in the second book of the *Argonautica*:

Regarding the inhabitants of the island of Öland <note>A Swedish island in the Baltic Sea.</note> in the Gothic Sea, who placate a mountain as if it were a God, see Olaus Magnus, <note>Olaus Magnus (1490–1557) was a Swedish writer and archbishop famous for his "History of the Northern Peoples" (1555), which chronicled the customs and myths of Scandinavia.</note> Book II, Chapter 23. Pompeius Festus <note>A 2nd-century Roman grammarian.</note> says: *Altars [altaria] are so named from their height [altitudo], because the ancients used to perform sacrifices to the gods above on structures raised up from the earth.* Lutatius <note>Likely referring to Lutatius Placidus, a scholar of the 5th or 6th century.</note> writes: *We sacrifice to the heavenly ones on built-up hearths, from which also they are named altars, because while sacrificing we stretch our hands toward the heights.* For this reason, Jupiter is also called *Epakrios* <note>original Greek: ἐπάκριος Ζεὺς, "Zeus of the Peaks."</note> according to Hesychius, <note>An Alexandrian grammarian of the 5th or 6th century who compiled an extensive dictionary of Greek words.</note> because altars to Jupiter were usually established on the tops of mountains and promontories. Hence Melanthes <note>A lost Greek author who wrote on sacrifices; his fragments survive in later commentaries.</note> rightly says in his book on sacrifices: *Every mountain is called the mountain of Jupiter, because it was the custom of the ancients to perform sacrifices to the God who is the Highest in a high place,* that is, *every mountain is called a mountain of Jupiter, since the custom of the ancients was such that, for the God who exists as the most high, they made sacrifices in the heights.*

# ON THE GERMAN GODS.

...they are called "Hermean heaps" <note>original Greek: ἑρμαῖοι λόφοι (*hermaioi lophoi*), mounds of stones dedicated to the god Hermes (Mercury).</note>; people used to pile them up on public roads, and travelers would increase them by frequently throwing stones in honor of Mercury. For Mercury was placed in charge of journeys by the Pagans: hence he is also called "the god of the road" <note>original Greek: ἐνόδιος (*enodios*), meaning "of the way" or "roadside."</note>. ## CHAPTER XXIV.

*Not just any grove, but the oak was chosen. Nothing more sacred than the hard oak. The Oak is Jupiter to the Celts; a Holy Tree. Theodo, King of the Bavarians. The method of choosing a tree. A scimitar suspended in the grove. The reason. The custom of the Poles. Dead kings hung in oaks. Dedicated to Jupiter. Silvani, gods of the woods. Dryads. From where they are named. The Celts, however, did not choose just any groves, but only those in which the most ancient and massive oaks and hard-woods flourished. For the <term>Druids</term> <note>The high-ranking priestly class among the ancient Celts.</note> held nothing more sacred than the hard oak, as witnessed by <term>Pliny</term> <note>Pliny the Elder, a Roman author and naturalist (23–79 AD).</note> in Book 16, Chapter 44: "Already by themselves they choose groves of hard oaks: nor do they perform any sacred rites without that foliage, so that from this, they can be seen to be called Druids according to the Greek interpretation" <note>original Greek: *drus* (δρῦς) meaning "oak." Pliny suggests the name Druid is derived from the Greek word for the tree they worshipped.</note>. <term>Maximus Tyrius</term>, the Platonist, writes in his 38th dissertation that the Celts worshiped a high oak and solemnly addressed it by the name of Jupiter. There is also a law of <term>Liutprand</term>, King of the Lombards, which states: "Whoever [worships] at a tree, which..."

<meta>This page continues Schedius’s exploration of the sacred groves and religious symbols of the ancient Germanic and Celtic tribes. This was dedicated to the God. The <term>Druids</term> <note>Ancient Celtic priests and judges known for their ritual use of groves.</note>, by their own consensus and that of the whole people, would choose the most beautiful tree in the entire grove. They would take its protruding branches from both sides and join them again at the top to the firm and main trunk, so that those two "arms" were united with the stem. At the top, where they joined, they would inscribe the word <term>Thau</term> <note>original: "Thau"; referring to the letter Tau (T), which was often viewed as a symbol of the cross or a divine mark in ancient religious contexts.</note> into the bark, as they did also below where the arms branched out. On the right branch, they inscribed the name <term>Hesus</term> <note>A powerful Celtic deity often associated with Mars or Mercury.</note>; on the middle trunk, they inscribed <term>Taramis</term> <note>original: "τὸ Taramis"; the Celtic god of thunder, comparable to Jupiter or Thor.</note>; and on the left branch, <term>Belenus</term> <note>original: "τὸ Belenus"; a Celtic sun god often identified with Apollo.</note>. By this conjunction, they signaled that there was indeed one God, but in three persons—and yet these were only one God. <note>The author, writing in the 17th century, is attempting to find a precursor to the Christian Trinity within ancient pagan tree-worship.</note>

However, regarding what some write—that they worshipped a <term>scimitar</term> <note>original: "acinacem"; a short, curved sword or saber typical of ancient Eastern and steppe cultures.</note> in the groves—that seems to be for another reason. Indeed, concerning the worship of the scimitar, <term>Pomponius Mela</term> <note>A Roman geographer of the 1st century AD.</note> writes in Book II, Chapter 1: "Instead of statues, they dedicate swords and tents, and they strike down men as sacrificial victims." Regarding the discovery of the sword sacred to <term>Mars</term> <note>The Roman god of war.</note>, <term>Priscus</term> <note>A 5th-century diplomat and historian who famously visited the court of Attila the Hun.</note> discusses this in <term>Jordanes</term>' work *On the History of the Goths* <note>original: "de rebus Gothicis"; Jordanes was a 6th-century historian who chronicled the origins of the Gothic people.</note>; see also <term>Bonfinius</term> <note>Antonio Bonfini (1427–1502), a Renaissance historian who wrote a monumental history of Hungary.</note> in Book III, Decade I. <term>Clement of Alexandria</term> <note>A 2nd-century Christian theologian and philosopher.</note> in his *Exhortation to the Greeks* <note>original: "in Protrept."</note> says: "And indeed, the Scythians of old used to worship the scimitar." The same author says: "Warlike Mars is called <term>Ares</term> in Greek, from the words for <term>lifting up</term> and <term>acting like a man</term> <note>original: "ἀπὸ τῆς ἄρσεως καὶ ἀνδρώσεως"; Clement uses a Greek wordplay to link Ares to destruction and rising up in violence.</note>, that is, from killing and insurrection." For this reason, it seems to me that many, when they have fixed only a sword in the ground, are sacrificing as if to Mars. 

Furthermore, this was a custom of the <term>Scythians</term> <note>Nomadic people of the Eurasian steppes known for their prowess in war.</note>, as <term>Eudoxus</term> <note>An ancient Greek geographer and astronomer.</note> says in his second book *On the Circuit of the Earth*. They used to anoint the sacred scimitar with the blood of captives, as <term>Herodotus</term> <note>The 5th-century BC Greek historian often called the "Father of History."</note> records in Book IV; consult him. They seem to have used this symbol, maintaining this custom, in order to signify to everyone that they [defended] their religion just as...

> *Touch the table with your hand in the manner that those*

...moreover <note>original: *terea*, continuing the word *interea* from the previous page</note> from the established customs of sacrifices, the number three was employed in sacred rites. As Porphyrius <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 234–305 AD) who wrote extensively on vegetarianism and ritual</note> wrote in his book *On Sacrifice*, it was the custom of the ancients to first offer herbs, branches of trees, and animals along with flowers to the Spirits <note>original: *Dæmonibus*; in this context, these are intermediary beings between humans and the high gods, not "demons" in the modern sense</note> before they were to immolate <note>To offer as a sacrifice</note> to the most high God. This they indeed did three times, so that those very Spirits might carry the vows and prayers of the men performing the sacrifice to the supreme God, for they were believed to be the messengers of the supreme God. > *Even if the whole sea should run through my hands,*

<note>original Latin: "Et tota Thetys per meas currat manus / Harebit altum facinus." This quote is from Seneca's tragedy *Phaedra* (also known as *Hippolytus*), here cited via the Church Father Tertullian. "Thetys" is used poetically to represent the entire ocean.</note>

Tertullian, in Chapter 5 of *On Baptism*, notes: Among the ancients, whoever had defiled himself with homicide would expiate himself with purifying water. On this point, Anticlides <note>A Greek historian from the 3rd century BCE who wrote about the "Nostoi" or the returns of Greek heroes from Troy.</note> rightly writes in Book 74 of his *Returns*: <margin>$\overset{\epsilon \theta}{\tau \eta}$ $\gamma \alpha \rho$</margin> "It was the custom of the ancients—a custom which is still in full force today—that whenever they committed the murder of men or other slaughters, they would wash their hands in flowing water for the purification of the stain." <note>original Greek: "ἔθε γὰρ ἦν τοῖς παλαιοῖς, ὅπερ καὶ νῦν ἀκμάζει, ὅταν ἢ φόνον ἀνθρώπων, ἢ καὶ ἄλλας σφαγὰς ἐποίην, ὕδατι ἀενάῳ τὰς χεῖρας ἀπονίπτειν εἰς τοῦ μιάσματος κάθαρσιν." Latin: "erat enim mos antiquorum, qui nunc quoque servatur, ut qui caedem hominum, vel aliorum animalium commisissent, perenni aqua manus abluerent, ad commissi piaculi lustrationem."</note>

From this custom also, Pontius Pilate in Matthew 27 prepares to wash away with water that murder committed against our most innocent Savior, as if he himself were innocent and in no way guilty of that killing, once he had washed himself with water: *taking water, he washed his hands, saying: "I am innocent of the blood of this just man."* <note>original Greek: "λαβὼν ὕδωρ ἐπενίψατο τὰς χεῖρας, λέγων: ἀθῶός εἰμι ἀπὸ τοῦ αἵματος τοῦ δικαῖου."</note>

# ELIAS SCHEDIVS

Hesychius <note>An Alexandrian grammarian from the 5th or 6th century CE, famous for his lexicon of rare Greek words.</note> also touches upon this ritual: <term>the lustral basin is used for purification by means of water containing barley and salt</term> <note>original Greek: χερνίβιον ἀγνισθῆναι, δι’ ὕδατος ἔχοντος κρίτας καὶ ἅλας</note>, which is to say, a basin containing water to purify the judges and their assistants. Not only were the sacrificial priests washed with water, but also the victims themselves; as Dionysius of Halicarnassus <note>A Greek historian and teacher of rhetoric who lived in Rome during the reign of Augustus.</note> writes in Book VII of *Roman Antiquities*: <term>having washed themselves and purified the sacred objects with pure water</term> <note>original Greek: χερνιψάμενοι δὲ γὰρ αὐτοὶ, καὶ τὰ ἱερὰ καθαρῷ περιαγνίσαντες ὕδατι</note>, which means they are washed themselves, and they purify the sacred rites with a pure stream. 

Moreover, they even poured water into the ears [of the animal] so that the victim might seem to nod <note>The original Latin text uses "abnueret" (to refuse or shake the head), but the Greek and the author's own explanation suggest "annuat" (to nod or assent). In ancient sacrifice, a movement of the animal's head was interpreted as its voluntary "consent" to be sacrificed.</note>; a practice that Myrtilus reports in Book II of *Lesbian Affairs*: <term>the priests were accustomed to pour water into the ear of the victim, as if it were nodding its assent to the sacred rites</term> <note>original Greek: οἱ μὲν ἂν ἱερεῖς τὸ ὕδωρ εἰώθασιν ἐμβαλεῖν εἰς τὸ οὖς τοῦ ἱερείου, ὡς ἐπινευούσης τελεταῖς</note>. That is, *for indeed the priests were accustomed to pour water into the ear of the victim so that it would assent to the sacrifices.* 

Indeed, even he who touched the altar of Jove <note>The Roman name for the Greek god Zeus.</note> with impure hands was struck by a thunderbolt, as Timarchides writes regarding Asterius in his book *On Crowns*:

> ->Therefore the Father burned him with a fiery<-
> ->thunderbolt,<-
> ->For it is especially necessary for a mortal to worship divine things in<-
> ->purity.<-

> ->*thunderbolt,*<-

> ->*things purely.*<-

# ON THE GERMAN GODS

## CHAPTER XXVIII.

*Fire and water were employed. From where this custom arose. God as a consuming fire. Among the Persians, sacred fire. The Magi of the Cappadocians. Heraclius extinguished the fire. The most ancient God of the Chaldeans. When the sacred fire of Jerusalem was extinguished. Sacred fire was carried before the Roman Empire. As before the Kings of the Persians. The drums of the Indians. The robe of the Syrians. The axes of the Romans. Gilded and naked swords for Kings and Princes. A silver trumpet for the Doge of the Venetians.*

**F**ire was employed for sacred rites, just as water was. It was also used for making treaties, as Servius <note>A 4th-century grammarian known for his commentary on Virgil.</note> witnesses in Book XII of the *Aeneid*: <term>water and fire are always employed</term> <note>original Latin: semper aqua & ignis adhibetur</note>. From this comes the practice that those whom we wish to exclude from our fellowship, we "interdict from fire and water," that is, from the very things by which social fellowships are joined together. Furthermore, fire always burned upon the altar, which the priest nourished, as is also written in the book of Leviticus; without this fire, it was divinely forbidden to perform any sacrifice. Pollux <note>Julius Pollux, a Greek rhetorician of the 2nd century CE whose "Onomasticon" is a major source for ancient terminology.</note> says: <term>That upon which we sacrifice, or where we kindle fire, is an altar, a censer, or a hearth</term> <note>original Greek: ἐφ' ὧν δὲ θύομεν, ἢ πῦρ ἀνακαίομεν, βωμὸς, θυμιατήριον, ἑσία</note>; <gloss>*</gloss> <term>for some have named it thus, but you might most properly call it the one in the Prytaneion, upon which the unquenchable fire is lit</term> <note>original Greek: ἔνιοι γὰρ οὕτως ὠνομάκασιν, ἥτω δ' ἂν κυριώτατα καλοίης τὴν ἐν πρυτανείῳ, ἐφ' ἧς τὸ πῦρ τὸ ἄσβεστον ἀνάπτεται</note>,

<meta>catchword: it</meta>

---

<gloss>*</gloss> The "sacrifices of God," which in Joshua 13:14 are called <term>ishei</term> <note>Hebrew: אִשֵּׁי (fire-offerings or "fires")</note>, show that these gave the origin to the name of the fires of Vesta <note>The Roman goddess of the hearth, whose temple held a perpetual sacred fire.</note>. This is demonstrated by Gale in his book *The Court of the Gentiles* (Part I, Book 2, Chapter 9, §5), by Vossius in *On the Origin of Idolatry* (Book II, Chapter 65, p. 652), and by Dickinson in *The Phoenician Delphic Oracles* (p. 120 and following).
