<meta>This page continues Schedius's exploration of fire as a sacred element, following his citation of the Greek scholar Pollux. He transitions from defining the physical locations of sacred fire (altars and hearths) to explaining the theological reasoning behind its use in both ancient pagan and contemporary Christian contexts, specifically focusing on the tradition of perpetual flames and Persian fire rituals.</meta>

...that is, those things upon which we sacrifice or kindle fire: an altar, a censer, or "Vesta" <note>Schedius uses the name of the goddess Vesta to refer to the hearth itself.</note>, for some have called it so. Indeed, you might most appropriately use that name for the fire which is in the <term>Prytaneum</term> <note>A public building in ancient Greek cities containing the community's holy hearth and perpetual fire.</note>, upon which that perpetual fire is accustomed to burn. *Polydore Vergil, Book V, Chapter VII of "On the Discovery of Things."* Thus, in fire more than in other elements, all sacred rites were established; because fire, I believe, is nearest to heaven; because God first spoke to Moses in the appearance of fire; and because he had snatched up the burnt offerings accepted from heaven. 

Among us likewise, the inhabitants of heaven <note>Likely referring to saints or the divine in Christian liturgy.</note> are decorated with no greater honor from the outside than with wax candles. For the same reason especially, as I think, the perpetual fire was preserved by the <term>Vestals</term> <note>The Vestal Virgins, priestesses of the Roman goddess of the hearth, who maintained a fire that was never allowed to go out.</note>: since our God is a consuming fire, and for that reason, it is rightly held sacred. Therefore, among the Persians, <gloss>*</gloss> fire was sacred, as Strabo <note>A Greek geographer and historian from the 1st century BCE.</note> testifies in Book XVII: <term>to whatever god they sacrifice, they first pray to the fire</term> <note>original Greek: ὅτῳ δ᾿ ἂν θύσωσι θεῷ, πρώτῳ τῷ πυρὶ εὔχονται</note>. Regarding the Magi, Phoenix of Colophon <note>A 3rd-century BCE Greek poet.</note> says in Athenaeus's *The Banquet of the Learned*, Book XII:

> The sacred fire is not rekindled by the Magi
> According to custom, by touching the god with rods.
> <note>Original Greek: Οὐ παρὰ μάγοισι πῦρ ἱερὸν ἀνέσησε / Ὥσπερ νόμος, ῥάβδοισι τοῦ θεοῦ ψαύων.</note>

---

* <gloss>*</gloss> <margin>That they pursued fire with divine worship was recently argued by Filippo della Torre in *Ancient Monuments of Antium*, p. 168 and following. The opposite view—that fire was a symbol rather than the god itself—is correctly defended by Thomas Hyde in *History of the Religion of the Ancient Persians*, chapters I, VI, XXI; Ralph Cudworth in *The True Intellectual System of the Universe*, p. 286; Jacques Gaffarel in *Unheard-of Curiosities*, p. 181; Pierre-Daniel Huet in *Alnetan Questions*, book II, chapter I, p. 100; Christoph Cellarius in *Academic Dissertations*, p. 635; and the Reverend Salomon Deyling in *Sacred Observations*, part II, p. 132.</margin>

# ON THE GERMAN GODS #

<meta>catchword: vir-</meta>

Euphrates the Persian, in Book III of Dioscorides's *Anthology*, forbids his body to be burned with fire, fearing perhaps that he might contaminate the fire with his corpse:

->To defile the fire,<-
->For us, is more bitter than a painful death.<-
<note>The original Greek text reads: *Πῦρ δὲ μιῆναι / Ἡμῖν τοῦ χαλεποῦ πικρότερον θανάτου.* Schedius also provides a Latin translation: *Ignem vero contaminare / Vobis difficilis mortis acerbissimum puto.*</note>

See more on this custom in Plutarch's book *On the Principle of Cold* <term>Peri tou protou psychrou</term>, and in Julius Firmicus Maternus's *On the Error of Profane Religions*, Chapter V. Strabo, in Book XV, writes the following concerning the Magi <note>Ancient Persian priests or Zoroastrian practitioners.</note> in Cappadocia who guard the fire:

"In Cappadocia there is a great multitude of the Magian people, who are also called <term>Pyrethi</term> <note>From the Greek *pyrethoi*, meaning "fire-kindlers."</note>. There are also many shrines to the Persian gods. They do not sacrifice with a knife, but by beating the victim with a certain club as if with a pestle. There are also <term>Pyratheia</term> <note>Fire-temples.</note>, which are certain noteworthy sanctuaries. In the middle of these is an altar, upon which there is much ash, and the Magi preserve an inextinguishable fire. Every day, entering for nearly the space of an hour, they chant before the fire, holding a bundle of rods <note>Known in Zoroastrianism as the *barsom*, a bundle of twigs used in rituals.</note>, and wearing felt tiaras which hang down on both sides so far as to cover their lips and cheeks."

This is to say: *In Cappadocia, there is a great multitude of the Magi, who are called Pyrethi. Likewise, there are many shrines to the Persian gods. They do not slaughter with a knife but with a staff, striking as if with a pestle. There are also Fire-temples, certain sanctuaries worthy of mention. In the middle of these is an altar, on which there is much ash. The Magi preserve an inextinguishable fire there. Entering daily for nearly the space of an hour, they chant together, [holding] a bundle...*

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the ritual use of fire among ancient peoples. # ELIAS SCHEDIUS #

...holding rods before the fire. They wear woolen tiaras <note>These caps, known in Persian contexts as *padams*, often featured flaps to cover the mouth to prevent the priest's breath from polluting the sacred flame.</note> which, being fitted on both sides, cover even the lips and the jaws. However, the Emperor Heraclius, while laying waste to Persia, destroyed those fire-temples <note>Latin: *pyrea*; Greek: *pyreia*</note>, as Suidas <note>A 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia.</note> writes: "Heraclius both demolished the cities and destroyed the fire-temples of the Persians" <note>original Greek: ὁ δὲ Ἡράκλειος τὰς τε πόλεις καθήρει, καὶ τὰ πυρεῖα διέφρε τῶν Περσῶν</note>. See the *Tripartite History*, Book 10, Chapter 30; Theodoret’s *History*, Book 5, Chapter 39; Procopius, Book 2, *The Persian Wars*; and Nicephorus, Book 14, Chapter 19. 

Indeed, the Hebrews record that this use of fire among the Chaldeans is very ancient, so much so that they affirm that <term>Or</term> <note>Hebrew: אור</note> denotes fire or light. Rabbi Moses Ben Maimon <note>The influential Jewish philosopher known as Maimonides (1138–1204).</note> records this in *The Guide for the Perplexed* <term>Moreh Nevukhim</term> in Book 3, Chapter 30; see his words cited in my first treatise. 

Furthermore, the sacred fire of Jerusalem, which was kept on the altar by the priest, was eventually extinguished of its own accord when King Antiochus sold the priesthood to Jason. This fire had previously survived, inviolate and eternal, for seventy years during the Babylonian Captivity in a hidden place beneath the waters, as Saint Augustine reports. 

<margin>An image of this kind of fire-temple <note>Greek: *pyreia*</note> or shrine is shown by Thomas Hyde in *The Religion of the Ancient Persians*, page 354.</margin>

Moreover, the Roman Emperors had proceeded to such a height of pride that they allowed a sacred fire—which was similarly a custom for the Kings of Persia—to be carried before them as if it were a symbol of their empire, and they used it as a distinguished mark of honor and singular adornment. Alexander ab Alexandro, *Genial Days*, Book 5, Chapter 28. For thus Quintus Curtius writes in Book 3: "The fire which they themselves called sacred and eternal was carried before them on silver altars." Drums were a delight to the Kings of the Indians, as Alexander [writes].

# ELIAS SCHEDIUS #

Alexander ab Alexandro <note>A 15th-century Italian humanist and jurist whose work *Genialium Dierum* (Genial Days) was a popular source for ancient customs.</note>, in Book 1, Chapter 38, writes: The Kings of India maintain as royal finery that when they go out in public, they appear conspicuous with a golden miter <note>A ceremonial headdress or cap.</note> adorned with many gems, and dressed in fine linen <note>Latin: *sindone*</note>, with drums and bells preceding them. The Syrians held the robe and scepter as royal finery. Indeed, in an earlier age, it is recorded that Kings held spears—which they now call scepters—as a sign of majesty and in place of a crown. 

It has been committed to memory by many that Romulus, once he had secured the kingdom, made himself more venerable by using the curule chair <note>A folding chair inlaid with ivory, a seat of high office in Rome.</note>, the *trabea* <note>A ceremonial toga with purple stripes worn by kings and augurs.</note>, and other specific garments. Most notably, he distinguished himself with twelve lictors <note>Bodyguards and attendants to Roman magistrates.</note> who carried the fasces and axes <note>Bundles of rods and an axe, symbolizing the power to punish and execute.</note> before him as insignia of majesty. He also utilized attendants, couriers, orderlies, and heralds. 

Silver trumpets, a golden umbrella, a golden chair, a golden cushion, and multi-colored banners are the insignia of the Venetian Duke <note>The Doge of Venice.</note>, granted to him by the Pope, as Sabellicus <note>Marcus Antonius Coccius Sabellicus (1436–1506), a noted historian of Venice.</note> writes in Book 5, Ennead 9. 

The head-insignia <note>referring to the Doge’s cap, the *Corno Ducale*.</note> originally rose into a cone in the style of a Phrygian miter, as the most ancient images of princes testify. Today, the headband <note>Latin: *infula*</note> is pressed down at the front and raised at the back into the shape of a bent horn, so that it appears that the height of dignity resides in that rank which accompanies the prince. Sabellicus, Book 7, Ennead 8. 

Whenever the Duke goes out in public, these insignia are carried before him. He himself follows, accompanied by the ambassadors of foreign Princes, appearing shortly thereafter with the most ornate display of clothing and a head covering so composed that a complete horn stands out. By this clear sign, he testifies that he is indeed the Prince of the entire Republic, yet in such a way that the Senatorial order, which follows in great numbers, claims a principal part of authority for itself alongside him.

## CHAPTER XXIX.

*Oak leaves in sacrifices. The same custom among the Greeks. Hecate <note>The goddess of magic, crossroads, and the night.</note> crowned with oak. Names of the oak. Oak crowns. Laurel in the rites of Apollo. Poplar in those of Hercules. Myrtle in the Dionysian rites. Crowned sacrificial victims. Vessels as well. The olive branches of the Supplicants. Among the Athenians alone. Oil in the sacrifices of Pluto <note>The god of the underworld.</note>.*

Alexander ab Alexandro <note>A 15th-century jurist who documented ancient customs.</note>, in Book 4, Chapter 15, notes: The Druids <note>The high-ranking priestly class among the ancient Celts.</note> performed no sacred rite without a branch of oak. For they held the oak in such great honor that they even established them as being vocal <note>original: *vocales*. Schedius refers to the ancient belief that certain trees could speak or deliver oracles.</note>. It is also told that a statue stood there which struck bronze cauldrons <note>original: *lebetes*. ## CHAPTER XXX.

*Turning during sacred rites. The Celts turn to the left. A passage from Athenaeus is interpreted. The custom of the augurs. Turning toward the East. The contrary custom of the Jews. Christian temples facing the East. For what reason Elxai was a heretic. The custom of the Greeks in receiving the sacred bath.*

It was a precept of Numa <note>Numa Pompilius, the legendary second king of Rome, credited with establishing many of Rome's religious traditions.</note> that you should turn yourself around while you worship the gods, and sit down once you have finished worshipping, as Plutarch writes in his *Life of Numa*. The turning of the worshippers is said to be a representation of the globe of the world: by which it might more clearly appear that he who worships the gods (inasmuch as he is turned away from the sunrise when temples face the East) turns himself in that direction, and then immediately turns back toward God, completing a circle and achieving his own fulfillment from both movements. Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, a 1st-century Roman author and naturalist.</note> in Book 28, Chapter 1 says: *In the act of worship, we bring the right hand to our lips to blow a kiss, and we turn the whole body around; the Gauls <note>A term often used by ancient authors to refer to the Celtic peoples of Western Europe.</note> believe it is done with more religious devotion toward the left.* They also looked toward the East. For an Augur <note>A Roman priest whose job was to interpret the will of the gods by observing the flight of birds or other natural signs.</note>, as Livy <note>Titus Livius, the famous Roman historian.</note> records in Book 1 of his *History of Rome*: *When, after taking a view of the city and the fields and praying to the gods, he marked out the regions from the East to the West; he called the parts to the right the South, and those to the left the North.* Callixenus of Rhodes <note>A Greek historian of the 3rd century BCE.</note> in his *History of Alexander*: <note>original Greek: "τοῖς μὲν οὖν κατοιχομένοις περὶ τὰς ἡλίου δυσμὰς ἐναγίζομεν. τοῖς δὲ οὐρανίδαις ὑπὸ τὴν ἕω τοῦ ἡλίου ἀνατέλλοντος ἱερεύομεν."</note> that is, *We perform funeral rites for those who have departed life around the setting of the sun; but to the heavenly gods, we sacrifice at the time*

Even among the Jews, this custom was carried over from the Gentiles. Ezekiel, chapter VIII, verse 16: *And behold, at the door of the temple of the Lord, between the porch and the altar, were about twenty-five men, with their backs toward the temple of the Lord and their faces toward the East, and they were worshipping the Sun toward the East.* For the Holy of Holies was placed in the Western part of the Jewish temple. Therefore, the Lord commanded through Moses in Deuteronomy that they should not enter facing the East in the manner of other nations, but that they should enter from any direction facing toward the temple while praying to God, so they might not seem to worship the Sun as the idolaters did, according to the testimony of Saint Jerome. 

However, we enter our temples from the West toward the East, not only because Christ when crucified looked toward the West from the East—and thus could be, as it were, looked up to by those praying toward the East—but also because He is the Sun of Righteousness, as written in Malachi, chapter IV, verse 2: ->but for you who fear my name, the Sun of righteousness shall arise.<- <note>original Hebrew: "וזרחה לכם יראי שמי שמש צדקה"</note> Also because from the rising of the sun, as the same prophet records in chapter I, verse 11, even unto its setting, the name of Jehovah shall be great among the nations, and in every place incense shall be offered to his name, and a pure offering. And just as the lightning moves from the East to the West, as in Matthew, chapter XXIV, verse 27, so shall be the coming of the Son of Man on that great day which we await. Cle-

# ON THE GERMANIC GODS

> Clement of Alexandria <note>An early Christian theologian (c. 150 – c. 215 AD) who sought to unite Greek philosophy with Christian belief.</note>, *Stromata* <note>Meaning "Miscellanies," his major work on Christian life and knowledge.</note>, Book VII: It is therefore permitted not even to utter a prayer with the voice, but only to direct whatever is spiritual within us toward that voice which is perceived by the mind, through an inseparable turning toward God.

Since the East is the image of the natural day, the light which first shone out of the darkness increases from that direction. Furthermore, for those who wallow in ignorance, the day of the knowledge of truth has arisen in the same manner as the Sun rises in the morning East—namely, through Prayers. For this reason, even the most ancient parts of the temples looked toward the West, so that those standing with their faces turned toward the images <note>Likely referring to the practice of placing cult statues at the western end of a temple so the worshiper faces East to see them.</note> might be taught while turned toward the East.

> Let my prayer be directed as incense in your sight, the lifting up of my hands as an evening sacrifice,

so say the Psalms <note>Psalm 141:2.</note>.

> Justin Martyr <note>An early Christian apologist and philosopher (c. 100 – 165 AD) who wrote defenses of the faith to the Roman Emperor.</note>, *Response 118*: Since among us we designate all the most excellent things for the honor and veneration of God, and in human opinion the East is more excellent than other parts of creation, for that reason, at the time of prayer, everyone turns their face toward the East. Just as we sign ourselves with the right hand in the name of Christ—at least those who require such a seal—because the right is thought to be better than the left (although it differs by position, not by nature), in no other way is the East designated for worshipping God as the more excellent part of creation. And as for our looking toward the East when we perform our prayers, that is not contrary to the words of the Prophets and Apostles. For in every place, the "East" exists for those who pray <note>Meaning that the spiritual "East" (Christ) is omnipresent.</note>.

> Tertullian <note>A prolific early Christian author from Carthage (c. 155 – c. 220 AD), known as the "father of Latin theology."</note> in the *Apology*, chapter 16: Looking up toward the East, Christians pray with hands spread out, because they are innocent; with heads bared, because we are not ashamed; and finally, without a prompter <note>original: "sine monitore." In Roman pagan ritual, a priest or "monitor" would dictate the exact words of a prayer to ensure no mistakes were made; Tertullian argues Christian prayer is spontaneous and heartfelt.</note>,

...they strike the victim across the back <note>original: "septū" - likely a contraction of "septum" (the wall of the body/back) or "septum" (enclosure), here referring to the physical strike of the sacrifice.</note> with a sword. Based on long observation from antiquity, this practice has gained belief among them.

*Julius Caesar, Book VI, Gallic Wars:* The whole nation of the Gauls is greatly devoted to religious observances; and for that reason, those who are afflicted with more serious illnesses, and those who are involved in battles and dangers, either sacrifice humans as victims or vow that they will sacrifice them, and they employ the Druids <note>Ancient Celtic priests, judges, and lore-keepers who were high-ranking members of society.</note> as ministers for these rites. This is because they believe that unless a human life is given for a human life, the power of the immortal gods cannot be appeased; and they have publicly established sacrifices of the same kind.

*Lucan, Book I, Pharsalia:*

> And those by whom the pitiless Teutates is appeased with slaughtered blood,
> ->and the terrifying Hesus with his cruel altars,<-
> ->Hesus,<-
> and Taranis <note>original: "Tharamis," a variant spelling of the Celtic god of thunder.</note>, whose altar is no gentler than that of Scythian Diana <note>In mythology, the "Scythian Diana" or Artemis of Tauris required the sacrifice of all shipwrecked strangers.</note>.

*Pliny, Book XXX, Chapter 1:* During the consulship of Gnaeus Cornelius Lentulus and Publius Licinius Crassus <note>97 BC.</note>, a decree of the Senate was made that no man should be sacrificed; for until that time, these monstrous rites were celebrated openly. This practice certainly possessed the Gallic provinces, and even within our own memory.

*Tacitus, Book I, Annals:* In the nearby groves were barbarian altars, where they had slaughtered tribunes and centurions of the first rank.

*Book XIV, Annals:* For they considered it lawful to consult the God by inspecting human entrails <note>original: "fibris" (fibers), referring to the organs used in divination.</note>.

In the same work: By publicly slaughtering a man, they celebrate the horrific beginnings of their barbarian rites.

the most noble among them used to sacrifice to this God, but later, they began to secretly buy and rear children to be sent for sacrifice. However, once an investigation was held, some of those about to be sacrificed were found to be substitutes <note>term: "subdititii" (fraudulent replacements, specifically children of the poor or slaves bought to save the children of the elite)</note>. Having weighed these matters, and seeing that the enemy had already struck camp before the city, they were seized by a religious dread, as if they had abolished the ancestral honors due to the Gods. Therefore, so that they might correct those errors without delay, they sacrificed two hundred children chosen from the foremost nobility in a public sacrifice. Others who were also vulnerable to accusations—no fewer than three hundred—offered themselves voluntarily. *Justin, book XVIII of his History:* indeed, they sacrificed humans as victims and brought children (*an age which provokes mercy even from enemies*) to the altars, demanding peace with the blood of those for whose lives the Gods are usually most fervently petitioned. If we investigate the origin of that horrific sacrifice, it will be manifest that it is to be derived from Abraham. For *Porphyry* <note>Porphyry (c. 234–305 CE) was a Neoplatonist philosopher who often sought to find common threads between different religious traditions.</note> (as *Eusebius* writes in *Preparation for the Gospel, books I & IX*) recorded that Saturn—whom the Phoenicians called *Israel*, as is clear from *Justin, book XXXVI*—was a very ancient King of Phoenicia. <sig>Nn 3</sig>

...was widespread. <note>This continues the sentence from the previous page regarding the diffusion of bloodthirsty rites.</note> Nor is it surprising that these rites were part of their sacred ceremonies; indeed, their Gods were parricides, adulterers, murderers, oath-breakers, and even worse than the worst of men, as is known everywhere from the writings of the Ancient Historians. Therefore, they also perpetrated the most cruel deeds, enticed by the crimes of the Gods, so that they might render them favorable through debauchery and blood. 

Of this cruelty, no slight mark is found in a certain law of the Twelve Tables <note>term: "Twelve Tables" (The foundational code of Roman law, traditionally dated to 451–450 BCE.)</note>, by which a debtor who was unable to pay was divided alive by his creditors, and each claimed a part of the divided body for himself, as Aulus Gellius <note>A 2nd-century Roman author whose "Attic Nights" preserves fragments of older Roman laws and history.</note> writes in Book 20, Chapter 1:

*For an acknowledged debt, and for matters legally judged, let thirty days be the lawful period. Afterward, let there be a "laying on of hands" <note>term: "manus injectio" (a legal procedure where a creditor physically seized a debtor to bring him before a magistrate).</note>; let the creditor lead him to court. Unless he satisfies the judgment, or unless someone intervenes as a guarantor for him by that law, let the creditor take him away, bind him either with a cord or with shackles of fifteen pounds weight—not less, or if he wishes, more. If he wishes, let the debtor live on his own means; if he does not live on his own, let the one who holds him bound give him a pound of grain every day; if he wishes, let him give more. Keep him in chains for sixty days. During those days, on three successive market days, let him be produced before the praetor in the assembly, and let the amount of money for which he was judged be proclaimed. On the third market day (if he has not settled in the meantime), let him suffer the capital penalty, or let him go across the Tiber to be sold abroad; and if there are several creditors to whom the defendant was judged liable, on the third market day let them cut him into pieces; if they cut more or less, let it be without liability.* <note>original: "sine fraude esto." This meant the creditors would not face legal charges if they accidentally cut a portion larger or smaller than their share of the debt.</note> 

And in the spectacles, in the circus, and in the theaters, men were everywhere torn apart by wild beasts in honor of that God to whom the games were dedicated. Salvianus <note>Salvian of Marseille, a 5th-century Christian writer known for his moral critiques of Roman society.</note> in Book 6 heavily reproaches and censures these depraved customs. "In the spectacles," he says, "the primary kind of delight is for men to die, and for the bellies of wild beasts to be filled with human flesh..."

...with the pleasure of those standing around and the joy of those looking on. And so that this may happen, it is at the expense of the world. For us, however, since murder is once and for all forbidden, we are not even permitted to destroy what has been conceived in the womb, while the blood is still being drawn into a human being. Today, in that very place, blood consecrated to Bellona <note>term: "Bellona" (The Roman goddess of war. Likewise, there are those who, at the shows in the arena, greedily catch the fresh blood flowing from the slit throats of the wicked to drink it as a cure for the falling sickness <note>term: "comitial disease" (A historical term for epilepsy. Where are those also who dine on the meat of wild beasts from the arena? Those who seek the boar or the stag? That boar has wiped off the blood he drew in the struggle; that stag has tossed in the gladiator's blood. The very bellies of bears are sought after, still digesting human internal organs. Thus, meat fed on man is belched up by a man. You who eat these things, how far are you from the feasts of <term>Christians</term>? <note>Tertullian is addressing the "Thyestean feast" rumors—the false accusation that Christians ate babies during their secret meetings.</note> Do those who, with wild lust, gape for human limbs do any less because they devour them while alive? Are they less consecrated to filth by human blood because they lick up the blood of those yet to be? They do not eat infants, clearly, but rather those who have reached puberty. 

Let your error blush before the <term>Christians</term>, for we do not even have the blood of animals in our edible feasts; for this reason, we also abstain from things strangled and from those that die of natural causes, so that we may not be contaminated by blood in any way, even if buried within our entrails. Many of them also skin the right hands of their enemies, including the fingernails, and use them to cover their quivers. Among all hides, human skin is almost the thickest and is of a brilliant whiteness. Many even carry about whole humans who have been flayed and stretched out over wood upon their horses. Diodorus Siculus, Library of History, Book V:* They hang the severed heads of enemies from the necks of their horses; they hand over the spoils of the enemy, stained with blood, to their attendants to be carried before them as if in a triumph, while they themselves chant a prayerful hymn of victory. *And they fix these first-fruits of the spoils <note>term: "manubiarum primitias" (the first and best portion of the war-booty, often dedicated to the gods).</note> to the vestibules of their houses, just as if they were wild beasts they had slaughtered. They carefully preserve the heads of the most noble enemies, anointed with cedar oil, in chests; showing them to guests, they boast that some ancestor, or their own father, or even they themselves, refused to trade this head even for a great sum of money. In this way, they demonstrate a barbaric greatness of soul.* Tacitus, *Annals*, Book 1: *Scattered about were fragments of weapons and the limbs of horses, as well as human faces fixed to the trunks of trees.* <note>Tacitus is describing the Roman commander Germanicus discovering the site of the Battle of the Teutoburg Forest, where the legions of Varus were massacred years earlier.</note> Sextus Rufus Festus in his *Breviarium* relates many things concerning the cruelty of the Scordisci— <note>The Scordisci were a tribe in the Balkans known for their fierce resistance to Rome and alleged sacrificial practices.</note>

That is to say, the aspects <note>original Latin: *vultus*, literally "faces" or "appearances," referring to the specific configurations of the stars.</note> of this world are subject to the celestial aspects, and therefore the Sages, who made **Images of the Stars**, looked for the entry of those aspects into the heavens, and then they performed the work they were meant to do. > "In this Chapter, Ptolemy wishes to reveal many secrets of **Images**, and the aspects which he said were in this world are the species of Animals and the species of Plants; and for this reason, he says that all these species are ruled by similar aspects remaining in the Heavens. The Sages of Images observed when a Planet emerged from beneath the rays of the Sun and entered these aspects, and they would place that Planet in the Ascendant; and the aspect which it entered, they would carve into stone, mixing with it other things necessary for these matters. By this adaptation or destruction, they did whatever they wished, and that power remained in the stone for a long time."

Having now been **devoted** <note>original: "devotus"; referring to the ritual of *devotio*, where a Roman general vowed his life to the gods of the underworld in exchange for the destruction of the enemy.</note> to the **Gods of the Dead**, he appeared to both battle lines as something more majestic than a human sight, as if sent from heaven, a sacrificial offering to appease all the anger of the Gods, who might carry the plague away from his own people and onto the enemies. "...[whatever] comes to meet me, when I return in peace from the Ammonites, shall be Jehovah’s, I say, or I will offer it as a burnt offering." <note>This continues the biblical quote from the previous page, Judges 11:31.</note> This vow is bipartite: the first part is this: "whatever comes out of my house shall be the Lord’s"; the second part: "or I will offer it as a burnt offering." For the conjunction *vav* <note>The Hebrew letter ו translated here as "or."</note> here is not copulative <note>meaning "and"</note>, but disjunctive <note>meaning "or"</note>, as in Genesis 26:11, Exodus 1:10, and Exodus 21:15. Thus, Jephthah’s meaning was that it would either be sacrificed to the Lord as a burnt offering, if it were of the kind that could be sacrificed; or, if it were not permitted to be offered, it would otherwise be consecrated to God. And Andreas Osiander <note>A prominent Lutheran theologian and scholar (1498–1552).</note> in that same place thinks that Jephthah vowed distinctively, so that whatever first came out of his house would either be assigned to the service of divine worship, or, if it provided suitable material for a sacrifice, it would be immolated. See also the annotations of Tremellius and Junius <note>Influential 16th-century biblical commentators.</note> on the Bible.

As for what is written in verse 39: *And it came to pass at the end of two months, that she returned to her father, who did with her according to his vow which he had vowed* <note>original Hebrew: ויהי מקץ שנים חדשים ותשב אל-אביה ויעש לה את-נדרו אשר נדר</note>. *It was indeed at the end of two months, when she had returned to her father, that he carried out upon her his vow which he had vowed.* However, these vows are to be understood far differently—not that he sacrificed her, but that he dedicated her to God; for he fulfilled the first part of the vow. For as to what some interpret regarding human sacrifice <note>original Greek: ἀνθρωποθυσίᾳ (*anthropothysia*), the ritual killing of humans.</note>, God is not delighted by such things, nor did Jephthah’s faith allow it. For God prohibits it and condemns it by law in Deuteronomy 12:31, and for that reason commanded that firstborns be redeemed; and He is so far from desiring the death of even a sinner that, on the contrary, He gave His own Son to die for sinners. For if He refused the sacrifice of Isaac, which He Himself had commanded...

Furthermore, no sacrifices were performed except by the Levites, and specifically the Priests, who offered victims to Jehovah on that bronze altar. Without a doubt, Jephthah consulted the high priest about this difficult case, who would by no means have permitted him to offer a victim that was not at all pleasing to God. Moreover, the Spirit of Jehovah was with Jephthah, as we read in verse 29: <note>original Hebrew: ותהי על־יפתח רוח יהוה, "And the spirit of the LORD came upon Jephthah"</note>. If this spirit is good and from God—and God Himself never performs evil—Jephthah would never have vowed something so far removed from God's law and so utterly impious <note>original: "piaculare," referring to an act requiring atonement or a grave sin.</note>. 

In the Epistle to the Hebrews, his faith is also greatly praised by the Apostle (Chapter 11, verse 32), such that he is numbered among those men most dear to God. This would by no means **have been the case if he had polluted that altar, dedicated to God the Best and Greatest, with such a wicked ritual. Rather, his daughter, the Virgin, remained celibate, as the same text implies:** <note>original Hebrew: והיא לא־ידעה איש, "And she knew no man"</note> **"and she had not known a man."** For he did not redeem her with a monetary payment according to the law found in the final chapter of Leviticus, verse 4 <note>Leviticus 27:4 provides a scale of monetary values to "redeem" or buy back a person dedicated to God's service by a vow.</note>, but left her consecrated to the Lord. Therefore, he did not allow her to marry, lest she should seem to belong to anyone other than Jehovah; this decision proceeded from an ignorance of the law (as the times were then corrupt). 

Indeed, he says in verse 37 that he cannot take back his word; and the girl, keeping faith with her father, bewails her virginity. Thus **Chytraeus** <note>David Chytraeus (1530–1600), an influential Lutheran theologian and historian known for his biblical commentaries.</note> **writes on this passage: "Some believe that Jephthah did not kill his daughter, but consecrated her to God in celibacy, so that as a virgin without a husband or children, she might end her life secluded from the company of other people and her peers. ...perpetual virginity, because she was to live without a husband and children, she deplores. Just as we read that Hannah, the mother of Samuel, wept with tears over her barrenness, because she would procreate no worshippers of God. Albertus Magnus <note>A 13th-century Dominican friar and philosopher known for his vast scientific and theological writings.</note>, in *On the Valiant Woman* <note>original: "de muliere forti," referring to the "Woman of Valor" in Proverbs 31.</note>, chapter 20, section 1, letter B, says: the daughters of nature who set their mind and will toward the propagation of nature, judging it the best thing to find joy in children and a husband, are signified by Jephthah’s daughter, who for two months wept for her virginity in the mountains, because she would leave no seed upon the earth. 

She was terrified that she would die a virgin, and she asked her father for a period of only two months to mourn her virginity. She also feared the curse of barrenness mentioned in Exodus 23 <note>Exodus 23:26 promises that "none shall miscarry or be barren in your land." In the ancient context, childlessness was often viewed as a divine curse or a great misfortune.</note>. If, indeed, she had been slaughtered, she would not have lamented over her virginity, but over her soul <note>original: "anima," here meaning her life or vital breath.</note>. Nor is it said in the history that Jephthah slaughtered his daughter as a burnt offering <note>original: "holocaustum," a sacrifice entirely consumed by fire.</note>, but only that he did to her as he had vowed: namely, that she would not know a man, but would preserve perpetual virginity.

*The spilled blood was collected. With it they burned offerings on the altars. They believed this burnt offering was pleasing to the GODS. Flies plagued the sacred rites of the nations. The god Achor, Jupiter the Fly-Averter <note>original Greek: "Ἀπομυῖος" (Apomyios) — a title given to Zeus at Olympia as the "averter of flies" from the sacrifices.</note>. They collected the spilled blood in shallow bowls <note>term: "pateris" — wide, shallow bowls used in ancient rituals for pouring libations.</note>, and with it they burned offerings upon the altars, as Tacitus <note>A Roman historian (c. 56–120 AD) who wrote extensively about the Germanic tribes in his "Germania" and "Annals."</note> reports in Book 14 of the *Annals*: *For the Druids <note>Ancient Celtic priests and ritual specialists.</note> held it lawful to burn offerings on their altars with the blood of captives, and to consult the Gods through the entrails of men.* <note>original: "Nam cruore captivo adolere aras, & hominum fibris consulere Deos fas habebant Druydae."</note> Lucan <note>A Roman poet (39–65 AD), author of the epic "Pharsalia."</note> writes in Book 3 of the *Pharsalia*:

> And every tree was purified with human blood. <note>original: "Omnis & humanis lustrata cruoribus arbos."</note>

Nor is it surprising that they did this, since other nations also believed such a sacrifice was pleasing to their GODS. Homer says in *Iliad* Book 1:

> If perhaps he might be willing, having accepted the fat of lambs and choice goats, to ward off destruction from us. <note>original Greek: "Αἴ κέν πως ἀρνῶν κνίσης αἰ γῶν τε τελείων. Βούλεται ἀντιάσας ἡμῖν ἀπὸ λοιγὸν ἀμῦναι."</note>

*If perhaps [the god], having caught the scent of sheep and whole goats, might wish to drive the plague away from us.*

Flies, attracted by the scent, would very frequently swarm the sacrificial victims. Therefore, in order to be freed from this <unclear>nuisance</unclear>, certain nations instituted sacred rites by which they might be driven away. Regarding the Cyrenaicans <note>The people of Cyrene, an ancient Greek and later Roman city in modern-day Libya.</note>, Pliny mentions in his *Natural History*, Book 10, Chapter 28: *The Cyrenaicans would invoke the god Achor* <note>original: "Achorem Deum" — a deity specifically invoked to ward off flies.</note> *when a multitude of flies brought pestilence; the flies perish immediately after a sacrifice has been offered to that god.* Regarding the Palestinians, Philastrius <note>A 4th-century bishop and writer on heresies.</note> says: *Those who worship a fly in the city called Accaron <note>Modern-day Ekron, one of the five ancient city-states of the Philistines.</note>.* Aelian, in Book 10 of his *On Animals*, says: *Sacrifices are made to flies in the temple of Apollo.* The Greeks prayed to Jupiter the Fly-Averter <note>original Greek: "Ἀπόμυιος" (Apomyios) — a title for Zeus at Olympia used to keep the sacrificial area clean.</note>, as Pausanias testifies in his *Description of Greece*, Book 1, regarding the Olympic games. The Arcadians, however, worshipped Hercules the Fly-Catcher <note>original Greek: "Μύιαγρος" (Myiagron) — an assistant deity or hero tasked with removing flies.</note>, whom the same author mentions in his *Arcadia*; Pliny, in Book 29, Chapter 6, calls him Myoides. Clement of Alexandria agrees with this in his *Exhortation to the Greeks*: *The Eleans sacrifice to Zeus the Fly-Averter, and the Romans to Hercules the Fly-Averter <note>original Greek: "Ἀπομυίῳ Διὶ θύουσιν ἠlei͂οι, Ρ'ωμαῖοι δὲ Α'πομυίῳ Ἠρακλεῖ."</note>.* Flavius Josephus <note>A first-century Romano-Jewish historian.</note> records the god of Accaron as "The Fly" <note>original Greek: "Μυῖαν" (Myian).</note>. Flies in great numbers used to infest the sacrificial victims, attracted by the constant stench <note>In this context, *nidor* refers to the heavy smell of burning fat and meat from sacrifices.</note>. Therefore, so that they might be freed from this plague, certain Gentile nations established sacrifices to drive them away. Regarding the people of Cyrene <note>An ancient Greek city in modern-day Libya.</note>, Pliny mentions in Book 10, Chapter 28 of his *Natural History*: *The Cyrenaeans used to invoke the god Achor when a multitude of flies brought pestilence; the flies perish immediately after a successful sacrifice has been made to that god.* Regarding the Palestinians, Philastrius <note>A 4th-century bishop and writer on heresies.</note> says: *There are those who worship the fly in the city called Ekron.* Aelian, in Book 11 of *On Animals*, says: *Sacred rites are performed for flies in the shrine of Actian Apollo.* The Greeks used to appease Zeus *Apomyios* <note>original: Ἀπόμυιον — "The Averter of Flies."</note>, as Pausanias testifies in his book on the *Eliacs*, during the Olympic games. The Arcadians, however, worshipped Hercules *Myiagros* <note>original: Μύιαγρον — "The Fly-catcher."</note>, as the same author records in his *Arcadics*; Pliny, in Book 29, Chapter 6, calls him *Myiodes*. Clement of Alexandria agrees with this in his *Exhortation to the Greeks*: *The people of Elis sacrifice to Zeus the Fly-Averter, and the Romans to Hercules the Fly-Averter.* Flavius Josephus records that the god of Ekron was a Fly. However, it is handed down that flies never infested the sacred rites of the true God; in the *Pirkei Avot* <note>A collection of ethical teachings from the Jewish Mishnaic period.</note>, Chapter 5, sections 6 and 7, it is written: *no fly was seen in the house of slaughter <note>The area of the Temple in Jerusalem where animals were prepared for sacrifice.</note>.* And in the judgment of the great Scaliger <note>Joseph Justus Scaliger, a leading 16th-century scholar of chronology and history.</note>, that which was called *Baal-zebahim* <note>original: "Baalzebahim" — a scholarly play on words.</note>, the God of victims, of slaughters, of sacri-

These men were driven mad after finding the idol of the Goddess; and soon after, an oracle gave a response during the goddess's own sacred rites, stating that her altar ought to be sprinkled with human blood. And whereas previously they were led to be sacrificed by lot, the practice eventually evolved into flogging, so that the altar would nonetheless be stained with blood. *...beaten with whips throughout the entire day at the altar of Orthian Diana <note>The Spartan title for Artemis, often translated as "Upright" or "Strict."</note>, they often endure the lashes even unto death, remaining spirited and defiant; indeed, this struggle is called the "flogging" <note>original: *flagellatio*</note>.* Philostratus <note>The OCR reads "Philastrius," but the quote is from the 3rd-century author Philostratus’s *Life of Apollonius of Tyana*, Book VI.</note> on Apollonius of Tyana: 

<note>The following is a translation of the Greek passage: "The custom of whips is performed for Artemis, originating from the Scythians, after oracles were brought forth, as they say. I have stated these things regarding the gods of the Greeks, whom I would not call wise if they became partners in whips for those practicing liberty. He did not say 'of whips,' but rather to sprinkle the altar with the blood of men, just as was demanded among the Scythians. But the Lacedaemonians <note>The Spartans.</note>, having cleverly bypassed the necessity of human sacrifice, arrived at the contest of endurance, by which it is possible neither to die nor to fail in offering the first fruits of their own blood to the Goddess."</note>

*That is, the custom of those who whip is observed for Diana among the Scythians <note>Ancient nomadic people of the Eurasian steppes; the Spartans believed their statue of Artemis was stolen from Scythian territory.</note>, even with oracles, as they say, commanding it. Furthermore, he did not call the Gods of the Greeks wise, unless they were to become masters of whips and exercise liberty. Nor did he say "of whips," but rather to sprinkle the altar with a great amount of human blood, just as they are occupied with doing among the Scythians. But the wise Lacedaemonians <note>Spartans.</note> established this inexcusable sacrifice into a contest for demonstrating fortitude: in which it is not easy to die, and yet nonetheless, drink-offerings of their own blood are offered to the Goddess.*

**See Lucian, *Icaromenippus*; Arrian, *Discourses of Epictetus*, Book I, chapter 3; Tertullian, *To the Martyrs*, chapter IV.** **For that which today is the greatest solemnity among the Lacedaemonians,** <term>diamastigosis <gloss>the ritual flogging of Spartan youths</gloss></term>, **is well known. In this sacred rite, noble youths are assigned to be whipped before the altar.** **Hence Petronius says in the *Satyricon*:** *And I indeed endured three blows with Spartan nobility.* **Seneca, *On Providence*,** chapter IV.

Chapter IV. Do you truly believe their own children were hated by the Spartans <note>original: *Lacedaemoniis*</note>, whose natural character they test publicly by applying whips? The fathers themselves encourage them to endure the strokes of the whips bravely; as they are torn and half-dead, they ask them to persist in offering wounds to wounds. Moreover, a priestess presided over the rites, who held up a small and light statue of the Goddess for as long as the boys were being beaten, as Silenus of Chios <note>A 4th-century BC Greek historian of Sicily and Carthage.</note> relates in his *Fabulous History*. But indeed, if those entrusted with the task of beating, moved by pity because of the beauty or distinction of the youths <note><term>ephebes</term>: young men of military age in ancient Greece undergoing training.</note>, performed it more sparingly or more gently, it was said that the statue became so heavy a sign that the priestess could not sustain its weight. On other occasions, there was a fixed number of lashes, as Zonaras <note>A 12th-century Byzantine chronicler and theologian.</note> writes in volume III: <note>original: "τοῖς δὲ λοιποῖς ἐκκόψας τὰ ὄμματα, καὶ περιγραπτοὺς ὁρίους συγκλείσας αὐτοὺς ἔνθα κατ᾿ ἐιαυτὸν πέμπων ἑκατὸν βυνεύρεις ἤκιτεν ἕκαστον"</note> *that is, to the rest, having gouged out their eyes and confining them within marked boundaries, he ordered a hundred lashes of ox-hide to be inflicted on each one sent there annually.* Saint Paul in 2 Corinthians, chapter 11: <note>original: "ἐν κόποις περισσοτέρως, ἐν πληγαῖς ὑπερβαλλόντως ὑπὸ Ἰουδαίων πεντάκις τεσσαράκοντα παρὰ..."</note> *in labors more abundant, in stripes beyond measure... from the Jews five times I received forty lashes less*

It is thought to derive from the word *Galal*, which means to remove or to cut away, just as the name *Gilgal* <note>original: *Gilgal*</note> became common among the people of Israel in Joshua 5. The reasoning is that just as the Israelites cut away the foreskin, so the *Galli* <note>Schedius is referring to the priests of Cybele, but also making an etymological connection to the Gauls.</note> would cut off their member, removing the disgrace from themselves so that they might be considered to be in a state of chastity. are still preserved even now. And Apollodorus <note>A Greek scholar of the 2nd century BC; his lost works often detailed ancient history and mythology.</note> reports that four Oannes emerged from the Red Sea over the course of successive ages, each of whom was half-human and half-fish. During the time of King Ardorachus of the Chaldeans, another figure of similar shape emerged, whose name was Odakon <note>original Greek: Ωδάκων</note>. Alexander Polyhistor <note>A Greek scholar from the 1st century BC who compiled vast amounts of information on various cultures.</note> also mentions Odakne <note>original Greek: Ωδάκνην</note>, a two-headed animal, otherwise a fish, from whose tail human-like feet grew. He attributes a human voice to it, and says that having emerged from the Erythraean Sea <note>The Red Sea</note>, it reached Babylon; at sunset it returned into the sea. From this being, men learned arts, letters, agriculture, the dedication of temples, architecture, and political laws. Abydenus <note>A Greek historian who wrote about the Chaldeans and Assyrians.</note> also mentions this Oannon and assigns to him a semi-divine <note>original Greek: ἡμιδαίμονα</note> form. Philo <note>Likely referring to Philo of Byblos, who wrote on Phoenician religion.</note> does not overlook him either. And this Dagon was half-man and half-fish, which is also what his name denotes; for *dag* <note>original Hebrew: דג</note> means "fish." Moreover, his form is elegantly noted in the Holy Scriptures in 1 Samuel, chapter 5, verse 4: *And when they rose early on the next morning, behold, Dagon lay prostrate before it, on the ground, before the ark of the Lord; and the head of Dagon and both the palms of his hands were cut off, upon the threshold;* only the Dagon <note>original Hebrew: רק דגון נשאר עליו. This is a wordplay; since "dag" means fish, the text implies only the "fishy part" remained.</note> was left of him, *that is, as Rabbi David Kimchi <note>A famous medieval Jewish commentator and grammarian, also known as the Radak (1160–1235).</note> explains, only the form of a fish was left in him.* Furthermore, after the sacrifices were slaughtered, they would afterwards pray, as is evident from Maro <note>Virgil's surname.</note> in the *Aeneid*, Book XII:

*Sacrificing their own girls and sons to demons.*
I pass over the history related by Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus (c. 37–100 CE), a Romano-Jewish historian.</note> in Book 9, Chapter 12, concerning King Ahaz, and the words of Philo the Jew in his book *On Abraham*. Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 234–305 CE) who wrote extensively on religion and vegetarianism.</note> writes in Book 2 of *On Abstinence*: The Phoenicians, in the midst of great calamities such as wars, droughts, or pestilences, would sacrifice one of their most dearly loved ones, chosen by vote, to Saturn. <note>original Greek: Φοίνικες ταῖς μεγάλαις συμφοραῖς ἢ πολέμων ἢ αὐχμῶν ἢ λοιμῶν ἐθύοντο τῶν φιλτάτων τινὰ ἐπιψηφίζοντες Κρόνῳ</note> That is, *The Phoenicians, in great calamities of either wars, droughts, or famine, would sacrifice someone very dear to them to Saturn, after collecting the votes.*

Diodorus Siculus <note>A Greek historian known for his monumental universal history, the Bibliotheca historica.</note> writes in Book 20 concerning the Carthaginians, who are descended from the Phoenicians: there was among them a bronze statue of Saturn which extended its hands palms upward, but so slanted toward the ground that a child placed upon them would roll off and fall into a pit full of fire. Philastrius <note>A 4th-century bishop and heresiologist.</note> says: they set up an altar, called by the name Tophet <note>A location in Jerusalem in the Valley of Hinnom where, according to the Bible, worshippers influenced by Canaanite religion sacrificed children to the god Moloch.</note>, after some person in the valley of the son of Hinnom. In that same place, the Jews sacrificed their sons and daughters to demons. And Eusebius <note>A Greek historian of Christianity and bishop of Caesarea.</note> in his *Oration in Praise of Constantine*: For every year the Phoenicians sacrificed the most beloved and only-begotten of their children to Saturn. <note>original Greek: Κρόνῳ γὰρ Φοίνικες καθ’ ἕκαστον ἔτος ἔθυον τὰ ἀγαπητὰ καὶ μονογενῆ τῶν τέκνων</note> That is, *For the Phoenicians sacrificed every year the dearest and only-born of their children to Saturn.*

These are the same sacred rites which the author of the Book of Wisdom <note>An apocryphal/deuterocanonical book of the Bible.</note> in Chapter 14, verse 23, and Chapter 12, verses 5–6, calls child-slaying rituals. <note>original Greek: τεκνοφόνους τελετάς</note> Some people, however, believe that the children were only "passed through the fire" without any harm, between two built-up pyres, as if they were being purified. <note>term: lustration <gloss>a ritual of purification or cleansing, often involving fire or water</gloss></note> * This opinion—

For it was held to be a <term>piaculum</term> <note>A religious sin or an act requiring atonement.</note> if the laments of the children or parents were heard during the <term>burning</term> <note>original Latin: "ustulationem."</note>. <term>Plutarch</term> also records this in his book *On Superstition* <note>original Greek: περι δεισιδαιμονιας (peri deisidaimonias).</note>. <term>Benjamin of Tudela</term> <note>A 12th-century Jewish traveler who documented customs across Europe, Asia, and Africa.</note> also reports that the same rite exists among the inhabitants of Dogbyn Cheneraga: all the relatives and kinsfolk leap and play with drums and dances with the greatest joy until the victim has been entirely consumed by fire. The etymology of the word offers no small support for this; for <term>Tophet</term> <note>original Hebrew: תופת. A location in Jerusalem noted for child sacrifice to Moloch.</note> refers to "drumming": a <term>toph</term> <note>original Hebrew: תוף</note> is indeed a drum, and <term>tophaphot</term> <note>original Hebrew: תופפות</note> are female drummers; this is because that place would resound on all sides with the beating of drums—a point which <term>Rabbi David Kimhi</term> <note>A medieval Hebrew grammarian and biblical commentator, often cited as R. D. Cimchi.</note> also transmits. Furthermore, it was a custom among the Romans to employ musical instruments **. Hence <term>Ovid</term> writes in the first book of *Letters from the Black Sea* <note>original: "de Ponto."</note>:

> *When the flute-player plays on his curved horn before the Mother Goddess, who would deny him the copper of a meager coin?* <note>original: "Ante Deum matrem cornu tibicen adunco / Cum canit, exiguæ quis stipis æra neget?" These lines are from Ovid's *Letters from the Black Sea* (Ex Ponto), 1.1.39–40, referring to the priests of Cybele (the Mother Goddess) begging for alms.</note>

It was believed that they achieved this—as <term>Natalis Comes</term> <note>Natale Conti (1520–1582), an influential Italian mythographer whose "Mythologiae" was a standard reference for Renaissance scholars.</note> records in Book 1 of his *Mythology*, Chapter 10—so that pipes might be used in sacred rites to divert the minds of the people present from private thoughts toward a reverence for the immortal Gods; this is because the power of music impresses something divine upon our souls. For **Jupiter**, when he was believed to be that supreme divine mind, only lights <note>Referring to lamps or candles symbolizing intellectual clarity.</note> were employed in sacrifices. However, when Jupiter was considered the highest part of the air <note>In many ancient systems, the gods were associated with physical elements; Jupiter often represented the ether or the upper atmosphere.</note>, then musical instruments were used, as they were in the rites of several other Gods. Indeed, it is said that through the noise of such "simulated" sacrifices, even a small child was snatched from his father's cruelty. <note>This refers to the myth of the infant Jupiter (Zeus), who was hidden from his father Saturn (Cronus) by the Curetes, who clashed their shields and instruments to drown out the baby's cries so Saturn would not hear and eat him.</note> In the ancient sacrifices of this God, the melodies of the **Strophe** and **Antistrophe** were sung in imitation of the movements of the stars, as <term>Aristoxenus</term> <note>A Greek philosopher and pupil of Aristotle who was one of the most important ancient theorists of music.</note> says in Book 1 of *On the Holes of Flutes*, and as <term>Biton</term> <note>An ancient Greek author known for his work on war machines and instruments.</note> writes in the book he addressed to Attalus *On Musical Instruments*. For they would turn, dancing now this way and now that, during those sacred rites; by the **Strophe** <note>original: "Strophen." The first part of a choral ode, performed while moving from right to left.</note> they signified the primary movement of this universe; by the **Antistrophe** <note>original: "Antistrophen." The second part of the ode, moving from left to right, returning the dancers to their original position.</note> the specific motions of the individual planets; and by the **Epode** <note>original: "Epodon." The final part of the lyric sequence, sung while standing still.</note> they signified the rest and firm station of the earth.

The Celts, as the divine Caesar writes in Book 6 of his *Commentaries on the Gallic War*, when they have decided to engage in battle, sacrifice the captured animals that have survived, and they gather the remaining spoils into a single location. In many of their states, one may see mounds of these things built up in consecrated places. It rarely happens that anyone, neglecting their religious duty, would dare to either hide captured goods at their own home or remove what has been placed in the mound; a most severe punishment involving torture is established for such an act. <note>original: "Celtæ Marti, ut D. Cæsar l. VI. Comm. Bell. Gall. scribit..." Caesar is describing the "Interpretatio Romana," where he applies the name of the Roman god Mars to a similar Celtic deity of war.</note>

<term>Florus</term> <note>Lucius Annaeus Florus, a Roman historian of the 2nd century AD.</note> in Book 2, Chapter 4, records that the Gauls, under the leadership of Astrionicus, vowed a <term>torque</term> <note>A "torquem" or torque is a large neck ring made of twisted metal, a characteristic piece of jewelry and a symbol of status among Celtic warriors.</note> from the spoils of our soldiers to their own Mars. Listen also to the cruelty of the <term>Mysians</term> <note>A tribe from the Balkans/Eastern Europe, often depicted as "barbaric" by Roman writers.</note>, who even fed upon the flesh of captives, as the same author left written in Book 4, Chapter 12: The Mysians, having sacrificed a horse immediately before the battle line, <margin>*</margin> <note>original: "Mysi statim ante aciem immolato equo..."</note> made a vow that they would both offer the entrails of the slain enemy leaders as a sacrifice and consume them. At other times, the most fearful of nations made their vows with a murmur, or conceived their vows silently in their minds. As <term>Juvenal</term> <note>Decimus Iunius Iuvenalis, a Roman satirical poet.</note> says in *Satire 10*:

-> *An anxious mother, seeing the shrine of Venus, prays* <-
-> *for beauty for her sons with a moderate murmur,* <-
-> *but for her daughters with a louder one.* <-
<note>original: "Formam optat modico pueris majore puellis / Murmure, cum Veneris fanum videt anxia mater."</note>

And <term>Persius</term> <note>Aulus Persius Flaccus, a Roman poet known for his difficult and stoic satires.</note> in *Satire 2*:

-> *It is not easy for just anyone to remove their murmurs* <-
-> *and low whispers from the temples, and to live* <-
-> *with a vow made openly.* <-
<note>original: "Haud cuivis promptum est murmur, humilesque susurros / Tollere de templis, & aperto vivere voto;" These lines suggest that people often whispered shameful or greedy prayers to the gods that they wouldn't want others to hear.</note>

*“A good mind, reputation, and faith—these things he asks for clearly, so that a stranger might hear.*

<note>original: "Mens bona, fama, fides..." These lines are from the Roman satirist Persius (Satire 2.8–13). He is mocking hypocrites who pray for virtue out loud but whisper selfish or murderous desires in private.</note>

Seneca, in *Epistle 10*: “Though you may release the Gods from your old vows, take up new ones from scratch: ask for a sound mind, and for the good health of the soul, then of the body. *Why should you not make such vows? Boldly ask God, for you will ask Him for nothing that belongs to another. But so that I may send this letter with some small gift, as is my habit, there is a truth I found in Athenodorus:* <note>Athenodorus Cananites was a Stoic philosopher and teacher of Augustus Caesar.</note> *know that you are free from all desires only when you have reached the point where you ask God for nothing except what you could ask for openly.* For now, how great is the madness of men! They whisper the foulest vows to the Gods; if anyone leans in an ear, they fall silent; and what they do not want men to know, they tell to God. See, then, if this can be a wholesome rule: *Live with men as if God sees you; speak with God as if men hear you.*” Therefore, Philemon the Comic poet, although a Pagan, wrote with no less wit and correctness regarding the offering of vows to God:

“If anyone, O Pamphilus, brings a sacrifice,
A multitude of bulls, or of kids, or by Zeus,
Other such things, or fashioned works...”
<note>original: "Εἴ τις δὲ θυσίαν προσφέρων..." This is a fragment from Philemon, a Greek New Comedy poet. He is arguing that God cares more for a person's character than for expensive sacrifices of livestock or gold.</note>

## CHAPTER XXXV.

*They used to sanctify friendship with blood. The Rituals. Similar examples from the Scythians. Catiline entered into a pact with blood. The Germans deliberated during banquets. A passage from Tacitus concerning Civilis. Those fond of wine. What the three drinks of the ancients were.*

**T**he Germans held it a sacred law to unite friendship by the tasting of blood. Athenaeus, in Book I, Chapter II of the *Deipnosophistae*, relates from the historian Posidonius: that the Germans, embracing one another in their <term>symposia</term> <note>A Greek term for a formal banquet or "drinking party."</note>, cut the veins in their foreheads and, mixing the blood that flows down into a cup, they drink it, believing they have reached the highest degree of friendship when [they exchange] blood...

After a drink of this kind, they anoint the head with ointments—especially rose-oil or quince-oil—lest they be overcome by the vapor of the wine; but if these are not available, they use wine or oil of nard. <note>original: "melino... nardino." Melinum was an oil made from quinces, and nard was a costly aromatic oil from the Himalayas, common in the ancient Mediterranean.</note> This was also the custom of the Scythians, who were themselves Germans, as Herodotus reports in Book IV: <note>Herodotus was a 5th-century BCE Greek historian. The author Schedius reflects an early modern belief that the Scythians of the Eurasian steppes were the ancestors of the Germanic tribes.</note> *For the Scythians, having poured wine into a large earthen cup, mix in their own blood; those striking a treaty cut their bodies slightly with a knife or a sword. Then, they dip a scimitar, arrows, an axe, and a sword into the cup. Once they have done this, they bind themselves with many oaths; afterwards, they drink the wine—not only those who made the treaty, but also their most high-ranking companions.* <note>original: "acinacem," a type of Persian or Scythian short sword or scimitar.</note> Pomponius Mela also writes of them in Book II, Chapter 1: <note>Mela was a Roman geographer of the 1st century CE.</note> *Not even their treaties are bloodless. Those who make a pact wound themselves, and once they have mixed the blood they drew, they taste it. They consider this the surest pledge of a lasting loyalty.* <note>original: "manisurae fidei pignus certissimum."</note>

The ancient Danes also, according to the testimony of Saxo in Book I, were accustomed to drench their footprints with a sprinkling of blood when they were about to strike a treaty, intending to strengthen the pledge of friendship by the exchange of each other's blood. <note>Saxo Grammaticus (c. 1160–1220) was a Danish historian. This ritual suggests that the "shared blood" literally marked the ground where they stood together.</note> By this pact, Lisenis the Pirate and Hadingus (the exiled son of King Gram of the Danes), bound by the tightest bonds of alliance, declared war on Loker, the tyrant of the Curetes. Furthermore, a Prince of the Saracens and a Byzantine Emperor, as Nicetas reports in Book II of *The Emperor Isaac Angelos*, established a friendship between themselves by cutting a vein in each other's chests and pledging their blood to one another. <note>Nicetas Choniates was a Byzantine historian. This anecdote illustrates that Schedius saw the "blood covenant" as a cross-cultural phenomenon extending even to the medieval Middle East.</note> There were also some, as Gaius Sallust reports in his book *On the Catiline War*, who said that after Catiline had delivered his speech, when he was driving the partners of his crime to take an oath, he handed round human <note>The text breaks off here at the catchword "cor-", likely referring to "human blood mixed with wine" or "human bodies." Sallust was a Roman historian recording the conspiracy of Catiline to overthrow the Republic in 63 BCE.</note>

...the blood of a human body, mixed with wine in bowls, was passed around; then, when everyone had tasted it following an oath of curse—just as is customary in solemn sacred rites—he revealed his plan. He claimed he did this so they would be more faithful to one another, each being conscious of such a great crime. <note>original: "tanti facinoris conscio." This passage likely refers to the historian Sallust's account of the Roman conspirator Catiline, who supposedly made his accomplices drink wine mixed with human blood to ensure their silence.</note>

But let no one wonder that the Germans confirmed their friendship or a treaty with a drink of blood. Indeed, according to the testimony of Tacitus in his book *On the Customs of the Germans*, <note>original: "Tacit. in l. de Mor. Germ.," referring to the *Germania*, written around 98 CE.</note> they often consult at banquets about reconciling enemies, joining families by marriage, choosing leaders, and finally about peace and war. It is as if at no other time is the mind more open to simple thoughts or more warmed to great ones. A people neither cunning nor crafty, they reveal the secrets of their hearts in the freedom of the place. Thus, the exposed and naked mind of everyone is reconsidered the following day, and the purpose of both times is preserved. They deliberate while they are unable to pretend; they decide while they are unable to be mistaken. 

To this also refer the words of Tacitus in Book IV of the *Histories*: *Civilis was heard with great approval and, by a barbarian rite and ancestral oaths, he bound them all together.* <note>Julius Civilis was the leader of the Batavian Rebellion (69–70 CE) against the Roman Empire. The Batavians were a Germanic tribe living in the Rhine delta.</note> For among the banquets, he urged the nobles of the Batavians to war, observing that deathly rite as a pledge of friendship. <note>original: "feralemque illum ritum." The "feral" or deathly rite refers to the grim nature of the blood-oath.</note> Furthermore, to continue drinking for a day and a night is a disgrace to no one. 

Xenophon also records this of the Persians in Book VIII of the *Education of Cyrus*. <note>original: "in Pæd. Cyri," referring to the *Cyropaedia*, a biography of Cyrus the Great.</note> Hence Seneca says: *Regarding the Germans, that thing was clearly monstrous in recent years in Gaul: the capacity of men for drinking was a miracle to everyone. Indeed, at individual tables, individuals drained four quarts of wine each, such that nine drinkers emptied nine amphorae.* <note>original: "quartarios... amphoras." Seneca the Younger was a Roman Stoic philosopher. An amphora was a large vessel, and Seneca uses this anecdote to marvel at (or criticize) the legendary drinking capacity of the northern tribes.</note>

...twofold. When the army of Emperor Charles V <note>Charles V (1500–1558), Holy Roman Emperor and King of Spain.</note> was besieged by the French at Naples, the Germans, loathing the drinking of water as if it were harmful to their internal organs, and demanding wine as if it were a fair and rightful due, searched through almost all the cellars of the city with a roar. They did not even fear to devastate the house of Alfonso del Vasto himself, the Emperor's commander. <note>Alfonso d'Avalos, Marquis del Vasto (1502–1546), was a celebrated Italian condottiero in the service of Charles V.</note> Based on the tip of a treacherous blacksmith, they uncovered several jars of Greek wine hidden in pits dug beneath the garden. Once the whole army had gathered, they exhausted the supply with extreme speed, drinking from their helmets and carrying it away in water-buckets—wine which, if shared moderately, was believed to have been enough to last everyone for several days. —Giovio, *History*, Book XXV. <note>Paolo Giovio (1483–1552) was an Italian physician and historian whose "Histories of His Own Times" is a primary source for the Italian Wars.</note>

And, when the wedding of Hippolyta, the daughter-in-law of King Ferdinand, and his son Alfonso was being celebrated with the most splendid preparations (for it was a day of a spear-running tournament, and everything was burning under the sun, and people of every kind had gathered to watch), many were praisers of the games, or rather, most everyone was an admirer. Yet, in the midst of the crowd of those praising and applauding, a certain German shouted: *Farewell to games where no one drinks.* And Diodorus Siculus, in Book V of his *Library*: <note>Diodorus Siculus was a 1st-century BCE Greek historian. Book V of his "Bibliotheca historica" describes the geography and customs of various European peoples.</note> Near them are hearths with burning fires, equipped with jars and spits which are filled with the meat of whole limbs. But as Timocles <note>Timocles was an Athenian comic poet of the 4th century BCE.</note> says:

# ELIAS SCHEDIVS

Calling it the "All-Healing" one in their own tongue <note>The Druids referred to mistletoe as *uile-ice* (all-heal) in the Celtic language, a term Pliny translated into Latin as *Omnia Sanantem*.</note>, and having duly prepared sacrifices and feasts under the tree, they bring forward two bulls of white color, whose horns are then bound for the first time. A priest, dressed in a white garment, climbs the tree. He cuts it down with a golden sickle, and it is caught in a white cloak. Then they sacrifice the victims, praying that God make His gift prosperous for those to whom He has given it. They believe that fertility is granted to any sterile animal by drinking an infusion of it, and that it serves as a remedy against all poisons. Such is the religious devotion of nations, often directed toward frivolous matters. However, the reason why they offered that branch, which they call "salutary" <note>original: *salutarem*, meaning health-giving or saving.</note>, is not easily found—unless, as I conjecture, they had heard from the earliest ancestors that the "offshoot of Jehovah" should one day blossom, which would be salvation for all nations.

---

<note>Sebastien Roulliard <note>Sebastien Roulliard (1560–1639) was a French lawyer and antiquarian known for his "Gallican" histories which sought to prove that the ancient Druids had pre-knowledge of Christianity.</note> in his book: *Parthenie, or the History of the most august and most devout Church of Chartres, dedicated by the Ancient Druids in honor of the Virgin who would give birth, etc., Paris 1609. Octavo. p. 51.* He trifles with the idea that Christ affixed to the cross was indicated under the symbol of mistletoe. For just as mistletoe—fixed into a tree not its own—is gathered in the winter time, is to be caught in a white garment, and attracts birds with the sweetness of its fruit; so Christ, born at the time of the winter solstice, was later affixed to a common and "alien" wood <note>Referring to the wood of the Cross.</note>, then taken down and wrapped in white linens, and through His burial and resurrection draws all hungry souls to Himself. Roulliard suspects that for no other reason than hatred toward Christians, Pliny omitted the name *Panchreston* <note>A Greek term meaning "good for everything" or "universal remedy."</note> for mistletoe, and substituted "All-Healing" in its place. Nor will the *Oration of François Meinardus Fristitus held at the Academy of Poitiers on October 10, 1609, and printed there in 1614*, persuade anyone that Jurisprudence was foreshadowed by the Druids under the image of mistletoe.</note>

And they believed the offering of that branch was a sign of that specific Offshoot <note>original: *germinis*. In a biblical context, "The Branch" or "The Offshoot" is a title for the promised Messiah.</note>; therefore, in their sacred rites, they represented that expectation through the offering of mistletoe. For the Pagans adopted many things taken from sacred biblical sources. Thus, in the rites of *Mithras* <note>Mithras was a Persian sun god whose mystery cult was a major rival to early Christianity in the Roman Empire.</note>, they practiced baptism, the breaking of bread, and the presentation of wine mixed with water, as *Justin Martyr* records in his work *Against Trypho* and in his *Oration to Antoninus Pius*, and as *Tertullian* <note>Justin Martyr (c. 100–165 AD) and Tertullian (c. 155–220 AD) were early Christian authors who argued that such similarities were "diabolical mimicry" of Christian sacraments.</note> notes in his *Apology*, among others. Mention of that Offshoot is made in Isaiah, chapter 4, verse 2 <note>The Latin text cites chapter 4, verse 1.</note>: *In that time the offshoot of Jehovah shall be for glory and honor.* And in chapter 11, verse 1: *For a rod shall come forth from the cut stump of Jesse <note>original: *Ischai*, the father of King David.</note>, and a sprout shall blossom from his roots.* Jeremiah, chapter 23, verse 5: *Behold, the days are coming, says Jehovah, in which I will raise up for David a righteous offshoot.* Also in chapter 33, verses 15 and 26. Zechariah, chapter 3, verse 8: *Behold, I am going to bring forth my servant, the Offshoot.* And in chapter 6, verse 12 <note>The Latin text cites verse 14.</note>: *Behold the man whose name is the Offshoot.* Nor is it a wonder that this was known to the *Celts*, since they even believed God would be born of a virgin, as mentioned above. For the pagans—having lost the true doctrine regarding God, the heavenly teaching, and the Sacraments that belong to the true worship of God—retained mere dreams: shadowy rituals of sacrifice instead of the true external ceremonies. Even these were corrupted in many ways, altered by the invention of new ideas, and amplified beyond measure. The scholar *Caspar Peucer* <note>Caspar Peucer (1525–1602) was a German scholar and physician who wrote extensively on divination and the history of religion.</note> pursues this argument more fully across several pages in his book *On Divination*; see his work there.

Calling it "The Healer" <note>original: *Sanantem*. Such is the religious devotion of nations, which is often directed toward trivial things.

However, the reason why they offered that branch, which they call "salutary" <note>original: *salutarem*, meaning "healing" or "saving."</note>, is not easily found: unless, as I conjecture, it is because they heard from the ancient fathers of old that the Offshoot of Jehovah <note>original: *germen Jehovæ*. Schedius links the mistletoe to the "Branch" or "Sprout" mentioned in Messianic prophecies like Isaiah 4:2 and Zechariah 6:12.</note> must one day blossom, which would be the salvation of all nations.

Sébastien Rouilliard, in his book: *Parthenie, or the History of the Very August and Very Devout Church of Chartres, Dedicated by the Ancient Druids in Honor of the Virgin Who Would Give Birth, etc. (Paris, 1609, octavo, page 51)*, trifles with the idea that Christ affixed to the cross was signified under the symbol of mistletoe. For he argues that just as mistletoe, attached to a foreign tree, is gathered in the winter time, is caught in a white garment, and attracts birds by the sweetness of its berries; so Christ, born at the time of the winter solstice, was afterward affixed to a vile and foreign wood <note>Referring to the cross, which was "foreign" to Christ’s divine nature.</note>, but then taken down and wrapped in white linens, drawing all hungry souls to himself through his burial and resurrection. 

Furthermore, Rouilliard suspects that for no other reason than hatred toward Christians did *Pliny* omit the name of mistletoe as *Panchreston* <note>original: *Panchreston*, a Greek term meaning "useful for everything" or "universal remedy."</note>, substituting "all-healing" in its place. Nor will the *Oration of François Meinardus the Frisian, delivered at the Academy of Poitiers on the 6th of the Ides of October, 1609, and printed there*, persuade anyone that Jurisprudence was foreshadowed by the Druids under the image of mistletoe.
