### ON THE GERMAN GODS.

And they considered the offering of that [mistletoe] to be a symbol of that "offshoot" or "branch" <note>original: *germin,* referring to the Messianic "Branch."</note>; therefore, they represented that divine offering in their sacred rites through the offering of mistletoe. For the Gentiles adopted many things taken from sacred [biblical] sources. Thus, in the mysteries of Mithras <note>Mithraism was a Roman mystery religion centered on the god Mithras, which early Christian writers often compared to Christianity as a "demonic imitation."</note>, there was baptism, the breaking of bread, and the offering of wine mixed with water, as Justin Martyr <note>An early Christian apologist (c. 100–165 AD).</note> records in his *Dialogue with Trypho* and his *Oration to Antoninus Pius*; Tertullian in his *Apology* and others also report this.

Mention of that "Offshoot" <note>original: *Germinis*</note> is made in Isaiah, chapter 4, verse 2: *In that time, the sprout of Jehovah shall be for glory and honor.* And in chapter 11, verse 1: *For a rod shall come forth from the cut stump of Jesse, and a shoot from his roots shall blossom.* In Jeremiah, chapter 23, verse 5: *Behold, the days are coming, says Jehovah, when I will raise up for David a righteous branch.* Also in chapter 33, verses 22 and 26. In Zechariah, chapter 3, verse 8: *Behold, I will bring forth my servant, the Branch,* and in chapter 6, verse 14 <note>The author likely intends Zechariah 6:12: "Behold the man whose name is the Branch."</note>: *Behold the man whose name is the Branch.* 

Nor is it surprising that this was known to the Celts, since they even believed God was to be born of a virgin, as mentioned above. For the heathens, having lost the true doctrine concerning God, heavenly teaching, and the Sacraments, retained only mere dreams added to the doctrine of true worship. In place of external ceremonies, they kept shadowy rites of sacrifice, and even those were corrupted in many ways, varied by new inventions, and expanded immensely. Caspar Peucer <note>A 16th-century German scholar who wrote on divinations and the history of religions.</note> pursues this argument more fully for several pages in his book *On Divination*; see him there.

...calling it "all-healing" <note>original: *sanantem*; Schedius is referencing Pliny the Elder’s *Natural History*, where he claims the Druids called mistletoe a name meaning "all-healing" in their own tongue.</note> in their own language. When the sacrifices and feasts have been duly prepared under the tree, they bring forward two white bulls, whose horns are then bound for the first time. The priest, dressed in a white robe, climbs the tree. He cuts it down with a golden sickle. It is caught in a white cloak <note>original: *sago*, a coarse woolen mantle or blanket.</note>. They believe that fertility is granted to any sterile animal from a drink made from it, and that it is a remedy against all poisons. ## CHAPTER XXXVII.

### The herb Selago. Its sacred use among the Gauls and the manner of gathering it.

They also held in honor another herb similar to the Savin <term>Sabina: A species of juniper (Juniperus sabina) used in ancient and traditional medicine</term>, called *Selago* <note>original: *Selaginem*; historically identified with various plants, including clubmoss or a type of hedge-hyssop</note>. As Pliny records in Book 24, chapter 11 of his *Natural History*: *It is gathered without the use of iron, with the right hand passed through the sleeve of the tunic, while the left hand is withdrawn as if one were stealing it. The person gathering it must be dressed in a white garment and have clean, bare feet; a sacrifice of bread and wine must be made before it is gathered. It is then carried in a new cloth.* The Druids of the Gauls taught that this plant should be kept to ward off all destruction, and that its smoke is beneficial against all defects of the eyes. These same people named the herb *Samolus* <term>Samolus: Often identified as Brookweed or Water Pimpernel</term>, which grows in damp places. This was to be gathered with the left hand by those who were fasting, to protect against the diseases of oxen and cattle. The person gathering it was forbidden to look back or place it anywhere other than in a water channel <note>original: *canali*; likely referring to a trough or a running stream where it was processed</note>, where it was to be crushed. On these matters, see the botanical writers in their herbals.

---

Sebastian Roulliard, in the work cited on page 57, interprets *Selago* as *Sebine*, that is, "venerable," and he believes it was an image and type <note>In 17th-century scholarship, a "type" was a natural or historical symbol that prefigured a Christian truth; Schedius often argues against over-extending these parallels.</note> of the Virgin Mary, though he erroneously twists everything toward Christian sacred rites. The opinion of Boxhornius <note>Marcus Zuerius van Boxhorn (1612–1653), a Dutch scholar known for his early theories on the common ancestry of European languages</note> in his *Origins of the Gauls* is no more pleasing; he derives the name of the herb *Samolus* (which Pliny mentions in the same place) from the superstitious rite of gathering it with the left hand, since in Hebrew שמאול <note>original Hebrew: *shemol*; meaning "the left" or "left side"</note> means the "left hand." Jacques Daléchamps <note>A 16th-century French physician and botanist famous for his commentary on Pliny</note>, in his commentary on this passage of Pliny, testifies that even today the people of Bologna call the herb *Pulsatilla* <term>Pulsatilla: Commonly known as the Pasqueflower</term> by the name *Samiolo*. Additionally, Nicolas Chorier, in Book 2 of his *History of Dauphiné*, page 90, considers *Selago* to be the *chamaepeuce* <term>chamaepeuce: Literally "ground-pine," a low-growing plant resembling a small conifer</term>.

<summary>Schedius describes the ritualistic gathering of the herbs Selago and Samolus by the Druids as recorded by Pliny, while critiquing contemporary scholars who attempt to find Christian or Hebrew etymologies for these plants.</summary>

# CHAPTER XXXVIII.

### *Verbena. Its description. The Gauls use it for casting lots. The custom of gathering it. Its use in Roman sacred rites. Used for crowns in the rites of Jupiter. Sacred to Venus. For what reason. Dedicated to Bacchus.*

But the use of Vervain <term>Verbena: A plant of the genus *Verbena*, specifically *Verbena officinalis*, long associated with divine forces and medicinal healing</term> was also very common among the Druids, or Celts, as Pliny also records in Book 25, Chapter 9: *No herb, however, among the Roman nobility, has more renown than "hierabotane"* <note>original: *hierabotane*; from the Greek for "holy herb"</note>. *Some call it "Peristerion"* <note>original: *Peristerion*; Greek for "pigeon-plant," as pigeons were thought to be attracted to it</note>, *and our people call it "verbenaca." This is the herb which we have noted that envoys carry to the enemy.* <note>Roman heralds, known as *fetiales*, carried bundles of Vervain to ensure their safety and religious authority when negotiating treaties or declaring war.</note> *With this, the table of Jupiter is swept, and houses are purged and purified. There are two kinds of it; the leafy one, which they consider the female; the male has fewer leaves. The branches of both are numerous, thin, a cubit long* <term>Cubit: An ancient unit of measurement based on the length of the forearm, roughly 18 inches</term>, *and angular. The leaves are smaller than those of the oak, and narrower, with larger divisions: the flower is grey-blue, and the root is long and thin. It grows everywhere in level, watery places. Some do not distinguish between them, but make them one genus entirely, since both have the same effects.*

*Both are used for casting lots by the Gauls, and they chant prophecies from them. But the Magicians* <note>original: *Magi*; here referring to practitioners of ritual herbalism and folk magic</note> *in particular are obsessed with these. They claim that those rubbed with the plant obtain what they wish, drive away fevers, win friendships, and there is no disease it cannot heal. It must be gathered around the rising of the Dog Star* <term>Dog Star: Sirius; its "heliacal rising" in mid-summer was considered a potent time for gathering medicinal plants</term>, *in such a way that neither the Moon nor the Sun sees it; with honeycomb and honey given to the earth beforehand as a propitiatory offering. After a circle is drawn around it with an iron tool, it is dug up with the left hand and raised on high. It should be dried in the shade—the leaves, stem, and root separately. They also say that if the dining room is sprinkled with water in which it was soaked, it makes the guests more cheerful...*

The Druids say that it is tossed high into the air by the serpents' hissing, and that it must be caught in a cloak <note>original Latin: *sago*; a thick woolen cloak worn by Roman soldiers and Gauls</note> so that it does not touch the ground. The one who snatches it must flee on horseback, for the serpents will pursue him until they are blocked by the intervention of some river. The test of its authenticity is if it floats against the current, even if it is bound in gold. And as the cleverness of the Magi is skilled at hiding their frauds, they declare it must be gathered during a specific phase of the moon, as if the timing of the serpents' activity were subject to human will. I have actually seen this egg; it is about the size of a small round apple, with a cartilaginous shell marked with numerous cavities like the suckers on the arms of an octopus—a distinctive mark of the Druid’s egg. It is remarkably praised for winning lawsuits and gaining access to Kings; it is an object of such vanity that I know of a Roman knight from the Vocontii tribe <note>A Gallic tribe in what is now southeastern France</note> who, during a trial, was put to death by the Emperor Claudius <note>original: *D. ...they have made. For it is not the custom for them <note>the serpents</note> to be crested on the caduceus <note>The herald’s staff carried by the god Mercury</note>. Hyginus <note>Gaius Julius Hyginus, a Roman mythographer</note> states: "Some, when they fashion caducei, depict two serpents entwined on a small rod: because this was the beginning of Mercury's peace." Regarding the Lithuanians—who are Sarmatians, or Scythians, and the very same as the Germans—who worship serpents, Martin Cromer <note>A 16th-century Polish historian and cartographer</note> agrees with those devoted to Pliny’s accounts in Book 15. These people, *he says*, once believed that serpents and vipers were not without a share of divinity, and they were nourished as if they were household gods <note>original Latin: *lares*; protective spirits of the Roman home</note> in individual houses and families. Milk was offered to them as a sacred drink, and roosters were sacrificed to them. It was considered ill-omened and an inestimable disaster for the entire family if anyone killed or harmed one of them.

And Guagnini <note>Alexander Guagnini, an Italian-born chronicler of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth</note> writes the same in his description of Lithuania regarding the Samogitians <note>A region in modern-day Lithuania where pagan traditions persisted late into the Middle Ages</note>: There are many rural idolaters among the Samogitians who nourish certain serpents in their homes as household gods <note>original Latin: *penates*</note>. These serpents have four short legs like lizards, with black and fat bodies, and are called *bivoytas* <note>Likely a corruption of the Lithuanian *gyvatė* (snake) or *žaltys* (grass snake). While grass snakes have no legs, early modern travelers often confused them with skinks or the "slow-worm" lizard</note> in the native language. On certain days, after the house has been purified, the serpents crawl out to the food set for them. The whole family stands around in a kind of fearful veneration until the creatures have eaten their fill and returned to their place. If any misfortune happens to the creatures, the family believes their domestic serpent-god has been poorly received and satisfied. He built ships with flat hulls to manage the shallow and uncertain shoreline. Thus the infantry crossed; the cavalry followed in the shallows, or, where the water was deeper, they crossed by swimming alongside their horses. A diverse battle line stood on the shore, dense with weapons and men, with women running between them like Furies <note>Deities of vengeance in Greek and Roman mythology, often depicted with snakes for hair</note>; in funeral garb, with their hair disheveled, they carried torches before them. And the Druids all around, pouring out dreadful prayers with their hands raised to heaven, struck the soldiers with the novelty of the sight—so much so that, as if their limbs were paralyzed, they offered their immobile bodies to be wounded. Then, encouraged by the exhortations of their Leader, and stimulating each other so that they would not fear a feminine and fanatical column, they carried forward the standards, struck down those in their way, and enveloped them in their own fire. A garrison was afterward placed over the villages, and the groves sacred to cruel superstitions were cut down. For they considered it lawful to nourish their altars with the blood of captives and to consult the Gods through human entrails.* <note>original: "Nam cruore captivo adolere aras, & hominum fibris consulere Deos, fas habebant."</note>

## CHAPTER XL. ##

*The Vates: Another order of priests. Their duties. The divination of Ismenian Apollo <note>Apollo Ismenius was a title for Apollo at Thebes, where he was consulted through the interpretation of burnt offerings.</note>. The custom of the Indians in consulting priests on the outcome of events. And these are the details concerning the Druids found scattered throughout the works of authors whose writings have reached our hands. Beyond these, however, there were also other orders, among whom those called the <term>Vates<note>A class of seers and diviners among the ancient Celts and Gauls, distinct from the Druids (philosophers/judges) and Bards (poets).</note></term> were prominent. Strabo mentions them in Book IV of his *Geography*: *Among all three nations, the Bards, Vates, and Druids are held in exceptional honor. The Vates, moreover, are devoted to sacrifices and the study of the causes of nature.* Diodorus Siculus, in Book V of his *Library of History*, writes: *There are also Vates of great esteem among them; they divine the future from the flight of birds and the entrails of sacrificial victims, and the entire populace obeys them; especially when a consultation arises concerning matters of great importance.* And these were perhaps the same as the *Vates* of the Romans, whose duties Orpheus described in these lines from the *Argonautica*:

> I have learned the many and various laws of the seers,
> Which concern the positions of wild beasts, birds, and entrails;
> And those things which the souls of mortal men,
> Struck in their hearts by sleep, prophesy in the paths of dreams;
> And the interpretation of signs and portents, and the courses of the stars.
> <note>original: "Ἀμφὶ δὲ μαντείης ἐδάην πολυπείρονας ὅρμους / Θηρῶν τ’ οἰωνῶν τε καὶ ἢ σπλάγχνων θέσις ἐστίν. / Ἢ δ’ ὅσα θεσπίζουσιν ὀνειροπόλοισιν ἀταρποῖς / Ψυχαὶ ἐφημερίων, ὕπνῳ βεβολημέναι ἦτορ. / Σημείων τεράτων τε λύσεις, ἄστρων τε πορείας."</note>

...in modern times, Nicolás Monardes <note>A Spanish physician (c. 1493–1588) who wrote one of the most important early books on the medicinal plants of the New World, despite never traveling there himself.</note> writes the following in his book on the *Herbs of the Indies*: *Among the Indians, it was the custom for Priests to consult about the outcome of wars and other matters of great importance. <margin>Book V of the [Historical] Library <note>original: "l. V. Bibl." — Likely referring to Diodorus Siculus’s *Bibliotheca historica*, which contains a famous description of the Bards.</note></margin> Among these peoples, there are also poets of lyric songs, whom they call **Bards**. To the accompaniment of instruments not unlike lyres, they sing the praises of some and the vituperation <note>scathing verbal condemnation or oratory abuse</note> of others. *Ammianus Marcellinus <note>A 4th-century Roman soldier and historian whose work is a primary source for late antiquity.</note>, Book XV:* The Bards recorded the outstanding deeds of brave men in heroic verses and sang them with sweet melodies to the lyre. *Asconius <note>Quintus Asconius Pedianus, a Roman scholar known for his commentaries on Cicero's orations.</note>* describes this manner of singing in his commentary on *Cicero’s Third Verrine Oration*: When <term>citharists<gloss>musicians who play the cithara, an ancient stringed instrument related to the lyre but with a larger wooden sounding box</gloss></term> sing, both hands perform their duty. The right hand uses the <term>plectrum<gloss>a small tool or pick used to pluck or strum the strings of an instrument</gloss></term>, and this is "singing from without"; the left hand plucks the strings with the fingers, and this is "singing from within." However, the citharist of Aspendos <note>An ancient city in modern-day Turkey known for its music and theater.</note> performed a difficult feat: he did not use both hands for the song, but rather performed everything—that is, the entire melody—from "within," using only his left hand. For this reason, all who were thieves were called "Aspendian Citharists" by the Greeks in a proverb, because just as that musician was a concealer of his technique, so were these men concealers of their thefts. *Orpheus* reports in the *Argonautica <note>An epic poem detailing the voyage of Jason and the Argonauts; the text attributes the invention of the lyre to the Sirens here.</note>* that the **Sirens** invented the lyres:

To these is added a fourth order, namely that of the Samotheans. <note>The Samotheans were believed by early modern scholars to be an ancient race of philosophers in Britain and Gaul, supposedly founded by Samothes, a descendant of Japheth. *That is to say*: For Kings have need of the most learned men in the greatest of affairs, so that they may serve as their advisors; and while they give commands to others, they themselves receive commands from those [learned men] regarding what is proper to do and from what they should abstain. Just as Homer says Agamemnon needed the counsel of Nestor; and as often as he did not obey that counselor, he lamented and immediately repented. 

Moreover, Philip, who seems to have been the most clever of Kings, summoned Aristotle as a teacher and guide for his son Alexander, because he himself was not fit for teaching the kingly art. Although he wished to command all others—the Macedonians, Thracians, Illyrians, and all the Greeks—he handed his son over to the command of another to be educated. While he gave orders to so many thousands of men, he did not venture to give orders to that one boy alone. For he did not think the risk was equal if he should fail in his duty toward others as it would be if he failed toward his son.

...he forbade him to be struck in the customary way by the lictor, and he—the one to whom the East and the West had submitted—lowered the lictorial fasces <note>The *fasces* were bundles of rods with an axe, symbolizing a magistrate's power. Aelian, in Book 7, Chapter 15 of his *Various Histories*, relates that the Mitylenians imposed laws on rebels by which they forbade them from teaching their children letters: <note>original Greek: "ἡνίϰα τῆς θαλάσσης ἦρξαν Μιτυληναῖοι, τοῖς ἀφισταμένοις τῶν συμμάχων τιμωρίαν ἐϰείνην ἐπήρτησαν, γράμματα μὴ μανθάνειν τοὺς παῖδας αὐτῶν, μηδὲ μουσιϰὴν διδάσϰεσθαι: πασῶν ϰολάσεων ἡγησάμενοι βαρυτάτην εἶναι ταύτην, ἐν ἀμαθίᾳ ϰαὶ ἀμουσίᾳ ϰαταβιῶναι"</note> *When the Mitylenians held command of the sea, they imposed this punishment on those allies who revolted: that their children should not learn letters, nor be taught the liberal arts; judging this to be the heaviest of all punishments: to live out their lives in ignorance and lack of culture.* For they saw that no Republic would be safe in which there was a poverty of learned men.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the vital necessity of education for rulers. Following the previous page's examples of how the deprivation of learning was used as a punishment (by the Mitylenians) or a tool for religious suppression (by Julian the Apostate), the author now cites the Greek orator Isocrates and the historical anecdote of Demetrius Phalereus to argue that monarchs are uniquely disadvantaged because they lack the honest criticism and daily struggles that naturally educate private citizens.</meta>

<page-num>640</page-num>

# ELIAS SCHEDIUS

Many things serve to educate, and especially the lack of luxury, but rather being compelled to struggle for one's life every day. Next are the laws, under which each citizen happens to live; furthermore, freedom of speech, and the ability to openly attack the faults of one another before enemies. In addition to these, some of the poets of old have left behind instructions on how one ought to live. Thus, from all these things, it is likely they become better men. But for tyrants, nothing of this sort exists; rather, those who most of all needed to be educated once they were established in power, continue on without any admonishment. For most people do not approach them, and those who do associate with them speak only to please them. <note>original: "πολλὰ τὰ παιδεύοντα... πρὸς χάριν ὁμιλοῦσιν" — This is a passage from Isocrates’ oration *To Nicocles*, an ancient Greek "mirror for princes" advising a young king on how to rule justly.</note>

*For there are very many things that might educate private men; and especially a life free from delights, and the daily necessity of struggling, as it were, to provide for one's livelihood. Then the laws, by which each are governed in their own states: furthermore, that liberty which allows friends to openly rebuke one another, and enemies to drive home faults: finally, certain ancient Poets have left behind precepts regarding the manner of living. By all which things it is agreeable that they should become better. To Princes, however, nothing of this kind happens: but those whom it was most fitting of all to be instructed, these, soon after undertaking the principate, live out their lives without any advisors. For the approach is open to very few: those indeed who live familiarly with them, say and do everything to win favor.* <note>The author provides a Latin translation of the preceding Greek text from Isocrates to ensure clarity for his contemporary scholarly audience.</note>

**Hence** Demetrius Phalereus <note>Demetrius of Phalerum (c. 350–280 BCE), an Athenian statesman and philosopher who advised Ptolemy I in Alexandria and was instrumental in the founding of the Great Library.</note> used to urge King Ptolemy to buy and read books written about kingship. For the things of which friends [fear to] warn Kings...

The men fear this fate much more for the sake of their women—so much so, that *the minds of the tribes are more effectively bound when noble girls are also demanded as hostages.* For it was the custom among the Germans that the mothers of their families (as *Caesar* reports in Book 1 of his *Commentaries on the Gallic War*) would declare through lots and prophecies whether it would be beneficial to engage in battle or not. 

From this, as *Jean Bodin* <note>A 16th-century French jurist and political philosopher who wrote extensively on demonology.</note> relates in Book 11, Chapter 5 of *On Demonomania*, drawing from *Caesar*, *Ariovistus* <note>A leader of the Suebi and other Germanic tribes in the 1st century BCE.</note>, the King of the Germans, was equipped with four hundred thousand men; yet he placed such faith in the prophetic women concerning the day of the conflict that he was forbidden by them from fighting before the New Moon. *Caesar*, having learned of this, immediately joined the battle.

The Celts <note>The author, following ancient sources, often groups Germanic and Celtic peoples together when discussing northern customs.</note> were suffering from internal rebellion. When they had already taken up arms for war, their wives, placing themselves between the opposing battle lines, pleaded against the crimes: and they arranged it so that the men, returning to favor, laid down their dispute. Therefore, in the treaties made with Hannibal <note>The famous Carthaginian general who crossed the Alps to fight Rome.</note>, it is specified that the Celts shall not complain to the Carthaginians that the Carthaginian Hipparchs <note>Greek term for cavalry commanders.</note> and leaders are the judges, nor shall the Carthaginians object to the Celts that the women of the Celts act as judges.

in turn, she herself brings something of the nature of arms to the man. This they consider the greatest bond, these their secret sacred rites, these their gods of marriage. <note>The author is quoting Tacitus, *Germania* 18. The passage emphasizes that Germanic marriage was a partnership in hardship and war, symbolized by the exchange of weapons rather than jewelry.</note> Nor should a woman think herself outside the considerations of virtue, or beyond the hazards of war; she is warned by the very omens of the beginning of the marriage that she comes as a partner in labors and dangers, destined to suffer and to dare the same things in peace and in battle. This is what the yoked oxen, the prepared horse, and the gifted arms proclaim. Thus she must live, and thus she must die. 

Therefore, as the same author <note>Referring to Tacitus.</note> relates, this is the chief incentive for their courage; it is not chance, nor a random gathering that forms the troop or the military wedge, but families and kinships, with their "pledges" <note>original Latin: *pignora*, referring here to their wives and children, who served as a physical reminder of what the men were fighting to protect.</note> close by. From there, the wailing of women can be heard, and from there, the crying of infants. These are the most sacred witnesses for every man, and these are his greatest praisers. To their mothers and to their wives they bring their wounds; and the women do not fear to count the gashes or to clean them. <note>original Latin: *exsugere*, literally "to suck out" or clean the wounds, a common ancient medical practice.</note> They also carry food and encouragement to those who are fighting. 

Hence, as the same author relates in Book 14 of his *Annals*, a diverse battle line stood before the shore, thick with arms and men, while women ran between them; in the manner of Furies, in funeral dress, with their hair hanging down, * they carried torches before them. <note>This refers to the Roman attack on the island of Mona (Anglesey), where Druids and women defended the sacred groves.</note> And as the soldiers were setting out for battle, according to the Divine Caesar in Book 1 of his *Commentaries on the Gallic War*, the women, with outstretched hands and weeping, implored the men not to deliver them into slavery to the Romans. 

Nor was the fight against the wives any less fierce, says Florus in Book 3, Chapter 3, than against the men themselves; for they had placed their wagons and carts all around like a rampart, and fought from high above as if from towers, using lances and pikes. We read, however, that women were also present with Dionysus <note>The Greek god of wine and ecstasy, who according to legend led a conquering army into India.</note> when he was subduing India.

## CHAPTER XLIV.

*Auspices. Lots. Mossolanus the Jew. Rhabdomancy <note>original Greek: Ῥαβδομαντεία. Divination performed by throwing or shaking rods, sticks, or arrows.</note>. A custom in use among the Rugians <note>An East Germanic tribe living on the Baltic coast.</note>. Also among the Frisians <note>A Germanic ethnic group native to the coastal parts of the Netherlands and Germany.</note>. They prophesied by means of tamarisk wood. Tamarisks are sacred to Apollo. The same ritual among Eastern peoples. The evil eye. Warding off the evil eye. They spat thrice into their bosoms to remove the evil eye or disease. Another method of consultation among the Rugians.*

The Germans pay the greatest attention to auspices and lots, says Tacitus in his book *On the Customs of the Germans* <note>Tacitus's *Germania*, written c. 98 AD, is a primary source for early Germanic culture.</note>. There were, however, many modes of divining, as Natale Conti <note>A 16th-century Italian mythographer.</note> writes in Book 1 of his *Mythology*: either from the sight of birds—from which we get the word <term>auspices</term> <note>From the Latin *avis* (bird) and *specio* (to look at).</note>; or from food, which gave rise to the *solistimum* and the *tripudium* <note>Ovens observed from the feeding habits of sacred chickens; a "tripudium" occurred when a bird ate so greedily that food fell from its beak and hit the ground.</note>; from chattering came auguries; from song came the <term>oscines</term> <note>Birds whose vocalizations, rather than flight patterns, were considered prophetic, such as ravens or owls.</note>; and furthermore from flight, whether to the right or to the left.

But how much value should be placed on this art of augury, says Polydore Vergil <note>An Italian humanist and historian who lived in England during the Tudor period.</note> in Book 1, Chapter 24, was clearly demonstrated by Mossolanus the Jew, a truly wise man. As Josephus relates in Book 1 of *Against Apion* (drawing from Hecataeus <note>Hecataeus of Abdera, a Greek historian and skeptic.</note>), while Mossolanus was in the army, a certain seer ordered everyone to halt their march until he could take an omen from a bird that was nearby. Mossolanus, saying nothing, quickly took up his bow and, having shot his arrows, killed the bird. When the seer and several others reacted with indignation, he said:

> "Why do you rage, you wretched spirits? For how could this bird, being ignorant of its own safety, predict the outcome of our journey for us? For if it had been able to foreknow the future, it would never have come to this place, fearing that it would be struck by the arrows of Mossolanus the Jew."

...ever <note>The text begins with the suffix of a word from the previous page, likely completing "auguries" or "auspices."</note> it may be, according to the testimony of Tacitus in his book *On the Customs of the Germans* <note>Tacitus, *Germania*, chapter 10.</note>, the custom among the Germans is simple. *They cut a branch from a fruit-bearing tree and slice it into little twigs; these they distinguish by certain marks and throw them at random and by chance over a white cloth. Then, if the consultation is public, the priest of the community—or if private, the father of the family himself—prays to the Gods and, looking up to the sky, picks up three twigs, one at a time. Once lifted, he interprets them according to the mark previously impressed upon them. If the lots forbid the matter, there is no further consultation on the same business for that day. But if they allow it, the confirmation of auspices is still required; and indeed, it is also known from this that they interrogate the voices and flight of birds.* Regarding the Rugians <note>An East Germanic tribe from the Baltic coast, known for their distinct pagan rituals persisting into the Middle Ages.</note>, Saxo Grammaticus <note>A 12th-century Danish historian.</note> writes the same in Book XIV of his *History of the Danes*: *The Rugians,* he says, *dwellers by the Baltic Sea, using three small pieces of wood—with one side white and the other black—cast them into the lap in place of lots; they signified prosperity with the white sides and adversity with the dark ones.*

In the laws of the Frisians <note>The *Lex Frisionum*, a legal code for the Frisian people recorded around 800 AD.</note>, Title XIV, as the jurist François Hotman <note>A 16th-century French legal scholar.</note> discusses in his *Discourse on Fiefs*, chapter XLIX, the following appears: *There must be lot-tellers: two sticks cut from such a branch (which they call <term>tenos</term> <note>A Germanic term for a lot or divining rod.</note>, one of which is marked with the sign of the cross and the other is left plain) are wrapped in clean wool and placed upon the altar or upon holy relics. If a priest is present—or if a priest is lacking, any young boy—he must lift one of these lots from the altar. Meanwhile, God is to be entreated to show by an evident sign if those seven men, who swore an oath regarding a committed homicide, had sworn the truth. If he lifts the one marked with the cross, those who swore shall be innocent. But if he lifts the other, then each of those seven men must make his own lot—that is, a stick (tenum) from a branch—and mark it with his own sign so that he, as well as the others standing around, may recognize it:* and

Furthermore, the Magi and the Scythians, according to the testimony of Natale Conti in Book IV of his *Mythology* <note>Natale Conti (1520–1582) was an influential Italian mythographer.</note>, practiced divination by means of tamarisk wood <note>original: *lignum Myricae*</note> and by many other twigs of shrubs. Moreover, that divination by tamarisk rods was common in Lesbos is attested by the very surname of Apollo himself, as he was called *Myricaeus* <note>meaning "of the tamarisk"</note> by the Lesbians for that reason. Furthermore, Archaeus left in the records he produced concerning Archenatis and the Erythraean War that Apollo appeared in a dream to Archagetas <note>A title meaning "the founding leader."</note>, the supreme commander of that expedition, carrying a branch of tamarisk; for this reason, they considered that plant to be pleasing to that God.

And Callimachus <note>A noted Greek poet and scholar from the 3rd century BCE.</note> says: *Why is it that women spit into their bosoms?* <note>original: "τί κόλποισιν ἐπὶ πτύσι γυν."</note> We draw further evidence of this power of spitting from Aelian, who writes concerning pigeons in Book 1, Chapter 15: *They say that in the succession of the brood, while the pigeons are brooding over the eggs and after the chicks are hatched, the male spits upon them to drive away envy, so that they might not be susceptible to fascination.* <note>original: "διαδοχῆς. Φασιν ἐπωάζειν τὰς περιστερὰς..." / "fascinationi sint obnoxii." In ancient folklore, even animals were thought to protect their young from the "evil eye" using saliva.</note> It was customary to spit not only to keep away the "evil eye" <note>term: *fascination*; the ancient belief that a malevolent glare could cause physical harm or bad luck.</note>, but also to reject every kind of bad omen. On this point, Seneca writes in *Consolation to Marcia*: *Who, if warned about the fate of their own children, would not spit as if at a dire omen, and command that such things instead fall upon the heads of their enemies?* Pliny, in Book 28, Chapter 4, says: *We spit to ward off the "comitial" diseases <note>term: *comitial disease*; an ancient name for epilepsy, so called because if someone had a seizure during a Roman assembly (*comitia*), the meeting was cancelled as a bad omen.</note>, which is to say, we spit upon the contagious force of the sickness.* Theophrastus, in his *Characters* regarding "Superstition," writes: *Upon seeing a madman or an epileptic, he shudders and spits into his own bosom.*

There was also another method of consulting the fates among the Rugians <note>A West Slavic tribe inhabiting the island of Rügen in the Baltic Sea, known for their distinct pagan rituals.</note>: sitting by the hearth of the house, they would draw lines in the ashes without counting them beforehand. If, upon counting them later, they found the lines were of an even number, they judged this a sign of a prosperous matter; if the number was odd, they considered it a prediction of misfortune, as Saxo Grammaticus <note>A 12th-century Danish historian famous for his *Gesta Danorum* (Deeds of the Danes).</note> relates in Book 14 of his *History of the Danes*.

### ON THE GERMANIC GODS.

It was, furthermore, a particular custom of the nation, according to the testimony of Tacitus in his book *On the Manners of the Germans* <note>original: "Tacit. in l. de Morib. Germ."; referring to the Roman historian Tacitus and his ethnographic work, the *Germania*.</note>, to test the omens and warnings of horses. These animals are maintained at public expense in the same sacred forests and groves—white horses, untouched by any mortal labor. These are yoked to a sacred chariot, accompanied by the priest and the king or the leader of the community, who observe their neighing and snorting. No other omen carries greater weight, not only among the common people but also among the nobles and the priests. For they consider themselves the servants of the Gods, and the horses to be their confidants <note>The Latin *conscios* implies the horses share in the secrets or knowledge of the gods.</note>. The last of all the Germans to observe the use of this omen were the Rugians <note>A tribe residing on the Baltic coast, particularly the island of Rügen; while Schedius calls them "Germans," they are often identified as West Slavic in medieval contexts.</note>, as Saxo writes in Book 14 of the *History of the Danes* <note>original: "Saxo l. XIV. Hist. Dan."; referring to the medieval chronicler Saxo Grammaticus.</note> and Cranzius in Book 5 of *Vandalia* <note>original: "Cranz. l. V. Vandaliæ"; referring to Albert Krantz, a 15th-century historian.</note>.

A sacred horse was kept among the Rugians, white in color, from which it was considered sacrilegious to pluck hairs from the mane or tail. Only the priest had the right to feed or ride it, so that the use of the divine animal would not be considered cheaper or less significant the more frequent it became. In this horse, it was believed their God waged wars against the enemies of his sacred rites. The chief proof of this matter was that, although the horse remained in its stable at night, it was often seen in the morning covered in sweat and mud, as if it had run great distances during exercise.

When it was decided to undertake a war against some province, a triple row of spears used to be arranged by the work of the attendants before the temple. In each of these rows, two spears were fixed crosswise with their points turned into the ground, with equal spaces separating the rows. At the time of leading the expedition, the horse...

## CHAPTER XLVI.

...they would flee to him, as if to the most righteous judge of all. The Senate, the people, and the Priests, who had come in crowds to watch the single combat or other such trials, would meanwhile implore divine aid—as is recorded in the Salic Law <note>The *Lex Salica* was the ancient law code of the Salian Franks, established in the early 6th century.</note>. They would recount from memory the favors that God had bestowed upon them in similar matters, praying that He would be present for the innocent person in the current case and grant victory from heaven. The accused was given the opportunity to choose and hire whomever he wished to fight on his behalf. The accuser himself, however, was forced to fight. The Lombards also introduced the use of the duel in Italy, such that King Agilulf <note>Agilulf (reigned 590–616) was a King of the Lombards who consolidated their rule in Italy.</note> even provided for them in his laws. By this means, ambiguous rights concerning possessions and more serious criminal charges, which might threaten one's safety or reputation, were decided.

They offer a threefold reason for this so-barbarous custom:

I. On account of the lack of laws by which ambiguous cases might be resolved. For since they wished to submit to neither divine nor Roman laws, they put forward that well-worn proverb: 
> *If the laws do not suffice, let us come to arms.* <note>original: "Si non sufficiunt jura, veniamus ad arma."</note>

II. Because they had received that custom from their ancestors on the Island of Scandinavia; and being accustomed to wars, with arms always at the ready, they embraced it as the most familiar and most direct method of declaring equity.

III. Lest, on account of the private enmities of a few, the tribes should engage in bloody battles among themselves, single combat <note>The text uses the term *monomachia*, a Greek-derived word for a duel or one-on-one fight.</note> was permitted between the principals of the contention as a remedy. This was done in such a way that whoever was hindered by age, illness, or sex could hire another in their place, whom the Italians call a <term>champion</term> <note>original: "campionem"</note> from the Lombard and also Germanic word <term>Kämpffer</term> <note>Modern German *Kämpfer*, meaning a fighter or combatant.</note>.

If he <note>Referring to a hired champion fighting on behalf of another.</note> should fall in battle, the patron in whose name he had fought was understood to be condemned, just as if he himself had been convicted of the crime. These details are from Bernardo Sacco’s *History of Ticinum* <note>Ticinum is the ancient name for the city of Pavia in Italy; Bernardo Sacco was a 16th-century historian of the region.</note>. In the laws of Charlemagne, it was established—as Hotman <note>François Hotman (1524–1590), a renowned French legal scholar and humanist.</note> discusses in his *Discourse on Feuds*, chapter 44, regarding the Lombard Law, Book II, title 54—that in criminal cases, the accuser and the defender should contend equally in the field with clubs; nor should the matter be decided by their swearing of oaths. It is clear, however, that this was to be understood as the procedure only when other forms of legal proof were lacking.

By a law of Emperor Otto IV <note>Though the text says Otto IV, the mention of Pope John XIII and the Synod of Ravenna (967 AD) indicates the author likely refers to Otto I, the Great. Historical texts from this era often contain such numbering discrepancies.</note>, a sentence was promulgated in Romagna by the Italian Princes, with the knowledge and agreement of Pope John XIII and the entire Synod that had then gathered at Ravenna (as appears in the Lombard Law, Book II, title 54, and the Laws of the Franks, title 4). It was decreed that henceforth throughout all Italy—even in those courts where they used Roman Law (that is, the laws of Justinian)—they should not settle controversies by the swearing of oaths, due to the great multitude of perjurers; instead, they should resolve them by duel and combat. Emperor Otto ordered this institution to be observed not only in the disputes of private citizens and laypeople, but even in the legal conflicts of the Churches.

Frotho III, King of the Danes, as Saxo Grammaticus <note>A 12th-century Danish historian and author of the *Gesta Danorum*.</note> relates in his fifth book, also ordained that any controversy whatever should be decided by iron <note>original: "ferro" – referring to the sword.</note>, believing it more honorable to conflict with strength than with words. If one of the combatants, by stepping back, should leave the boundary of the drawn circle, he was treated as defeated and would suffer the loss of his case. But if [a man] should attack a champion [on behalf of another] regarding any matter, the champion would receive him while armed, though [the challenger] was to fight only with a staff. This was the ancient custom...

*Sidonius Apollinaris, Book I, Letters* <note>Gaius Sollius Apollinaris Sidonius (c. 430–489 AD) was a Gallo-Roman poet and bishop whose letters describe the transition from Roman to Germanic rule.</note>: an armor-bearer stands around the chair; a crowd of fur-clad attendants is admitted so they do not block the way, and removed so they do not make noise. *Apuleius, Before the Court* <note>Referring to the Roman author Apuleius (c. 124–170 AD); this passage describes the high status of royal guards.</note>: Brave men and attendants of the royal sides maintained guardianship through the strength of the brave with ever-watchful protection. Thus, duties were divided among them in the royal retinue of arms.

*Firmicus Maternus, Book III, Chapter IV, Mathesis* <note>Julius Firmicus Maternus was a 4th-century lawyer and astrologer; his work *Mathesis* is one of the most complete handbooks of Roman astrology.</note>: [The stars] will make shield-bearers, or protectors of the Emperors, or those who preserve the safety of leaders through their own watchfulness. Then, in the assembly itself, either one of the leaders, or a father, or a relative, adorns the youth with a shield and a <term>framea</term> <note>A Germanic word for a spear with a short, narrow iron head, used for both close and distant combat.</note>. This is their version of the toga <note>A reference to the Roman ritual where a boy put on the *toga virilis* to mark his entry into manhood.</note>; this is the first honor of youth. Before this, they are seen as part of a household; afterward, they belong to the state.

Distinguished nobility or the great merits of their fathers assign the rank of leader even to young men. They are joined with others who are more robust and have already been tested, and there is no shame in being seen among the followers. The retinue itself <note>original: *comitatus*</note> also has its ranks, based on the judgment of the one they follow. There is great rivalry among the followers as to who holds the chief place with their leader, and among the leaders, as to who has the most numerous and fierce followers. This is their dignity, this is their strength: to be always surrounded by a large circle of chosen young men—a distinction in peace, a protection in war. Nor is this famous name and glory only within their own tribe, but also among neighboring states, if their retinue stands out in number and valor; for they are sought out by embassies, honored with gifts, and often settle wars by their very reputation...

Since the Fates <note>The Parcae, the three personified goddesses of destiny in Roman mythology who spin, measure, and cut the thread of life.</note> have granted an endless thread of life to no man, and all must be resolved back into the earth—even if one exists as the most powerful of Kings—as Sotades <note>A Greek poet of the 3rd century BCE known for his satirical and moralizing verse.</note> says:

For a corpse, every form of burial is a punishment if the dead can still feel; but if they do not feel, the very speed of the body’s destruction is a remedy.* Thus, among the Gauls, as witnessed by Julius Caesar <note>The Roman general; this refers to his *Commentaries on the Gallic War*.</note> in Book VI, the dead were cremated. This rule alone is observed: that the bodies of illustrious men are burned using specific types of wood. ...they cast in things to be read by the deceased. Indeed, the opinion of Pythagoras <note>Pythagoras of Samos was a Greek philosopher whose followers believed in metempsychosis, or the transmigration of souls into new bodies after death.</note> gained strength among them; namely, that human souls are immortal and, having entered another body, take up life anew after a defined period of time. But this has already been investigated above. 

Truly more fortunate are those for whom Death is both the release and the end of all sorrows: beyond which our misfortunes (these are the words of Seneca <note>Lucius Annaeus Seneca, a Roman Stoic philosopher, writing to a mother grieving her son.</note> in *Consolation to Marcia*) do not extend, and which restores us to that tranquility in which we lay before we were born. If someone pities the dead, let them also pity those not yet born. Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, a Roman author and naturalist.</note> says in Book VII, chapter 53: *For everyone, from their final day onward, things are as they were before their first day; nor is there any more sensation of body or soul after death than there was before birth.* These are the verses of the Emperor Hadrian <note>Hadrian ruled the Roman Empire from 117 to 138 AD; he reportedly composed this poem on his deathbed.</note> in which he bids farewell to his soul:

> Little soul, wandering and charming,
> Guest and companion of the body,
> Into what places will you now go,
> Pale, stiff, and naked,
> Nor will you tell your jokes as you used to.
<note>original Latin: *Animula vagula, blandula, / Hospes comesque corporis, / Quæ nunc abibis in loca, / Pallidula, rigida, nudula, / Nec ut soles, dabis jocos.*</note>

Arrianus <note>Flavius Arrianus, a Greek historian who chronicled the campaigns of Alexander the Great.</note> in Book I of the *Expedition of Alexander* writes: *Eat and drink, and play, since other human affairs are not worthy of this applause.* <note>original Greek: ἔσθιε καὶ πίνε, καὶ παῖζε, ὡς ἄλλα τὰ ἀνθρώπινα οὐκ ὄντα τούτου ἄξια.</note> Aristobulus <note>A Greek historian who accompanied Alexander the Great; his works are often cited by later authors like Athenaeus.</note> in Athenaeus <note>A Greek rhetorician and grammarian, author of the *Deipnosophistae* or "The Banquet of the Learned."</note>, Book XII of the *Banquet*: *Eat, drink, play; for all other things are not worth a round of applause.* Another says:

> I possess only what I ate, and the wantonness and 
> pleasures I experienced with love. 
> But all those many and wealthy things have 
> dissolved.
<note>original Greek: Κεῖν' ἔχω ὅσσ' ἔφαγον, καὶ ἐφύβρισα, καὶ σὺν ἔρωτι Τέρπν' ἔpathon. τὰ δὲ πολλὰ καὶ ὄλβια πάντα λέλυνται.</note>

Furthermore, in Athenaeus’s <note>Athenaeus of Naucratis was a Greek rhetorician writing in the 3rd century AD; his *Deipnosophistae* (The Banquet of the Learned) is a vast collection of snippets of ancient wisdom and table talk.</note> *Deipnosophistae*, Book VIII, he says this:

Sotion <note>A Greek philosopher and teacher of the famous Roman Stoic Seneca.</note> said these things in the same work:

> You will possess only those things which you have eaten and drunk; 
> the rest is merely ashes—even for Pericles, Codrus, or Cimon. <note>Pericles, Codrus, and Cimon were all legendary or historical leaders of Athens; the author uses them to show that even the most powerful men are reduced to the same dust as everyone else.</note>
> <note>original: "Ἕξεις δ’ ὅσ’ ἂν φάγῃς τε, καὶ πίῃς μόνα, Σποδοὶ δὲ τ’ ἄλλα, Περικλέης, Κόδροι, Κίμων."</note>

And one of the Poets—I know not which of the Greeks—grunts <note>The author uses the word *grunnit* (grunts) to mirror the "swine" metaphor in the verse.</note> thus:
> We are all kept for death, and we are fattened,
> just like a herd of irrational swine 
> to be slaughtered.
> <note>original: "Πάντες τῷ θανάτῳ τηρεύμεθα, καὶ τρεφόμεθα, Ὡς ἀγέλη χοίρων σφαζομένων ἀλόγων."</note>

In Aragon <note>A historic kingdom in what is now Spain.</note>, such a monument is said to exist:

->I DO NOT KNOW WHERE I AM GOING.<-
->I DIE UNWILLINGLY. FAREWELL.<-
->TO THOSE WHO COME AFTER.<-
->M. POSTUMIUS, KNIGHT.<-

Likewise at Rome:

They were wiser than those who believed the soul perished along with the body, and that no span of life was to be expected after death. For this reason, they called their monuments and tombs *eternal homes*, <note>original: "aeternas domos"</note> and [said] they were indulging themselves in sleep

...as if any gods might show the way to the death <note>The Latin *niciem* is likely a fragment of *perniciem* (destruction/death) or *necem* (slaughter).</note> of Commindorigis. From this, Clement <note>Clement of Alexandria, a 2nd-century Christian theologian who sought to harmonize Greek philosophy with Christianity.</note>, with whom Eusebius agrees, thinks that the origin of sacred buildings is derived from no other source than from tombs, which, being more magnificently built, were called by the name of * temples. 

Eunapius <note>A 4th-century Greek historian and staunch defender of paganism.</note> certainly, in his *Lives of the Sophists*, mocks the Christians for gathering at the funeral pyres of the dead as if at the altars of new gods. Brodæus <note>Jean Brodeau (1500–1563), a French scholar known for his annotations on classical texts.</note> mentions this in Book III. 

But Necromancy <note>original Greek: Νεκυομαντεία; the practice of communicating with the dead to predict the future.</note> is to be numbered among the most ancient forms of Magic. Thus Ulysses, in Homer’s *Odyssey*, calls forth his mother in the land of the Cimmerians. Maro <note>The poet Virgil.</note>, imitating these accounts, does the same in the sixth book of the *Aeneid*. In later centuries, Rome had something similar at a place named Tarentum <note>A site on the Campus Martius in Rome associated with the secular games and subterranean altars to underworld deities.</note>, near the banks of the Tiber. See examples of this matter in Peucer’s work *On Magic* <note>Kaspar Peucer (1525–1602), a German reformer and physician who wrote extensively on divination.</note>. 

But that madness also pervaded the people of God. And God sternly rebukes it in the Holy Testament, Leviticus chapter 20, verse 6. Now, the "Ob" <note>original Hebrew: אוב; a term referring to a medium or a "familiar spirit" through which the dead were consulted.</note> was either a rite or a Demon, which issued forth from the unclean parts—which cannot be named honorably—rather than from the head or armpits; or it refers to the Soothsayers...

...belly-speaker <note>original: ἐγγαστριμύθω (*engastrimytho*)</note>. Therefore, the *Ob* <note>The Hebrew term for a spirit of the dead or a "familiar spirit," often associated with ventriloquism in this period of scholarship.</note> is a ventriloquist. Those who were initiated into these sacred rites would hold branches of myrtle in their hands and be purified with incense, as Rabbi Moses Ben-Nachman <note>Nahmanides (1194–1270), a leading medieval Jewish scholar and mystic.</note> says in the *Jad-Chazeka* <note>The "Strong Hand," referring to Maimonides’ code of Jewish law, the *Mishneh Torah*.</note> in the section on Idolatry <note>original: עכו״ם (*Akum*), an acronym for worshippers of stars and planets.</note>, chapter VI. Furthermore, Rabbi Abraham Ben-David <note>Raavad (1125–1198), a critic of Maimonides known for his glosses on the Mishneh Torah.</note> maintains that the location for these rituals was the grave of the dead. Regarding the *Jideonei* <note>original: *Jideonei* or *Yiddua*, another type of spirit mentioned in the Bible alongside the *Ob*.</note>, the Talmud contains references to it, and Rabbi Simson, as quoted by Rabbi Moses of Coucy in Negative Precept 39, affirms that it consists of a bone from an animal called the *Yiddua* <note>original: ידוע (*Yadua*), literally "the known one."</note> which, when placed in the mouth, would teach regarding the future and resolve those things being sought. Others, however, write of a certain unknown creature called the *Jadoa*, which possesses a human form in every part, but which is attached from its navel by a cord of a certain root to the place of its birth; it remains alive as long as it is attached, until those who do not dare to approach closer due to its innate ferocity kill it with arrows. <note>This refers to the *Adne HaSadeh*, a legendary humanoid creature from Jewish folklore, sometimes described as a "man of the mountain" or a plant-animal hybrid that dies if its umbilical root is severed.</note>

## CHAPTER XLVIII.

*The funeral procession. The body placed upon a stone. Dearer items were cast into the funeral pyres. Monuments erected. Bread placed on the pyre. Sacrifices of the Easterners. Living humans slaughtered. Trumpeters and scene-players.*

The manner of leading the procession, or the funeral pomp, was as follows. First, chosen young men <note>original: *lecti juvenes*</note> went ahead, who represented the brave deeds of those killed in war, and they dragged with them captured enemy shields, standards, weapons, and horses. These were followed by others, whom they intended to slaughter as offerings for the dead <note>original: *inferiis mortuorum*—sacrifices made to appease the souls of the deceased</note>. Then, the weapons of the slain enemy leader were carried, fixed upon a massive wooden post. There followed the sorrowful horse which the deceased had been accustomed to ride into battle. Then the weapons of the deceased himself were carried. Finally, they brought out the corpse itself, which the entire company followed all the way to the funeral pyre. Virgil <note>original: *Maro*, referring to the Roman poet Publius Vergilius Maro</note> describes this procession in most elegant verses in the *Aeneid*, Book 11; see those.

We see this same pomp still observed today among Princes and those of high rank <note>original: *Purpuratos*, literally "those clad in purple," referring to royalty or high-ranking church officials</note>. Albert Krantz <note>original: *Cranzius* (1448–1517), a German historian and theologian.</note> recorded the manner of this in his *History of the Vandals*, Book 14, chapter 34: The Grand Duke of Mecklenburg was entombed in Doberan <note>original: *Dobram*</note> near Wismar. The service was performed in the Church of St. George. On Sunday toward evening, a solemn vigil was held. Before dawn, a solemn Mass of the Holy Trinity was sung. Meanwhile, at all the altars of the church, the Friars Minor <note>The Franciscans, a mendicant religious order</note> of that place, summoned from Rostock and Schwerin, performed the sacred ministry one after another. Offerings were made in order at the high altar. Then, after a funeral oration was delivered in Latin, a solemn sacrifice was prepared for the dead, with the prelate performing the rites— <note>original: *sacra faciente Pontifice*</note>

A second horse, with similar trappings, displayed the arms of Vandalia. A third group, with the same number of men, weapons, and candles, bore the insignia of the County of Schwerin <note>original: *Suerinensis*</note>. A fourth horse bore on its forehead the arms of the Lordship of Rostock, along with standards and candles. A fifth bore the insignia of the Lordship of Stargard. A sixth horse, which the Duke himself used for splendor, came forward armored in gleaming iron, bearing the arms of the Prince.

# ELIAS SCHEDIVS

...[burned along with the body.] <note>Continued from previous page.</note> We read that monuments were also erected for certain animals by their living masters. Julius Capitolinus <note>A historian from the *Historia Augusta*.</note> writes that when the horse **Volucris** died, the Emperor **Verus** <note>Lucius Verus, co-emperor with Marcus Aurelius.</note> took care to have a tomb built for it on the Vatican hill. And Cassius Dio records that a tomb and a column with an epigram were erected by **Emperor Hadrian** for his horse **Borysthenes**. Likewise, **Statius**—in the first book of his *Silvae* <note>A collection of occasional poems.</note>—is the authority stating that **Domitian** erected a colossal statue to a horse. I pass over the inscriptions for dogs, which may be seen everywhere in **Italy**. The ancients, however, placed bread and other necessities for life onto the funeral pyre—as Victor <note>original: *Victor. l. XXI. V. L. c. IX.*</note> adduces—as if the dead were able to feed upon them. Moreover, certain filthy and abject individuals would sit nearby to snatch those things from the fire while the human corpse was burning. **Catullus** indicated this in a verse regarding **Rufus of Bologna**, when he wished to declare his beggarliness and filth; for he says:

> — — often in the graveyards
> you will see him snatching his dinner from the pyre itself. <note>original: *sæpe in sepulcretis / Videbis ipso capere de rogo cœnam*; Catullus 59.</note>

***

The place in which the funeral feasts <note>original: *epulæ in funere*</note> are burned is called the **Culina** <note>literally "Kitchen"</note>, says **Festus** <note>Sextus Pompeius Festus, a Roman grammarian.</note> under this word entry. In this sense, **Jacob Spon** in his *Voyage to Greece* <note>original: *Voyage de la Grece*</note> (Volume III, page 47) applied the term **Culina** while explaining an inscription from Tibur <note>Modern Tivoli, Italy.</note>, which **Gruter** <note>Jan Gruter, a scholar of ancient inscriptions.</note> also reports on page 493. There, since it is said that **Sulpicius** restored, among other things, a **Culina** to **Hercules Saxanus** <note>A title of Hercules associated with stone-quarries.</note>, Spon says this was a place near the temples where the funeral banquets were prepared. Compare **Filippo della Torre** in his *Monuments of Ancient Antium* <note>original: *Phil. a Turre Monumenta Veteris Antii*</note>, Roman edition, 1700, who on page 308 thinks that the **Culina** was not only a place where funeral feasts were held, but also where sacred rites were performed.

## ELIAS SCHEDIUS

> ->*He seizes living victims as offerings to the underworld, to sacrifice them to the shades:*<-
> ->*And to drench the flames of the funeral pyre with the blood of captives.*<-
<note>original: "Viventes rapit inferias, quos immolet umbris: / Captivosque rogi perfundat sanguine flammas." From Virgil's *Aeneid*, Book 10, lines 519–520, describing Aeneas taking prisoners to kill at the funeral of Pallas.</note>

The same author says in Book 11 of the *Aeneid*:

> ->*He had bound the hands of those behind their backs whom he would send as offerings to the shades below,*<-
> ->*to sprinkle the flames with blood shed in sacrifice.*<-
<note>original: "Vinxerat & post terga manus, quos mitteret umbris / Inferius cæso sparsuros sanguine flammas." From Virgil, *Aeneid* 11.81–82.</note>

**Julius Caesar** records in Book 6 of his *Commentaries on the Gallic War* that this custom also flourished among the **Celts**: indeed, shortly before the era of his own memory, the slaves and clients whom it was established were beloved by their masters were burned together with them once the proper funeral rites were completed. **Jordanes the Goth**, a historian, described the funeral of **Attila**, King of the Huns <note>The text uses "Belæ Hunnorum Regis," likely referring to the account of Attila's death in Jordanes' *Getica*.</note>, in this way: the body was placed in the middle of the camp within a circle of tents. The most elite horsemen of the **Huns** rode around him in a circle, much like the chariot races of the Circus, performing a **pyrrhic dance** <note>A traditional Greco-Roman war dance performed in armor.</note> and singing his praises in a rhythmic chant. Soon after, they honored the body with a gathered offering of gifts; they celebrated a feast <note>term: *comessationem* (a ritual banquet or carousal)</note> that combined joy with mourning. Subsequently, they buried the body in the ground at a predetermined location secretly at night; they dedicated the spoils of their enemies to him, and then offered sacrifices with much human blood. Meanwhile, an armed cohort circled the funeral pyre, and the entire sky echoed with the blare of trumpeters. For they employed these musicians in their funerals. As **Persius** says in his *Sixth Satire*:

> ->*Hence comes the trumpet and the candles; and at last the "dear departed,"*<-
> ->*laid out on his high bier...*<-
<note>original: "Hinc tuba, candela, tandemque beatulus alto." From Persius, *Satire* 3.103. The term "beatulus" is a diminutive, ironic way of referring to the deceased as "the little blessed one" or "the late lamented."</note>

Among the Romans, when someone passed away, flute players <term>tibicines|Musicians who played the "tibia," an ancient wind instrument similar to an oboe or flute, essential in Roman religious and funerary rites.</term> would play, and friends were summoned to serve as witnesses to testify that the person had died of natural causes rather than by poison or the sword (Victor, Book 9; V. L. Chapter 14). The Carians and Phoenicians likewise used pipes in mourning that were a palm's width in size, which produced a mournful and shrill sound. These pipes are called *Gingrae* <note>original: "Gingræ"</note> in the Phoenician language because they are typically used during the lamentations for **Adonis**, whom they call *Gingras*. (Erasmus in his *Adages*, citing Athenaeus, *The Banquet of the Learned*, Book 4; Seneca on the Death of **Claudius**). Seneca notes that the funeral of Claudius was the most beautiful of all, arranged so that one might know a god was being carried out, accompanied by such a massive crowd of horn players and flute players. **Xiphilinus** also records: *while others went before the funeral litter, some beat their breasts in grief, while others played mournful tunes on their pipes.* <note>original Greek: "οἱ μὲν οὖν ἄλλοι πρὸ τῆς κλίνης προΐει μὲν, καὶ τινὲς ἐκόπτοντο, ἑτέρων πενθιμῶν ἐπαυλώντων"; author's Latin translation: "alii vero sub lectica procedebant, quidam vero plangebant, aliis lugubriter præcinentibus."</note> **Statius** writes in the *Thebaid*, Book 5:

> ->When the heavy horn bellows its signal of grief<-
> ->with its curved tip<-
> *The Pipe.* <note>original: "Cum signum luctus cornu grave mugit adunco / Tibia."</note>

Artemidorus in Book 1 of his *Interpretation of Dreams* <note>original Greek: "αὐλεῖν δὲ πυθικοῖς αὐλοῖς, πένθος σημαίνει"; original Latin: "canere vero pythicis tibiis luctus indicat"</note> writes that to play upon Pythian pipes signifies mourning. For it is considered inhuman if human bones found at a crossroads <term>trivio|A 'trivium' is a place where three roads meet; such spots were considered spiritually significant and often haunted in antiquity.</term> are not sprinkled with at least a light dusting of earth. That is to say, *By sending a meal to the earthly Hecate upon the ground, he established it to avoid and appease death through atonement.* <note>Hecate was the goddess of magic, crossroads, and the underworld; offerings were left to her to prevent the restless dead from wandering.</note> Suetonius writes in his life of *Vespasian*: *While he was dining, a dog brought a human hand from a fork in the road <note>original: "bivio"</note> and threw it under the table.* <note>This was considered a divine omen that Vespasian would one day hold the power of the Empire in his hand.</note>

For those who see an unburied corpse and do not cast dust upon it were thought to be accursed. <note>original Greek: "οἱ γὰρ νεκρὸν ὁρῶντες ἄταφον, καὶ μὴ ἀπα- μενοι κόνιν, ἐναγεῖς εἶναι ἐδόκουν"</note> That is to say, *those who discern a dead man unburied, and do not scatter dust, are held to be abominable.* <note>original Latin: "id est, qui mortuum cernunt insepultum, neque pulverem regunt, execrabiles habentur."</note> Aelian, in Book 5, Chapter 14 of his *History*, states: There is also this Attic law <term>Attic law|Laws pertaining to ancient Athens. In this context, it refers to the religious duty imposed on citizens to respect the dead.</term>, that whoever happens upon an unburied human body must by all means cast earth upon it, and bury it facing the west. <note>original Greek: "νόμος καὶ οὗτος Ἀττικός, ὃς ἂν ἀτάφῳ τύχῃ σώματι ἀνθρώπου, πάντως ἐπιβάλλειν τῇ γῇ, θάπτειν δὲ πρὸς δυσμὰς βλέποντα."</note> 

<margin>\* Regarding the custom of casting earth upon the dead, see Salmasius' notes on Attic matters, page 563.</margin>
That is, *this law is also written among the Attic laws. If anyone should happen upon the unburied corpse of a man, let him at least cast earth on it,\* and bury it in such a way that it looks toward the setting sun.* <note>The west, where the sun sets, was traditionally associated with the land of the dead in many ancient cultures.</note> Quintilian, in his *Declamations* VI, writes: *Truly, it [the sight of a corpse] produced in us not only pity but also a sense of religious duty; thus, burial is provided even for the bodies of passing travelers, and earth is cast upon them by strangers. They declare that from this arises the impulse that we heap earth on unknown corpses.*

Horace, in Book 1, Ode 28, writes:

> *But you, sailor, do not be so stingy as to withhold*
> *a small portion of shifting sand from my unburied*
> *bones and head.*
> *Although you are in a hurry, it is not a long delay;*
> ->it will be permitted<-
> *that you run on once dust has been thrice cast.*
<note>In Roman tradition, casting three handfuls of earth was legally and religiously sufficient to constitute a burial, freeing the soul to cross the river Styx.</note>

---

On almost all ancient monuments, you will find these letters written at the beginning: *D. M.* or *D. M. S.*, or even spelled out as *TO THE SPIRITS OF THE DEAD* <note>original: *DIIS MANIBVS*</note> or *TO THE MANIAS* <note>original: *MANIABVS*</note>, by which they intended to denote that the monument was sacred to the Spirits of the Dead—that is, to the bones and the ashes. However, ancient writers do not agree on who these "Manes" gods were, or from where they received their name. Some confuse them with the *Lares* and *Penates* <note>Household gods who protected the family and the home; see Daniel Gerdes, *Dissertation on the Lares and Penates*, included in Volume 15 of the *Critical History of the Republic of Letters*, published in French, p. 84 and following</note>; others identify them with *Genii* <note>Guardian spirits assigned to people or places</note>, whether good or evil; some even understand them to be *Lemures* <note>Restless or malevolent ghosts</note> and *Larvae* <note>Terrifying spirits of the dead</note>. <note>Compare the Abbot Jean-François Simon’s *Dissertation on the souls of the deceased and their state according to the doctrine of the Pagans*, which is found in Volume 2 of the *Memoirs of the Academy of Inscriptions*, p. 32 and following, and the *Memoirs of Trévoux*, 1708, p. 499 and following.</note> They are also commonly used to refer to the souls of the deceased; indeed, they are even taken to represent the Underworld <note>original: *Inferis*</note> itself. <note>See Brisson, *On Formulas*, Book 1, p. 51, and Claude Nicaise in his very learned explanation of the *Ancient Monument found in Aquitaine, in the Diocese of Auch*, Chapter 5, p. 17.</note>

I GIVE, DEDICATE, AND MAKE THIS MONUMENT <note>original: *DO. D. F. M.*, abbreviations for *Do, Dico, Facio Monumentum*</note>. GIVE NINE... TEN SESTERCES <note>A Roman silver coin; *HS* is the standard abbreviation</note> AND ASSIGN THE MAKING OF IT. FAREWELL, LIFE.

Hence Virgil <note>original: *Maro*, the family name of the poet Publius Vergilius Maro</note> in Book VI of the *Aeneid* sings thus:
> - - *Give me lilies with full hands,*
> *let me scatter purple flowers, and let me at least heap*
> *these gifts upon the soul of my descendant.* <note>original: *Manibus date lilia plenis...*</note>

Juvenal, *Satire VII*:
> *May the Gods grant to the shades of our ancestors a thin earth and without weight,*
> *and fragrant crocuses, and an eternal spring in the tomb,*
> *those who wished a teacher to be*
> *in the place of a holy parent.* <note>original: *DI majorum Umbris tenuem & sine pondere terram...*</note>

And Tacitus, in his book *On the Manners of the Germans*, reports the same concerning the Germans:
*A mound of turf raises the tomb. They despise the steep and laborious honor of monuments, as being heavy upon the deceased.* <note>original: *Sepulcrum cespes erigit...*</note>

For the ancients used to wish a heavy grave upon those for whom they felt ill will, so that they might return less quickly to the rest of the Spirits of the Dead <note>original: *Manes*</note>, or might swim across the Styx <note>The principal river of the underworld in Greek mythology, over which souls were ferried</note> with the greatest effort. Seneca in the *Troades*:
> - - *She fell so as to break the earth*
> *heavy upon Achilles, face down, and with an angry force.* <note>original: *Cecidit ut Achilli gravem...*</note>

## CHAPTER L.

*Hair laid aside in mourning. Sometimes used to be burned together with the body. The custom among the Jews. They performed funeral offerings by the cutting of hair. It was believed to be shorn by Proserpina. Sacred to the GODS in youth. Also offered to rivers. The firstfruits of the beard offered to the GODS. No one was allowed to shave their hair while on a ship. The origin of this. Half-shaven servants. Being shaved was considered ignominious among certain people. On those who had promised their hair as a vow.*

Furthermore, it was the custom to cut the hair and place it upon the tomb, so that through this act of mourning the deceased might be made well-disposed toward them. <note>original: "ἔθος ἦν τέμνειν τὰς κόμας... ἵνα διὰ τούτου πένθος ἵλεως αὐτοῖς ὁ νεκρὸς ᾖ"</note> That is, it was the custom to cut locks of hair and place them on the grave, so that the dead might be pleased by this grief. Euripides writes in *Iphigenia in Tauris*:
"Raise a mound, and let them see memorials for me; and give tears, sister, and hair to the tomb." <note>original: "Τύμβον δὲ χεῦσον, κ' ἀπίδες μνημεῖά μοι, Καὶ δάκρυ, ἀδελφή, καὶ κόμας δότω τάφῳ."</note>
Statius, in the funeral poem for his father:
->Lay your hair upon the burial mound.<- <note>original: "Crines pone super tumulum."</note>
Sometimes the shorn hair was thrown onto the funeral pyre or placed upon the corpse and burned. Homer's *Iliad*:
"Standing apart from the pyre, he cut off his golden hair." <note>original: "Στὰς ἀπάνευθε πυρῆς ξανθὴν ἀποκείρατο χαίτην." This refers to Achilles cutting his hair for Patroclus.</note>
Herodian, Book IV: "Certainly Philocarfes <note>Likely a reference to the Emperor Caracalla, who, according to Herodian, cut his hair to lay on the pyre of his friend Festus, imitating Achilles.</note> sought to place a lock of hair upon the flame." <note>original: "παῖυτε ὁ Φιλοκάρσης πλόκαμον ἐπιθέναι τῷ πυρὶ ζητῶν ἐγιλᾶτο"</note> Nor was this custom found only among the Western peoples, but also among the Easterners themselves and even among the people of God, as the words of Micah, chapter 1, verse 16, clearly show: "Make yourself bald and shave your head for your delicate children; enlarge your baldness like the eagle, for they have gone into captivity from you." <note>original: "Glabra te & tonde propter filios deliciarum tuarum: dilata calvitium tuum, ut aquila, quia migrant a te."</note> And with this cutting of hair they performed <term>inferiae</term> <note>Sacrifices or offerings dedicated to the spirits of the deceased.</note>. Heliodorus, Book VI:
"To you, who were my only sweet concern—if indeed you are dead—I offer these libations; and at the same time she plucked out her hair and threw it upon the bier..." <note>original: "ᾧ μόνη μοι γλυκεῖα Φροντὶς... τὰς ἐπιφέρω χοὰς καὶ ἅμα ἔτιλλε τὰς τρίχας, καὶ ἐπὶ κλίνῃ ἐπέβαλλε." From the *Aethiopica*.</note> This was done in place of the absent person, as if it were for Theagenes himself. The ancients also believed that those who were in the final struggle of death were shorn of a lock of hair by Proserpina <note>The Queen of the Underworld; it was believed no one could die until she cut a golden lock from their head to release the soul.</note>.
