# ELIAS SCHEDIUS

<page-num>696</page-num>

Nonius <note>Nonius Marcellus was a 4th-century Roman grammarian who preserved many fragments of earlier literature.</note> states: *those who were being set free were bald for this reason: they appeared to have escaped the storm of slavery, just as those liberated from shipwreck are accustomed to do.* <note>original: "qui liberi fiebant, ea causa calvi erant, qui tempestatem servitutis videbantur effugere, sicut naufragio liberati solent."</note> Petronius Arbiter, in the *Satyricon*, mentions a man who noticed a barber clinging to him with untimely service by the light of the moon; he cursed the omen, as it imitated the final vow of the shipwrecked. <note>In ancient Rome, shaving one's head was an "extreme measure" or a "vow of last resort" taken during life-threatening storms at sea; seeing a barber in a non-emergency context was thus considered a bad sign of impending doom.</note> Hence Saint Paul, in Acts 27, encouraging the sailors to cast off their sadness, says: *For not a hair from the head of any of you shall fall.* <note>original: "οὐδενὸς γὰρ ὑμῶν θρὶξ ἐκ τῆς κεφαλῆς πεσεῖται." St. Paul uses this phrase to reassure the sailors that they will not need to make the "shipwreck vow" of shaving their heads because they will survive intact.</note> Among the pagans, however, slaves of lower status were kept half-shaved. Apuleius <note>Author of the 2nd-century Roman novel *The Golden Ass* (or *Metamorphoses*).</note> writes in Book 9 of the *Golden Ass*: *Their foreheads were branded with letters, their hair was half-shaved, and their feet were ringed with shackles.* <note>original: "Frontes literati, capillum semirasi, & pedes annulati." Branding a slave's forehead was a common punishment for theft or attempted escape.</note> Yet for others, hair was shaved away when freedom was granted, as is clear from Plautus’s *Amphitryon*. <note>Plautus was a Roman playwright; the ritual of "shaving for freedom" symbolized a fresh start.</note> Lucian, in his work *Timon*, writes: *...a lewd servant, highly prized since childhood, with his jaw still partially shaved.* <note>original: "ἡ καταπύγον οἰκέτης ἐκ παιδικῶν τίμιος, ὑπεξυρημένος ἔτι τὴν γνάθον."</note>

Among most nations, however, it was considered disgraceful to be shaved, as we noted previously in the general discussion regarding the Germans. Nicolaus of Damascus <note>A historian and philosopher from the Augustan age.</note> writes: *The King orders the man who has committed the greatest crime to be shaved, as this is the ultimate disgrace.* <note>original: "τὸν δὲ μέγιστα ἀδικήσαντα ὁ βασιλεὺς κελεύει κείρασθαι, ὡς ἐσχάτης οὔσης ἀτιμίας."</note> Indeed, the King commanded those most guilty of crimes to be shaved as the final mark of punishment. Philostratus, in his *Life of Apollonius of Tyana*, Book 7, writes: *From that point, the abuse of the man began: his beard and the hair on his head were shaved off, and he was bound among the worst criminals.* <note>original: "ἄρχεται τὸ ἐνθεῦτε τῆς ἐς τὸν ἄνδρα ὕβρεως, γενείων τε ἀποκείρας αὐτὸν καὶ χαίτης ἐν τε τοῖς κακουργοτάτοις δήσας." Apollonius was a Neopythagorean philosopher whose long hair was a sign of his ascetic holiness; shaving him was an attempt to strip him of his dignity.</note> In a similar way, he began to devise another kind of punishment for the man, shaving his cheeks and treating his hair as if he were among the most wicked. Harmenopulus <note>Constantine Harmenopulus was a 14th-century Byzantine jurist; his *Hexabiblos* became a fundamental legal code.</note> in Book 6, Title 6, Section 18: *Let the one who has been beaten and shaved be sent into exile.* See also Title 5, Section 18; Title 7, Section 10; Title 8, Section 7; and throughout the work. This punishment was also applied to adultery. Harmenopulus, Book 6, Title 2, Section 20: *Adulterers are to be beaten and shaved...*

<meta>catchword: ELIAE</meta>

...lived for a long time between the Rhine and the Danube, and 51 years before the capture of Troy, he came to Latium. After killing the tyrant Cacus, he was received as a guest by Evander. It is suspected that he introduced various superstitions, including those used in funerals; these Numa <note>Numa Pompilius, the legendary second king of Rome credited with establishing many of its religious rites</note> later partly rejected and partly approved, but the Decemvirs <note>The *Decemviri*, a commission of ten men who compiled the Twelve Tables, the foundation of Roman law</note> eventually abolished them through laws brought from Greece. Among those ceremonies accepted from a barbarian nation were these: that women should "shave their cheeks"—that is, they would tear their faces with their fingernails—and that they should "make a *lessum*" <term>lessum: an archaic Latin term for ritual lamentation or bloodletting</term>, which is to say, they would draw blood from their veins to testify to their grief. This is what the Germans call in their native tongue *Ein låssn thun* <note>German: "to perform a bloodletting"</note>, or *haben* [to have]. Even today, the Italians—having borrowed the term from the Goths or Lombards—say *Salasser* and *far Saluffo* <note>Italian: *salassare*, meaning to bleed a patient for medical or ritual reasons</note>. In sacred matters, Moses forbade the Israelites from cutting their flesh for the dead or branding themselves with marks (Leviticus 19). Plautus certainly mentions the *lessum* in his play *The Boor* <note>original: *Truculento*</note>, Act 4, Scene 2, speaking through the character of the procuress:

> *Thetis also made a ritual lamentation*
> *for her son while grieving.* 
<note>original: *Thetis quoque etiam lamentando lessum fecit filio.* Thetis was a sea-nymph and the mother of the hero Achilles.</note>

The words that follow prove that the young man Dinarchus had done something similar to a *lessum*. 

This barbarian custom was propagated through Italy and Greece all the way to Palestine. Solon <note>the famous Athenian lawmaker and poet</note> first abolished it in his *Axones* <note>the revolving wooden tablets upon which Solon's laws were inscribed</note>, and from there the Decemvirs, borrowing the idea, abolished it in the Laws of the Twelve Tables, as it was considered more fitting for Germans than for Athenians or Romans. For as Tacitus testifies in his book *On the Customs of the Germans* <note>original: *de Moribus Germanorum*</note>, men quickly set aside their wailing and tears, but they are slow to abandon their grief and sadness; for women, however, mourning was always considered honorable, both in general and especially when their husbands were killed in war. This information is from Theodor Zwinger <note>a Swiss physician and humanist scholar</note>, Volume 1, Book 1, of the *Theater of Human Life* <note>original: *Theatrum Vitae Humanae*</note>.

It links this "barbaric" custom to linguistic roots in German and Italian and cites prohibitions in Biblical and classical law.</summary>

-> Columns, stelae, and sepulchral pillars worshipped as divinities. <-

Having now traversed those matters which concern true sacred rites—regarding both those who administer them and the things administered—which have certainly been noted from the best and most reliable authors, it remains for us to show other rites of the ancients and hand down their origin with as much faithfulness as can be achieved. Whatever was added after the initial form of worship flowed from that same source as the rest of the sacred rites. Of this kind are the solemn gatherings at the massive bulks of statues, likenesses, columns, and <term>sepulchral pillars: *cippi*, stone pillars used by the Romans as monuments or landmarks</term>. For these statues, columns, pillars, and likenesses were not erected in honor of the Gods, but were placed in memory and glory of deceased Heroes.

<summary>Schedius begins his third treatise by arguing that many ancient religious structures, such as statues and columns, did not originate as divine icons but as funeral monuments for deceased heroes that were later deified.</summary>

<page-num>703</page-num>

<header>CONCERNING THE GERMANIC GODS.</header>

placed. For those who had been the founders of some illustrious family, or the authors of some remarkable victory, were honored—after they had died a premature death—with some surviving monument. Later, they instituted certain religious games at the close of the year; they dedicated and scattered flowers and crowns, offered <term>funeral sacrifices: *inferias*, offerings specifically intended for the souls of the deceased</term>, and applied whatever could serve as either an honor or an ornament. From this, as the sacred rites grew daily in a greater manner, posterity venerated them as Heroes or as <term>Demons: *Dæmonia*, here referring to tutelary spirits or lesser deities in the classical sense, rather than purely evil beings</term>.

Nor indeed at that time did they distinguish between Demons or Heroes, as the Theologians of a later age did. For to unrefined men, God, Demon, and Hero were one and the same. And craftily, the Demons mocked the superstitious with a heap of illusions; they thrust themselves into the bodies of inanimate statues and deceived the <term>Hierophants: priests who interpret sacred mysteries</term> themselves in a certain frenzied <note>original: *lymphatico*; Schedius uses this term to describe a state of divine madness or ecstatic possession often associated with ancient oracles</note> manner, so that they might more easily entice them into offering honor to the statues. Nor did they refuse the name of some Mortal, provided that they were thereafter regarded as immortal GODS.

Truly, when many of the deceased had discovered certain remarkable arts for human use, or had achieved illustrious victories, or had given rise to certain noble families, posterity pursued them with such great honor that they gathered at their statues as if at sacred temples. For they seemed to be of a certain greater nature than was right to determine were infected by mortal decay; or, by the sense of a more excellent nature, those who were worshipped were the Heroes of the Demons.

A most clear testimony of this matter is indeed handed down by the Author of the <note>Schedius refers here to the "Book of Wisdom" (Wisdom of Solomon), an apocryphal/deuterocanonical text often cited in early modern scholarship to explain the origins of idolatry.</note> Book of Wisdom, from chapter 14, verse 12 through to 22...

# ELIAS SCHEDIVS

...records: For by the empty pride of men, idols entered into the world <note>original: Κενοδοξίᾳ (Kenodoxia); this refers to groundless conceit or vainglory</note>, and for this reason a swift end was devised for them. For a father, consumed by untimely grief, having made an image of his child who was snatched away too soon, now honored as a god the one who was then but a dead man, and passed down secret mysteries and rites to those under his authority. Then, as time passed, this impious custom became entrenched and was observed as law; by the decrees of tyrants, graven images were worshipped. And when men could not honor them in person because they lived far away, they reproduced their distant likeness, making a visible image of the king they wished to honor, so that by their diligence they might flatter the absent one as if he were present. Furthermore, the ambition of the craftsman drove even those who did not know the king to a greater intensity of worship. For the artist, perhaps wishing to please the ruler, used his skill to force the likeness into a more beautiful form. The common people, lured by the grace of the work, now regarded as an object of worship <note>original: σέβασμα (sebasma); a term for a sacred object or deity</note> the man who shortly before had been honored merely as a human. And this became a snare for human life: for whether men were enslaved by misfortune or by tyranny, they bestowed the <term>Incommunicable Name: the unique name of God (Jehovah/Yahweh) which cannot be shared with created things</term> upon stones and wood. That is:

*Since through the vain opinion of men they came into the world, and therefore a brief end for them was devised. For a father, tormented by bitter grief, when he had made an image of a son taken away quickly, now treated with honors as a god him who then indeed was a dead man, and handed down to his subordinates mysteries and sacrifices. Then, as time proceeded, this impious custom growing stronger was kept as law, and by the commands of tyrants worship was attributed to engraved things. Whom when men could not honor in person...*

Regarding the first maker of statues, it was discussed in the first treatise; we deem it a sin to repeat it here. And certain families first offered sacrifices to their own founder, which were finally transferred to others. ...divine honors. Among the Germans, in a similar way, certain statues were erected in honor of the ancient Heroes. The first of these was dedicated to the founder of the race, namely Tuyscon—or "Dis" among the Celts. Indeed, Tuyscon and the Celtic "Dis Samothes" are the same figure, as has been demonstrated above. Julius Caesar, in the sixth book of his *Commentaries on the Gallic War*, recorded this for posterity: *The Gauls claim that they are all descended from Father Dis <note>The Roman god of the underworld, whom Caesar used to describe a native Celtic creator deity</note>, and they say this tradition was passed down by the Druids. Both the Germanic people (under the name Tuyscon) and the Gauls (under the name Dis) honored this figure after his death as the father of the family, and they erected statues to him in sacred groves.*

## CHAPTER II.

->Hercules. King of the Boii. Otherwise known as Alemannus. The etymology <note>original Greek: ἔτυμον (etymon)</note> of the name. Several figures named Hercules. The twelve labors. Remarkably voracious. Mocked for that reason. The Celtic Hercules.<-

Tacitus, in his book *On the Customs of the Germans* <note>original title: *de Moribus Germanorum*, a primary Roman source on Germanic tribes</note>, records that there was also a Hercules among the Germans; they sing of him above all other brave men when they are about to go into battle. This man was the last of the Kings of Germany (according to those whom Berosus <note>A reference to the writings of "pseudo-Berosus," which were popular in the Renaissance for reconstructing ancient king-lists</note> enumerates), says Aventinus in the first book of the *Annals of the Boii*. He was called Alemannus, with the surname "Hercules," and was the first founder of the Boii <note>A large Celtic/Germanic tribe that gave their name to Bohemia and Bavaria</note>. His emblem was the Lion, which was the reason for his nickname; therefore, the practice of keeping lions is a traditional custom among our local princes.

It was also the surname of Alemannus, the King who was the forefather of the Boii <note>The Boii were a large Celtic tribe; in this context, the author identifies them as ancestors of the Bavarians</note>, whose heraldic emblem was a Lion. # ELIAS SCHEDIVS

<margin>Schedius incorrectly cites Thietmar <note>Thietmar of Merseburg (975–1018) was a bishop and chronicler; the author here notes a scholarly error in Schedius's references</note> as having seen this himself, though no such mention of the Irminsul is found in Thietmar’s work.</margin>

...a full-bodied statue, which held in its right hand a military standard—our people call it a banner—displaying a rose. Just as the rose has but a brief moment of beauty and is easily born and easily perishes, so too is the outcome of battles. In its left hand, it held out a scale <note>original: "libram"</note>, representing the uncertain fate of combatants which easily tips one way or the other. Its unprotected chest displayed a bear, suggesting the internal spirit of the warriors. Upon the shield was a Lion, who rules over the beasts, showing an invincible drive for brave deeds. The statue stood upon a field sown with flowers: because nothing is seen as more joyful to the brave than to demonstrate their valor in the line of battle, according to Albert Krantz <note>A German historian (1448–1517) who wrote the "Saxonia," a history of the Saxon people</note> in Book II, Chapter IX of his *Saxonia*. 

There is also doubt regarding the location. It is written by Krantz in Book II, Chapter IX of his *Saxonia* that this idol was worshipped by the Saxons in Westphalia at Heroburg, or in the fortress of Hermopolis, as Gregory of Tours <note>A Gallo-Roman historian and bishop (c. 538–594)</note> calls it. However, Thietmar in Book II, page 15, places a statue at Merseburg on the river Saale with this inscription: 

**I AM THE LEADER OF THE SAXON PEOPLE;**
**I PROMISE CERTAIN VICTORY TO THOSE**
**WHO WORSHIP ME.**

And this is indeed correct. For this column was erected in honor of Arminius <note>original: "Harminii"</note>; it was called the **Pillar of Herman** <note>original: "Hermans saul"</note> by the ancients. This name was later corrupted and called the **Irminsul** <note>original: "Irmans saul"</note> by descendants who were ignorant of its origin. For this Arminius was the Leader of the Cherusci, a man brave in war and quick in counsel, who afflicted the Romans with a heavy slaughter. This occurred when Quinctilius Varus <note>The Roman general famously defeated at the Battle of the Teutoburg Forest in 9 CE</note>—as Velleius Paterculus <note>A Roman historian (c. 19 BCE – c. 31 CE) who served under Tiberius</note> writes in Book II of his *History*—a man born of a family more illustrious than noble, and a man mild in character and...

...[he was] quiet in temperament, as if more immobile in both body and mind, more accustomed to the leisure of the camps than to active military warfare. How little he despised money was made clear by Syria, which he had governed; he entered that wealthy province a poor man, but left it a wealthy man while the province itself was left poor <note>This is a famous quote from the Roman historian Velleius Paterculus describing Publius Quinctilius Varus, the Roman general who would eventually lose three legions in the Teutoburg Forest</note>. When he was in command of the army in Germania, he conceived the idea that these people—who seemed to possess nothing human but their voices and limbs, and who could not be tamed by swords—could be softened by the rule of law. With this purpose, he entered the heart of Germania as if among men enjoying the sweetness of peace, spending the summer season holding court and conducting legal proceedings from the tribunal. 

But the Germans—which can hardly be believed unless experienced—are a people of the greatest ferocity yet most cunning, a race born for falsehood. They simulated a series of fictitious lawsuits, now provoking one another with injuries, now expressing gratitude that Roman justice was settling these disputes, and that their own wildness was being softened by the novelty of an unknown discipline, so that matters usually decided by arms were now terminated by law. They led Quinctilius Varus into such a state of utter indolence that he believed himself to be a city praetor <note>A high-ranking Roman magistrate responsible for justice within the city of Rome</note> administering justice in the Forum, rather than a commander leading an army in the heart of Germany's borders. 

Then a young man, noble by birth, strong of hand, quick-witted, and possessing a brilliance beyond that of a barbarian, named Arminius—the son of Sigimer, a prince of that nation—showed the fire of his soul in his face and eyes. He had been a constant companion in our previous military campaigns, and had already obtained the rights of Roman citizenship and the rank of a Knight <note>original: "equestrem gradum"; the Equestrian order was the lower of the two aristocratic classes in Rome, often granted to loyal foreign allies</note>. He used the general's sluggishness as an opportunity for his crime; he observed, not without wisdom, that no one is more quickly crushed than the man who fears nothing, and that a sense of security <note>original: "Securitatem"</note> is the most frequent beginning of disaster. XII.

as Florus relates in Book IV, Chapter XXII, it seemed as if the people were changed, the land was different, and the very sky appeared milder and softer than usual. Finally, not through flattery but because of his merits, when that most brave young man died there, the Senate granted him a surname derived from the province—an honor they had never bestowed elsewhere <note>original: "cognomen ex provincia dedit." This refers to Nero Claudius Drusus, who was posthumously granted the title "Germanicus" for his victories in Germania.</note>.

But it is more difficult to hold onto provinces than to create them. They are acquired by force; they are retained by law. Therefore, that joy was brief. For the Germans had been defeated rather than tamed; they had adopted our customs more than our weapons while under the command of Drusus. However, after he died, they began to hate the lust and pride of Quinctilius Varus no less than his cruelty. He dared to hold a judicial assembly <note>term: "conventum" (a formal assembly for the administration of justice)</note>, and he had positioned himself in the camp as if he could restrain the violence of the barbarians with the rods of a lictor <note>A lictor was a Roman officer who carried the 'fasces' (a bundle of rods and an axe) representing the power to punish or execute</note> and the voice of a herald. 

But they—who had long mourned their swords being covered in rust and their horses being idle—as soon as they saw the togas <note>The toga symbolized Roman civil law and administration, which the Germanic tribes found more oppressive than military force</note> and legal systems more savage than weapons, seized their arms under the leadership of Arminius. First, therefore, Arminius took a few men into his partnership of planning—as Velleius Paterculus testifies in Book II of his *History*—and soon many more. He both claimed and persuaded them that the Romans could be crushed. He joined actions to his decrees and established a time for the ambush. 

These were the leading men, as Aventinus lists them in Book II of the *Annals of the Boii*: Liber, a priest of the Chatti; Segimundus, son of Segestes and a priest of the Cherusci; Veromarus the Chatti; Egimarus and his son Sosithacus of the Cherusci; Berthorites, the brother of the aforementioned Melo, along with his son Theodoric, of the Sicambri. They conspired secretly at the instigation of Arminius, the son of Sigimer, of the Cherusci tribe—those who live between the Weser <note>original: "Visurgin"</note> and the Elbe <note>original: "Albin"</note> and are now known by the common name of Saxons.

XII. Varus possessed such confidence in the peace that he was not even moved when the conspiracy was predicted and brought forward by Segestes, one of the Germanic leaders. For as Velleius Paterculus <note>Marcus Velleius Paterculus (c. 19 BCE – c. 31 CE) was a Roman historian who served as a military tribune under Tiberius.</note> relates in Book II of his *History*, the plot was disclosed to Varus by Segestes, a man of that nation who was faithful and of illustrious name; but fate was already prevailing over human counsel, and had dulled all the sharpness of his mind. For so it is: usually, when fortune is about to change, it corrupts wise counsel; and it brings it about—which is most wretched—that what happens seems to have happened deservedly, and misfortune is transformed into a fault. And so Varus denied he believed the warning, and declared that he measured the hope of the people's goodwill toward him by his own merit. 

Segestes himself recounts the conspiracy he reported, as recorded in Tacitus, Book I of the *Annals*: 

*“Therefore, I brought an accusation against Arminius—the kidnapper of my daughter and violator of your treaty—before Varus, who then presided over the army. Delayed by the general's sluggishness <note>original: "dilatus segnicia Ducis"</note>, because there was too little protection in the laws, I demanded that he bind me, Arminius, and our fellow-conspirators. That night is my witness—would that it had been my last! And what followed can be more lamented than defended.”* 

Nor, as Velleius Paterculus relates in Book II of his *History*, was any opportunity for a second warning left after the first informer. We shall not attempt to set forth the sequence of that most atrocious calamity—none was more grievous to the Romans among foreign nations since the loss of Crassus <note>Marcus Licinius Crassus suffered a disastrous defeat against the Parthian Empire at the Battle of Carrhae in 53 BCE, where the Roman eagles were lost.</note> among the Parthians—in full volumes, as others have done. 

Now the sum of the tragedy must be lamented. An army, the strongest of all, foremost among Roman soldiers in discipline, strength, and experience of wars, was hemmed in by the lethargy of their leader, the treachery of the enemy, and the unfairness of fortune. Not even an occasion for fighting honorably was given to the wretched men as much as they had wished; even those who were being punished...

By this disaster, it was brought about that the Empire, which had not stopped even at the shore of the Ocean, was forced to halt at the bank of the Rhine river.

*The first camp of Varus, with its wide perimeter and measured headquarters, showed the labor of three legions; then, by the half-ruined rampart and the shallow ditch, it was understood that the broken remnants had now settled there. the craftsman had joined seven swords in their sheaths to his side, all hanging from a single belt. He held an eighth sword drawn in his right hand. This one was fastened into his fist with a most firm connection by an iron nail, such that it could not be torn from his hand unless the hand itself were cut off. Its thickness was beyond the proportions of a human body, and its length far exceeded the stature of a man. The inhabitants believed this deity to be endowed with powers like those of Mars <note>The Roman god of war</note>, and they believed he presided over war.

In the nearest shrine, the image of Porevithus <note>A Slavic deity, likely a variant of Perun or a local multi-faced god</note> was worshipped; it was fashioned with five heads but lacked any weapons. A third shrine was made conspicuous by the idol of Porenutius. This statue, representing four faces, had a fifth inserted into its chest; its forehead was covered by the idol's left hand and its chin by the right. 

Who these figures truly were remains a matter of doubt. I suspect, however, that they were certain ancient kings descended from the lineage of the Vandal kings <note>Schedius, like many early modern historians, often conflated the Germanic Vandals with the Slavic tribes of the Baltic</note>. Yet, who they were exactly is reported with total uncertainty, nor does their specific identity appear in the accounts of other writers. We might conjecture, at least, that Porevithus was perhaps Burvanus, the son of Anthyrius I (King of the Vandals and the Obotrites <note>A confederation of West Slavic tribes located in modern-day Mecklenburg and Holstein</note>), while Rugievithus was actually Rugilandus—otherwise called the brother of King Anthyrius III and the son of Alimer, King of the Obotrites. Lacking certain reliability from historical writers, we shall refrain from bringing forward further details about them.

### ON THE GERMANIC GODS

There was also a famous statue which was corruptly called *zedutt* or *Iodutte* <note>original: "zedutt, vel Iodutte"</note>. Etymologists twist themselves in various ways here as well. Some derive *zeduck* from "summoning" <note>original: "citando"</note>, as if by invoking this statue for some crime, people were summoned to its tribunal; this term is indeed quite famous among legal experts. Others derive it from the word *zeter*, from which comes the German *zeter geschrey* <note>original: "zeter geschrey"; a traditional Germanic cry for help or an outcry against injustice</note>. To some, however, it seems to be derived from the word *Gedeute* or *Gedaute*, meaning a sign, a monument, or the indication of a deed performed. Reiner Reineccius, on page 51 of *On the Origins of the Mansfelders*, thinks that *zedutte* is the Saint Jodutte, and he brings forward another of the same name who was worshipped in the territory of Delbrück, where a certain song is commonly sung to this god, the beginning of which is:

> Saint Jodutte was a holy man,
> When the enemy came, he went at the front, etc.

But the true origin of this idol is as follows. When Lothair, Duke of Saxony, was attacked in war by Henry V—who wished to snatch from him the Electoral dignity with which he had been invested by Henry III and grant it to Count Hoyer of Mansfeld—Lothair gained victory on the field called Lark-field <note>original: "Lerchenfeldt"</note> at Welf’s Wood <note>original: "Welphes holtz"</note>. In that battle, 45,000 men fell. To serve as a perpetual memorial of the victory, he erected a trophy, and for a more illustrious testimony of the event, he took care to build a chapel nearby, according to the custom of that time for all frequent—

## CHAPTER VII.

->*Flints, the Idol of the Vandals. Visilaus, King of the Obotrites.*<-

Among the Vandals <note>The author refers here to the Slavic tribes of the region</note> who inhabited Lusatia <note>a historical region in eastern Germany and western Poland</note>, there was also an idol, as the *German Saxon Chronicle* records, named *Flints*. By this name the Saxons refer to flint <note>original: "filicem"</note>; the idol was placed upon a massive flint stone. It bore a form such as the image of Death is usually depicted, but it was covered with a long cloak, carrying a staff in its hand and holding a swollen pig's bladder. On its left shoulder sat a lion; the barbarians believed that they would eventually be raised from the dead by its power. No historian has left a record of this idol's origin. I suspect, at least, that this monument <note>original: "cippum"</note> was erected in honor of Visilaus (commonly called Vislauu), who was King of the Heruli and the Obotrites. ## CHAPTER VIII.

->*Basanwow. Basanus, King of the Franks. Desirous of divinity. He withdrew himself from the council of nobles. Worshipped as a god by his people.*<-

Certain writers also make mention, though by name only, of a certain god called **Basanwow**, commonly known as **Basanus**. He was also an illustrious hero, the younger son of Diocles, King of the **Sicambri** <note>The Sicambri were a Germanic tribe often identified by early modern historians as the ancestors of the Merovingian Franks</note>. He ordered a shield and a sword to be carried before him as a clear sign of justice. In the thirty-third year of his reign, he led an army toward the peoples of the Upper Rhine, toward **Trier** <note>original: "Treviros"</note> and **Mainz** <note>original: "Moguntini"</note>, and killed the minor king Thaborinus, adding that entire region to his own dominion. This Thaborinus was the King of the **Angrivarii** <note>A Germanic people located in what is now Lower Saxony</note>, and from his name the fortress of **Thabor** was named, which Basanus ordered to be built in memory of this deed. In the *Henetic* <note>Wendish or Slavic</note> tongue, this city was called **Altenburg** <note>German: "Old Castle"</note>, or *megapolis* <note>original: "μεγάπολιν", Greek for "Great City"</note>, from which his descendants took their name, and which the inhabitants also named **Mecklenburg**, as well as *Werle* (or *Herula*), and other fortifications. 

Because of the memory (as *Wolfgang Lazius* states) of *Bucephalus*, that most celebrated horse which history records Alexander used in war and which bore the mark of a bull’s head, Anthyrius carried the emblem of a bull’s head upon the sail of his ship. Furthermore, because he had placed the figure of a golden **Griffin** upon the prow, the annals relate that all the Princes descending from him—who obtained rule over the *Heruli*, *Winuli*, *Rugians*, and *Obotrites*—adopted these same insignia of the bull’s head and the golden griffin. ### ELIAS SCHEDIUS, CONCERNING THE GERMAN GODS.

Our own poems, written in our native tongue <note>The author refers to Germanic vernacular songs or "carmina," which served as primary historical sources before written records.</note>, treat these matters more extensively. But we also establish **Ora** as a Vandal Princess, about whom nothing has reached us besides her bare name. However, we suspect that she is **Orithyia**, or **Oritha**, otherwise known as **Oraja**, for whom the name "Ora" was used as a corruption by the ignorance of the common people. She was the daughter of the King of the **Sarmatians** <note>A large confederation of Iranian people who lived in what is now Southern Russia and Ukraine.</note>, and was married to **Anaras**, King of the **Heruli** and **Obotrites** <note>West Slavic tribes located in modern-day Mecklenburg and Holstein.</note>, who was the son of **Anthyrius the Great**. 

As for why female leaders were counted among the number of the Goddesses, **Tacitus** <note>Publius Cornelius Tacitus, a Roman historian who wrote 'Germania' around 98 AD.</note> relates this in his book *On the Customs of the Germans* <note>original: "l. de Mor. Germ."</note>: "For they believe there is something holy and prophetic within women; they neither despise their counsel nor neglect their responses." We saw **Veleda** <note>A priestess and prophetess of the Bructeri tribe who played a prominent role during the Batavian rebellion against Rome.</note> under the Divine **Vespasian**, who was long held in the place of a deity by many. But long ago they also venerated **Aurinia** and many others—not out of flattery, nor as if they were making them into Goddesses. Furthermore, the passage in Tacitus seems corrupted, and it should be read as **Alironia**. This reading comes closest to the truth. For they were called *Alironiae*, women who provided prophecies and looked ahead to the outcome of future events; we have already discussed these in the first Treatise <note>original: "Syngramm."</note>, Chapter XLIII.

# OF THE GERMAN GODS.

Maimonides, in Book III of *The Guide for the Perplexed* <note>original: "More Nebochim"</note>, Chapter 47, writes that it was the custom among the Zabians <note>A group of Near Eastern pagans often identified by medieval scholars as star-worshipers.</note> or Chaldeans to sacrifice to Demons who manifested themselves in the form of a Goat. Certain people of the Zabian nation served Demons and believed that they appeared to men in the form of Goats. And for that reason, they called the Demons "kids" <note>original: "hædos," referring to young goats or the Hebrew *Se'irim*.</note>. This opinion was widespread in the time of Moses, just as the Scripture said: *they shall no longer sacrifice their victims to kids or goats.* <note>Leviticus 17:7.</note> These were the kinds of Gods belonging to both the Romans and the Greeks, whom some also write were worshiped by the Germans.

It is a popular fable that Julius Caesar, having built a bridge at the Colony of the Ubii <note>Modern-day Cologne</note> across the Rhine and led his army across, conquered all of Germany. They say that after obtaining Victory, as an everlasting memorial of this distinguished achievement, he built seven Cities in honor of the seven Planets. The first, they claim, was erected in honor of Saturn and called Saterburgh; the second, Hamburgh, in honor of Jupiter Ammon; the third, Marsburgh, in honor of Mars; the fourth, in honor of the Sun, called Solwedel; the fifth, called Magdeburgh, in honor of Venus; the sixth, dedicated to Mercury, called Heresburgh; and the seventh, Luneburgh, in honor of the Moon. These are trifles, more nonsensical than any old wives' tales, devised at the hearth by idle women. For who is so perver-

See what the celebrated Le Clerc <note>original: "Clericus"</note> opposes to this in the *Select Library* <note>original: "Bibl. Select."</note> Volume III, page 160 and following. ### ELIAS SCHEDIVS

...who is of such a mind that they would believe and give credit to their trifles, which are supported by no pillar of worthy authors? Hellebore <note>Hellebore was a plant used in ancient medicine to treat insanity; Schedius is suggesting these "historians" are literally out of their minds.</note> was needed to purge the small brains of such unwise men <note>original: "ἀσόφων" (asophon)</note>—I will not call them Historians—who, while better men enjoy their leisure, attempt to mock them with useless and ill-intentioned writings, smearing their work with nonsense perceived in dreams. 

Or do they not know that even that magnificent writer <note>Julius Caesar</note>, who elsewhere thinks quite highly of himself, stayed no more than eighteen days beyond the Rhine, but retreated for fear of the Suevi <note>A large confederation of Germanic tribes</note>? For so he writes in Book IV of the *Commentaries on the Gallic War*:

*From them he learned that the Suevi, after finding out through scouts that a bridge was being made, had held a council according to their custom and sent messengers in all directions, ordering that they should depart from their towns; they should deposit their children, wives, and all their possessions in the woods; and that all who could bear arms should assemble in one place. This place had been chosen almost in the center of those regions which the Suevi occupied; here they decided to wait for the arrival of the Romans and to fight there. When Caesar learned this—having completed all those things for which he had decided to lead his army across: to strike fear into the Germans, to take revenge on the Sugambri <note>A Germanic tribe that had raided Roman territories</note>, and to liberate the Ubii <note>A Germanic tribe allied with Rome, living near modern Cologne</note> from siege—having spent exactly eighteen days across the Rhine, and judging that he had progressed enough for both honor and utility, he withdrew into Gaul and broke the bridge.*

But on the second occasion when he crossed the Rhine, fearing a shortage of grain, as he himself writes in Book VI of the *Commentaries on the Gallic War*, he decided not to proceed further. However, so that he would not entirely remove the fear of his return from the barbarians, and in order to delay their reinforcements, having led back his army, he broke the far part of the bridge which touched the bank of the Ubii... <note>The text ends here mid-sentence, concluding on the following page.</note>

...which reached a length of two hundred feet, he cut down, and at the end of the bridge he established a tower of four stories, and placed a garrison of twelve cohorts for the sake of guarding the bridge, and strengthened the place with great fortifications. It is incredible, nor does it agree with the truth, that within eighteen days these seven cities, separated from one another by such a long and remote distance, were built. Nor were they built by Drusus <note>Nero Claudius Drusus (38–9 BC), a Roman general who led several campaigns into Germany but died after a fall from his horse.</note>: for he did not hold that small portion of Germany around the Rhine for long; but while waging war, he was put to flight, and while being carried away by his very swift horse, he fell; and with a broken leg near Bingen <note>A town in modern-day Germany on the Rhine.</note>, he breathed out his hostile soul. So says Johannes Aventinus <note>A 16th-century Bavarian historian and philologist.</note> in Book II of the *Annals of the Boii*. 

Neither did Germanicus <note>The nephew of Emperor Tiberius, famous for his campaigns in Germania to avenge the Roman defeat at the Teutoburg Forest.</note> found them: for regarding the construction of these cities, neither Tacitus, nor Florus, nor Paterculus, nor Strabo, nor Ptolemy make any mention. Nor did the Romans ever lead an army beyond the Elbe <term>Albis; the Elbe River served as a major boundary between the Roman sphere and the unconquered Germanic tribes</term>. Strabo, in Book I, writes: *Indeed, that region which faces beyond the Elbe is utterly unknown to us. For we have received no word of any of the ancients having completed this journey by ship to the East, as far as the mouth of the Caspian Sea; nor did the Romans ever cross beyond the Elbe.* 

Tacitus, in his book *On the Customs of the Germans* <note>This work is commonly known as the *Germania*.</note>, says: *In the land of the Hermunduri rises the Elbe, a river once famous and well-known, but now it is only heard of.* But concerning this, see the first chapter of our first Treatise <note>original: "Syngrammatis"</note>. 

Rightly, therefore, should those men be driven out <note>original: "explodendi" - literally "hissed off the stage," a theatrical metaphor for rejection.</note> who busily endeavor to thrust forward trifles cheaper than a shadow, not only with the Muses opposing them but even against the will of Truth itself; and they should be expelled from Germany who fabricate tales that those seven Germanic cities were built by the Romans. However, I do not deny that Roman sacred rites passed over to the Germans; but it happened in another [way...]

The reasoning and origin of those things is far different. Indeed, the Germanic nobles Segestes <note>A nobleman of the Cherusci tribe who was an ally of Rome.</note> and his son Segimundus—who, according to the testimony of Tacitus in Book I of the *Annals*, had been a priest at the Altar of the Ubii <note>original: *Ara Ubiorum*; a major Roman religious center located at modern-day Cologne.</note>—as well as Flavius (the brother of Arminius), Julius Paulus, and Claudius Civilis <note>The leader of the Batavian rebellion against Rome in 69 AD.</note> of royal lineage, Italus, and others, were granted Roman citizenship. Having been educated in Italy, they served in the Roman military and were initiated into their sacred rites. These men, if we are to believe our own historians, undoubtedly changed their ancestral gods and sacred rites to the Roman custom. Tacitus, in Book XI of the *Annals*, testifies to this very thing: *It was in vain that Arminius was put forward; for if his son, raised on hostile soil, had come into the kingdom, it was to be feared that he would be tainted by foreign nourishment, servitude, and every external custom.* For the minds of subjects, being lighter than a bit of straw, are easily bent and changed by the authority of Princes. For when a King or Prince devotes himself to something and applies himself to it, you will see his subjects immediately doing the same thing. This truth, like all others, is skillfully touched upon by Claudian <note>A Roman court poet of the late 4th century.</note> in his poem *On the Sixth Consulship of Honorius*:

> ->If you command anything for the common good and think it should be kept,<-
> ->Be the first to undergo your own orders. Then the people become more observant of fairness,<-
> ->And they do not refuse to bear the burden when they see the author himself<-
> ->Obeying his own law. The world is formed<-
> ->After the example of the King; nor are edicts so able to bend human<-
> ->Sentiments as the life of the ruler.<-

However, those "demons" <note>original: *daemones*; in this period, the term often referred generally to pagan deities or spirits rather than strictly "evil" beings.</note> whom they write were worshipped in Germany were these: Crodo, Ammon, Mars, the Sun, Venus, Mercury, the Moon, Castor and Pollux, Triglas, Prono, Svantovit, Zernebug, and Juterbug—each of whom we shall examine individually.

## CHAPTER II.

*Crodo. Believed to be Saturn. The form of the Idol. Its location. The etymology of the name. A ritual of execration among modern Saxons.*

In the fortress of Hartesburg by the Hercynian forest <note>The Harz Mountains of northern Germany.</note> near Mount Melibocus and the city of Goslar, the Saxons worshipped the idol Crodo; <margin>*</margin> the Romans <note>original: "Latini"</note> called him Saturn. He was an Old Man, standing upon a fish which they call a Perch <note>original: "Percicum"</note>, dressed in a tunic, with bare feet, and girded with a linen band: he held a wheel and an urn filled with grain, roses, and fruit. The nakedness of his head signified that the God should be worshipped with a pure heart and an uncovered head; with the linen cloak they represented liberty, for the sake of whose inviolate strength they would oppose their enemies—just as a Perch <term>Perca: the European perch, known for its sharp defensive fins</term> opposes the "sea-wolf"—even at the risk of their lives. And the wheel foretold this: that the people ought to be united, and must advance against the enemy with gathered strength. That linen belt signified friendship, which ought to be preserved without pretense or blemish. The urn with its fruits marked time, which brings forth the crops of the year for the use of humanity and all of nature. The *Chronicle of Brandenburg* imagines that the city of Gardelegen <note>original: "Garleben"</note> takes its name from Crodo: because there Crodo was worshipped together with Isis. <meta>catchword: fuerit.</meta>

---

<margin>*</margin> *Regarding Crodo, see Tollius in "Travel Letters," page 31 and following; Jo. Mich. Heineccius, "Dissertation on the Ancient State of the Region Surrounding Goslar and the Harzburg Crodo," chapter II, which is appended to the "Antiquities of Goslar"; and Wilhelm Ernst Tentzel’s "Monthly Dialogues," 1689, page 382.*

## CHAPTER III.

*Jupiter Hammonius. His Form. Worship in the image of a Ram. Etymology of the name. Gambrivius, King of the Germans. The grove of Hamme.*

They write that Hamburg was dedicated to Jupiter Hammon <note>Also known as Ammon, an Egyptian deity later identified with the Greek Zeus and Roman Jupiter; often depicted with ram's horns.</note>, as if Jupiter Hammon had abandoned Africa to migrate into Germany. The idol sat upon a throne, brandishing a scepter in its left hand and a glittering sword in its right. From the right side of its mouth issued a lightning bolt; from the left, thunder with flames. An eagle sat upon its head, and a dragon was trampled beneath its feet. Around the deity sat twelve GODS: namely Neptune, Pluto, Vulcan, Mars, Mercury, Apollo, Juno, Ceres, Vesta, Pallas, Diana, and Venus. This is recorded in the *Saxon Chronicle*, folio 43; by Albert Krantz, Book II, Chapter 33; and by M. Petr. <note>Likely Marcus Petrejus, a 16th-century chronicler.</note>

...among the Germans, *Hamm* signified a forest. For this reason, the people of Dithmarschen <note>Latin: Ditmarfi</note> call their forests *Suderhamm* and *Norderhamm*. # CHAPTER IV.

**Mersburg**. *A town dedicated to Mars. Built by Marsus, King of the Germans.*

They write that the town of Mersburg was built for Mars. Some claim that the fortress of Eresburg in Westphalia was called Aresburg, which they believe is derived from the Greek. In *The Chauci*, page 116, he says: *Ham*, to a German, denoted a grove or a wooded thicket. From this, across the Elbe <note>Latin: Albis</note> and opposite the Chauci, the city of Hamburg began to be called by its name; and in the land of the Chauci itself, the names Stolham, Efensham, and Hamhusen represent fading traces to those honoring their companions. # CHAPTER V.

->*Salzwedel. A town of the March. An image of the Sun. The etymology of the name.*<-

Furthermore, they imagine that the city of Salzwedel <note>original: "Soltwedell"</note> in the Old March <note>Latin: "Marchia vetus"; a historic region in modern-day Saxony-Anhalt</note> was built for the fourth of the planets, the Sun <note>In the geocentric model used in antiquity and the Middle Ages, the Sun was counted as the middle or fourth "planet"</note>, and that the temple there was dedicated to the Sun by the Divine Julius Caesar. The form of the idol was that of a man who held a flaming wheel before his chest with both hands. It does not seem inconsistent to them that this idol was erected to the Sun: for from *Wedell*, which to us signifies a tail <note>German: "Wedel"; originally meaning a tail, a fan, or a tuft of hair</note> such as a lion has, they say the Sun was so named because of the flames of its rays spread around its chest. More learned men, however, think it should be called *Soltwell*, which is to say, the "House of Salt." For *Will* and *Wedel* also signify "house" in the ancient Germanic language.

With this image, the pagans <note>original: *gentilitas*</note> worshipped Venus. As for what might be understood by these mythological explanations, see the *Saxon Chronicle*, to which the eager reader is referred. It should rather be thought that the city <note>Magdeburg</note> was named after the **Amazons**, those warlike women of the Germans, whom we have previously proven existed in Germany.

### CHAPTER VII.

->Everything regarding the City of Mercury is uncertain. *Hermes’ life.*<-

Regarding Mercury, such uncertain accounts are related that neither the location nor the name is agreed upon. Some think the place was called **Hermesleben** <note>The author is debating the etymological origin of a place name, possibly modern Ermsleben</note>. However, the true origin is **Hermolauben**, from **Hermione**, a king of the ancient Germans. Concerning him, consult Johannes Aventinus <note>A famous Renaissance historian and philologist, 1477–1534</note> in Book I of the *Annals of the Bavarians*. Mercury was certainly held in great honor among the Celts and Germans, as authors mention throughout their works; they even considered it lawful to perform sacrifices to him with human victims <note>original: *humanis hostiis*</note> on certain days. But I cannot be brought to believe that he was called by the Greek name **Hermes** <note>original: ἐρμῆς</note> by the Germans, since it has been sufficiently demonstrated above that he was regarded as **Theutates** <note>A prominent Celtic deity often identified by Roman writers as Mercury due to his role as a protector of trade and travel</note> by the Romans.

## CHAPTER VIII.

### Lüneburg, sacred to the Moon. The true etymology <note>original: ἔτυμον (*etymon*)</note> of the name.

Authors write that **Lüneburg** was dedicated to the **Moon** <note>original: *Luna*</note>, and that a column of the Moon was erected there, upon which sat the image of a man with long ears, holding a golden image of the Moon in his hands. They write that this was demolished by **Charlemagne** <note>original: *Carolo M.*</note> in the year 800. However, this city drew its name from elsewhere. For it was named either after the river **Luna** or **Elmoa** flowing past it, or from the rich abundance of **flax** <note>original: *linum*</note> that grew there, which in the dialect of Upper Germany is called *Lein*, but in Lower Germany is called *Lyn*. This city is called **Marionis** by **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century Greco-Egyptian geographer</note>. Concerning its location, consult the cosmographers, since it is not our purpose to report these things with exactness.

---

<margin>* Regarding what some relate about Lüneburg, says **Johannes Scheffer** of Uppsala <note>A 17th-century humanist scholar and professor at Uppsala University</note> in *Antiquities of Uppsala*, page 113: "That it comes from 'Luna' [the Moon] cannot be proven to me. Indeed, the Moon was never called 'Luna' by the Germans; from where, then, would the word 'Lüneburg' come, being composed from two different languages <note>i.e., a Latin root and a German suffix</note>? Nor is the argument valid which is brought forward by **Schildius** <note>Johannes Schild, a 17th-century historian</note> in *Concerning the Chauci*, Book II, chapter 1, page 106—namely, that this was done through some interpretation of the name by the Romans. For why would the Germans have observed the interpretation of the Romans and joined it to a German word, rather than using their own name? You might say the same was done in **Mersburg**, **Soltwedel**, **Isena**, and other similar places. I will respond that for all of these, it is no more clear than for Lüneburg; in fact, the whole thing is false."</margin>

* **Heinsius** <note>Daniel Heinsius (1580–1655), a famous Dutch scholar.</note> in his notes on **Silius Italicus**, Book XIV, page 484, contends that the images of the Gods placed on the stern were the "protection" <note>original: *tutela*</note>, while those placed on the prow were the indices of the signs or "insignia" <note>original: *παρασήμων* (parasēmon), the identifying mark or name-sign of a ship</note>. **Scaliger** (notes on Eusebius, p. 39), **Bochart** (Volume II of his Works, p. 712), **Turnebus** (*Adversaria* XIX, 2), and others hold the same view. However, there are passages from ancient authors which establish that both the prow and the stern had insignia, and that the tutelary Gods were also placed on the prows. On this point, see **Johannes Alberti** (*Sacred Observations*, p. 290 ff.) and the great **Salmasius** <note>Claude Saumaise (1588–1653), a French classical scholar.</note> in his *Plinian Exercises*, Volume I, p. 403, who observes that the same object often served as both the protection and the insignia on a ship. For the complete condition of these "insignia" among the ancients, read the authors diligently cited by the Reverend **Johann Christoph Wolff** in his *Philological and Critical Care*, p. 1388 ff.

## CHAPTER X.

->Triglas. *An Idol of the Vandals. Three-headed. Diana. A sacred horse of black color.*<-

Triglas <note>The name originates from the Slavic "Triglav," literally meaning "three-headed."</note> was an idol of the *Vandals* and the people of *Stettin* <note>Modern-day Szczecin in Poland.</note>: they dedicated a temple to it on the Mountain of the *Harlingi*, which was later converted into a monastery of the *Premonstratensian* Order. *Pirnensis* <note>Johannes Pirnensis, a 16th-century chronicler.</note> reports that even in his own time, around the year *1526*, that idol existed in a certain hidden location; its head was formed of three faces, and it held a curved *Moon* in its hands. *Sabinus* <note>Georg Sabinus (1508–1560), a scholar and poet from Brandenburg.</note> writes in his book on the *Margraviate of Brandenburg*: "Yet nothing adorns either city quite like that temple of the *Blessed Virgin*, which Emperor *Henry the Fowler* <note>reigned 919–936 AD.</note> constructed. In their shrine once stood the three-headed idol called *Triglas*, which the *Wends* <note>original: "Venedi," a historical term for Slavic peoples living near Germanic settlements.</note> formerly worshipped with the highest veneration." This was an image of *Diana*. For *Eustathius* <note>The 12th-century commentator Eustathius of Thessalonica.</note> mentions that Diana was called *Trigla*; a claim supported significantly by the *Moon* depicted with it. As for why she was depicted as three-headed, the reason is that she possesses a triple power, as *Servius* <note>Maurus Servius Honoratus, a famous 4th-century grammarian.</note> reports: *Diana* on earth, the *Moon* in the heavens, and *Proserpina* <note>Goddess of the underworld.</note> beneath the earth. Nor is this inconsistent with the historians. For *Tacitus* reports that *Isis* was worshipped by the *Germans*, whom *Caesar* called the *Moon*. And it was proven earlier that *Isis* is the same as the *Moon*. To this deity, a noble horse was sacred—as the author of the *Life of Otto* <note>Referring to St. Otto of Bamberg, who led missions to Pomerania.</note> reports in Book II, chapters 20 and 22—specifically one of black color, which was tended with great devotion by one of the priests. Those about to go into war would use this horse to seek out the outcome of the event, following a certain method—

# ON THE GERMAN GODS.

...derives the etymology from the Greek *pronoia* <note>original Greek: πρόνοια, meaning "foresight" or "providence"</note>, because the world is ruled by God's providence. Rather, as we conjecture, it refers to Brennus, a King of ancient Germany, to whom posterity erected a statue and dedicated a temple in perpetual memory; which later the ignorant and simple common folk called "Prono" instead of "Brenno." For he was King of the Vandals or Germans in that place, as Aventinus <note>Johannes Aventinus (1477–1534), a prominent Bavarian Renaissance historian</note> reports in Book I of the *Annals of the Boii*. Certainly another Brennus lived in the same region, an Anglo-German by nation, from whom those English who later invaded Britain descend; consult Aventinus in the same work. Finally, he was followed by that famous Brennus who sacked Rome; the last Brennus was the one who plundered the temple at Delphi; regarding these, consult the works of Livy, Florus, Velleius Paterculus, Justin, Plutarch, Diodorus Siculus, Dionysius of Halicarnassus, and others.

## CHAPTER XII.

->*Suantovitus. Worshiped by the Rugians. The origin of this rite. The image. The priest enters the temple while holding his breath. A sacred horse. Spoils and plunder were sought for the Idol. The statue is cut down. The Bohemians do not abandon his memory.*<-

<margin>* Regarding Suantovitus, perhaps <note>Latin: "f." for "forte"</note> Witislaus, the God of the Slavs and Moravians, consult Johann Peter von Ludewig, Dissertation I, section 8 and following, and Masius.</margin>

Before all other peoples on the shore of the Baltic Sea, the Rugians <note>A West Slavic tribe inhabiting the island of Rügen</note> worshiped Suantovitus: whose primary sanctuary and the statue itself were in the capital city, Arkona.

# ELIAS SCHEDIUS

<margin><unclear>The...</unclear> <unclear>b...</unclear> <unclear>rel...</unclear> <unclear>ch...</unclear></margin> <note>Text in the margin is partially obscured by the book's binding gutter.</note>

Jan Dubravius <note>A 16th-century historian and Bishop of Olomouc</note> in Book I, Albertus Krantz in Book V of his *History of the Vandals*, and Saxo Grammaticus <note>A medieval Danish historian famous for the Gesta Danorum</note> in Book XIV, all hand down the origin of this deity in the following manner: Once the Rugian Slavs <note>A West Slavic tribe on the island of Rügen</note> were conquered by Charlemagne <note>original: "Carolo M."</note>, they were ordered to worship Saint Vitus of Corvey <note>original: "S. Vitum Corvegiensem"; Corvey was a powerful Benedictine abbey in Westphalia</note> as a martyr. However, after they eventually threw off the yoke of subjection, they altered the religion they had received, even while keeping the name. In contempt of the monks of Corvey, they bestowed the name **Suantovitus** upon their idol. They continued to pay the tribute formerly intended for Saint Vitus every year until the time of King Eric of the Danes <note>original: "Ericum Danorum Regem"</note>, who, having captured the town, destroyed the idol.

In the city of **Arkona** <note>The religious center of the Rugians on Cape Arkona</note>, his temple was a double structure, enclosed by a sequence of barriers and accessible by a single door. The exterior was composed of walls covered by a roof of purple color. The interior, however, rested upon four pillars; in place of walls, it shone with hanging tapestries. It shared nothing with the exterior part except for the roof and a few decorated ceiling panels.

Saxo Grammaticus, in Book XIV of his *History of the Danes*, describes the form of the idol in this way: Within the building stood a massive statue with four heads and as many necks, of which two appeared to look toward the chest and two toward the back. Furthermore, of those placed both in front and behind, one looked toward the right and the other toward the left. The beards were shaved and the hair was closely cropped, according to the custom of the Rugians. In its right hand, the statue held a horn crafted from various types of metal, which the priest was accustomed to fill every year with wine <note>original: "mero," referring to pure wine</note>; from the very level of this liquid...

The latter conjectures that **Suantevitus** is named not from Saint Vitus, as is commonly told, but from *Swynso*, which is to say the "Sun" <note>original: "sole"</note> of the Slavic lesser gods.

### CONCERNING THE GERMAN GODS

...expecting the supplies of the following year. His left hand formed a bow, with his arm bent back toward his side. His tunic reached down to his shins, and his feet touched the ground, with their base hidden within the floor. Not far away were the bridle and saddle of the image, along with several other insignias of divinity. The wonder of these was increased by a sword of conspicuous size, whose scabbard and hilt, besides the excellent beauty of the carving, were enhanced by an exterior appearance of silver.

Once a year, as Münster <note>Sebastian Münster (1488–1552), author of the *Cosmographia*</note> writes in Book III, after the harvest was gathered and victims sacrificed before the temple door, there was a solemn feast of the nation. The priest would tend the temple while holding his breath <note>original: "spiritu oris compresso"</note>; whenever he needed to draw breath, he would run to the door, so that the presence of the deity would not be offended by a human breath. 

At early dawn, while the people kept watch before the doors, the priest entered and examined the horn which he had filled the previous year. If the measure of fullness corresponded to what it had been, he pronounced that the coming harvest would be bountiful; if it was diminished in any part, he ordered the crops to be stored more carefully, as a scarcity <term>caristia</term> <note>a period of high prices or famine</note> was imminent. Then, tasting the old wine <term>merum</term> <note>pure, undiluted wine used in libations</note>, he poured it at the feet of the idol, drank the refilled horn, and restored it, full of wine, to the right hand of the deity in the same manner. 

They also fashioned a honey-cake <term>placenta</term> <note>a sacrificial cake; here it refers to a massive round loaf</note> of such size, using mead <note>original: "mulso", a mixture of wine and honey</note>, into a round shape so that a man could hide behind it. To this god belonged a sacred horse, which was believed to carry him into battles; of this, more is said in the second *Syngramma* <note>likely referring to a specific chapter or "composition" within this or a related work</note>. Both payments and spoils were sought for this idol. For a coin was paid annually by everyone, as Saxo <note>Saxo Grammaticus</note> relates in Book XIV, for the cult of this image, along with [a share] of spoils and plun... <note>The word is completed on the next page.</note>

# ELIAS SCHEDIVS

...of the third part. This idol also possessed three hundred horses and just as many attendants <note>original: "satellites," referring to a mounted military retinue</note> serving as soldiers upon them. All the profit they acquired, whether by land or by sea, was placed under the guardianship of the priest. From the spoils of these activities, the priest forged various kinds of insignia and diverse ornaments for the temple, which he committed to the locked enclosures of the treasury. In these storehouses, besides an abundance of money, a great deal of purple cloth, eaten away by age, had been piled up. There, a huge quantity of public and private gifts could also be seen. 

This statue, worshipped through the tributes of all Sclavia <note>the land of the Slavs</note>, was also honored with gifts by neighboring kings. At last, Waldemar <note>Waldemar I (1131–1182), King of Denmark</note>, King of the Danes, as the same author relates and as Helmold <note>Helmold of Bosau (c. 1120–1177), a Saxon historian</note> reports in *Book II, chapter XII*, having captured Arkona, the city of the Rugians, cut down the statue of Suantovitus and overthrew it. 

Abundant purple fabric hung around the temple, so rotten with decay that it could not bear to be touched. Nor were there lacking the unusual horns of wild beasts, no less wonderful in their natural state than in their decoration. A demon, appearing in the shape of a dark-colored animal <note>original: "furvi animalis"</note>, was seen to depart from the inner sanctuary and suddenly vanished from the sight of those standing around. 

When the townspeople were ordered to throw ropes onto the idol to pull it down, they were unwilling to carry this out for fear of their ancient religion. Therefore, the Danes commanded captives and foreigners who were seeking profit in the city to cast it out. Indeed, the locals believed that the majesty of their household deity, which they had been accustomed to follow with such great worship, would immediately exact heavy punishments from those who violated it. Then, truly, the various voices of the inhabitants could be heard: some followed the injuries dealt to their God with lamentation, while others followed with laughter. As evening approached, all who were in the kitchens...

...they were, they attacked the idol with axes, reducing it into small fragments and into logs fit for the hearth. Nevertheless, the superstition regarding that same idol, as Dubravius <note>Jan Dubravius (1486–1553) was a Bishop of Olomouc and a historian known for his history of Bohemia.</note> writes in *Book I*, flourished among the Bohemians for a long time, until Wenceslaus <note>Saint Wenceslaus I (c. 907–935), Duke of Bohemia, known for his Christianization of the region.</note>, the Prince of Bohemia, changed the religion after obtaining the relics of Saint Vitus <note>A 4th-century Christian saint; the author suggests his name was used to replace the pagan Svantevit.</note> from the Emperor Otto. But even then, he was unable to erase the memory of Santovitus <note>A variation of the name Suantovitus or Svantevit.</note> from the minds of the Bohemians. Indeed, even now they have no greeting more solemn than that which is made under the name of Vitus. For when they are about to receive a guest, a friend, or any unarmed person arriving from abroad, they cry out "Witæus, Witæus!" <note>original: "Witæus, Witæus ingeminant"</note>, as if congratulating them on the safety <note>original: "sospitati"</note> granted by Suantovitus. Since it so happened that while a plague was spreading among their neighbors, those alone who worshipped Suantovitus remained untouched and unharmed by the contagion.

EL. SCHED. ON THE GERMANIC GODS.

...calling him *Belbuch*, according to the testimony of Sebastian Münster <note>Sebastian Münster (1488–1552) was a German cartographer and scholar whose *Cosmographia* was one of the most popular books of the 16th century.</note> in Book III of his *Cosmographia*. Among the Vandals <note>The author frequently uses "Vandals" to refer to the Wends, a group of West Slavic tribes.</note>, the word *Zcerne* means black; from this, *Zcernewitz* means "black light," and *Zcernebitz* means "black ground." *Bel*, however, is white, and *Belbuch* is the "White God"; *Zernebuch* is truly the "Black God." They considered them as a good and an evil spirit <note>original: "genium"</note>, and viewed Satan as the author of both good and evil, following the Manichaean error <note>Manichaeism was a dualistic religion that taught a fundamental struggle between a good spiritual world of light and an evil material world of darkness.</note>. But others call that *Belbuch* by the names *Iuterbuch* or *Iuterbock*, and they attach I know what sort of fable about the goat <note>original: "capro"</note> of a certain woman named Jutta <note>This refers to a folk etymology for the town of Jüterbog in Germany.</note>. We pass over these absurdities in silence, lest we detain the reader any longer or delay our own progress.

<note>
The distinguished Sperling <note>Otto Sperling (1634–1715) was a Danish jurist and historian.</note> says in his *Danish Valerius Maximus*, page 6: "The pagans had certain gods among the whites and others among the blacks." For instance, among the Pomeranians and the people of Wollin <note>original: "Julinenses"</note>, one was called *Belbock* and the other *Zernebock*, which mean "White Lesser-God" and "Black Lesser-God." These they once worshipped, which is why Gauka Thorus <note>A figure likely from the Scandinavian sagas or history who interpreted Christian figures through a pagan framework.</note> believed Christ to be among the white gods. Philip a Turre <note>Filippo del Torre (1657–1717), an Italian bishop and antiquarian.</note>, in his *Dissertation on Belenus*, page 273 and following, thinks the first of these gods was Biele, who was worshipped with great superstition among the Thuringians. Saint Boniface <note>Known as the "Apostle of the Germans," an 8th-century missionary who famously cut down Donar's Oak.</note> cast down the idol of this god once and again, as reported by Johann Letzner, who wrote the life of that same Apostle of the Germans from an old manuscript held by Nicolaus Serarius <note>A Jesuit historian (1555–1609) who wrote on the history of Mainz.</note> in his *History of Mainz*, book 3, note 21, page 474. The other, *Zernebock*, based on the meaning of the name, could be "Black Jopher" <note>original: "Jopher niger"</note>—though others read "Black Jove" [Jupiter]—about whom Bollandus <note>Jean Bolland (1596–1665), the namesake of the Bollandists, who compiled the *Acta Sanctorum* (Lives of the Saints).</note> writes in the *Acts of Saint Juliana*, February 16, page 875.
